Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Dominion Rands Act, chapter twenty of the statutes of 1908, and to increase the rate of interest changed by the Dominion upon deferred payment of money due to the Grown in the right of Canada, for the sale, lease, or other disposition of natural resources under the provisions of the said Act.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
By amendment
to the Dominion Lands Act of last session the rate of interest on school lands was increased from five to six per cent, with provision for seven per cent to be charged upon arrears. The seven per cent chargeable upon arrears applies to past as well as to future sales. The purpose of this amendment is to make the same rates apply to all cases of sales of natural resources, and particularly to arrears due the Crown in respect of pre-emptions and purchased homesteads. The amendment will have application to all sales of course that it is within the power of the Governor in Council to make of the natural resources of the Dominien. The object is to, if possible, correct an abuse which is all too prevalent at the present time-that is to say, of purchasers of lands from the Crown and of other resources as well, but chiefly lands, financing upon the Dominion, inasmuch as our rate of interest has been far below that ordinarily obtaining in the locality.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Act as amended
last session added to the rate of interest in sales of school lands in the way I have described. This resolution is to make the same addition to the rate of interest upon the same principle, apply to all sales of natural resources.

On motion of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance), Bill No. 28, to confirm two Orders of the Governor General in Council respecting the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-Orders in Council 7th and 13th March, 1919, confirmed:

Mr. Chairman, it is highly regrettable that this Bill, confirming the Orders in Council putting the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System under a receivership, should be proceeded with in the absence of a decision on the part of the Government as to what our future railway policy is to be. It is also to be regretted that the Government thought it advisable to take any step which would have the effect of causing the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to cease operating that portion of their system which is called the Grand Trunk Pacific. A more democratic and a more constitutional way of dealing with this matter would have been to bring it before Parliament and to examine into it carefully before taking any such important step as is now under consideration.
The people of Canada at large and this Parliament in particular have not been fully seized of all that is involved in the nationalization of the Grand Trunk Pacific and consequently, of the Grand Trunk Railway system; nor have they had opportunity of studying the matter carefully. Last year, during the session of Parliament, it was announced by the Prime Minister, in answer to a question put by this side of the House, that pourparlers or negotiations were in progress between the Government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company concerning the sale to the Government or the nationalization of the two systems. When we inquired as to the policy of the Government in this matter, the Prime Minister said that it would not be in the public interest to advise the House and the country of the nature of negotiations which were under way. Notwithstanding that, however, the Government have committed the country to a definite policy

which they have consistently carried out- because they had absolutely made up their minds at that time to expropriate the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific. How did they do it? First, they refused to agree to the proposal made by the two companies; they did not agree as to the amount to be paid.
We all agree that the Government should oblige the Grand Trunk Railway Company to live up to all its obligations. The Government should not allow the country to undertake all the obligations of that company. But, as I say, the Government had made up their minds to take over the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific, although they would not let the House know under what conditions they intended doing so.
The Acting Prime Minister gave the House the other day the first comprehensive information that we have received since the beginning of the negotiations. He read at length various letters which passed between the Government and the company. He gave the House full details of the difficulties which the Government had met in attempting to reach an agreement with the Grand Trunk Railway Company. We now know that that company, which in 1903 or 1904. had entered into an agreement with the Government for the building of the section of the Transcontinental from Winnipeg to the coast, could not live up to their obligations on account of various difficulties which had arisen between them and the Government in the carrying out of the original scheme. Under the original scheme the Government was to build the section of the Transcontinental from Moncton to Winnipeg, and the Grand Trunk Railway Company was to build the section between Winnipeg and the Pacific coast. This new undertaking was to be called the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, its shares being entirely in the bands of the Grand Trunk.
At various stages of the operations carried on under the agreements of 1903 and 1904, difficulties arose between the Government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company as regards the building by the Government of the Transcontinental railway. For instance, in 1912, 1914 and 1915, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company advised the Government that the changes which had been made by the Government in the construction of that section of the road which the Grand Trunk Railway Company was ultimately to lease from the Government, would render it impossible
for the company to take over the National Transcontinental, and to live up to the obligations undertaken under the agreements of 1903 and 1904. May I speak more plainly what is in my mind? Under the? agreements of 1903 and 1904, the Government was to build that section of the road which extends from Moncton to Winnipeg according to certain specifications, plans and details which had been agreed on between the Government and the company. Subsequently, particularly after 1911, when the change of Government took place, the Government took upon itself, through the Department of Railways and Canals, (because at that time the Transcontinental Railway Commission had been superseded by the Minister of Railways and Canals), to change, without the approval of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, not only the grading but the specifications and the terminals of the railway. The Government, therefore, did not live up to the agreements of 1903 and 1904, and by so doing gave to the company the right to refuse later on to take over the National Transcontinental railway.
The House is now in possession of the correspondence exchanged between the Government and the company. In 1912 the president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company stated clearly to the Government that any change in the grading or in the specification of the railway would put that company in an impossible position because they would not be able to take a lease of the Transcontinental railway as per the agreement of 1903. The Government did not take any notice of this formal protest by the company, but went on changing the grading in such a manner that the Transcontinental railway would not have for the company the same usefulness. Some time after, when the Government had completed the construction of the Transcontinental railway from Moncton to Winnipeg, the Government offered to the company a lease of the Transcontinental railway. That offer was flatly refused. I have not been able to put my hand on the document by which the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company declined to take over the National Transcontinental on the conditions of the agreement of 1903, but from my recollection of that document, I think I can cite the three main reasons advanced by the company for declining to live up to the agreement.
The reasons were, first, because the cost of the railway had been greatly in excess

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: To what company does the hon. gentleman refer that should have been compelled to lease the National Transcontinental?

According to the agreement of 1903 the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company should have been compelled to lease that section of the road which had been built by the Government from Monc-ten to Winnipeg. That would amount to the same thing as compelling the Grand Trunk Railway Company itself to live up to their agreement, because we know that all the shares of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company are in the treasury of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. I think I am right in saying that according to the agreement of 1903 the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company was bound to take over under a lease that section of the road which had been built by the Govern-ment._ The Government have impliedly admitted the contentions of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. They have taken over the National Transcontinental railway from Moncton to Winnipeg; they
|Mr. Vien.]
have connected it up with the Canadian Government railway system and they are continuing to operate it as a Government railway.
What was the effect of the Government's failure to compel the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to live up to the agreement of 1903? The effect was, first, impliedly to admit the company's contention that it had no further obligations in respect of the National Transcontinental. Secondly, the effect was to deprive the Grand Trunk Pacific of a very important part of its transcontinental system. The National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific were built for the purpose of establishing a second transcontinental railway in Canada. That transcontinental system could not exist except as a whole; that is, the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific. The taking over of the Transcontinental left the Grand Trunk Pacific without any connecting link with its own system, which extended from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast, and naturally the Grand Trunk refused to admit any further obligations in respect of the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific which it had guaranteed. Then what happened? The Grand Trunk Pacific Company advised the Government that as they had been deprived of their connecting link they could not meet their obligations. Again the Government advanced money to the Grand Trunk Pacific, impliedly admitting the contention of the company that it could not continue to operate without the National Transcontinental, and admitting also that the Government had a certain responsibility in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Then what happens? The Government, seeing that it would be compelled to vote money year after year to make up the deficit in the operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific, immediately opened negotiations for the expropriation of both the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Government was in negotiation with the company last year, but would not disclose to this House or to the Canadian people the exact nature of those negotiations. When, however, it became imperative for the Government to advance further moneys to meet the interest on the bonds, the Government, after the opening of the present session, and without apprising Parliament of the condition of affairs, made up their minds to threaten the company They said to the company:	"We will not
ask Parliament to vote any further advances so long as the negotiations between the company and the Government remain in

their present unsatisfactory condition." That was a threat, designed to bring the company into such a position that it would be bound hand and foot to the Government. The company replied: " We will cease to operate that section of the road extending from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast." What did that declaration amount to? It was tantamount to saying: " We have a section of the road which does not pay, and therefore we are going to close it up." As the company had refused to take over the National Transcontinental, and as it owned the entire stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific, that section of the road from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast was simply a branch line of the Grand Trunk Railway system; there was no difference whatever between that section of the road and a branch line of the Grand Trunk system. The company therefore said to the Government: "As you will not subsidize our branch line from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast, we will close it." Now, if the Canadian Pacific Railway were to find one morning that one of its branch lines was not a paying proposition, would it not be perfectly right for it to say that it would close that branch liner I submit that the Government had absolutely no right to compel either the Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk Pacific to operate that section of the road from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast, until the company had defaulted in paying the interest on its bonds. We know from the information laid on the Table that neither the Grand Trunk nor the Grand Trunk Pacific had defaulted in their interest payments. But when the company said to the Government: " We will cease to operate that section of the road from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast," the Government said, " Then we will put the road in the hands of a receiver, under the authority of the War Measures Act."
We all agree on the principle that Canada should not take over the liabilities of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. We all agree that the Grand Trunk itself should not be relieved of its obligation in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific. It was the policy of the Government not to relieve either the Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk Pacific of their obligations. Yet I contend that, at law, the Government has done exactly what it intended to avoid. I contend that the action of the Government has absolutely relieved the Grand Trunk Railway Company of its obligations in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific. I contend that the Government's action was the last step in impliedly admitting the contentions of the company in respect of the agreement of 1903.
Let us consider the action of the Government when they were informed that the Company would cease its operation of that section of the line. Did they compel the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Grand Trunk Railway Company to meet their obligations? No. They could not do so because the companies were not in default; and under the provisions of the Winding-up Act they could take no steps for the same reason, that the company had fulfilled all its obligations. Instead, they invoked the authority of the War Measures Act and forcibly took over that section of the road extending from Winnipeg to the coast; and in order to establish that point clearly we need only read the first paragraph of the Order in Council, which says:
Re-Grand Trunk Receivership.
Provisions of Order in Council.
(1) Order recites that the continued operation of the G.T.P. System is essential in the present position of Canada resulting from the war, especially in connection with the transport of returning Canadian troops and of supplies, equipment and freight, and that the duty of continuing such operation is thrown upon the Government of Canada inasmuch as there are no effective provisions in the existing laws whereby such continued operation could be otherwise secured and that therefore immediate action is imperative.
In that first paragraph the Government admit that the company has fulfilled all its legal obligations, while the paragraph is also an admission that there was no other course open to the Government than to proceed under the War Measures Act. But I unhesitatingly say that it was never the intention when the Act was passed to allow them to forcibly take the railway, and I am of opinion that taking over that section of the road by virtue of that Act is tantamount to an expropriation of it by the Government. If, then, it is an expropriation, surely the Government is liable for compensation just as much as they would be if they took a house or a farm, or any other property for a public work. There is an Expropriation Act under which the Government could have taken over that section of the road. They did not elect to proceed under that Act. But under the terms of the Order in Council which 1 have just read, their action amounts to an expropriation, and in doing so the Government incurred the obligation to compensate the company for the forcible taking of their property. Now, I hardly think the Government could very well act more imprudently. If they did

not desire to advance any further moneys for the purposes of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company-which might be an advisable and even a commendable policy- they should at least have waited until the Grand Trunk Railway or the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway was in default. Had they done so, the Government would then have had a legal right to wind up the company and put it into receivership. They did not do so, but from the very beginning of their negotiations with the company the Government have impliedly admitted the contention of the company that they had no further obligations in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and have virtually relieved them of all such obligations. I believe that the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company have a good case at law and can meet the contentions of the Government and repudiate their obligations by the argument, that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company having been forcibly expropriated under the War Measures Act, they are now relieved of any responsibility in connection with that railway. The Government should they decide to forcibly take not only the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway but also the parent company, will be obliged to pay a compensation to the Grand Trunk Railway Company which will be calculated, without taking into account its obligations in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. 1 want to be clear on thait point. At law the Grand Trunk Railway Company will contend that it is relieved of its obligations in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company; and the Government if they take over the Grand Trunk Railway Company will have to pay the price. And in calculating the assets they will not be able to put by way of set-off the obligations of the Grand Trunk Railway Company in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.
I think it is a matter for very much regret that the Government did not see its way clear to take Parliament into its confidence, particularly when Parliament was in session, before taking an important step that will undoubtedly mean a heavy responsibility, financial and otherwise, on the shoulders of the people of this country. It is regrettable that they did not consult Parliament in the matter, and that they did not wait until the Grand Trunk Railway Company were in default before relieving it, as they have virtually done by their Order in Council, of all obligations in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.

It is true that the Government says in its Order in Council that it takes over that railway without incurring any resppnsibil-ity in connection with its operation, but surely, Sir, regard must be paid to the general underlying principle that we cannot forcibly take over a property without first justly and fairly indemnifying the owner. Whatever the Government might say in its Order in Council as to declining to assume any responsibility due to the forcible taking over of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, surely in accordance with common law and the dictates of common sense, it will have to indemnify the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Railway Companies for the property so forcibly taken. Moreover, the Grand Trunk Railway Company can now say: You have taken one of our branch lines. In so doing you have undertaken all the obligations of operating this branch line, and we are relieved of our obligations in respect of it. I say, Sir, I would be very much surprised indeed if the law courts, and the highest legal tribunals, did not maintain such a contention. Therefore I say that before committing the country to suoh an important policy as the forcible taking over of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, Parliament should have been consulted, and the Government should have made a careful study of the subject in consultation with it. It would have been a more democratic and constitutional way of dealing with the question.

It is not my intention to attempt any reply to the points that my hon. friend from Lot-biniere has attempted to make in connection with this question. The members of the Government will be able to make that answer, and I think they "will not find it an exceedingly difficult task.
I wish to say at the outset that if the opinion which the hon. gentleman has expressed on railway questions, and particularly in reference to the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Grand Trunk, is shared by his friends who sit on that side of the House, and by any very large number of the people of Canada, God help the country. If there is one question-

Might I ask the hon. member if he is in favour of relieving the Grand Trunk of their obligations in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway? That is the point the hon. member for Lot-biniere was making.

The hon. member for Lotbiniere was blaming the Govern-

ment for insisting that the Grand Trunk should live up to its obligations.
No.

That is what I
understood.
The hon. gentleman says that if members on this side of the House share my views in respect to the policy that should be followed as to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, " God help the country."
Yes, and I repeat the statement.
What view has me hon. gentleman particularly in mind that causes him to say that? On what expression of views by me does he base that statement?

If the hon. gentleman will just allow me, I hope to be able to make myself and my position perfectly clear and I hope to present facts to the hon. gentleman that will satisfy him that he is entirely wrong in his attitude on this question. What course could the Government pursue but take over the Grand Trunk Pacific railway-when the Grand Trunk threw it on their hands and refused to operate it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are only taking the Grand Trunk Pacific railway as receiver.
They might have given it bonuses as they did the Canadian Northern.

But the Grand Trunk Pacific was in an entirely different position; it was thrown on the hands of the Government. Had the Government refused to act as it did, what would have been the position? That vast country in the West, depending on the Grand Trunk Pacific railway,-because it has a very large mileage throughout that territory,-would have been absolutely deprived of any railway accommodation whatever. I am not here to defend the Government especially, but it seems to me it had no option in the matter; it did the only possible thing it could do. Had the Government refused to appoint a receiver, under the War Measures Act, the position to-day would have been one of chaos, and my hon. friend from Lot-biniere would probably have been denouncing the Government in the strongest possible language for permitting such a state of affairs.
Not in the least.

It was a case of
" You will and you won't, you shall and
you shan't; you'll be damned if you do, and you'll be damned if you don't." That was the situation, and the Government was obliged to do something. My hon. friend from Lotbiniere says that as a result of its action the Government has probably given the Grand Trunk a legal hold, probably a stranglehold, on it, but this Parliament is supreme. It represents the people of Canada, and can correct any situation at will.
Parliament was not consulted.

Never mind, the
Government had to act hastily and without the opportunity of consulting Parliament.
I think that when the people of this country get through their brains what this railway problem means, they will see that the Government and Parliament do the right thing by them in regard to the railroad question. Does my hon. friend not know that the party with which he is associated, in order to solve the transportation problem as they put it, loaded this country with a debt of one billion-just a round billion-in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental Railways? They brought about a state of chaos, the like of Which Dante could scarcely describe. Now that is the position we are in at the present time.

Will you itemize the
billion?

I was struck the
other day by a statement in a speech delivered by the Hon. George P. Graham, who was Minister of Railways, when my hon. friends opposite were in office, upon accepting a nomination in Essex county. That gentleman said:	" If you will put us
back we will resort to those Liberal principles that made Canada such a great nation after 1896."
Hear, hear.

In using the expression " Liberal principles " he must have meant " Opulent principles," because the Liberals spent money like drunken sailors on the railways, and did nothing but hopelessly tangle up the situation, as I shall prove before I conclude my speech. If that is what Air. Graham meant by Liberalism I entirely agree with him.

Perhaps at this stage
matters can be cleared up if I ask the hon. gentleman, does he say that this road should not have been built?

Decidedly it should not have been built. Sir Robert Borden was
ms

opposed to the building of this railroad and proposed as an alternative the double tracking of the C.P.R. around Lake Superior with running rights to other lines. That was 'the correct policy. I think it was the most insane policy that -was ever entered into by a free people, and I think that can be demonstrated. The construction of the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific railways represent the fastening of a debt of a billion of dollars on this country, because we now have to take those roads over. There is no use in my hon. friend from Lotbiniere, and other gentlemen, saying: "The Government is going in for public ownership, and God help the country when it adopts that policy." The Government cannot help itself. These railway children are unloaded on the Government as a result of the policy of the so-called Liberal party in 1896. I would like to, and perhaps later on I shall, give a brief sketch of the inauguration of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental railway projeobs, because, as hon. gentlemen know, the Canadian Pacific Railway had had the monopoly in the West up to a certain date. In the early days the Canadian Pacific Railway was very arrogant, sometimes insolent, although the people of Canada, let me tell my hon. friend from Lotbiniere, gave to that company enough money, in cash and donations of one kind and another, to build and equip the road two or three times over. I want the hon. gentleman to rivet that fact upon his mind [DOT]-the people of Canada gave, in cash and other donations, enough to build and equip the road two or three times over.
Will the hon. gentleman detail the amounts?
Did not the Canadian Pacific Railway give value for what it got?

In answer to my hon. friend from Lothbiniere, I cannot give the exact amount of the several subsidies offhand, but I have the information in my desk and am willing to go into details with him.
I certainly do not overstate the facts; they are as I have told you. I freely acknowledge that the Canadian Pacific railway is a well managed and a courteously conducted railway to-day. But in the old days they were very domineering and dictatorial to the people of the West, and they swaggered about that country just as if they owned it. When the so-called liberal Government got into office they undertook to solve the transportation problem by supplying a com-
peting railroad. Now, competition is not desirable even if it is possible; and it is not possible even if it is desirable. If the Canadian Pacific had been taken over by the country as it should have been-because I believe in public ownership if properly administered; there is no reason why we cannot get men to run transportation companies as well as private corporations can-I repeat that if the Canadian Pacific had been taken over by the people in the early days, properly operated and branch lines built to accommodate the settlers where necessary, it would have developed that country and would have furnished the people of the West with the railroad transportation that was necessary, instead of which, as my hon. friend knows and as the members of this House know, subventions in land were given to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and to other railway companies, and those lands were held by those companies in order that they might profit by the unearned increment, by the settlement in that country of a large population. Those companies did not sell their land holdings, and the result was that the settlers were obliged to move off ten, fifteen and twenty miles from the railway lines, instead of occupying these rich railway lands that were available for settlement. The result was that the people there almost reached a state of armed rebellion in one case, for they did not want that kind of policy. Thereupon the friends of my hon. friend undertook to "solve" the question, and they talked with indescribable foolishness about the whole proposition. They said: "If you endow another great railway corporation and let them into the West, then that will help solve the problem." The outcome of that talk was the contract with the Grand Trunk for the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Transcontinental. While I think of it, let me tell my hon. friend this- fact-and I want him 'to put a pin in the argument and just keep it there, because it is the crux of the whole thing-it was not the Government of Canada that forced the Grand Trunk to build the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Transcontinental; the Government-of Canada had nothing to do with it: it was the directors of the Grand Trunk, lead by the late Charles M. Hays, the Grand Trunk president, that forced this contract on the people, and if by virtue of this contract we find this state of chaos at the present time, and that the Grand Trunk has piled up this enormous debt on the coun-

try, why should we come to the rescue ot the Grand Trunk?
We are all agreed on that.

I am delighted to know that my hon. friend agrees with me on that point, because I did not so understand him; I thought he was arguing that the Grand Trunk had got a legal grip. I must tell my hon. friend that neither he nor his friends will ever get into office by defending these corporation tactics, and that it is high time that the people's representatives took a right position on questions of this kind. The people of Canada have been swindled in the most appalling style for the last twenty-five or thirty years, and our politicians on both sides of the House are almost equally to blame-there is a frank confession. But, in the name of all that is sensible, has not the time come when we should put an end to it? Let the Grand Trunk live up to its obligations. Why should we come to the rescue of the Grand Trunk at the present time? They got themselves into the difficulty; let them get out of it the best way they can.
But you have come to the rescue by the Order in Council.

My hon. friend having interrupted me, will he tell me in a word what should have been done?
iMt. VIEN: I said it was only necessary to wait until they were in default, and they would have been in default in a very few days.
Yes, but let me inform my hon. friend again that not only were they in default, but they notified the Government: "Take the road; we cannot operate it any longer."
They did not say any such thing. The hon. member will not find anything in the papers to substantiate his statement.
I appeal to the hon. leader of the Government whether the Grand Trunk did not say that they would cease to operate. What does that mean?
They closed a branch line.

Oh, they closed a
branch line ! No wonder the Acting Prime Minister laughs, as everybody in this House must laugh who knows the facts. What is closing down the road but ceasing to operate? Why, of course it is.
Oh, no.

My hon. friend is
somewhat younger than I am and I am going to give him a little advice. When you undertake to criticise a policy, you are in duty bound -to propose an alternative. If the Government had not done this, just the state of affairs that I have already described would have existed, and my hon. friend and the other members of the Opposition would have been railing at the Government about the outrage perpetrated on the West, of allowing the Grand Trunk Pacific to cease operation. And what sort of situation would we have had in the West where this line serves the people? It would have been indescribable. There was absolutely no other course for the Government to take.
But my hon. friend must know, and his friends must know, that they have been guilty of bringing about a highly disturbing state of affairs in this country, and we are to-day faced with difficulties that I would hardly like to describe. This railroad question is almost of as great, if not as great, importance as the tariff, because it means so much to the people, and we are so tangled up at the present time with its intricacies that I do not know how we are going to evolve ourselves from the difficulty. It will take the Government all its time to pilot the ship through the rough waters created by our railroad policy, and unless there is some criticism that should properly be directed towards the Government, I do not know that anything of the tenor offered by my hon. friend from Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) ought to be indulged in this afternoon.
Before the hon. gentleman spoke I had my notes prepared, and I proposed to go into this question very fully. I was going to criticise the Government somewhat, for its failure, through the Acting Prime Minister to speak out in as plain Anglo-Saxon as I think the circumstances of the case demand, because although I was not in the House-unfortunately I was sent for last week and did not hear what my hon. friend the Acting Prime Minister said-but in reading the papers I gathered the impression that he said, " We want to treat the Grand Trunk with fairness if not with generosity. We must be pretty fair to them." Now, it seems to me that the position is not one of generosity at all, it is one of simple justice, and this country may just as well understand now as later that it cannot any longer afford to be generous. It has been too generous-generous with the railway exploiters and promoters to the extent

that has almost involved the country in disaster. The time for generosity is past. The Grand Trunk is not entitled to generosity, because its own financial management got the country into this difficulty. Let it take the consequences, whatever the consequences are, instead of railing at the Government. I should think that if the members of the Opposition desired to stand right with this country they would, like me. be demanding that the Government should make the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific toe the mark. That is the only kind of policy that will appeal to the people of this country; no other policy, I think, should be tolerated.
Now, I intended at the outset to refer to what I regard as a press conspiracy in this country to try and do the work which my hon. friend from Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) was attempting to do, to help the Grand Trunk inferentially at the expense of the public. I have three or four newspaper clippings here. Perhaps I should first refer to the financial papers. With one or two honourable exceptions, the financial papers that derive their living from the corporations are, of course, disposed to excuse and to help the Grand Trunk-we might expect that. But to have a string of newspapers in this country pursuing a similar policy is very disturbing to the people and must be very distressing to the Acting Prime Minister. I assume that the Acting Prime Minister is going to stand absolutely by the people and by his duty, and until I find him taking another position I propose to give him my confidence.
Here is the Montreal Gazette, a virulent opponent of public ownership. It is all very well to oppose public ownership by pointing to the Intercolonial and saying: "The Lord forbid; let us have no more public ownership." But the Intercolonial was built-begun decades ago-as a condition of Confederation. It was not run as a commercial enterprise. It tapped this place and that place; it ran along around the coast; it was designed to cement the Maritime Provinces together and to weld that part of the country to the rest of Canada. Many things were done that should not have been done; we have had political management of that road and it has not been good. But let me tell my hon. friend that until recent years the people of the Maritime Provinces had their freight carried at one-quarter the rates prevailing on privately-owned railways. Had the rates prevailed on the Intercolonial that prevailed on other lines, I believe that the 
Intercolonial would have paid. It has been making ends meet; occasionally it has had a little deficit and occasionally a surplus. So that it is not quite to the point to refer to the Intercolonial, hold up our hands in horror and say that we must not have public ownership.
When the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier undertook to make this deal with the Grand Trunk, Sir Wilfrid himself said that public ownership was a dangerous fad and should be avoided; that out railways should be built by private enterprise. And that marvellous man, Clifford Sifton, who always looked like a sphinx and went about with his mind absolutely concealed, giving the impression that there was a reservoir of deep wisdom in his cranium, went out into his constituency and denounced public ownership in the strongest terms. He even said: "I do not want anybody who believes in public ownership to vote for me."
Does the hon. gentleman wish to be complimentary to Clifford Sifton?
I give my hon. friend credit for sufficient intelligence to place his own interpretation on my words.
My hon. friend may be sarcastic.

I may tell my hon. friend en passant that I ran against Clifford Sifton that time and I had him pretty well beaten up to a night or two before the election; but the "Liberal" emissaries spread over the constituency like a miasma, and it took me all my time to make a decent showing at the polls.
The overseas vote came in.

The point I wish to make is this: even as prominent a man as Sir Wilfrid Laurier and as great a bluff as Clifford Sifton utterly ignored what history showed that the nations of the "world had accomplished. I dislike quoting Germany in this House; everybody dislikes Germany so that I mention the name under my breath. But Germany's railroads are owned by the State, and were a great success. Hungary owns its own railroads, or most of them. Italy owns most of her railroads. Aly hon. friend will agree that when I speak of that glorious and glorified country, France, in this connection, I am giving a good instance: France owns most of her railroads. The Australasian colonies own their railroads; in fact, the best of the countries all over the earth own their own

railroads. I bring this up merely to emphasize the indescribable foolishness that those men talked when they denounced public ownership as a fad or a fancy and said: "In Heaven's name, let us not have it here." And then they entered into contracts entailing a liability of a billion on the country-to get rid of what? Of public ownership. And ye gods! That very expenditure has forced public ownership on our country. Just think how the wheel of fortune turns; just think of the irony of fate: these people who undertook to solve the transportation question by springing these contracts and these railroads on the country did the very thing that now forces the Government to adopt public ownership. The Government cannot do anything else.
Take the Canadian Northern, which we discussed last session and which I shall not spend any time referring to this afternoon. But what an appalling mess the Canadian Northern is or was:	four hundred millions
of liabilities, to say nothing of the liabilities of all these other railroads, and yet we have prominent newspapers lauding private ownership as if it had always proved a great success. How are we going to avoid public ownership? The Montreal Gazette, the Montreal Star, and one or two other publications that I might mention, think that we ought to continue private ownership. But if we do, we shall keep pouring the country's millions into the same capacious maw-and at that, where are we going to get to. Absolutely nowhere. I am not a prophet or the son of a prophet,, but if the policy of the Government is followed; if we have an intelligent, responsible, wise, businesslike commission of management for the publicly owned system-and I think we will get it; my hon. friend can help force the Government to see that we get it-appalling as these mistakes have been, appalling as the liabilities in connection with these railroads are, we shall be able to co-ordinate the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Canadian Northern, perhaps utilize the Transcontinental, and, get rid of unnecessary mileage, and furnish this country with a proper transportation system. And in addition-mark my words: I may not live to see it but you will-we will force much better rates than we have at present.
If there is one question that hon. gentlemen should study it is the railway question, because we have to deal with it at the present time; it is knocking at our door. Letting politics into it will not help us. We are up against the real thing in Canada, with an expenditure of nearly
$500,000,000 contemplated this session. Half a billion-where are we going to get the money? It behooves every member of this House and every individual in the country to consider carefully what policy we ought to adopt in order to save this country from ruin. Nothing will be gained by playing politics. I am an old Liberal.
I believe in what I regard as Liberal principles. But we shall not get anywhere by-blaming this Government or blaming that Government or by making legal arguments about this point or legal argument about that point. To do that may sound clever and may have an effect upon a few of one's own partisan constituents who vote for you once when you are right and twice when you are wrong; but it does not help the country and it will not get the individual member anywhere. We have a great task to perform.
I had hoped that my hon. friends opposite would be absolutely sound on this railway question. I hope the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien), who has just spoken, is the only one on the opposite side from whom we shall, during this session, hear a similar kind of criticism on the railway question.
What does the hon. member mean when he hopes that we shall be absolutely sound? Is he speaking of public ownership?

In my judgment, there is no other solution for the question than public ownership. The railroads-the babies have been placed on our laps, and we have to nurse them. Would my hon. friend hand back the Canadian Northern to Mackenzie and Mann or would he continue pouring tens of millions of dollars into that enterprise? Would he still keep pouring tens of millions of dollars into the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific? The hon. gentleman has asked me a question. I would like him to answer that.
I just asked my hon. friend what he meant when he said that he hoped we would be absolutely sound. If he says " public ownership," that is an answer; but I do not agree with him.
My hon. friend, between whom and myself has existed a lifelong friendship, will have an opportunity later on of telling the House what policy he would adopt.
I shall.

As I have stated before, a man who criticises what you do

is in duty bound to suggest what should be done.
Not necessarily.

If the hon. membei for Three Rivers thinks this country should go on pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into the maws of these railroad corporations and exploiters to fatten upon, then he is out of touch with the spirit of this country and he is following a policy that is bound to result in disaster later on.
That is a question of opinion.

Only one position can possibly be taken. I was going to read some extracts from the Montreal Gazette and the Montreal Star. Let me read one from the Montreal Standard, and I want to commend it to the consideration of the Acting Prime Minister. The Montreal Standard is a paper, I understand, owned by Lord Atholstan, proprietor of the Montreal Star. Lord Atholstan came out to the West two or three months ago to study the railway question, and since his return the Montreal Star and the Montreal Standard have opposed public ownership and denounced those who advocate it as faddists and dangerous men. This is from the Montreal Standard, and it rather startled me:
Here Canada stands to-day bent under the burden of war's aftermath;-
Always bringing in the war. What a multitude of sins it will cover in the future.
-with a war debt whose interest is bigger than her total income a few years ago; with problems of repatriation and reconstruction which are staggering the Government; with a financial obligation to the men who fought for her honoui and safety, which will constitute a vast first * lien on her treasury for a generation to come; with a smouldering discontent against Government in general which could easily be fanned into red flame!
It is almost incredible that in a time of such stress and peril the public ear should be open to wild projects for further national expenditure and commitments on a scale that would startle sane financiers in our most prosperous times.
I wish the Acting Prime Minister would listen to this:
Yet it is a fact that a clique of scheming politicians at this moment is frantically endeavouring to induce the Government of Canada to force the Grand Trunk Railway to sell out to the Government as a part of a wildeyed policy for the nationalization of all Canadian railways-careless of present financial dangers and future obligations; oblivious to the fact that great experiments in national operation are already under way both here and in

* the States, and deaf to the voice of common sense which urges a waiting time while these attempts are on trial.
In the name of national safety and business sanity, let the people of Canada call a halt to this folly! We have now on our hands the National Transcontinental which was to cost ?13,000,000 and has already cost over ten times that sum, with its operation by the Government only begun.
I think about twenty times would be nearer the mark.
We have the huge blunder of the Canadian Northern and its infinite possibilities of further waste, as a burden by day and a fear by night. We have the Intercolonial, with its lamentable record.
Is it sane to assume more loads until we see if we can carry this?
Then it says further on:
Is it sensible for Canada to plunge headlong into a similar pot of trouble before we are in a position to profit by what our neighbours shall learn, as well as by our own dearly bought experience? . . . This is no time for gambling. Even if there were prospect of something great to gain and not the risk of utter disaster.
Let the voice of prudence be heard. Let the Government repel the exploiters and close its ears to the specious pleadings of the plungers who would perpetrate another gigantic railway folly that would bring us to the very verge of financial ruin.
What is the title of that article?

not a very formidable sum in these day's of billions. What course should be adopted? Arbitration. Arbitration is the normal procedure in such cases. Arbitration was had to determine the value of the common stock of the Canadian Northern Railway.	.
If we arbitrate, what we witnessed with regard to the Canadian Northern arbitration last year will be repeated. In that case the Government set a limit of $10,000,000 which the arbitrators should not exceed. Yet the arbitrators gave the Canadian Northern nearly $11,000,000. If the

Grand Trunk was referred to arbitration, we can be quite sure of what the result would be. The country would be heavily mulcted in the long run doubtless for tens of millions. Just here, I want to make this point, lest I forget it. These papers that are opposing public ownership, when it comes down to the inevitable and the railways simply must be taken over by the Government, want to impose conditions that will make public ownership if not impossible at least to suffer from an irreparable handicap. They say:	Treat the Grand
Trunk generously. But in view of the enormous liabilities the country has to face in respect of the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific, if we increase the amount which the old Grand Trunk should get, how can we ever make a success of public ownership? If you load public ownership with conditions in advance that make it practically impossible, you are taking the course that is directly opposed to the interests of the country, and opposed to the successful carrying on of public ownership.
I have another extract to read. 1 hope I do not weary the House, but this is an important subject, and I am talking not only for the purpose of reaching the members who are here; I want to spread before the Country some aspects of this question, and if I take up the time of the House, I do it in the hope that I shall be able to render some little service to the people of this country. I want to read an extract from a letter which I received from a prominent gentleman in Toronto, who is also a very strong Liberal. He says:
I am of opinion that emissaries of the C.P.R. are at the back of the Gazette and Star performances and I warn that corporation that, whilst its importance as an economic factor is recognized, it is no longer regarded as a governing force in this country; that any efforts on its part to exercise functions of government or to obstruct openly or indirectly any public policy will re-act disastrously upon itself, and that the carryings on of the Gazette and Star cannot fail to do it injury.
The country recognizes that the whole source of railway troubles has been a disastrous policy of allowing the railways to be made a tool of the exploiters and stock operators like the Grand Trunk directors in Canada, that the country is determined to eliminate this element and is going to have a show-down to the very last card with these fellows. The "credit of Canada" bogey must be exploded. Financial bluffers and fakirs who reside in London are not less fakirs than those who reside in New York or Montreal. As a matter of fact they are merely groups of the same Camorra. All the tricks that are being worked just now, such as the threatened tying up of the American ends of the G.T.R., are part of the game of the Camorra. Nothing is too mean or despicable for them. But the Government holds the trump cards, and it must not delay in playing them. It is strictly
[Mr. Richardson.!
up to the Government. Assuming that they are in earnest, they have the game in their own hands and can easily win. In the West there is but one view on the question. Opinion is even more unanimous than on the tariff. The West is thoroughly " on " to the " big interests " and will not tolerate any more of that pretence of following the public) wishes whilst really working in with the grafters, of which we have had so long and painful experience in past years. Why should the " credit of Canada " be used as an excuse for handling the Grand Trunk with gloves, and excusing the authorities from fulfilling their credit and just obligations. The [Government ought to be asked to define what the " credit of Canada " means and to explain how the " credit of Canada," under any common sense definition, could be injuriously affected by Canada demanding not that the Grand Trunk live up to its contracts (it has already hopelessly fallen down) but that it perform at least sufficient of its obligations to enable the Government to avoid the catastrophic loss which would be entailed by having those frightful white elephants, the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific both thrown helplessly on its hands, without the link which is absolutely necessary to give them any value whatsoever. The Grand Trunk financiers are acting more like a crew of pirates or blackmailers than the preposterously high-grade persons whom they pose as being.
That is pretty strong language, but probably it is justified.
It seems to me that the offer which the Government is understood to have made to take over the Grand Trunk system incorporated with the G.T.P.R. and go on paying the Grand Trunk Guaranteed and Preferred shareholders dividends at the rate which they were receiving for a term of years prior to 1917 in a quite generous one under the circumstances and should have been readily, if not eagerly, accepted by the company. Unless its members desired to flout and defy decent public opinion instead of eagerly jumping at such a proposal, the managers ostentatiously rejected it and assume a most ridiculous and offensive attitude of pained surprise and offended dignity. They affected to regard the proposal as the initial step in an effort of the people of Canada to deprive them of their property. Did they make reference to the Grand Trunk Pacific contract, their delinquencies and their huge obligations to the country in connection therewith, all of which they were responsible for dragging the country into? They did. They proposed that this contract should be annulled,, that the Grand Trunk indebtedness to Canada should be cancelled and that the money of its own, which the Grand Trunk had actually invested in the Grand Trunk Pacific, should be repaid to it by the Government, which, of course, as in the case of the National Transcontinental, meant taking over the costly and unwieldy white elephant.
The reasons or conditions by which they supported this proposal were some of them even more monstrous and insolent than the proposal itself. In short, for icy effrontery and for cold-blooded disregard of all the decencies, this proposal probably excels anything, even in the annals of Canadian high finance.
In addition to the offer which the Government had made, I fancy, under all the circumstances, public opinion might support an offer

of say two or three millions for the ordinary stock. That would be generous but it ought to be the limit and if it be not accepted the whofe issue should be fought to a finish, by receiver's proceedings if necessary, leaving as a matter entirely for secondary consideration what might happen to the American ends. The only way to deal with these financial buccaneers is to let them understand that the people of Canada, through their representatives in Parliament, are going to fight them to the bitter end.
I have been referring to what the newspapers say and to the criticisms that have been made, and now I want to briefly mention some points brought out in the Dray-ton-Acworth Report-one of the most valuable reports ever presented to Parliament. In view of the position of the country with regard to the transportation question and the difficulties that have been rapidly piling up, the Government appointed a commission composed of Sir Henry Drayton, Mr. Ac-worth, an English railway expert, and Mr. Smith, an American railway expert. It was a strong commission and cost the country a large sum of money, but they went very carefully into the whole question and submitted an important report. Now, if we select a commission that goes over the entire ground and considers the subject in all its bearings, would it not seem to be the duty of Parliament and of the country to accept the findings of that commission? Hon. members will no doubt expatiate on the question of justice to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and will probably, as the session progresses, indulge in considerable "camouflage," if I may use the term; but I shall read to the House from the report of this commission an extract or two which I think will serve to put the subject in its proper light. These commissioners have no axe to grind; they have no desire to injure the Grand Trunk Railway Company or the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, their duty being simply to consider the whole question as experts and to suggest to this House the best solution of the transportation problem. I do not want to weary the House, but the time I spend in reading these extracts will not be wasted. On page 26, under the caption "Grand Trunk Company's Proposal" the following appears:
The Grand Trunk Company have, in the letter of their president, addressed to the Prime Minister and dated December 10, 1915, officially acknowledged that they cannot fulfil their obligations in reference to the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Grand Trunk company have already obtained a tacit release from their contract in reference to the Transcontinental half of the original Grand Trunk Pacific undertaking. They have now, by their chairman's

letter, put it on record that they are " at the end of their tether." They say that it is " quite impossible for them to meet the extra liabilities arising from the Grand Trunk Pacific company." They propose to retire altogether from the concern; that in return for their handing over to the Government the $25,000,000 common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, which is in their possession, but for which they only paid a nominal amount of actual cash, the Government shall not only relieve them of all liability for the interest on the securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific and subsidiary companies, and for any deficiencies of operating expenses of the Grand Trunk Pacific system, but shall " repay the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company any money advanced to the Grand Trunk Pacific or its Branch Lines and Development Company and other subsidiary companies."
We cannot think that this is a reasonable proposition or one that we could advise the Government to accept. What would be thought if one partner in the business were to say to the other: "We entered Jointly on an enterprise which we thought would be profitable. It has turned out the reverse. I propose that you settle with the creditors, pay out to me the whole of the capital I put in, and let me retire. Provided I go free, I am content that you make what you can out of the business." We think the Grand Trunk Company cannot thus escape the consequences of its own action. We quite agree that the Grand Trunk Company cannot meet its Grand Trunk Pacific liabilities. But, if the Government is to relieve the Grand Trunk Company of liabilities which, it voluntarily incurred, but which it now finds it impossible to meet, it is for the Government, not for the company to fix the terms.
Surely that is clear. Now I will read another extract from page 30:-
If the company has been taken advantage of, or in any way deluded or defrauded by the Government-
I would like hon. members to pay particular attention to this language:-
-the fair name of Canada requires immediate redress. On the other hand, the country ought not to be called upon to accept on the ground of good faith, a large loss and responsibility unless this ground is well established. We accordingly arranged to hold a viva voce examination.
Now I turn to page 32:-
Our inquiry has fully satisfied us that the Grand Trunk management was content at the time with the arrangement made; that it deliberately took its business chances, and proceeded with the undertaking. On the evidence there is nothing whatever to Justify any charge of lack of fairness or good faith on the part of the Government in its dealings with the company. We have no hesitation in saying that, neither legally or morally, have the promoters or shareholders of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company any basis for a claim that the country shall make good the Grand Trunk's mistaken investment in the Grand Trunk Pacific. Any aid given to them must be looked upon not as a matter of obligation, but as spontaneous bounty. The question is really so left by the Grand Trunk officials themselves. The record reads (page 176), as follows:-

" Sir Henry Drayton: Doesn't it really come down to this, that the statements in your letter mean that in your view, in order to protect the finances of the Grand Trunk, and as a corollary to protect the finances of the country, the Government ought to relieve the Grand Trunk in regard to its investment; isn't that the whole thing?
Mr. Chamberlain: That is the whole thing.
Sir Henry Drayton: There is nothing else to it?
Mr. Chamberlain: Nothing else."
It is obvious from the report that in the judgment of the commissioners the Grand Trunk has no claim whatever upon this country. The Grand Trunk exploiters-or shall I call them the financial managers- induced the Government of the day to enter into these contracts. Hon. members will recall that the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, speaking of the necessity of haste, when the proposal to construct the Grand Trunk Pacific was before Parliament, said, " We cannot wait, because time will not wait, and unless we go on with this contract at once the future of Canada will be bound in shallows." And those who have good memories will also probably call to mind the retort of the Hon. Mr. Blair, who, I think, was then Minister of Railways. He said that it was not time that would not wait, but Cox, who was one of the men associated with the Grand Trunk exploitation at the time. Cox could not wait. That, however, by the way.
Now, the credit of Canada bogy has been raised by the Grand Trunk exploiters in the Old Country.
They say, " If you do not treat the Grand Trunk generously you will interfere with the credit of Canada," and they use that statement on every conceivable occasion. Let me read an extract from the Financial Times, of London, England. I was almost forgetting it, but it has just occurred to me, and it is very important that hon. members should hear this. The journal in question speaks as follows:
Are these unfortunate shareholders to get nothing, as apparently suggested in the Drayton report? It is quite impossible to believe that a government which has during the great war-
The war is invoked again-

which has just ended acted so splendidly could ever behave in such a disgraceful manner. It would be a serious blot on the Canadian Government if, by taking advantage of the adverse factors which have forced these stocks to their present low levels, they were to endeavour to obtain the railway at a knock-out price. The railway has fought gallantly against adverse conditions for many years, and has never paid to the ordinary shareholders any dividends, and now, after sixty-five years, has got a system in completeness and efficiency second to none on the American oontinent, capable in normal times

of earning good dividends. It would be beyond belief that its property should be taken from it at anything but a fair price.	.
A writer who quoted this extract comments on it, and I adopt his language because I think it is admirably adapted to the subject under the circumstances, as follows :
Note the insidious appeal to the just pride oi the people of Canada, in the vigorous, wholehearted, and effective manner in which they discharged their duty of Imperial patriotism, and in doing which they "acted so splendidly."
If the people of Canada should absolutely ignore those ordinary shareholders of the Grand Trunk, they would, from no moral standpoint, be acting in any way inconsistently with their record in the war, although the Financial Times insidiously and menacingly suggests that such a course would be " disgraceful behaviour," and in violent contrast with Canada's war record. This, however, is quite in keeping with the sordid ethics and ideals of exploiting finance, which are those of Prussianism, and which justify such doctrines as that necessity knows no law, that the end justifies the means, and that no subject of human thought, or no field of human effort, however lofty, need be sacred, if its invasion will further the ' invader's purpose, however sordid or base it may be.
Note also the whining and mawkish appeal to the sympathies. This appeal is also based on falsehood, and false inference. The "adverse circumstances," against which the railway fought, were not created by the people of Canada, tout almost entirely by the bad judgment, bad management, and devious financing, of its directors in the past.
It is a gross travesty on the facts to say that the Grand Trunk Company "has got a system in completeness and efficiency second to none on the American continent, capable, in normal times, of earning good dividends." In view of the fact that the railway did not, in times, some of which were better than normal, earn half the dividends which it actually paid; in view of the written statement of its own officers that it would at present require a sum of $51,000,000 to put it in a " state of completeness and efficiency," and in view of the whole report of the Royal Commission, such stuff as the quoted paragraph must be published by men who either are grossly ignorant of, or uninformed upon, their subject, or who care nothing about the accuracy or falsehood of these facts or conclusions, provided they create the desired impression in the minds of their readers. It is time the public should be thoroughly awakened to the publicity methods and devices of exploiting finance, and of its press mouthpieces. At the present moment an insidious hut vigorous and unscrupulous press campaign, in the interest of financial exploitation, is being conducted in nearly every part of Canada, with the purpose of preventing the release of the great public services of the country from the paralyzing and corrupting tentacles of high finance.
With regard to the four issues of preferred shares, the suggestions in the Financial Times which doubtless embody the views of the Grand Trunk magnates, are even more extravagant and impertinent than those with reference to the ordinary shares. In short the Times writer thinks that for the shares of all kinds, which had a stock exchange value of some $70,000,0'0 to $75,000,000, which value, at that, was based

on unearned dividends and fictitious net earnings Canada should pay the holders at rates, *which would bring the total payments to over $1©0,0'00',000 !
When we think over the facts relating to these shares, already recited, when we reflect upon the methods by which such commercial value as they had was sustained, when we reflect further on the actual condition of the property as disclosed in the report of the Royal Commission, when we remember the summing up of that report in regard to these shares, " we regard the share capital of the company as being Intrinsically at small value at the present time," it is only when we mass all these reflections before our mind's eye that we may adequately appraise the " gall " and the greed and the moral turpitude which are necessary to enable such claims as those in the Financial Times article to he even suggested.
I want to deal with another point or two, although I realize that I have already spoken at too great length on this subject. The Grand Trunk Company during the last ten or twelve years, as pointed out in the Drayton-Acworth Report, actually failed to make the necessary improvements for upkeep, etc., on the line, actually failed to keep the line in proper condition, and in doing so, jeopardized the interests of the country, because they were unable to give the adequate service that was required. These payments they have neglected to make in the upkeep of the road amount to a very large sum. I think it is something like $21,000,000, but hon. gentlemen will find the exact figures in the Drayton-Acworth report. Notwithstanding their failure during that period to meet the necessities oi the road, they paid to their own shareholders during the period of deferred improvements the immense sum of $36,000,000 in dividends. Now they have the audacity to blame the Government for the position in which they find themselves at the present time. To ask for relief, and to raise the 'bogy of the credit of Canada suffering unless they get that relief. If the credit of Canada is so fragile that a pistol can be held at the head of the Government by any exploiter, then the Dominion is in a very serious condition indeed.
I would like to say in conclusion that I trust the Government will deal with this matter in the only way in which it should be dealt with. I reiterate that the Grand Trunk got the country into the present trouble of their own seeking, and this Government has no right whatever to come to the rescue of the company at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I might take advantage of the question asked by my hon. friend (Mr. Cahill) to explain the present position, and in doing so answer my hon. friend from Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) with regard to certain matters which he raised this afternoon. This legislation which we are asking from Parliament is for the purpose of confirming and ratifying an Order in Council passed under the War Measures Act which, as I stated when the resolution was under consideration, has the force and effect of a statute. The Minister of Railways, under that Order in Council has been appointed a receiver of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System, and is operating that system by virtue of the powers conferred upon him by that Order in Council, and under the direction and control of the Exchequer Court.
Mr. hon. friend from Lotbinifere this afternoon appeared to me to be under a misapprehension as to the true position. He seemed to be of the opinion that the Government, as a government, had expropriated the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System. Now the Government has not expropriated that system; it has merely appointed a receiver, with the statutory powers of a receiver, under Section 26 of the Exchequer Court Act. The Minister of Railways as receiver is precisely in the same position as a receiver appointed by the Exchequer Court, because the Order in Council states that he is in that position. This Parliament has given the Exchequer Court power to appoint a receiver in certain cases; this Parliament has likewise I>ower to name the Minister of Railways as receiver, with the powers given by Section 26 of the Exchequer Court Act, and subject to the jurisdiction of that court.
Under what statute?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Under the authority of Parliament. When we pass this legislation my hon. friend and all others in this House, together with the Senate, and with the assent of the Crown, will have made the Minister of Railways receiver of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. He is now receiver, as I stated before, by virtue of the Order in Council which has been passed.
Let me elaborate that again from my point of view for my hon. friend's information. Parliament authorizes the Exchequer Court to appoint a receiver in certain eases. Parliament can also author-

ize an individual to be the receiver of a railway system, subject to the Exchequer Court jurisdiction. That has been done in this case. Why has it been done? Because, as I pointed out when the resolution was under consideration by the House, an application could not be made to the Exchequer Court except for foreclosure and sale. My hon. friend said this afternoon: Why did not the Government, instead of taking possession of the road immediately under the War Measures Act, wait a few days until default took place? My hon. friend has evidently not looked up the trust mortgages-and I hardly blame him for that because they are very complex documents-securing the various issues on the Grand Trunk Pacific system. For example, the Dominion Government has guaranteed the first mortgage securities on the Grand Trunk Pacific system. Now, if we desired to apply to the Exchequer Court for the appointment of a receiver under the Exchequer Court Act, we should have had to wait until default occurred upon the payment of interest on the Government guaranteed securities and for a period of six months afterwards as provided for in the trust mortgages. The Canadian. Government was confronted with this position: The Grand Trunk Pacific Company was unable to continue in operation. Why? Because the company had no money. The Grand Trunk Railway of Canada having decided to wash their hands of the Grand Trunk Pacific system, so to speak, said: "We cannot give you any money." -The Dominion Government had reached the point where it said, "We shall not continue to pay seven or eight million dollars a year to carry on this system while the negotiations with the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada are in their present unsatisfactory position." Now, what would have happened, supposing the Government had not appointed a statutory receiver? I have shown the committee that the Dominion Government could not have applied to the Exchequer Court for the appointment of a receiver under the Exchequer Court Act-
Until the company made default?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Until the company made default, and six months afterwards under the terms of the trust mortgages. No trust mortgages that I have ever seen provide that immediately on default of payment of interest application can be made for the appointment of a receiver. There is usually a waiting period of three or six months, and quite properly,

because a company might recover. In this case, as I have stated, the Government was confronted with this notice: We have not any money. We are going to discontinue operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific system. The Government in the public interest had to act, and it did act, but it did not expropriate the system. What it did was to appoint a receiver, because, having regard to the Exchequer Court Act, it was not possible to make application in the usual way to the Exchequer Court for the appointment of a receiver. Further than that, there is not complete jurisdiction in the Exchequer Court to grant a receivership in the case of a system like the Grand Trunk Pacific, for the reason that there are telegraph lines in connection with it over which the Exchequer Court has no jurisdiction, and also a development company, a branch lines company, and a provincial line. Therefore, under all the circumstances the Government, as I have stated, acted so as to ensure in the public interest the operation of the system. I am sure that every one in the committee will agree that it would have been disastrous to the country at this time to have permitted its discontinuance.
Now, as to the question of liability that my hon. friend has raised. I am sure that he has not studied the matter seriously or he would not have put that forward. The Minister of Railways, as receiver, is precisely in the same position as a receiver appointed by the court and subject to direction and control by the court. He is there to carry on the system. That is made perfectly clear by the Order in Council. More than that, that Order in Council has the force and effect of a statute, and Parliament now, by its ratification, will enact that the Minister of Railways, as receiver, shall have no liability towards the Grand Trunk Railway Company or to any bond holders or other creditors. My hon. friend seemed to doubt whether that would be valid. Well, it is valid because Parliament has said so, in the War Measures Act, which gave the Dominion Government the authority to pass this Order in Council, which Order in Council, as I have stated, has the force and effect of a statute. If my hon. friend has any doubt about that, then when this Bill becomes law and this Order in Council is validated by Parliament, no doubt possibly can arise, because the Order in Council is embodied in the Act of Parliament..

At that point might I ask a question? The hon. leader of the Government says that the Minister of Railways

in this case "will be to all intents and purposes the same as a receiver ordinarily appointed. The receiver so appointed has to manipulate his finances by virtue of the property that is put in his hands, and is receiver under the direction of the court. Vv ill the Government in this case supply moneys to the receiver to run the enterprise?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The money which the Government will furnish will only be to the extent necessary to continue the operation of the system upon the receiver's certificates authorized by the Exchequer Court, precisely in the way that my hon. friend has in mind. In other words, this receivership does not differ essentially from the receivership of an industrial concern or a railway over which the Exchequer Court usually has jurisdiction to appoint a receiver. That is the legal position, and what we are asking Parliament to do is to ratify and confirm that Order in Council; and I have no doubt it has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, for this reason: If hon. gentlemen will look at the War Measures Act they will find the question of transportation during the war is made subject to the jurisdiction of the Government by Order in Council. The Minister of Railways as receiver is in possession of the system and is running it.
Now then, what is the position to-day so far as the Grand Trunk Railway Company is concerned, because, after all, hon. gentlemen want to know. At the meeting of the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, held in London March 21, 1919, they passed a resolution, which I brought down in the papers which were laid upon the table of the House recently, and which I have no doubt hon. gentlemen have seen. This was the resolution :
That this meeting, having heard from the chairman a statement of the course of negotiations which have taken place between the Government and the board, approves of the action of the board and is of the opinion that the amount offered by the Government for the purchase of the Grand Trunk Railway is inadequate and will not enable the board to formulate a friendly and agreed scheme which would satisfy claim of different classes of stockholders; but it urges the hoard to convey to the Government the desire of all classes of stockholders to arrive at a friendly understanding:
And that the board be asked to form a committee selected from the largest holders of various stocks to consult with the board on the subject.
Since this matter was before the House, Mr. Kelley, the President of the Grand Trunk Pacific and of the Grand Trunk
Railway Company has returned from England. He came up to see me, presented this resolution and opened up negotiations on behalf of the Grand Trunk Railway Company That is the situation to-day so far as the Grand Trunk Railway Company is concerned.
