The member for Lothbiniere spoke of there being no default. I am sure he realizes that the only reason why there has been no default is that the Government of Canada has been voting seven and a half or eight million dollars a year to pay not only the deficit on operations of the Grand Trunk Pacific, but also the interest upon the guaranteed bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific, including those guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company itself. In other words, the Government has borne the entire burden. To give my hon. friend an idea of what the situation would have been this coming year, I may say that the interest which would have been payable upon all the securities this year is estimated at $8,000,000, to which must be added $4,000,000, estimated deficit in operating expenses, or a shortage of about $12,000,000 on the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system for the year 1919-20.

Which the Government is
going to pay in any case? The receiver will have to pay it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, the receiver will not pay the guaranteed interest. The receiver will, on the order of the court, raise money by receiver's certificate to the extent necessary to meet deficit in operating expenses only. The Government, under legislation passed previously is liable, of course, to pay the interest upon bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific which it, the Government, has guaranteed; but the receiver will not pay the interest upon securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific which have been guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company.

Was the Government
of Canada advancing money to pay interest on Grand Trunk Pacific bonds guaranteed by the Grand Trunk and not by ourselves?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Absolutely, and that is what has not been clear to the House. The Government of Canada has been paying everything; the Grand Trunk Railway Company has been paying nothing.

And paying out dividends to their shareholders meanwhile.
Sir THOMiAS WHITE: Well, they have not paid out any dividends recently, I think

But the whole load of the Grand Trunk Pacific has been cast upon the Government of Canada. What I think my hon. friend did not understand, and what has, perhaps, not been made plain in London, is that the Dominion Government, by its votes every year has been providing money to pay for all guaranteed interest, including, of course, interest guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada.
My hon. friend spoke of the National Transcontinental, Eastern division, and said that the Government should have compelled the Grand Trunk Pacific to take it under lease as provided by the statute. Theoretically that is correct. But my hon. friend knows what various defences would have been raised and what litigation would have resulted-for what good? To what end? The interest which would have been payable by the Grand Trunk Pacific in respect of the Eastern division of the National Transcontinental would have been $5,000,000 or $6,000-, 000 a year. So that if what my hon. friend suggests had been done, the present position would simply be this: Instead of there being an amount of $12,000,000 to meet for 1920, there would be $17,000,000 to meet, representing the interest upon the Eastern division of the National Transcontinental. My hon. friend needs no counsel from me on the question whether the Grand Trunk Pacific would have been able to bear that burden; so that I think we can dismiss that phase of the question. It belongs to the past, and I do not see very much object in discussing it.
The question of our credit in London has been touched upon. Well, we are always very desirous of maintaining our credit in London, in New York, and elsewhere. Canada has always had a very self-respecting position in London. We have appreciated the opportunity of placing loans there, but we have thought that while there was a degree of sentiment in the matter, at the same time the transaction was advantageous to the lender as well as to the borrower I therefore emphasize the assertion that our position with respect to loans which we have made in London has been an entirely self-respecting one.
A certain section of the London press- the matter was referred to this afternoon by the member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson)-has endeavoured to give the impression that Canadian credit would suffer by reason of the action which we have been compelled to take. I noticed some little time ago a despatch from London in the Montreal Gazette which stated:

Canada is expected to meet her loans in the British market as they fall due. Ahout twenty-five million becomes due in June. The British claim that if Canada can offer credits to European countries, she cannot expect Britain, who needs all her available money, to extend credits to Canada. This view is endorsed by Canadians here, who feel that we must finance our growing foreign trade on our own money, and not on British loans.
It struck me as rather strange that a despatch should come to Canada indicating that Canada was not to be allowed to renew an existing loan in London at a time when I was using my best efforts as Minister of Finance to renew a loan of $100,000,000 made to the Imperial Government by the chartered banks of Canada. It occurred to me that if this view prevailed, it must prevail in very narrow circles. It could not be the view of the Imperial Government, because my relations with them could not have been more satisfactory than they have been, not only during the war but ever since I have been Minister of Finance. I took the opportunity of cabling Sir George Perley, Canadian High Commissioner, to inquire as to the truth of this despatch. I have this from him, dated March 24:
Have seen nothing in press and have no information of anything which would give ground for report that Canada would be expected to meet her loans maturing here. Have seen Treasury who say no foundation for press despatch. Am authorized to send you following message:
" Chancellor Exchequer states that Treasury appreciates greatly assistance given by Canada in financing war as the Dominion has been able to loan to British Government more than she has borrowed from it. Regarding loan maturing next June, Treasury will, on request, immediately grant permission for fresh issue here to replace it, or will consider favourably proposal that they should pay it off and offset same against portion of their dollar Indebtedness to you if you prefer that course."
All we are asking the committee to do this afternoon is to approve of the ratification of this Order in Council under which the Minister of Railways is placed in the position of statutory receiver of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system.
The minister has not answered my question. I asked the Government what they expected this matter would lead to; what would be the ultimate course.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I thought I had answered what my hon. friend had in mind when I stated that the Grand Trunk had opened up negotiations through Mr. Kelley.
I cannot, of course, forecast what the course of these negotiations will be, but my view is that the Grand Trunk railway of Canada will come into the possession of the Domin-

ion Government. I am not in a position tc say that definitely, because we have not reached an agreement in the negotiations. My hon. friend probably has in mind: Supposing that our negotiations with the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada continue in their present unsatisfactory condition, what will the Government do? I stated the other day that the Dominion Government had many remedies which it could pursue. For example, when legal action can be taken, an application to the Exchequer Court for foreclosure under*the first mortgage securing bonds of the Grand Trunk Railway Company guaranteed by the Dominion Government, may be made. There are other mortgages under which the Dominion Government, in the event of default, can proceed-and there has been default-to foreclose and offer for sale. Then the Dominion Government is in a position to sue upon obligations which have matured. I have answered my hon. friend. I think it is unwise to indicate the precise course which the Government will pursue. There is the Grand Trunk Railway situation, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway situation, the Government guarantor of securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Grand Trunk Railway Company guarantor of securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and with a large amount owing from the Grand Trunk Railway system. I cannot tell my hon. friend what will happen out of all that. I have indicated to him what is in my mind.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Just before six o'clock, the Acting Prime Minister stated that negotiations were proceeding with the Grand Trunk Railway Company. I should like to ask if it is the intention of the Government to acquire the Grand Trunk railway system, in accordance with the proposals made previously.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I stated that negotiations had been resumed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company with the Government. I think it undesirable to add anything to that statement.

What I should like to find out is whether the Government has definitely made up its mind to acquire the Grand Trunk as a public-owned railway, if that road can be got on terms approximating the offer which was made some time ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can only repeat that I do not think it desirable to make any specific statement respecting the negotiations that are under way.

In view of the very important announcement just made by the Acting Prime Minister, may I with all respect say that it is unreasonable to ask the House to proceed with this legislation in view of the negotiations that are afoot, and in view of the bearing these negotiations may have on the effect of the present legislation. Surely we ought to be in possession of that information before we are asked to advance this legislation another stage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think the negotiations have any bearing upon the question before the House, with all due deference to my hon. friend.
We cannot tell.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The question before the House is this: The Government by Order in Council has made the Minister of Railways receiver for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system. He is acting under the authority of that order, and under the direction of the Exchequer Court. We are asking Parliament to validate our action. Irrespective altogether of the negotiations with the Grand Trunk, a certain situation exists with respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. That situation is that the system cannot Operate, cannot discharge its duties to the public, without this receivership. We are asking Parliament to ratify the Order in Council under which that receivership was created for the purpose of carrying on the Grand Trunk Railway system, so as to serve the public in Western Canada.

What, then, was the meaning of the statement made by my hon. friend in introducing this legislation, when he said that the next move was up to the Grand Trunk? If we are taking over this road under a receivership, how long are we to be expected to continue in that position? If a receiver were appointed in the ordinary way, he would not be coming to the Treasury of Canada for money to operate the road, but would have to get the money elsewhere. Are we going to assume all the obligations and continue to manage the road until we have arrived at some conclusion with the Grand Trunk? What bearing has the Grand Trunk on the present legislation? If the Government do not make a deal with the Grand Trunk, what

then? How long shall we continue to operate the road under present conditions? Will the Government foreclose and take the road over, put it up for sale, or what?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is for the Government to determine. The immediate situation is that a receivership is absolutely necessary in order that the Grand Trunk Pacific may continue to operate and discharge its duty to the public. The immediate cause of this receivership was that the public interest might be served through the continued operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system. My hon. friend asks how long? That depends upon the course which the Government pursues. The Minister of Railways is acting as receiver under the authority of the Exchequer Court. Money is needed to make good the deficits in operating expenses, so that the system can carry on. The Minister of Railways could offer his receivership certificates, authorized by the Exchequer Court, to private individuals if he so desired, but there is no necessity for doing that. The Government is quite content to take receivership certificates, which would be made a first charge on the system prior to all existing charges, under an order of the Exchequer Court. Our . immediate duty, however, is to operate the road. That is so obvious that it does not seem to me to be debatable. If the Government had not appointed a receiver, the alternative would have been to allow the system to come to a standstill, resulting in great disorder, and almost disaster, to the western sections of the community which the road serves. Apart altogether from any negotiations with the Grand Trunk, our immediate duty is to provide for the operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and that is what we are doing. My hon. friendi asks, what further? I have already stated that the'Government have many remedies. We could resort to foreclosure and sale proceedings, under the first mortgage securing the bonds guaranteed by the Dominion Government, or under other mortgages securing issues which the Government has in its possession. What course the Government may take will be as we may be advised, and as we may decide, but I submit that the immediate question before the committee is whether this receivership order shall be validated by Parliament.

Would it be a correct
interpretation of the remarks just made by the Acting Prime Minister to say that he has informed the committee that no matter

what the outcome of the present negotiations may be, they cannot have any bearing upon the effect of the legislation now before the committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say that exactly. I said that, apart altogether from the negotiations with the Grand Trunk, the Dominion Government had the duty of providing for the operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system. A receivership was essential to that, and we have established the' receivership. The reason negotiations with the Grand Trunk came into the question was that the Grand Trunk had not been discharging its liabilities to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system. As I have already pointed out, the company sought to cast the entire burden upon the Dominion Government. We stated to the company, in reply to their request that we should continue to finance the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system and find the money to pay the interest on the bonds for that system, whmu bonds were guaranteed not only by the Dominion Government but by the Grand Trunk Pacific as well, that the Dominion Government did not propose to do that in view of the present unsatisfactory condition of the negotiations with the Grand Trunk. That was explained to the House when the resolution was under discussion, and before six o'clock I stated that the Grand Trunk Railway had entered upon negotiations with the Dominion Government since this matter was last before the House. I think I gave a perfectly frank and clear statement of the matter.

It is not quite clear to me yet. If this legislation has no relation to the Grand Trunk, I do not. think it. is unreasonable to ask the Government what their proposals are with respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific. Do they intend to hold it, and for how long? Why not let it go into the hands of a receiver?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is in the hands of a receiver.

Why not let it go to sale? Why should we by -this legislation tie up the Dominion Government and the people of Canada to an indefinite expenditure of money? I do not quite understand what the Acting Prime Minister means by "the present unsatisfactory condition of negotiations with the Grand Trunk." If I understood him correctly, he said that this legislation had nothing to do with the Grand Trunk, and then in the same breath he said we must pass this legislation because

of the present unsatisfactory state of the negotiations with the Grand Trunk. I think the Government should tell us whether it is their intention to acquire the Grand Trunk, and whether they have committed themselves to a policy of public ownership of railways. I do not think there has been any discussion here about public ownership of railways, and I think before we embark upon this great expenditure we should have more information as to the intentions of the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) made a full statement on the subject at the last session of the House.
Oh, no. He refused to give information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not wish
to repeat unduly, but it seems to me that what I have stated is perfectly clear. That is, when the directors of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company served notice on the Dominion Government that they would no longer operate the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system, the Government was at once confronted with a situation that called for the appointment of a receiver, as the best means of protecting the public interest. That action was taken and is now before Parliament for ratification. I do not think it has been seriously contended by any one that the Government of Canada should allow the operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific system to be discontinued.
There would be no necessity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
says that there is no necessity.

I say there would be no
necessity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member says there would be no necessity for it, and that would be true under certain circumstances. If the Dominion Government, in addition to putting up all the money it has advanced since the original agreement was entered into between the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the Government of 'Canada-that is to say, $10,000,000 advanced in 1909,	$15,000,000
more in 1913, $16,000,000 in 1914 and $22,000,000 since-if, in addition to all that, we are prepared to put up $12,000,000 for the coming year and assume all future liabilities of the Grand Trunk Pacific system, then there certainly is no necessity.

Has not the Government the same power, under the War Measures
Act, to amend the law regarding the Exchequer Court as they have to appoint this receiver?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is precisely what we have done. My hon. friend has not read the Order in Council. We have enlarged the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court so as to enable this receiver to act exactly as if he had been appointed by that court. The jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court was enlarged because it was not applicable to a railway system like the Grand Trunk Pacific system, and the Minister of Railways, as I have pointed out, is in the same position as a statutory receiver as regards duties and powers, and is under the direction of the Exchequer Court. For this reason it is entirely inaccurate to say that the Government has taken over the system. The Minister of Railways is receiver, and to-morrow, if the Government or Parliament decided to appoint a private individual as receiver in his stead, he would stand in precisely the same position and be subject to the Exchequer Court of Canada. The Grand Trunk Railway Company desires the Government to continue making advances by way of loans, eight, ten or twelve million dollars a year, relieving them entirely of their liability in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific. This the Government said they would not do while negotiations with the Grand Trunk were in their present unsatisfactory condition. Since this matter was before the House on resolution, the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company have passed a resolution indicating a desire to resume negotiations with the Dominion Government, and Mr. Kelley, President of the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, has come to Ottawa to see me with a view to re-opening these negotiations.
With regard to what?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With regard to acquiring the whole system of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. My hon. friend knows perfectly well the enormous liabilities which the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada has assumed in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. It is obvious that if the receivership goes on to a legitimate end-in which probability the Dominion Government would apply for foreclosure and sell under its first mortgage-the Grand Trunk Railway system would have no other alternative than to come to the Government either for assistance or to be taken over.

That is the situation. The Government cannot allow the Grand Trunk Pacific system to continue as it has heen in the past, or as it is to-day. We certainly have no intention-and have so expressed this view in the correspondence brought down-of voting this money every year. This year it would mean $12,000,000 more. The Grand Trunk is quite well aware of that, and as I have stated, they have come to negotiate with us.
Is it the intention of the Government, before committing the country, to submit to Parliament the agreement that is in course of negotiation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Government would have to come to Parliament for legislation.
Yes, but before or after?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would depend. An agreement might be entered into subject to ratification by Parliament. If my hon. friend thinks that an extraordinary thing I would refer him to the legislation of 1903-4. That is the usual course, which is entirely in accordance with the principles of responsible government. The Government will have no desire to conceal from Parliament any completed negotiations they have with the Grand Trunk Railway Company.

It appears to me that the gist of the situation is this: Everybody agrees that we should not undertake any new obligations, nor relieve the Grand Trunk Railway Company of its liabilities in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. Our serious complaint is that the Government has just adopted the worst course it possibly could, in that it has actually given the Grand Trunk Company a new argument in their contention that they have no more obligations in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. In the correspondence which was laid before the House by the Acting Prime Minister some time ago, the Prime Minister stated that the difficulty between the Grand Trunk and the Government has been mainly the contention of the Grand Trunk that they are no longer under any obligations as regards the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. That is one of the difficulties that arose in the discussion between the ministers of the Crown and the Grand Trunk in London. The ministers offered two million odd dollars a year, three millions after a certain period, and eventually $3,600,000 in perpetuity. The Grand Trunk contended 
that this amount was not reasonable, and to establish their case they claimed that the liabilities of the Grand Trunk Pacific should not be considered, since they were no longer responsible for such obligation . But the Grand Trunk were armed with several arguments, one of them, which I explained this afternoon, being that the Transcontinental railway having been taken over by the Government they had been deprived of a connecting link which was essential to their system. Their second argument is that during the war the Government, under the War Measures Act took 150 miles of rails which they sent to France and other countries; while the third argument is that the Grand Trunk Pacific, being disconnected with the east, cannot be a paying proposition. They impliedly admitted them in 1912 or 1913, when the Transcontinental railway was completed and the Grand Trunk Railway Company refused to take it over. And in the Dray-ton-Acworth Report, at page 26, we see this:
The Grand Trunk Railway have already obtained a tacit release from their contract in reference to the Transcontinental half of the original Grand Trunk Pacific Railway undertaking.
The Drayton-Acworth report has ascertained that by virtue of the various understandings which haven taken place between the Government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company, the undertaking of 1903 and 1904 has practically by common accord between the company and the Government been laid aside. Surely if the company sets up that contention the Government has helped it in establishing its case if it goes to court. What has occurred for years? The Government has paid the indebtedness of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. The company came to the Government and said that it could not make both ends meet. The Government accordingly paid the bill, and applied yearly to Parliament for the money wherewith to do so. When the Grand Trunk, said, on the 4th of March, that it was gbing to close its branch line on the 10th, what did the Government do? It virtually expropriated that line. The Acting Prime Minister has stated that it was not an expropriation, but to realize that it is we need only read the terms of the Order in Council which recites:
And' whereas the continued operation of said system is essential in the present position of Canada, resulting from the war, which has not yet been terminated by peace, especially in connection with the transport of returning- Canadian troops and of supplies and equipment and freight, and other services made necessary by the war.

The Government could have done two things. It could have taken the Grand Trunk purely and simply and 'transferred to itself the ownership of 'both systems.
It could have caused the title of the Grand Trunk Pacific to be vested in the Crown. That would have been an expropriation, not only of the administration or the use of the road, but of the property itself. The Government has not done that but it has expropriated the road to a certain extent. It has forcibly taken the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, which is a branch line of 'the Grand Trunk, and put it undeT the supervision of the Minister of Railways, who, for the time being, is called a receiver. The Government may call this anything it likes, but surely the objects are clearly set forth in the Order in Council under which the Grand Trunk Pacific is taken over and placed under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Railways as receiver. Well, if the Grand Trunk Railway Company does not satisfy the Government, and if 'the Government has to go to court, I say, the company will be in a far better position to decline iany responsibility in respect to its obligations to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. The company will say: We have closed the branch line and you have taken it over; that being so, you are not going to be responsible merely for the operations of the road, you will also be responsible for all the other obligations and we refuse to" assume further responsibility.
I think the Government could have done otherwise. It could have taken other measures so as not to force the issue just now. It could have 'ascertained whether it really was advisable to take over the Grand Trunk at this period, and if deemed not advisable, the necessary legislation could have been introduced. If the Government thought it inadvisable to take over the Grand Trunk Pacific until the Grand Trunk was in default in meeting its obligations, it could have maintained the system that had hitherto prevailed until an agreement could be reached. The Government says: We are not going to advance any further money for the purposes of the Grand Trunk. And yet it has not taken over either the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Grand Trunk, but has simply placed the former road under a receiver. What is going to be the immediate result? The immediate result will be that all the operating expenses will have to be carried by the Government, or by the re ceiver acting for the Government. The Government will have no recourse against either the Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk
Pacific for these operating expenses. If the Grand Trunk Company chooses to close a branch line and the Government decides to operate that branch line, surely the operating expenses will be a charge on the Government. And not only the operating expenses, but the interest on the bonds, and this not because of the Order in Council .taking over the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, but because of the other reasons advanced by the Grand Trunk for some years past, and which have been impliedly accepted by the Government, and which reasons I have fully explained.
Besides all this there is the other question, that Parliament has been absolutely ignored in this matter. The Government was advised on the 4th of March that the Grand Trunk would cease to operate the Grand Trunk Pacific railway on the 10th. Surely the Government could have taken Parliament into its confidence before entering upon a course, which, in my opinion, if the Grand Trunk Company fails to reach an agreement with the Government, will tend to do exactly what we wish to avoid. That is, it will give further ground to the Grand Trunk to claim they are relieved of, and to decline their responsibilities in respect of, the Grand Trunk Pacific railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend,
I think, has not a proper conception of the Grand Trunk Company's obligations in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. He thinks the Government has made itself responsible for those liabilities. I pointed out, before the committee rose at six o'clock, that the Minister of Railways was in the position of a receiver; that there had been no expropriation, and consequently there is no legal liability in respect of the interest on any of the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. My hon. friend says that we have put the Grand Trunk Railway Company in the position that it is relieved of its liabilities in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway system. The hon. gentleman does not appreciate the fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company has issued many million dollars of securities that are in the hands of the public, guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. The coupons will be presented from time to time, as interest becomes due, and it will be for the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada to make good its guarantee. In the meantime the advantage is this as far as the Government of Canada is concerned: If we had gone on as before-and that is

all that my hon. friend suggests, he says you must go on-we should have had to bring down an estimate to this House for $12,000,000 to enable the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to go on this year as it did last. In doing that we should be relieving the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada from its liability in respect not only of the bonds which it has guaranteed, but really in respect of the system whose stock it owns.
Did not the Grand Trunk Railway Company decline to admit their responsibility in connection with their obligations for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: But do they not contend that they are no longer responsible for their obligations in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I do not think so; I do not see how they could.
Will the acting Prime Minister allow me to read this from his recent speech?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

He Said:
The Grand Trunk Hallway Company said to the Dominion, " We want to assume no responsibility for the Grand Trunk Pacific."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is what they still say. They say, "We want to assume no responsibility." The Dominion Government say, "You will have to assume certain responsibility." That is the difference.
That is the legal issue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is the legal issue. The Dominion Government's policy is not to provide money in payment of the interest upon all the securities; in other words, the fixed charges, and also the deficit upon operation. That is where the issue lies between the Government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company.
If the Government is wrong in that policy it is for the House to say so; but I do not believe the House will say
I

anything of the kind. On the contrary, I am satisfied that if the Government brought down an estimate this year of $12,000,000 in order to carry on the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, this House would say to the Government that we should not have done it. That is the position, and that is the issue before the House. The Grand Trunk Railway Company has a liability toward the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and in any negotiations we have for the acquisition of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system that liability must be taken as an important factor, and for .that position I say the Government is entirely responsible, and is willing to take the responsibility.
Mr. GEORGE B. NICHOLSON (Algoma East): I would not presume to detain the House while it is in committee on this Bill but for two reasons. I spoke briefly on the resolution in connection with this Bill two weeks ago, but there seems to be a manifest effort in the press throughout the country and in the House to jockey the country into a wrong position in its relations with the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, and I feel it to be my duty, as a member of this House and in justice to my constituents, to place my opinion clearly before the House and the country in regard to that issue, and in doing that to give the House and the country some information that I believe neither has yet been really seized of. Another reason is because the Acting Prime Minister has announced that further negotiations are being entered upon between the Government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada in connection with the solution that must be found for the situation in which we find ourselves in relation to the Grand Trunk Railway and its subsidiaries, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental. The hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) this afternoon, in building up a case for the Grand Trunk Railway Company, laid down three reasons why the Grand Trunk Railway Company should not be called upon to assume their obligations in relation to the Transcontinental-and he used these as an argument why we were being placed in a wrong position in respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. The first reason was the cost of the National Transcontinental Railway east of Winnipeg; the second was the change in grades, and the third was the change in terminals. Now, at the risk of wearying the House I am going to give you the reasons put forward by the President of the Grand Trunk Railway Company as to why they could not assume their obligations in relation to the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific. When being examined by Sir Henry Drayton, Mr. Chamberlin gave these reasons;
Sir Henry Drayton:	There is the other
matter; You think that the Government as a matter of fairness to the Grand Trunk, ought to relieve the Grand Trunk Railway Company of its total Grand Trunk Pacific investment?
Mr. Chamberlin; I do.
Sir Henry Drayton; And repay to the Grand Trunk the money it has in the Grand Trunk Pacific, and relieve the company of all its responsibility. That is a large order. We want to give you every opportunity to state every ground on which you think that should be done.
Mr. Chamberlin; Well, Sir Henry, if you will look at this map you will see where the Grand Trunk Pacific stretches away off up through the north country, while the Grand Trunk is away down in this part of the country. It is not a natural connection of the Grand Trunk, is it? It is not only not a connection of the Grand Trunk, but it is not of any benefit to the Grand Trunk.
In the first place, we are under contract to send all business over this north line, away from the Grand1 Trunk. The Grand Trunk cannot derive any benefit from it, under the oontract with the Government.
I want the House to take particular notice there-

Will the hon. member let me mention this-and even from a Bolshevik it may be of some use-that I never said any such thing in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. I said that those were the reasons put forward by the Grand Trunk Railway 'Company for not taking over the National Transcontinental railway.

If the hon. member will listen carefully he will note that I am not referring to the Grand Trunk Pacific exclusively. I am referring to the Grand Trunk Pacific and the National Transcontinental, and Mr. Chamberlin in his answers was referring to the whole system.
When he says " We are under contract to send all business over this north line," what does that mean? They entered into a contract with the Canadian Government to send their western business over the north line, away altogether from the Grand Trunk. Would that not be sending it over the Transcontinental? Mr. Chamberlin goes on to say:
The Grand Trunk cannot derive any benefit from it under the contract with the Government.
Commissioner Acworth: That is a new point, to me.
Mr. Chamberlin: In addition to that, the company is bound to put steamers on the Atlantic and steamers on the Pacific, to accommodate all that business.

Were they going to put steamers on the Atlantic to accommodate business that they were bringing as far east as Winnipeg, and no further? It is obvious that he was referring to the National Transcontinental and its terminal on the Atlantic ocean. The evidence continues:
And yet it does not bring one dollar of business to the Grank Trunk.
Commissioner Acworth:	How does that
obligation arise?
Mr. Chamberlin: It arises out of the contract with the Government.
Commissioner Acworth: The original contract with the Government?
Mr. Chamberlin: The original contract.
Mr. Biggar: Of July 29, 1903.
Commissioner Acworth: Is the agreement a schedule to the Act?
Mr. Biggar: Yes, sir, a schedule to the Act of. 1903. Chapter 80, I think it is.
Commissioner Acworth:	Therefore, if the
Grand Trunk, as it does at present, operate or control the operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific, were to send traffic through Portland instead of through Halifax, it would be a fraud on the agreement?	\
Mr. Chamberlin: Yes. We are bound to go on with all that tremendous outlay and to carry that load, and yet not get one dollar of benefit from it. The Grand Trunk simply cannot carry it.
And a little further on:

This whole question relates to what is ultimately to become of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. I think it is well, therefore, that we should just consider for a minute the relationship that this has to that company, who are not only the stockholders1-the proprietors-of the Grand Trunk Pacific, but who are also the guarantors of a large block of the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and as such cannot escape their responsibility. Let me qualify that by saying that the solicitor of the Grand Trunk Railway Company a few days ago questioned these figures, and when challenged to give the correct figures he stated he could not give the exact figures, bust he presumed it would be about $200,000,000. I have made a calculation of the obligations of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, based on the figures given by the chief solicitor of the company, Mr. Biggar. The outstanding bonded indebtedness is $200,000,000. Then add to that for betterments, rolling stock, etc., as per page 28 of the Drayton-Acworth report, the sum of $51,000,000. I should just like to supplement something that was said by the hon. member for Springfield in connection with Grand Trunk financing, because there has been a persistent effort made to put this country in the position of exacting the pound of flesh, and, as some of the newspapers say, not dealing fairly with the widows and '
orphans who own the Grand Trunk Pacific stock. As the hon. member for Springfield pointed out, during the very period when the Grand Trunk officials themselves stated that they were not maintaining their system as it should be maintained, they paid out in dividends $36,000,000, and I want to refer to this particularly. The Drayton-Acworth report says (page xxxii):-
A few weeks after the chairman's letter acknowledging that the company could not meet their Grand Trunk Pacific liabilities-with short-term notes, issued to make advances to Grand Trunk Pacific companies, which those companies evidently cannot meet at maturity, outstanding to the amount of $25,000,000-the Grand Trunk Company paid away $2,500,000 in dividends.
At the very same time they came before the Government of Canada and said: We cannot maintain our system unless you advance us further sums of money, or provide means by which we can get the money. Grand Trunk financing from its inception has been based on the payment of dividends out of money that should have been used for the maintenance of the system itself. Is it a reasonable proposition for the president of the Grand Trunk to come forward and say, as he did (page 28 of the Drayton-Acworth report): " If we had $25,000,000 now from some other source than the earnings of the company we would be in a fairly good position." What did they want that $25,000,000 for? Was it to project needed railway lines in parts of Canada that required to be served by railways? WTas it to do anything for the development of the resources of Canada? It was to put in ties and rails and repair cars and locomotives that had become	derelict because the Grand Trunk railway had been starved in order to pay dividends to the shareholders in London. And dividends on what? Dividends on stock that in my judgment, if the whole situation was analysed, would not represent one single dollar that ever went into the physical assets of the Grand Trunk railway. The Grand Trunk railway has been built up and financed and maintained by the sale of bonds and debenture stock on the English market and, as was stated in this report, one reason why they desired to pay large dividends was in order that they might stabilize the money market in London so far as the Grand Trunk railway was concerned.
In view of the fact that the people of Canada are faced with the obvious necessity of getting out of this difficulty by taking over all the physical assets of the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pa-

eific, I believe it would be well for us to stop and consider some of the reasons why the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada has not been able to operate as economically as other railways running parallel to it, and through territory very similar and handling equal quantities of freight and passengers on just as favourable terms. In that connection I have made some very brief personal investigations to satisfy myself as to some of the possible causes.
Before the Drayton-Acworth Commission the officers of the Grand Trunk Railway Company said that they required then 200 locomotives and at least 10,000 box cars. I stated in this House last year that the last locomotive I had seen turnpd out of the shops for the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada was obsolete before she turned a wheel, but in order that I may make this point clear I am going to deal very briefly with the question of equipment of the Grand Trunk. Taking the capacity of a modern freight car as 40 tons, the locomotive of a train made up of 1,000 tons net freight, loaded in 40-ton cars, hauls 500 tons of non-productive dead weight in the form of tare, or the net weight of the car before it is loaded. With the same amount of freight in 30-ton cars the locomotive hauls 612 tons of non-productive dead weight.
Take a twenty-five ton car and move 1,000 tons of freight and you have 650 tons of non-productive weight to move. Take a 20-ton car and for the same quantity of freight you move 750 tons of non-productive weight. As between a 20-ton car and a 40-ton car you have a 20 per cent increase on account of wheelage, bringing the total amount of non-productive weight that must be moved up to 900 tons as against 500 tons. The Grand Trunk railway moved in 1916, the last year for which a complete report is available, 37,686,255 tons of freight a distance of 100 miles, equal to 37,686, 1,000-ton trains for 100 miles. So that if the tare and wheelage was only increased 25 per cent on account of defective or inefficient rolling stock-from personal investigation, my opinion is it would be 5C per cent, but we shall assume it is only 25 per cent-they would have 37,686 trains each hauling 100 tons of unnecessary unproductive load a distance of 100 miles, or a total waste of 3,768,600 ton miles at a minimum cost or minimum waste of $2,826,450.
I shall now refer briefly to locomotives, and I may repeat that one of the reasons why the Grand Trunk are in the position

in which they find themselves as regards their old lines is the fact that they have never had, and have not yet, modern rolling stock. Equipment oeing standard, a freight train 1,00(1 net tons should be hauled 100 miles at a fuel cost of $33.75, assuming that the locomotive is of modern type and in a proper state of repair. The same net load with an obsolete type of locomotive consuming an increase of 25 per cent of coal would cost $45, or an excess of $11.25 for every 1,000-ton train handled 100 miles. Multiply this by 500 locomotives in daily use and you have an approximate sum of $2,000,000 wasted in fuel alone. I shall refer briefly to the condition of the Grand Trunk locomotives, as stated by the company's officials in the Drayton-Acworth report. They required at that time 200 locomotives. If you take all the locomotives that the Grand Trunk Railway Company have in their service-1,055 I think is the exact number-you will find that 50 per cent of them if taken into repair shops could be converted or remodelled at a cost of about $3,000 each making them fairly modern locomotives that could operate in competition with locomotives of a similar type on other railways. Of the remaining fifty per cent, one half, 25 per cent of the total-would cost $10,000 each to remodel.
Mr. MoMASTER: What is the cost of a new locomotive?

In the present condition of the steel and labour markets a new locomotive of modern type 170 to 200 per cent is worth about $65,000 to *$70,000. iln pre-war times the same locomotive could be obtained for about $43,000, but as conditions are, and, I fear, will be for some time to come, the cost will be as much as I say, namely about $70,000. Then the remaining 25 per cent of the locomotives to-day in the service of the Grand Trunk railway might very well be thrown on the scrap heap. If 300 locomotives in the Grand Trunk service were absolutely scrapped and 200 new ones built to take their place there would be an enormous saving, because each of those locomotives is not only consuming 25 to 50 per cent more fuel than it should in doing the work for which it was built, but it is not able to do the work that a modern locomotive can do. We are therefore faced with this condition, that to bring the motive power alone of the Grand Trunk railway up to standard in order that they can compete with railways in Canada or the United States that have standard equipment, will take $35,000,000.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that 33i per cent of the locomotives of the Grand Trunk railway might just as well be relegated to the scrap heap-that is about 300 of them?

From the standpoint of economical operation I state, without fear of contradiction, that if the Grand Trunk railway were efficiently managed and properly financed, and if it had officers such as any modern railway company should have, 300 of these locomotives would have been in the scrap heap five years ago, and 200 modem locomotives substituted for them.
Did I understand the hon. member to refer to locomotives to be repaired at a cost of about $10,000 each?

I say that about 300 Grand Trunk locomotives should be abandoned and, in addition, 25 per cent of their locomotives should be rebuilt and remodeled at a cost of $10,000 each; while every one of the remaining locomotives should have $3,000 to $3,500 spent on it. Hon. members need not take my word for it. Any one, if he desires to verify my statements, may consult any modern mechanical engineer, or appeal to the man who, as I stated in this House last year, is second to none as a mechanical engineer and who is now Chief Mechanical Superintendent of the Canadian Government Railways,-Mr. Hungerford.

I do not wish to question the hon. member's statements. I merely wish to get the facts. So far, we have 25 per cent which can be repaired at a cost of $10,000 each, 33 per cent which should be thrown on the scrap heap, and a certain number which can be repaired at a cost of $3,000,-I understand, another 25 per cent. Therefore, there would be about 20 per cent of real locomotives on the Grand Trunk Pacific.

The hon. member misunderstood me. B. Nicholson. 1
scrapped as utterly obsolete and worse as far as operation is concerned, and 20C modern ones built.
In addition to that let me say this: That due to wrong practice in the whole question of motor power and rolling stock, the lack of standards on the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, has cost these roads hundreds of thousands of dollars each year. I had the privilege, and took the liberty, of spending one whole day with one of the mechanical superintendents of the Grand Trunk, going through one of their shops, and I counted forty-six different types of one kind of casting used in connection with the drawbar equipment on their locomotives. Any man who knows anything about this subject, not only with regard to locomotives but anything else in the mechanical line, can realize in a moment what that means in connection with keeping up the whole system -what it costs in unnecessary repairs, and all that kind of thing. So that I say I believe one of the reasons why the Grand Trunk is in the position in which it is today, the reason why it has never been able to maintain itself out of revenue as it should have done, is because it has never been efficiently managed and efficiently operated. What the cause is I do not undertake to say. In the final analysis the question of the operation of the Grand Trunk is not at the moment the matter we are interested in. The question that intersets us is how we are going to finance the railway situation in which we find ourselves.
Is the hon. gentleman in favour of paying the Grand Trunk, or the Grand Trunk Pacific, anything for their stock if the Government takes over the road?

So far as I am personally concerned, I would simply take the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific and value their physical assets, having in view all the time the obligations of the former company with respect to the latter company. I would treat the whole thing on that basis. Let me say this: All these ideas with regard to being charitable and generous to the stockholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, so far as I am concerned, may sound very nice, but are not the right pleas to be advanced in this House. We have some responsibility, I bedieve, to at least see to it that the Canadian people get a reasonable measure of justice, notwithstanding all this talk of charity towards the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. However, that company comes to be in the position it is in with Tegard to the Grand Trunk Pacific it is entirely and solely liable. If it placed men in charge of its operations in Western Canada who squandered its money ruthlessly, as was done without question, then the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, and not the people of this country, is responsible ; and go far as I am concerned my final word is simply this: If negotiations are being opened up with the Grand Trunk Railway Company its responsibility must always be kept before it, or the people of Canada will not get even-handed justice. As against any question of fair play to the Grand Trunk stockholders, to whom dividends were paid out of moneys that, the officials themselves admit, should have gone into upkeep, I am one of those who say we should uphold the interests of the people of Canada.

I would like to say a few words about the resolution that is before the House, as it has a bearing upon the railroad that we are really taking over. That, as I understand it, is the question in which the committee is particularly interested. A certain- section of railway, known as the Grand Trunk Pacific, extending from Winnipeg to the coast, has been taken over by the Government through the instrumentality of a receiver. The last
time I spoke upon this question I took the ground that we should have taken that road over, if through a receiver, in the ordinary way, that we should have proceeded as the courts, and the laws governing those courts, provide. The Acting Prime Minister gave as a reason for the procedure adopted by the Government, that the Winding-up Act should not apply to certain branches of the company. Now the minister may give perfectly good reasons from a financial point of view, but when he cites reasons of law, we are bound to call his attention to the statutes. Section 6 of the Winding-up Act, which is Chapter 144 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, declares as follows:
This Act applies to all corporations incorporated by, or under the authority of an Act of the Parliament of Canada.
That provision is wide enough, Mr. Chairman-, to comprehend any company regardless of its character, whether it is a telegraph company or a railway company, or any other corporation. If it receives its existence or incorporation by virtue of the powers of this Parliament, then the Canadian Winding-up Act applies to it. Therefore, there is sufficient scope in the Winding-up Act to deal not only with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company itself, but with all its subsidiary companies. The reason which the Acting Prime Minister gives for not following the ordinary procedure was that the Winding-up Act would not apply to some branches of the company. He told us further that there would have to be a default before foreclosure could take place, and the Order in Council itself makes reference' to section 26 of the Exchequer Court Act. Now, referring to the Exchequer Court Act, being chapter 140 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, subsection 3 of section 26 says:
The Exchequer Court in any of the cases in this section mentioned

[DOT]-and let me say, Sir, that the cases mentioned are clearly within the circumstances which apply to this railway-
*-shall have all the powers for the appointment of a "receiver either before or after default.
Now that is perfectly clear. First, that the Winding-up Act applies to every phase of this company with which we are dealing, and secondly, that section 26, which is quoted in the Order in Council, has within its scope the power of appointing a receiver before,-as well as after, default.

The section is too long for me to read. I am taking the responsibility of saying that it covers such a case as this. If the company is unable to go on with its work, and that is the ground-

I refer to the whole of section 26. It is a long story, and I am not fond of reading in this way and taking up the time of the committee. I say that the sections are there for any person to read them.
