They will be unable to go on with the work. That is one of the conditions.	.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think you had better read the whole clause.

Very well, 1 will read it:
The Exchequer Court shall have Jurisdiction as regards any railway, or section of a railway, not wholly within one province, and as regards any railway otherwise subject to the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada, to order and decree in such manner as it may prescribe,-(o) The sale of such railway, or section of railway, and all of the rolling stock, equipment, and other accessories thereof.
(1) At the instance of the Minister of Railways and Canals, or, with the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, at the instance of any creditor of any person or company owning or operating such railway, or section, whenever such company has become insolvent, or has for more than thirty days failed to efficiently continue the working or operating of such railway, or section, or any part thereof, or has become unable to do so.
Now I submit to you, Sir, that the reasons put forward here for the last two weeks are that a letter was received from this company that on a certain day they would not operate beyond that day. That clearly comes within this proposition: or has become unable to work or operate the road. If the evidence received by the Government was good one way it was good the other. They received a letter from an official of this corporation which said: Beyond the 10th day of March we are not going to operate this road. Then the railway company must have become unable to do so, and it was because they had become unable, to do so that the Government appointed the receiver; and if the Government was justified in moving upon that

letter, they would also be justified in going before the judge of the Exchequer Court with that evidence and saying: We ask for a receiver because the Company says it has become unable to operate the road..

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
How long does it say
we have to wait before proceeding? .

You have not got to
wait at all, I submit.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Before the operation is continued under a receiver how long does it say we should wait?
My hon. friend knows that he can get an interim receiver appointed on the spur of the moment.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Are you sure of that?

Yes, he can get an interim receiver. All my hon. friend has to do is to go before the Exchequer Court and say: Conditions are such that I must immediately have an interim receiver; put him in to-day, we shall issue a notice, and ten days from to-day everybody interested will appear before this court and say whether this receiver should be continued or not. Therefore no notice is necessary, and so far as expeditiously taking hold of this road is concerned, the one method was just as expeditious as the other. It would not take any longer, except of course it was in the hands of the Government in the one case, and in the other they would have to go to a friendly court that would be willing to help them out when the necessities of the country required it. So it seems to me that the practice of the courts and the provisions of the law do not justify the contention of my hon. friend. I am not saying that the course taken by the Government will not lead to the same result, but I do not want the Acting Prime Minister or any other member of the Government to give laymen in this House reasons which are not good reasons, and reasons which those laymen appear to accept with alacrity and say: Of course that was all right, and the Government was perfectly justified in taking the course they took because they could not do anything else.
Some of my hon. friends on this side of the House were asking the Acting Prime Minister to-night: What are we going to do with this road? We can call the Minister of Railways a receiver or any other name that we please, but he is nevertheless the Minister of Railways, he is subject to the directions of this House, and he represents the Canadian people. I care not what he

calls himself, he is Minister of Railways in charge of this system, and the people of this country are paying for its operation. That is where the striking and material difference is between the ordinary receiver and the Minister of Railways as receiver. The ordinary receiver would have to so operate the property placed in his hands as to get money out of it to run it, and the creditors of that company could take an interest in seeing that the property was run as efficiently and economically as possible. In this case the receiver does not need to care how things go; he gets the money from the Treasury.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Where would the other receiver get his money?

By selling some part
of the property.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What would he sell?

He would have the
stock and could sell the property. But the Acting Prime Minister, says that this receiver gets money now on certificate, on the credit of this road. That is what I understood him to say. If that is the case, why would not an ordinary receiver get it just as well?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The receiver is an officer of the Crown and he gets any necessary money from the Treasury* of Canada; the other receiver "could get money by selling the road. What would become of the road when sold? What was it built for?

This company is in default. We are told that this is an insolvent concern, and that every step that the Minister of Railways is to take in connection with it is to be under the direction of the Exchequer Court, as is the case with every other receiver. Now, if we are to introduce other elements into it, according to the Minister of the Interior, which are foreign to what we have been told by the Acting Prime Minister, it is an entirely different case. We have a right to believe what the Acting Prime Minister told us, that this is to be conducted in every respect under the laws governing receivers. If that be the case, why finance this concern and go on with it indefinitely? That is what hon. members on this side of the House want to know. How long is this condition of things going to last; are we going to bring the receivership to a speedy determination and know where we stand? If we are going to take this road over and own it as part of the Canadian National system of railways, we must do a good deal
of housecleaning, we must not take it over with all its concommitants, with all this $200,000,000 of debt. Surely this process that must be gone through by the receiver should be gone through as speedily as possible, he should eliminate what we have not got to carry, and let us know what we have to pay.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. member mean that the debt now represented in the bonds of the road can be avoided? Does he desire that we do that? If so, who loses the money?
There are some bonds, I understand, in connection with this road that we have guaranteed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We lent all the money ourselves. Would not the first money we squeezed out be our own?

It is penny-wise-and-pound-foolish to try to protect those moneys if it would cost us too much to do so. Even if we lose 'some of them, it is better to get this property down to a business basis. The idea of a receivership is to get a property down to a proper working basis, down to what it is worth. Are we to carry $10,000,000 of somebody else's simply because below that there is a substratum of a few thousand dollars of our own? That is not business.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not want the hon. gentleman to misunderstand me. The first mortgage is guaranteed by us; the second by the Grand Trunk. Subsequent to these are a series of mortgages that are our own; consequently, the only advantage we could get would be by taking proceedings under our first mortgage and then seeking to eliminate-unless it was protected-the mortgage guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. As to the rest, it is all our own money; nothing is to be gained by squeezing that out.

This railroad has a certain value. The business of the receiver is to get that much money for it and to divide it equitably and fairly, under our laws, among the creditors. Let us get at the value of this road and let the money that it brings be properly divided. If we are going to take the property and keep it, that we do not get the cash out of these second or third mortgages does not make much difference. To-day the property is owned by nobody; let it be put in the category of proper ownership. If it is the intention of the Government to own it, we should get at it as speedily as possible.

clean out the wreckage and get down to business. Whatever we are obliged to pay for it, under the law, let us pay it. The Acting Prime Minister tells us that unless we take this system over we may have to pay $12,000,000 this year to keep it going. That is a large sum, but the Acting Prime Minister should tell the House what it will cost us under the present plan. The receiver is not obliged to account to Parliament; he accounts to the court. Possibly it will cost us more than $12,000,000 before the end of the year. Why should we be frightened into doing extraordinary things on the supposition that we are [DOT] saving money if we do not vote the $12,000,000? We may have to vote more. The Government should tell us what money they are going to save and when they are going to bring this thing to an end. To keep it going indefinitely under the receivership of the Minister of Railways is not going to get anywhere, except in a continuance of the wild expenditure of money which this railway has involved ever since we had anything to do with it.
The member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) said that the Grand Trunk Pacific should not have been built and that he was always opposed to its construction. On that ground the hon. gentleman is in conflict with a great many people in this country. In 1903 an agreement for the building of this road was entered into and a contract signed between the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Government. Parliament was dissolved and a general election was held in 1904. The principal issue before the people was whether the Government should go on with that agreement and build that road. The agreement itself was discussed on the hustings from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and the Canadian people, by their votes at this election, said:	Go
on with the construction of the road. I think that is the most democratic way of -finding out what the will of the people is on any given subject. In 1908 the people had another opportunity of discussing the matter, which they did, though not so vigorously as four years before. The Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier was again returned to power, while the work on the project was proceeding. In 1911, when the whole conduct of the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier was again under fire, the question of building the Transcontinental was not under discussion; everybody had accepted it as the proper policy. The only criticism made by Sir Robert Borden against the Laurier Government in 1911 was that it was moving too fast; that it was too pro-

gressive; that the Canadian people had better " let well enough alone." In view of the fact, therefore, that the Canadian people took that stand with regard to the building of this road, it does not lie in the mouth of any of us to say that the Government which undertook that work ijad no mandate and no authority from the people. Whether it was right or wrong, whether it was a sound proposition or not, is a question which the Canadian people have to answer. We are all stopped from saying anything further on that subject. For many years in this House the railway critic on the Government side was our good friend the late member for Hamilton, Mr. S. Barker. Mr. Barker was regarded as an authority on railway matters; always when the question of railway building or railway management was under discussion in the House, he was put forward as the authoritative speaker on the Conservative side.
Speaking in the House of Commons in 1912 on the subject of building this road, he said:
If I understand the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) aright, he is under the impression to-day that when this question was first opened in the country, there were a great many people who thought that the construction of the railway was not needed then, that it was premature. I do not know just what my hon. friend is referring to. If he says that many people at that time thought there was no need for additional railway facilities for the transportation of the grain produce of the great Northwest to the ocean, then he is altogether outside the facts. I was in the House at that -time and I can vouch for the opinion of every member of the Conservative party; I venture to say there was not one man on the Conservative side who doubted for a moment the absolute need of another through railway at the earliest possible moment.
That is the position taken by the railway critic of the Conservative party at that time, and I never heard Mr. Barker's authority of his right to speak for his party questioned. 1 will direct the attention of hon. gentlemen to the first Burget Speech made by the hon. gentleman who leads this House (Sir Thomas White). They will find in that speech entire and absolute approval of the policy of building this road and of what was being done. Perhaps the hon. gentleman might have complained that the amount spent was too much, but there was not one word of criticism as to the building of the road. Hon. members will also find that in that speech the Minister of Finance, now also Acting Prime Minister, said that this road was an asset to the country and not a debt as it was certainly bound to be of vast usefulness and impor-

tance to the great development that was then taking place and that would take place in Canada.
As regards hon. gentlemen taking shelter under the excuse that the Liberal party was responsible for building this road, there is nothing to that. We were all responsible for it and it looked like a splendid enterprise up to the time that there appears to have been a so-called conspiracy to smash the whole thing. A successful effort was made to break the first agreement, and when that agreement was broken, then of course the whole thing went to pieces and the Transcontinental railway was disconnected-the eastern part was disconnected from the western. The letter that Mr. Chamberlin wrote to the Government on the 13th July, 1912, which the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) refused to-night to read to the committee, throws a flood of light on this whole business. 'The argument and evidence of Mr. Chamberlin, speaking at any time since the date of that letter, must be read and construed in the light of the position that he took at that time. Mr. Chamberlin said: We truly have made a contract with the Government; we are prepared to carry it out, hut we are prepared to do so on the terms of the agreement; if the Government breaks the agreement and will not keep up their part, the whole business is broken up. This is Mr. Chamberlin's letter:
July 18, 1912
Major R. W. Leonard.
Chairman, Transcontinental Commission, Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir:-1 learn from our engineers that the standard of work on that portion of the Transcontinental Railway between Lake Superior Junction and Cochrane, which was at the outset adopted and has so far been complied with, is being departed from, and that instead of four-tenths grade and permanent structures, you have authorized grades up to one per cent and the erection of temporary wooden structures. In regard to this I would call attention to clause 7 of this agreement of the 29th July, 1903, which provides that the work of construction of the eastern division shall be done according to the specifications approved by the company and shall be subject to the joint supervision, inspection and acceptance of our chief engineer and the chief engineer of the commission. I beg to say if this work is done in accordance with what I understand to be your recent instructions, it will not be in compliance with the agreement nor satisfactory to this company and cannot be accepted.
E. J. Chamberlin.
That is the origin of the difficulty. This Government, after they came into power, began to put up wooden bridges where it was agreed to put up steel bridges; they
changed the grades, putting momentum grades in place of practically level grades, and they so changed the bargain that the company could not any longer 10 p.m. agree to carry it out. There is not, and never was, any denial of this letter. The hon. member for East Algoma refused to read it because it appears in a speech delivered in this 'House by the Hon. George P. Graham. His speech was delivered in this House; it is not like a speech that he might have delivered somewhere in the country, and for which there would be no very grave responsibility. This letter was quoted; it was not questioned then, and it was read in the presence of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Cochrane) himself who was then Minister of Railways. I do not question it to-night, but it already throws a whole flood of light as to why Mr. Chamberlin was speaking in this way. He says:	You have taken
away from me the eastern end of the road; you can no longer carry out the old agreement because you are changing the whole road, and if that be the case, how can you expect me to carry out my part of the agreement?-we will not do it. For that reason he and his company had a perfect right to assume that if they were getting out of part of the bargain, the whole thing had fallen to the ground and there was no reason for any struggling to keep up with it.
I want to be absolutely fair in this matter.
I am not going to say whether the full carrying out of this agreement -would be a good thing for the Canadian people or not, because 1 do not know. All I say is this, that the entering upon this agreement and the breaking of it have, at all events, landed us in a position in which we are to-day that we must either take over the road or deal with it in some other way. I ask the Government not to drag the matter along and involve the country in unnecessary expense. 'Let us own this road-and run it, like any other property we possess in a business like way.
Mr. MEIGiHEN: The committee has been very patient in listening to this discussion and has had its patience pretty sorely tried, but I earnestly ask that it bear with me for a moment while )I make some reference to the address just delivered by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie). He comes back to a subject very frequently referred to throughout the day, and alluded to in the letter quoted from Mr. Chamberlin of some date in 1912, namely to a claim put forward by the Grand Trunk Railway Company that there had been some violation of the agreement in respect of four

momentum grades east of Cochrane, which violation gave them the right to recede entirely from their obligation to take over the line.
And, to use the graphic language of the hon. member, that throws a flood of light on this whole situation, and he intimates to the House that but for these four momentum grades we would now have a good proposition in the Transcontinental and Grand Trunk Pacific; the Grand Trunk would be anxious to take over the road and operate it, and all the troubles of these later years would have been avoided. These four momentum grades have been discussed for a long time, and no one knows better than my hon. friend that when a company or an individual gets into difficulty it is ready to hang its hat on any little peg it comes across,-four momentum grades or anything else-in order, if possible, to have an excuse for getting out of its obligations. But of all the allegations attaining the very perfection of humbug that could be addressed to this or any other assembly, to say to any intelligent mind that the fact of the four momentum grades is any appreciable factor whatever in the determination of the question before the committee, or in the determination of the value of the Transcontinental or the essential soundness-
Will my hon. friend permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I should like to finish my sentence, but perhaps the hon. gentleman would prefer not.

Has the Government
made any demand on the Grand Trunk in respect of the deficits which they have made in the operation of the Transcontinental, and if not, why not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Because we have no agreement with the Grand Trunk. Unfortunately, in the original bargain there was no agreement with the Grand Trunk to take over the Transcontinental; the agreement was with the Grand Trunk Pacific. Undoubtedly we made demand on the Grand Trunk Pacific, and repeated demands, to take over the Transcontinental, and they resisted those demands and put up their plea, and put everything in their plea they could think of. They put in the four momentum grades-and smiled as they put them in. They told us frankly, as Mr. Chamberlin told the Drayton-Aeworth Commission, that the reason they did not take the Transcontinental over was be-

cause they could not take it over. With respect to making them take it over, litigation was contemplated, I am not certain, but I think a writ was issued and a defence put in. We might have launched upon a lot of needless, purposeless, and aimless litigation, but where would we have been if we had won? We would have had a judgment against them ordering them to operate the Transcontinental, but what practical value would that judgment have been? How could they operate the Transcontinental ?
Are the guarantees of the Grand Trunk no good?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The guarantee of
the Grand Trunk is not there. It is too bad the hon. gentleman did not have something to do with framing the bargain, but the fact remains that it was not in the bargain. The Grand Trunk never guaranteed that the Grand Trunk Pacific would live up to all its obligations. We have the undertaking of the Grand Trunk Pacific to take over that line and pay three per cent on the cost, but we have no guarantee of the Grand Trunk at all.
Not that the Grand Trunk would take it over?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, none whatever. Is this the first the hon. gentleman knew of that? We have just the undertaking of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and it cannot possibly perform its undertakings.
Bid not the Grand Trunk guarantee the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh yes, but the bonds are not an undertaking to take over the Transconti nental.
It is the same company.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Well, I will try once
more. The Grand Trunk Pacific issues certain bonds which the Grand Trunk guarantee. They issue certain others which the Grand Trunk do not guarantee. The Grand Trunk Pacific makes a covenant to take over the Transcontinental upon completion of construction. That covenant the Grand Trunk never guaranteed. For the fulfilment of that obligation we have the Grand Trunk Pacific and nothing else. What condition did we face? We faced capitalization of approximately $200,000,000 and an annual charge approximating $6,000,000. We are faced with a road that showed no reasonable chance of paying

operating expenses, to say nothing at all of fixed charges. There was a deficit, as a result of operation, of $2,000,000 a year. How could the Grand Trunk Pacific undertake an obligation which entailed an expenditure for rental of $6,000,000, and a loss in operation of $2,000,000-$8,000,000 altogether-when to operate its own line it had to borrow $7,500,000 every year? What is the use of talking of four momentum grades? You might as well talk about the colour of the rails. The four momentum grades is a mere flea bite. I consulted the engineer to-night, and he tells me that these grades were put in the same as any other grades, that no objection was made by the Grand Trunk at all. The objection was an after-thought on their part. It was not the practice to have the signatures of each engineer to all these things, he says. The grades were put in by the consent of both, not in writing, but by consent, the same as any other graces. But what has that to do with the thing to-day? The fact is that no matter what kind of grades the road had, no matter whether the company had legal rights that enabled them to escape or not, it really makes no impression on the situation at all. The fact was, whether they had legal rights or not, they could not operate. They frankly admitted that before Sir Henry Drayton. Here is what Mr. Chamberlin said:
Sir Henry Drayton: Doesn't it really come down to this, that the statements in your letter mean that in your view, in order to protect the finances of the Grand Trunk, and as a corollary to protect the finances of the country, the Government ought to relieve the Grand Trunk in regard to its investment?
M. Chamberlin: That is the whole thing.
Sir Henry Drayton: There is nothing else to it?
Mr. Chamberlin: Nothing else.	.
Nor was there anything else to it. And that is the reason why we did not relieve the Grand Trunk Pacific. They are not relieved to-day. Their legal obligation stands to-day as good as ever it was. In practice we operate because they cannot operate. A receiver has been appointed because they cannot operate the Grand Trunk Pacific. How could they operate the Transcontinental if they cannot operate the Grand Trunk Pacific? Why not see the real big things that count?

Sure.
Mr. MEIG'HEN:	Certainly. I am glad
the hon. gentleman does see them. I have not laboured in vain if he sees anything at all about it. We are in this position. We have gone in as receiver. The hon. gentleman says we could have gone in as receiver in another way. We could have had a receiver appointed under the Exchequer Court Act, also passed by this House. I do not want to get into an involved legal argument. Suffice it to say, that the legal advice tendered the Government in this regard was that that Act was not applicable to enable us to do as my hon. friend says. But whether or not, we would have been in the same position we are in to-day; we are simply operating under another Act. We would have had a receiver put in under the Exchequer Court Act, and we have a receiver now. We are in the same position one way or the other, and we are operating the road. It was the necessity of operation that compelled us to do it this way. It is quite true we could have waited for default, that is, in the sense of default on the bonds; and that default probably would have come. But what was to become of the road while we were waiting for default? Could jwe have done without the road? No; once you have built a road, and towns and industries have sprung up along it, it is a bounden necessity to operate that road. We could not afford to wait one or >
two or three months until the conditions stipulated in the trust deed matured. We had to see that not a day nor an hour was lost. And that is why we acted as we did. Our rights are safeguarded in every possible way.
I do not want to enter into a general discussion, which is not at all relevant to the immediate issue before the committee, as to what should be the conduct of our negotiations with the Grand Trunk from this. Suffice it to say that this Government has taken no step which in any way impairs or reduces the liability of the Grand Trunk Railway as originally entered into. The Grand Ttunk say to us:	Consider the
Grand Trunk on one hand and the Grand Trunk Pacific on the other; take our earnings and pay us our average of what we have made for ten years and then consider the Grand Trunk Pacific, and we will talk to you about that. We say, however, that-the two are one and inseparable. We say further:	It is true you paid dividends for
ten years averaging perhaps $3,600,000 a year, but while you did that we were taking care of your obligations; we were lending money to a company which you owned, in order to discharge obligations in respect of which you were liable; had you been taking care of all the obligations you would not have been paying $3,600,000 a year; indeed, were you to-day to take care ol all your obligations it is doubtful whether

you would pay your shareholders anything at all. That is the language we used to the directors of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. At the same time the people of Canada, and this Government as representing the people, are anxious that no impression shall be justifiably created among British people or others that we seek to confiscate or to take any step that favours of confiscation. We intend to see that the just rights of the shareholders are protected as much as the rights of anybody else. .But we say to them: In estimating the value of your shares there must be taken into account all the obligations of that road, not merely the obligations you yourselves have recognized in days gone by. The question is asked us, if this Bill goes through, what will you do? The acting Prime Minister said a few nights ago that the negociations had reached such a stage that the principles upon which we were acting were quite clear, the next step being on the part of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Apparently they are taking that step now. In fact, they have taken it, and have requested that negociations be resumed. Do hdn. gentlemen suggest that before negotiations are again entered into we should announce exactly what we intend to say? If we did that there would be no negotiations to conduct. The first step is the passing of this Bill. Before anything is done, oi course, it must be ratified by Parliament, and the Government has taken Parliament fully into its confidence as to the principles by which it desires to be guided. We say: we already have something in the nature of judicial determination of the value of the shares of the Grand Trunk railway, and that we cannot take the Grand Trunk Pacific. You may ask us to do it, conditions may compel us to do it, but conditions do not compel us to do it to the relief of the Grand Trunk railway and in such a manner that we cannot acquire the Grand Trunk railway under fair conditions. We claim that there has been something in the nature of a judicial determination and make you an offer based on the finding of that tribunal. We believe we make you as fair and generous an offer as we can, based and anchored upon that finding. If you refuse it we make you the same offer we make our own people in all cases of acquirement of private property, namely, settlement by arbitration, and we set down the terms of arbitration, that is to say, the principles by which the arbitrators should be appointed. It has never been alleged 
that these principles are unfair. We offer the same to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company as, through all time, we have offered to the holders of private property in this Dominion wherever that property has been taken by the Crown. We say to them; We offer you just the same; We do not impose restrictions as in the case of the Canadian Northern; otherwise just the same system of determining values is adopted. Nothing that we ever gave the Canadian Northern have we ever sought to refuse the shareholders or directors of the Grand Trunk; on the contrary, having regard perhaps in some degree to the fact that the shareholders of this road are widely scattered people in another land, and to the fact also that the road is an old historic Canadian institution that has played a great part in early days in the development of older Canada, we say [DOT] we will not impose on you the special restraints we did in the case of owners of proprietary interests in the Canadian Northern, and offer you a fair open arbitration with no limit fixed as the maximum which the arbitrators may award. Now I submit to the House that it does not lie in the mouth of the President of the Grand Trunk railway, or of the directors, or of the editors of financial journals in England or anywhere else, to say that we have refused the Company anything that we have ever conceded the owners of private property in this Dominion. There is nothing we have given to others that has been refused them, and when we are threatened by the proprietors or others with a condition of unfriendly negotiation it will be well to realize-and the sooner the better-that we cannot by any threats of that sort be brought to take a stand inconsistent with sound principle, the principle that has guided us in other matters of a similar kind.

The leader
of the Opposition,, when I was speaking this afternoon, asked me if I was opposed to the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and I replied in the affirmative. Perhaps the bald statement without an explanation might be used to my prejudice. While I am opposed, and always was opposed, to the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and while I still believe it was a colossal blunder, I would not want the House to understand that I take the position that the West does not need further railway accommodation. Settlement was extending in that country very rapidly and additional railway accomodation was required, but that in my opinion should have been

provided by arranging with the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian Northern to build branch lines under certain conditions. One of the reasons why I have been and am opposed to the Grand Trunk Pacific is the fact that it parallels for hundreds of miles some of the existing lines in that part of the country, consequently doing damage to the lines that were there-the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific. If the leader of the Opposition has been through Yellowhead Pass-if he has not he probably will some day-he will have witnessed or will witness the melancholy spectacle of two railways running parallel within a few yards, or a few hundred yards as the case may be, for hundreds of miles, the rails on one of those roads having been torn up for hundreds of miles. This seems to be a piece of gigantic folly, building a railway parallel to others and destroying their value. That was my position on that point.
While on my feet this afternoon I neglected to express the opinion that the capitalization of the old Grand Trunk is away beyond reason. It has a mileage of something over 3,000 miles and is capitalized for ?444,000,000, I think. If you divide the capitalization by the mileage you find that the Grand Trunk has cost over $127,000 a mile. It cannot possibly pay interest on that; no railway could. The Canadian Pacific, which was built under reasonable conditions, is capitalized at some $68,000 a mile, while the Canadian Northern, which we took over last year, is capitalized at $54,000 a mile.
One other point before I resume my seat. I think the Government owes it to itself and to the people of Canada to let the shareholders of the Grand Trunk, of whom, I suppose, there are some thousands in the old land, know exactly what the position is and what stand the Government and Parliament of Canada take in the matter. These shareholders are in the hands of a little clique of manipulating managers who are making a mighty good thing out of their job, and of course they are fighting for the continuance of the Grand Trunk Corporation.
Let the Grand Trunk pass into the hands of the Government, as it probably will, and the occupation of these financial manipulators and exploiters is gone, they will lose their job. They are working on the shareholders to give the idea that the Canadian Government is not acting fairly towards the Grand Trunk shareholders, that in fact this Government is discriminating against them because they are British. All sorts
of insidious statements are being made in order to prejudice the Grand Trunk shareholders. I think the Government ought to make a point of issuing a statement which would be circulated among those shareholders letting them know exactly what position we take. Because the shareholders, if they accepted the offer which the Government has made, to pay the average rate of interest on the preferred and guaranteed capital that prevailed for a period of years prior to 1917, would be in as good a position as ever they were, and in a very much better position than they are ever likely to be if matters are left to these manipulators. If the latter position is taken the result will be that the shareholders will be left in the lurch. I am not certain whether I understood the Minister of the Interior to say that the Government had offered arbitration to the Grand Trunk.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, persistently ever since February last.

I am rather sorry about that. I have no faith in arbitrations, particularly where too many lawyers are set to work on them. I want to state it here, because I like to take a public opportunity of doing so, that I have a great prejudice against too many lawyers handling our business. I believe a great deal of the losses of the country are due to the fact that we have had too many lawyers manipulating our affairs. I don't believe that we ought to arbitrate with the Grand Trunk. We arbitrated with the Canadian Northern, and we lost out, as I said this afternoon. The Government limited the amount it should give to $10,000,000, and these lawyers granted them about $11,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh, no.

What was the
amount?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There was a clause in the agreement which provided that no matter what the value of these shares was found to be no greater amount should be paid than ten millions. The Commission found the value of the shares to be, I think, $10,800,000, but the whole ten millions has not been paid, because certain shares have not been able to be delivered. When all are delivered there will not be a dollar more than $10,000,000 paid.

That is a matter for congratulation. We are about a million ahead of what I thought this afternoon, and I want to tender the Government mv

sincerest congratulations that in one case at least the country has saved that large amount. This is the first case on record of the kind, and I think we ought to rejoice over it. Of course the Government has offered arbitration to the Grand Trunk railway corporation, that settles it, but I believe it is a mistake. We can deal with perfect justice to the Grand Trunk without offering arbitration and paying immense fees to lawyers in order to obscure the whole situation.
The hon. gentleman might explain to the House his particular reason for not liking lawyers?

The lawyers are all right, and personally I have the sincerest friendship for them, but they have a way of tangling things up legally, and looking at everything through legal spectacles, which inclines me to the belief that the lawyers have been a greater curse to this country than any benefit they have ever conferred on it.
Has the hon. member forgotten the statute of limitations?
I shall have to plead ignorance.

From the information which has been vouchsafed this afternoon in regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, it appears to be pretty well understood on both sides of the House that the Government must take this road over and operate it. Whether the Government adopted the wisest method in taking the road over under the War Measures Act, or whether they should have obtained an order from the Exchequer Court, or should have adopted some other means of appointing a receiver, may not perhaps be very material. Whether this action was necessitated by the violation of some contract on the part of the Government, or whether the Grand Trunk were unable to carry out its agreement, may not matter very much either. The situation would appear to be that the Government will have to take over and operate the Grand Trunk Pacific.
What would be interesting to know is, what is our position with respect to the Grand Trunk itself? I have always understood that the agreement entered into by the Government for the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific was a specific one under which the Grand Trunk undertook to take over the road and operate it. Now, if I understood the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) correctly, and I think I did, he said that the Government had no con-

tract with the Grand Trunk, the contract was with the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In respect of the operation of the Transcontinental.

What puzzles me is how the Grand Trunk proper would guarantee the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific if there was no obligation on the part of the former company to take over and operate the latter road. I also understood the Minister of the Interior to declare that we had no contract or agreement whereby we could hold the Grand Trunk Company proper to the obligation to operate the road, but we had a claim against the Grand Trunk because it had guaranteed the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Now, I cannot understand why the Grand Trunk would guarantee the bonds of a road in respect of which they had no contract or liability.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Because the Grand
Trunk owns all the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific it presumably would interest itself in that road to the extent of guaranteeing certain of its bonds, but the Grand Trunk did not convenant with the Grand Trunk Pacific railway to take over and operate the Transcontinental.
Although it owns all the shares?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It owns all the shares of the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Transcontinental was built by the country.
^ Mr. McCREA: We are told that the Grand Trunk has guaranteed certain bonds, and we are also told that the Grand Trunk is responsible for the payment of these bonds, and that the Government has a good and valid claim against the company. On the other hand, the letter which was read a few minutes ago by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) would denote that as far back as 1912 the president, or general manager, indicated that the company was not going to be responsible for the carrying out of the contract referred to. The Government would have been well advised if, before this date,-and I suggest it is not yet too late if they have not done so,-it arranged a conference between solicitors representing the Grand Trunk and solicitors acting for the Government to see if an agreement could not be arrived at as to whether the Grand Trunk is responsible or not. Neither of the parties to this dispute has presented any legal opinion to the House stating definitely whether or not the Grand Trunk is liable. If the company is responsible, it has, by its officials, given us to understand from time to time, that it did

not consider itself responsible in any way for the payment of these guaranteed bonds.
I think it would be a good thing for the Government to invite the Grand Trunk to have their solicitors meet the Government's solicitors and go over all the details in order to decide whether the Grand Trunk are responsible or not, and if they are-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am glad the hon.
gentleman has more faith in lawyers than the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson). There happens to be no need of them this time. The Grand Trunk Railway Company have never repudiated their legal responsibility in respect of the bonds guaranteed by them; so there is nothing to discuss.

I do not always agree with the hon. member from Springfield, but I am pretty nearly in accord with him on the lawyer question. I am not a lawyer myself, and perhaps I may be all wrong, but the fact of the Government having stepped in and paid the interest on those bonds, as we have been told by the Acting Prime Minister this afternoon, would seem to indicate to some extent that we are acquiescing in the contention of the Grand Trunk Railway Company that they are not responsible for that interest, and I think if you proceed to the courts to enforce your claim the. Grand Trunk Railway Company will raise that as one of the reasons why they should be relieved from payment. If it is true that the Government are responsible for the interest on those bonds, I think the Government should have proceeded to pay it. Is the fact that they have not done that the reason why the Grand Trunk think the Government should enter into negotiations for acquiring the Grand Trunk proper? And if the Cabinet are unanimous on the point that we should nationalize the Grand Trunk and all other roads-and I am not so sure that the Cabinet are unanimous in that respect yet; I think there are members of the Cabinet who do not believe in it-but if they are unanimous, would it not be better parliamentary procedure to get the authority of Parliament to enter into negotiations, rather than for the Cabinet to complete the whole transaction, and then come to this House and say:	Now, take your choice:
either support the Government in this measure, or vote yourselves out of office. I do not believe that is the proper way to proceed.
For my part, I have not any faith in Government ownership of railways. I do not
believe that the Government of Canada, oi any other Government, can operate a railway as well as a good, sound corporation which employs men for their ability, whereas the man who gets a Government position, whether on a Government railroad or in any other branch of the service, usually acquires that position through his political friends, and once he gets it he has always enough political friends to keep him there, whether he is qualified or not.
Has the hon. gentleman in view any private corporation that would take over the white elephant that the Government have had thrust upon them and operate it as a private concern?

I do not know whethei
there is any private corporation that would take over the white elephant you have on hand. I am not finding fault with that; I said at the commencement of my remarks that I think we are in such a position that we have to take over the Grand Trunk Pacific. But, as far as I understand, the Grand Trunk proper are not asking anybody to take them over. On the contrary, they are claiming that the Government is attempting to ill-treat them and to take from them their property that they have operated for sixty years and that they built at a time when this country was in very great need of railway transportation and the railway business was not a paying proposition, but now that Canada has reached such a point in its development that their road will become a paying proposition, the Government steps in and wants to take it away from them. That is what I am finding fault with. If I were inclined to, I would find fault with the methods and means adopted for taking over the Canadian Northern. I think that this country paid a whole lot more money than it would have been called upon to pay had the Government adopted the proper means for acquiring that system.

How does the Minister of the Interior figure that he is going to get from the Grand Trunk the money that they are liable for to the Grand Trunk Pacific, and thereby to the Government? I presume he hopes to make the Grand Trunk responsible for their guarantees for the Grand Trunk Pacific; Am I correct in that assumption?	*

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We do not have to make them responsible; they are responsible.
You hope to gather something from that responsibility?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
You expect to be able to realize on that responsibility?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: To consider that responsibility in fixing the value of their shares.

What have their shares got to do with this transaction? If you hope to make them pay in respect of their responsibility, then, of course, your argument that the contract between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental holds good is a very poor one, for the, reason that the Grand Trunk guaranteed the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Grand Trunk Pacific in turn are oeing relieved of a portion of their responsibility to the people of the country, or whoever has got the money in that investment, by reason of the fact that you have allowed them to relinquish, or have relinquished for them, their contract with the Transcontinental.
In other words, if you made the Grand Trunk Pacific live up to their contract with the Transcontinental, instead of there being a deficit of $2,360,000 to $3,000,000 a 5 ear on the Transcontinental now, which the people of Canada are paying, you would be charging to the Grand Trunk Pacific $6,000,000 a year; and if, as the Acting Prime Minister stated, the Grgnd Trunk-Pacific are losing $12,000,000 in operation, they would also be losing another $3,000,000 on the Transcontinental, which would make $15,000,000. It might be possible for them to take up these securities and get something for them, but if they are loaded with a $15,000,000 obligation, in all probability the securities will be worth nothing. So that the leader of the Opposition is quite right in saying that measures should be adopted to take out the unnecessary expenditures or the money it will be impossible to pay interest on. From the questions which the Minister of the Interior has put, I take it that the Government does not intend to make the Grand Trunk responsible for their obligations to the Grand Trunk Pacific. If they do, how do they propose to do it?
It is a contractual relationship.
I want to know how you propose to get the money from the Grand Trunk.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I hardly know where to commence to disentangle the knot of absurdities which the hon. gentleman has made. We do not, in the first place, have to make the Grand Trunk responsible for anything. You cannot make the company

responsible; it made itself responsible; its bond is there. That is to say, it is responsible for the second mortgage bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific; if the Grand Trunk Pacific does not pay, it must. All we are anxious to do with respect to that responsibility is to make them realize it; to make them realize that it still exists and has to be taken into account in connection with the value of their shares. The difficulty is that some years ago they dropped the Grand Trunk Pacific in their tracks as they walked along and have forgotten about it. They have put it away; they do not like any too well to be reminded of it. So that all we have endeavoured to do in that respect is to bring home to them that that responsibility still exists and is an essential factor in the determination of the value of their share.
If I extracted anything else that had meaning from what the hon. gentleman said, it was this: If we had got an order of the court directing the Grand Trunk Pacific to take over the Transcontinental, and if the Grand Trunk Pacific, which was not able to do so, had done so and therefore had lost $2,000,000 a year more in operation and $5,000,000 more in rental-that is $7,000,000 a year more-then I think he tried to say that the Grand Trunk would more likely have to pay something on its bonds.

You would not say that
the Grand Trunk bonds would be any more valuable would you?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They would not be affected at all. The Grand Trunk bonds were the second mortgage bonds. It depends on the value of the road itself as an operating road whether these bonds are good or not and whether the Grand Trunk might be called upon to pay them. If the Grand Trunk Pacific as a commercial proposition is worth the amount of the first and second mortgage bonds up to the end of where the Grand Trunk guarantees, then the Grand Trunk will not be called upon on its guarantee.

The hon. gentleman has
a curious process of reasoning.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It might lose money on the operation of the Transcontinental, but the value of the Grand Trunk Pacific as a commercial proposition, as effecting the security of the second mortgage bonds, would be worth just the same whether they had to deal with the Transcontinental or not. These bondholders would sell the road aside altogether from its Transcontinental obligations. Now, that really has nothing to do with this question or with what the hon.

gentleman got up to speak about. It has nothing to do with their liability; they are liable, if they are called on to pay, now. The liability is great or small just in proportion to the value of the Grand Trunk Pacific enterprise itself as a distinct commercial entity. Whether great or small, all we say is that it exists. It is there, a fixed responsibility, binding on them, and we insist that it be taken into account in the determination of the value of their shares.
Well-
Carried.
You will carry it in plenty of time, now; don't-
Order. The hon. member is supposed to address the Chair.

Mr. Chairman, hon. members will kindly bear with me for a few moments. I hope that the Minister of the Interior will have patience; I regret that he got peeved a few minutes ago when I asked him a question, although he was quite ready to cross-question and examine the leader of the Opposition when he was speaking. The Minister of the Interior is very lucid in his explanation of everything except of the questions that are put to him. He jumps up and says: "This fellow does not say anything that we can understand;" he seems to think that the idea is to split hairs and work around in a circle. In one breath he says that the Grand Trunk have an equity in the stock of the Grand Trunk because the Grand Trunk liability does not amount to anything; in the next breath he says they have no equity in it. The Prime Minister says that the Grand Trunk directors have not said that they were responsible on their guarantee, and the Minister of the Interior says they are responsible on their guarantee. We have conflicting opinions from different hon. gentlemen opposite. We are only trying to get some information on this very interesting and apparently intricate Bill-information that we are clearly entitled to. Hon. gentlemen on the Government side have spent hours in discussing this matter, and when we on this side, who have not spent a quarter of that time in discussing it, ask a question or seek information it is not very becoming to hon. gentlemen opposite to say, "Carried," "Hear, hear," and so on, and run away with the idea that people are scared of them or that they are going to shoo us out of the Chamber. We are entitled to certain information, 74
and I intend to ask for it and to continue asking for it until the Government either attempt to .furnish it or say that they will not give it to me. I am not a bit particular whether they give it to me now, five minutes from now, or two hours from now. Apparently this question has evolved into a consideration of taking over not only the Grand Trunk Pacific but the Grand Trunk as well.
The question of taking over the Grand Trunk hp,s been discussed here in the last hour or two, but tl)at matter has not previously been considered by the House. There was a report that negotiations were taking place some time ago, and honourable members on the Government side of the House seem to take it for granted that some member on this side is trying to protect the interests of the Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk Pacific. They are not taking that from anything any honourable member on this side may have said, but they seem to have that idea fixed in their minds. If the 'Grand Trunk have a responsibility to the Grand Trunk Pacific, and if you can define that responsibility, it is just possible the Grand Trunk Railway Company have no equity whatever in the stock of the iGrand Trunk or of the Grand Trunk Pacific; and if they have not, I am anxious to know the reason of the anxiety on the part of members of the Government to pay the Grand Trunk Railway Company some money. If the Grand Trunk are responsible for some seventy or eighty million dollars of guarantees of securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific, as they apparently are from statements that have been made, it seems as if they have no equity in the Grand Trufik, as if the equity guaranteed in the Grand Trunk Pacific might exhaust the equity in the Grand Trunk. If the deficits in the Grand Trunk, the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific are so great that they will show a deficit in the combined three roads of which the Grand Trunk is a guarantor, then it is possible that the equity in the Grand Trunk is nil; that it will not bear the carrying charges nor the operating expenses. If that be the case, I do not see why honourable members opposite are so keen about paying the Grand Trunk something, insisting that the company are under this guarantee and that they must live up to it. And yet when we ask the minister how he purposes making them live up to the guarantee, he refuses to answer, saying that he cannot because of negotiations which are under way, and he circles around

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is, I think, under a misapprehension. The bonds to which he refers as being sold are the bonds of the Grand Trunk, not the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

I said the Grand Trunk Bailway Company. The Grand Trunk Bailway Company sold some $14,000,000 worth of bonds. If their obligation is binding to the Grand Trunk Pacific, if the Grand Trunk Pacific will hold them to their contract, then it would be impossible for them to sell the $14,000,000 worth of bonds, if the people understood the situation. When the Acting Prime Minister stated that the British people could not misunderstand the attitude of the Government in this matter, I think he was making some mistake because those bonds were sold after members of the Government had left London and had terminated for the time being their negotiations with the Grand Trunk people. What I want to find out from the Government is this:	Why are
they anxious to pay the Grand Trunk something for their stock if the jGrand Trunk have no equity in that stock? And if they have an equity, why should the Government take this summary action? Suppose the amount of bonds the Grand Trunk have guaranteed is $70,00,000. Provided that the Grand Trunk Pacific is losing only $6,000,000 a year, with the expectation in one or two years of recovery and making up their operating expenses and the interest on their bonds, then the guarantee would not be so heavy on the Grand Trunk; but if the Grand Trunk Pacific is hopelessly in the hole, as it would be if it were held to its contract with the National Transcontinental, then the Grand Trunk Pacific securities guaranteed by the Grand Trunk would come back in their entirety on the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk would be responsible for the total guarantee of the Grand Trunk Pacific bonds. I hope the Minister of the Interior can understand that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, I am lost. .

The minister is lost because he has been assuming all along that members of the Opposition are all opposed to this because they were opposed to taking over the Grand Trunk and to taking over the Grand Trunk Pacific without giving the Grand Trunk something. Let us put it in another way. If the Grand Trunk Pacific were not able

to pay, their securities would drop in the market, hut if their obligation was so great that they could never pay, then their securities would be of no value whatever.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What securities?
The Grand Trunk securities.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not necessarily.
If the Grand Trunk Pacific were losing say $10,000,000 a year, how long would it take to wipe out the Grand Trunk securities in the Grand Trunk Pacific? Can the minister follow that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, easily.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would not like my hon. friend to think that the Government is intentionally denying him any information. Since we brought down the resolution, I have laid upon the Table the very fullest information that we had respecting the transaction, including the balance sheet of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and those of its subsidiary companies, and all the correspondence that has passed between ourselves and the Grand Trunk railway. I apprehend, I think quite clearly, the point my hon. friend has in mind. He says that the Grand Trunk Railway Company has heavy liabilities of a contractual character in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific; that is, they have guaranteed in the first place $20,000,000 of the bonds secured by a second mortgage, and some $35,000,000 or $40,000,000 of the debenture stock, of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. He makes the point that the liabilities of the Grand Trunk Railway Company are so heavy in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific that in his view the shares of the Grand Trunk Railway Company would be, in the strictly legal position, of comparatively small value, and he asks why the Government is anxious to pay the Grand Trunk Railway Company the money in respect of their shares or in respect of the system if taken over. I will read what I think has been read before from the Drayton-Acworth report. The commissioners are speaking of the value of the shares of the Grand Trunk which they have recommended the Government to take over and have vested in a holding company to be controlled and managed on account of the people of Canada. They first touch on the very heavy liabilities of the Grand Trunk in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific, which they assume at $5,000,000 per annum, and then
74}
speak of the capital expenditure of $30,000,000 required by the Grand Trunk to put its own lines in proper condition, and then go on to say, which is precisely in point:
We regard the entire share capital of the company as being intrinsically of but small value at the present time. On the basis of present value of maintainable income the fair compensation would be very small. But we do not think that this is the only basis on which the people of Canada should proceed. We think this is a case for generosity rather than strict justice. Canada is under obligation to tho Grand Trunk shareholders, who in the early days, with but small Government assistance, and in competition with the railways of the United States with their vastly greater resources, built up the first Canadian railway-system.
Then they go on to recommend that tbs' average net earnings of the Grand Trunk for a period of ten years preceding the war be adopted as the basis in negotiating for the acquisition of the shares.
There is just one other point to which my hon. friend has referred. He spoke of the obligations of the Grand Trunk Railway in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Now, I assume he was speaking of the legal obligations. Those legal liabilities-some $20,000,000-are in respect of bonds which the Grand Trunk guaranteed under the original agreement. Secondly, there is the sum of $35,000,000 or more-I think more-of debenture stock since issued, and which they also guaranteed. Then there, are the guarantees which they gave the Government in respect of the loans made in 1909 and 1914. I think the total amount of the liabilities of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway guaranteed by the Grand Trunk is in the neighbourhood of $100,000,000-about $98,000,000, to be more accurate. The system also owes the Grand Trunk Railway Company on open account some $20,000,000 or more. That is the situation.
My hon. friend has spoken of the Eastern Division of the National Transcontinental, the title of which has always been in the Government, because the Government built it, and it was to be leased to the Grand Trunk Pacific. Now the Grand Trunk, while it is a guarantor of the securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific, did not guarantee to the Dominion Government that the Grand Trunk Pacific would carry out the lease of the Eastern Division of the National Transcontinental, which was in contemplation when the arrangement was originally entered upon and which was stipulated in the agreement, and in the legislation confirming it, between the Government of Canada and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway company. I

think I have cleared up all the points to which my hon. friend drew attention. I do not intend for a moment to refer to the circumstances under which the system was built or as to the wisdom or otherwise of building it. As I stated to-day, we have got past that; that water has gone over the millwheel. We have been confronted with a situation of immediate urgency, requiring in the view of the Government certain action in the public interest, and the action that has been taken by the Government to protect the people of Canada by maintaining continuous operation of the Grand 'drunk Pacific has, so far as I can see, been approved by all. It seems to me the matter has been very fully and amply debated, and I have to thank all hon. gentlemen for the -contributions they have made to the debate.

There in one point that I think the minister did not quite understand. Apparently the object of this transaction is to take over the Grand Trunk. Suppose you do not make a deal with the Grand Trunk; what position shall we be in then with respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific? Will the Government foreclose? How would they ever get the money from the Grand Trunk? Will they make the Grand Trunk responsible, under its guarantee, for the Grand Trunk Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We would not make the Grand Trunk responsible for the Grand Trunk Pacific except to the extent that it is now legally responsible. The point that was made by the Minister of the Interior, and which I made earlier in the day, is this: In estimating what the Government should pay by way of rental, if the Grand Trunk Railway system was taken over under lease (which was involved in the offer made by the Government to the Grand Trunk Railway Company last summer) there must be taken into account the legal liabilities which the Grand Trunk have in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific. My honourable friend says: suppose you do not take over the Grand Trunk, what then? Well, the Dominion Government have a first mortgage charge upon the Grand Trunk Pacific, and it could proceed under that first mortgage to foreclose, offer for sale, and get the system at a much lower price than is now represented by all the securities which have been issued in respect of it. That is what the Government could do. That would involve the elimination of the second mortgage securities guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, upon which their liability would still continue.
Suppose the second mortgagee were to take up the first mortgage; where would you stand then?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The purchaser
would have to consider whether this road which is not only not earning its fixed charges, but is making a deficit this year of $4,000,000, would be able to repay him if he assumed the first mortgage. I do not think my hon. friend need worry about that. Hypothetically, the Government would have to estimate whether the third and subsequent charges would justify it in paying a higher price I do not think it would, but if my hon. friend asks what the business position is I have no hesitation in telling him.

I understand that this
Grand Trunk Pacific Development Company is an entirely different concern from the Grand Trunk Pacific. It has separate assets and creditors and is a hotel system. tVhy this property should be taken over with the other is something I would like to know.
iSir THOMAS WHITE: The Grand Trunk Pacific Development Company is owned by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway company and therefore is one of the subsidiaries of the system. It owns hotels, steamships and other properties and real estate throughout the West. Any great railway system, as my hon. friend knows, embraces not only railway lines proper but subsidiaries.

Whaji provision will be
made with regard to the payment of creditors and other claims against this company? While by a stretch of imagination we can understand that a railway system may be taken over by Order in Council, I cannot possibly see why it is necessary by Order in Council under the War Measures Act to take over these hotels, seeing that is an entirely separate and distinct company from the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is run in connection with it and the stock is owned by the Grand Trunk Pacific. It. is part of the system. It was necessary to appoint a receiver not only for the railway company proper but also for the subsidiaries forming part of the system. My hon. friend asks what about the creditors? Well, he does not need advice from me as to the position of creditors. This system has been put into the hands of a receiver.

Why is this company referred to as the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System? I understand that term has never been used in connection with the

railway. There is "The Grand Trunk System" but not "The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System", which it seems to me is a misnomer.

We have heard so
much of late about the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System that I begin to fear they hardly convey an idea to our mind. I would suggest that our leader might propose to the leader of the Government that we adjourn.
I have no other questions to ask.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The "Grand
Trunk Railway System " is a term used to designate all that is embraced within the ownership of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company would own physical properties vested in it. It would own stock of express companies-although I do not think it does-telegraph companies, development companies, hotel companies, steamship companies, and the word " system " would properly apply to the company itself and all the subsidiaries.
Has the Grand Trunk Railway Company been completely relieved of the interest which it failed to pay and which was paid by way of grant from the Government, approved by Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The votes by Parliament during the past few years have been by way of loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific, secured by blanket mortgage in each case.

Does the Government not fear that its action will place it in a very awkward position before the courts in view of paragraph 6 of Chapter 24, 4 Edward VII, which reads:-
Notwithstanding anything in the said contract contained the Government shall not exercise any rights in respect of possession, foreclosure or sale, by reason of non-payment of interest by the company under the 31st, 32nd, or 33rd paragraphs of the said contract, or under all or any of them, unless .and until these shall be such default to the extent in the whole of a sum equal to five years of such interest, as the company is not relieved from payment of or permitted to defer or capitalize by the provisions of the said paragraphs.
According to this paragraph the Government appears to have no right to foreclose or to take possession of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway before five years of accrued interest is due. The Government by way of loan has surely, impliedly at least, authorized the company to defer its payments, to say the least, if, indeed, it has
not been entirely relieved. If that is so, it seems to me that the Government had no right to take over the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway or to force a foreclosure, and that in so doing it assumes all the liabilities of the Grand Trunk Pacific, or at least, is liable to the Grand Trunk Pacific for all damages which the company , may incur as a result of the forcible taking of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I dealt with this matter pretty fully this afternoon, and I hope that my hon. friend will not think me discourteous when I say that we have given the whole subject the most careful consideration and are satisfied that the appointment of the receiver has not exposed the Government to liabilities or in any way weakened our position.

I am anxious that we should get through with this Bill to-night, and it will perhaps be the only opportunity we shall have of saying a word to the Government before it enters upon the negotiations which are in contemplation. There appears to be an attempt on the part of iion. gentlemen on the other side of she House to create the impression that we have a special retainer from the Grand Trunk	and	from	the Grand Trunk
Pacific,	and that we are defending
their case. It is scarcely necessary to say that such is not the fact. We are here to represent the people of Canada, and are actuated by the desire to get out of this mix-up in the very best way we can. I would impress upon the Acting Prime Minister, if such negotiations are to be proceeded with, that as I understand the situation the Grand Trunk is in debt to this country to a very large amount in obligations that have already accrued due or will accrue due. We on this side of the House would impress upon the Government in the most urgent and solemn manner that all those obligations should be properly marshalled, and the position of the Grand Trunk as to its liabilities to the people of Canada ascertained in the most businesslike manner. If the road in question is taken over, and if any. money is bo be paid, our position is that that money shall be paid less the amount the Grand Trunk owes to this country. I "do not think that we can enter into sentiment in the matter at all, it will have to be a respectable business transaction. Whatever the shareholders of the company, or the company itself, are entitled to get from us, they should get-no more and no less. I trust the obligations in question will be fully considered in any negotiations

that may take place between the Government and the company.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

speechtext: Hon. N. W. ROWELL (President of the Privy Council) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 46 respecting the puichasing of departmental and other supplies and materials for His Majesty.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of the House will recall that by Order in Council of 8th May, 1915, a War Purchasing Commission was constituted, its duties being to supervise purchases for which payments were to be made out of the war appropriation. The commission carried on its duties from the date of its appointment, supervising all purchases made out of the war appropriation and dealing only with

those branches of the public service until the month of February, 1918, when on the recommendation of the Prime Minister the duties of the commission were enlarged so as to embrace the other branches of the public service. The Prime Minister, in his report recommending the enlargement of the duties of the commission, pointed out that, pending consideration of permanent provision for that purpose after fuller study of the problems involved, the commission would continue to perform these larger duties. With the coming of peace, as the commission was appointed under the provisions of the War Measures Act, its duties would automatically come to an end unless other provisions were made. The work of the commission has been so satisfactory that the Government believe that it should be continued, and the present Bill provides for the appointment of a Purchasing Commission for Canada which shall do the purchasing of all supplies required by all departments of the Government. That does not include the Government railways, which now form part of a larger system and are being operated under the Railway Board. This, in brief, is the object of the Bill.
