speakeroldname: Hon. N. W. ROWELL (President of the Privy Council):
speechtext:
moved the second reading of Bill No. 37, respecting. the Department of Health.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving the second reading of this important Bill, it is fitting that a statement should be made to the House indicating the reasons why the Government has felt it necessary in the public interest to bring down this Bill. The proposal embodied in the Bill is one of the most important features of the Government's policy during the period of reconstruction. I may say that the war has impressed upon all citizens more than ever before the value of human life. There has certainly never been such a prodigal expenditure of human life in any war in history. On the other hand, never has human life been so valuable and never has the physical fitness of the men in the respective armies played so important a part in determining the final issues of the struggle. This war made an unexpected drain upon the energy and resources of the

soldiers engaged in the conflict. During many periods of the war, the question was as to the ability of the men to stand the strain and not break down under it. The men who had the greatest physical strength, who were the most capable of bearing the burden of the struggle, were those who in the end rendered the greatest service.
Not only has the war emphasized the importance and value of human life, but the -losses of the waf have made a great drain upon the best life in this and every other nation engaged in the struggle.
I am sure we all realize, Mr. Speaker, that the men who went to the front were not the weaklings, the physically unfit, but the very best blood of the nation. The men who enlisted were of course the strongest and the most vigorous in the national life, and all the countries which were at war suffered most severely by reason of the number of their strong, vigorous, young men who laid down their lives in this struggle. Canada has lost approximately 60,000, the majority of these having fallen in battle or died of wounds, while a limited number died of disease. Canada is to-day the poorer to that extent. Not only has there been this drain upon our people, but a large number of the men who went overseas to fight for us have returned to Canada less physically fit; they have been maimed in the struggle and have suffered from disease, and to-day tens of thousands of them are less able to carry on their work and take their place in the life of the nation than they were before the war.
When one takes into account these war losses, one realizes rwhat has been the drain of the war on the life of a young nation like Canada. . We must also bear in mind the heavy financial burdens which this war has imposed upon Canada as upon every other nation engaged in the struggle, and that the only way we can carry these burdens is by developing our resources, by increasing ithe output of our forests, our farms and our factories. And as that development can only be obtained by increasing the productive power of the nation, we realize with additional force what a loss it is to Canada that these vigorous young men are no longer available to us. Just at the time when the burden upon us is the greatest and when we need the best blood of the nation to bear that burden, we are suffering from these war losses.
It has been the policy of Canada for many years, Mr. Speaker, to spend large sums of money to foster immigration in order to people our unoccupied lands and

to develop our natural resources; and yet while we have been spending these large sums of money for this purpose, we have not been nearly so active in spending even a-moderate amount of money to conserve the lives, the health and well-being of the people here at home. We have not paid nearly so much attention to caring for the young children bom in Canada who would make good 'Canadian citizens as we have in bringing in immigrants to settle here and become citizens.
At this time when we are 'suffering from the losses due to the war, and when the value of human life has become of greatest moment, it is fitting that the House and the country should turn attention to considering better measures for conserving the health of our people.
, Now, do the conditions existing in Canada justify action at this time? What are the facts as disclosed by the medical examinations under the Military Service Act? I regret, Mr. Speaker, that the figures are not available of the rejections on the ground of physical unfitness while the voluntary system was in force. Of course, a record was kept of the men accepted, but not a corresponding record of the men who were rejected. But I have the figures of those who were accepted and rejected during the period the Military Service Act was in operation, and I am sure that these figures will, surprise hon. members. Hon. gentlemen will recall the fact that the class called up for service under the Military Service Act were young married men and unmarried men from 20 to 34 years of age. Now 361,695 men were medically examined under the Military Service Act; of these 180,440 were accepted as physically fit; of the remainder 181,255 were found to be more ot less physically unfit. In other words, of the adult male population of Canada of military age more than one-half were found physically unfit for active service. Those are startling figures, and they disclose to us the room there. is for improvement in caring for the health and well-being of the people of this country. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that no citizen would have believed that of the young men of this country between those ages 50 per cent would not have passed the test for entrance into active military service. It shows that there are thousands of young men in Canada who are not up to the physical standard, and that the majority of them are not up to that standard from quite preventable causes.
Not only do the facts in connection with enlistment disclose those conditions, but similar conditions are disclosed, so far as
statistics are available, in connection with infant mortality in this country. I regret to say, Mr. Speaker, that at the present time we have no vital statistics covering the whole Dominion, and it is not possible therefore to make a comparison with any other country which has a good system of vital statistics; but it is possible to make comparisons, between different countries in which they have adopted improved methods of caring for their children and the countries in which those methods have not been adopted. It is possible to make a comparison between some of these countries where the Governments have given special attention to the question of public health, and particularly child welfare, with the cities and towns of Canada where such great care has not been exercised. Let me give you some most interesting figures relating to this matter. These figures have been furnished to me by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, and I give them as furnished. The country in which the Government has taken the most active interest in child welfare, and in which its measures have touched practically the whole people, is Neiw Zealand.	The figures for New
Zealand are for the year 1915, and I understand that they are the latest available, but that they are fairly representative of the situation there. The deaths of children under one year of age per 1,000 births in New Zealand are 50. How do other countries compare with New Zealand? Australia comes next with 68 deaths to 1,000 births; Sweden, 70 to 1,000; France 78 to 1,000; the Netherlands, 87 to 1,000; Switzerland, 91 to 1,000; Ireland,, 92 to 1,000; England and Wiales, 110 to 1,000; and then when you pass over to countries like Russia you get 248 deaths per 1,000 births, and Chili, which has the highest mortality, 286 deaths per 1,000 births.

Mb at are the years to
which these figures have reference?

New Zealand, 1915; Australia, 1915; England and Wales, 1915; France, 1912, Netherlands, 1915; Russia, 1909; Sweden, 1913; Switzerland, 1914; Chili, 1914. These are the latest figures that we have been able to get.

Are the figures not
affected by the war in any way?

I should think that they are not appreciably affected by the war. I mention them only as indicating the general standard or scale which I understand the general figures support.
116*3

I now come to the situation in Canada as indicated by the statistics so far as they are available. It should be borne in mind, of course, that there is always the possibility of a percentage of error because of the fact that in some countries the statistics are not as accurately kept as in others; and the same may be true of the provinces. The figures, as given in the official records of each province, are as follows:
The lowest on the list is Saskatchewan, 91-2 per thousand for the year 1916. The rest follow in this order:	Prince Edward
Island, 93.6, 1917; Ontario 107-2, 1916; British Columbia 107-3, 1916; Manitoba, 113-5, 1914; Nova Scotia, 120-9, 1916; Quebec 153-4, 1916.
But it is when you come to the cities of Canada that you find the more startling results. First let me give you the rates of infant mortality under one year of age in certain cities in the Old Country for the year 1916; London, 89 per thousand; Bristol, 95; Edinburgh, 100; Glasgow, 111; Manchester, 111; Nottingham, 116* Liverpool, 118; Leeds, 129. In England they believe that the rate of infant mortality is unnecessarily high. They believe that attention must be paid to the question of public health as relating not only to children, but to older people as well. So serious do they consider the conditions that one of the most important proposals of the present British Government is the creation of a department of health. Last month a Bill designed to accomplish this end received its second reading in the British House of Commons.
Compare the figures which I have just given with those for our own Canadian cities. I have the figures for six cities, two in Quebec, two in Ontario and two in Western Canada. The lowest percentage of infant mortality per thousand is found in Sherbrooke, Quebec, 101. Then comes Toronto, 109; Winnipeg, 126; Vancouver, 144; Quebec, 203; Montreal, 207; Ottawa, 224. Compare these figures of infant mortality in Canada with those of cities in Great Britain. We are willing to spend money to bring immigrants to Canada, yet there are dying in some of the great cities of our country, during the first year of their lives, twenty-five per cent of the babies born. I mention these facts to point out the urgent reasons why we in Canada should give serious consideration to this most important matter.

To what years are the figures for the Canadian cities applicable?
[Mr. Rowell. 1

Sherbrooke, 1917; Toronto, 1916; Winnipeg, 1917; Vancouver, 1916; Quebec, 1917; Montreal, 1917; Ottawa, 1916. In the light of these facts I am sure every one will realize that the question is one to which, the House and the country should devote their most serious thought.
May I inquire who compiled the figures which my hon. friend has just read?

up too much time, editorials from the leading journals of Canada very strongly supporting the proposal, in fact, demanding that the Government should establish a Department of Health. Now under the terms of its constitution the department will deal not only with matters relating to public health, but also with the social welfare of the people of Canada.
I presume that the minister has studied the constitutional aspect of the Bill and is satisfied that it does not invade the civil rights in the provinces.
Yes, that matter has been carefully considered. I do not think any question of civil rights arises under the terms of the Bill as drawn. As a matter of fact the public health-

Can the minister say
whether this question was brought up before the last Interprovincial Conference?
I do not remember, but I think it was not. However, there was this special conference called later, at which representatives of the province were present, when this proposal was made.
I asked the question I put to the minister because he stated that this is done at the request of the medical representatives of the different provinces.

They have requested it, but I do not mean to say that the Government is taking action because they did so.
I mentioned the fact only as indicating that they support the proposal and that it is their desire that this Bill should be passed. The British North America Act does not specifically deal with health, the only reference to health is the matter of quarantine which is expressly placed uiider federal authority. As a matter of fact, in the Act creating the Department of Agriculture passed in 1868 provision was made for public health and quarantine as being a matters over which the Parliament of Canada had jurisdiction. A number of sections of that Act dealt with public health and others with quarantine.
Which Act does the minister refer to?

The Act creating the Department of Agriculture passed in 1868. Ever since iConfederation the Federal Parliament has dealt with public health in various aspects under many Acts. I shall come to that in a moment. We have probably no fewer than fifteen Acts dealing with various phases of public health.
I observe in subsection B of section 4 a reference to the conservation of child life. I do not wish to anticipate the discussion, but is not that a matter which falls entirely within civil rights?

Every province is deeply and vitally concerned in that question, and it is its duty to do everything in its power to conserve child life. But I should think that it is equally important to the Dominion, which is spending thousands of dollars to bring immigrants here, to see that its native born do not unnecessarily die and the nation suffer.

I understand that, but I asked a direct question, and would like a direct answer. Has the minister studied the Bill sufficiently to be able to tell the House whether that section, for instance, does not fall within civil rights of the provinces?

I think the provinces clearly have jurisdiction, but the Federal Government also has jurisdiction. It seems to be a case of both having jurisdiction, but (so far as the Federal Government is concerned its action might very properly be limited to collecting information and furnishing it to all who may desire to take advantage of it, there is no question that there is a very important field of activity open in that respect. In the United States the isame situation exists as here. The States primarily deal with public health, and it was only in recent years that the Federal Government took up the question as a matter of self defence, originally in connection with quarantine and immigration, because people entering the country were bringing diseases and the Federal Government had to protect its citizens, lit gradually extended its work until it now includes many phases on which I shall give the House information shortly. Section 4 of the Bill provides limitations so that we are clearly not invading any provincial rights.
As regards the words " over which the Parliament of Canada has jurisdiction," it might be well to give a definition of the term "jurisdiction."
It covers all matters specifically enumerated in the Bill, and possibly a few others. I shall be glad to go into that in a few minutes when we come to discuss ithe general sections of the Bill.
Has a copy of the Bill been submitted to the provincial authorities?

No, I think not. I think no Government authority has asked for it. Several requests have come in for copies and they have been sent out but I do not recall that any have come from provincial governments. The Bill deals *with the question not only of public health but of social welfare and I am sure that the members of the House will agree that after all the most important thing is not to cure disease but to prevent it. The most important thing is to endeavour to create conditions favourable to good health rather than to treat disease after it has developed. In connection with the health of the people, no question is more important than good sanitary housing and the avoidance of slum conditions. I think it would be a natural development that the administration of the Federal Government's housing policy would be entrusted to a department like this. At present it is being administered by a committee of the Cabinet. 1 would expect that it would be entrusted to a department such as this because it is so intimately associated with the social welfare of our people.
Does the minister suggest that such a question as housing should come under federal jurisdiction?
I would suggest to my hon. friend that the policy which the Federal Government has adopted of assisting the provinces in housing would fall under federal jurisdiction.
The policy of increased subsidies.

A full discussion of that question can take place when the Estimates are submitted, but I think that what the Government has done is unquestionably within the jurisdiction of the Federal Rar-liament and it has been accepted in that spirit by every province, many of them having passed Acts in order to take advantage of the federal housing policy. There are many other matters that one might mention in the same light. I referred a moment ago to the United States situation being very similar to ours as far as the Federal jurisdiction is concerned. In the United States their Public Health Department which has grown from very small beginnings, has developed into a very strong and efficient department. They have now eight divisions as follows:
1. Division of scientific research.
That is clearly within the competency of the Federal Government there. It is as clearly within the competency of the Federal Government here and it may be one of the important features of the work of a department such as this. That, of course, would depend on whether an appropriation were proposed in order to carry it out.
2.	Foreign and insular quarantine and immigration.
3.	Domestic and inter-state quarantine.
4.	Sanitary reports and statistics.
5.	Division of marine hospitals and relief.
G. Division of personnel and accounts.
7.	Miscellaneous division, various activities in the matter of the publication of public health reports and bulletins.
8.	Division of venereal diseases (which was added last year).
They have developed a very strong department of health and they are now making large appropriations for it, many millions of dollars being appropriated in the United States for the promotion of public health.
Is it the in- . tention of the Government to proceed with the establishment of a department of scientific research?

That question has not been considered as yet. It is a question for future consideration, but I should think that one of the natural and inevitable developments of a Federal department of health would be that we should develop a bureau of scientific research in connection with it. I have been asked why that was not specifically mentioned in the Bill. The reason is that it is not necessary. Clause 4 gives power and it is a question of a vote to establish it. It comes up on the vote for an appropriation and so soon as the Government is prepared to recommend ito the House a vote for such a bureau that question would come up for consideration.

The minister has dwelt at considerable length during the course of his remarks with the infantile death rate. Could not that be very easily handled by making the Criminal Code a little more drastic in the passages that refer to murder?
My answer would be that I do not think the instances of infantile mortality in connection with what my hon. friend refers to would be any more numerous in Canada than in the other countries.

You would not like to answer that, perhaps. The second question is in connection with those unmentionable diseases; is it wortn this Government's

while to spend time legislating to cure those diseases, or would it not be better to clear those people out altogether?

The policy of the Bill is to prevent rather than cure.
Mr. BUTT'S:	You cannot prevent it by
Act of Parliament.

One can prevent the
spreading of many diseases. My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) asked in reference to the Federal Government's jurisdiction. I should like to draw his attention to certain Acts already passed by Parliament dealing with various health matters. In .the Department of Agriculture, we deal with the health of animals. We have undertaken in this House to care for the health of animals and to prevent the spread of contagious diseases. I should think that we had just as much right to preserve the lives of human beings as animals.

It would be a good
principle of law to say that if we had jurisdiction over agriculture it would follow, as incidental to that, that we should deal with the health of animals.

In connection with agriculture both the provinces and the Dominion have concurrent jurisdiction. They are legislating in connection with agriculture and' it is the same situation in connection with publi^ health.
Does the minister not think this is an unnecessary duplication?

No, I do not think so
at all. I think the figures I have given show the necessity of the action. Public opinion in the country demands action. The Government would be recreant to its duty, With its knowledge of these facts, and in view of the public demand, if it did not take action.
We maintain in the Department of Agriculture in connection with animal diseases a laboratory for investigation and the supply of sera, and we maintain inspectors to investigate outbreaks of disease. In the Department of Inland Revenue we exercise certain jurisdiction in the inspection of foods and beverages in regard to adulteration. That is one of the important matters that comes under the Federal Bureau of Health in the United States, but we have dealt with it here by the Department of Inland Revenue. The Department of the Interior deals with the medical and sanitary side of Indian Affairs. The Department of Immigration deals with the inspection of immi-[Mi*. Butts.]
grants' detention hospitals, investigation oi immigrants' subsequent condition as regards mental and physical health, quarantine arrangements at sea ports and on the frontier, leper lazarettos, administration of Public W'orks Health Act, inspection of vessels in ocean ports, and supervision of public health in the Yukon territory; the Department of Marine deals with marine hospitals and sick seamen; the Department of Trade and Commerce deals with vital statistics; the Department of Militia and Overseas Military forces deals with the army medical corps and army'military hospitals service, sanitation of camps, and food supplies for the army; the Department of Public Works deals with sanitary inspections of public buildings; the Department of Finance deals with infectious diseases transmitted through handling of money; the Department of Justice deals with the sanitation of prisons and the disease of criminals; the Department of the Naval Service deals with the sanitation of ships and food supplies for the naval service, and also with the diseases of fish and health in fish hatcheries; the Department of Customs investigates the quality of dutiable foods and drinks in relation to public health; the Post Office Department deals with infectious disease as transmitted through mails, and the sanitation of post offices. The Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Estatolishment deals with the physical and mental restoration of invalided soldiers; and the Commission of Conservation investigates into general, questions of public health. There is also the subject of patent medicines, which is under the Department of Inland Revenue, too, I think. Not only have we dealt with the question of health, but we have voted hundreds of thousands to.f dollars a year 'to various branches of the Government dealing with different aspects of the health problem.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I will deal briefly with the scope of the Act. It will be noticed that section 4 defines the duties and powers of the minister administering the Department of Health, and covers all matters relating to the promotion or preservation of the health and social welfare of the people of Canada over which Parliament has jurisdiction, and particularly the following matters and subjects. The first is:
(a) Co-operation with the provincial, territorial, and other health authorities with a view to the co-ordination of the efforts proposed or made for preserving and improving- the public health ;
At the present time there is no co-ordination; each province takes its own course, as

it does in any other matter. A Federal Department might be a clearing house in which information of 'the results of work in one province would be gathered up and made available to every other province, and the largest measure of co-operation worked out. It has been done in other branches of the Government in connection with other phases of work carried on by the provinces and the Dominion.

What does the hon. minister mean by "co-operation" and "co-ordination "? Does he mean that all literature to be distributed will be sent to the provincial boards of health to be distributed by them, or will it be distributed independently of the provincial boards?

I can give my hon. friend illustrations covering many matters, but I will take only one, the case of contagious disease. It is a matter of the greatest importance to the welfare of the whole nation that there should be to some extent at least corresponding provisions in all the provinces for the protection of public health against contagious diseases. If a contagious disease breaks out in any one province it is a menace to all the provinces, for we know how rapidly it spreads. In such a case co-operation should secure the enactment of legislation in the different provinces for the suppression of such a disease. I am quite lure that it would be feasible, and that the health authorities in the different provinces would be very glad to co-operate in order to secure such a result.
You will see that provision is made in section 6 for a Dominion Council of Health consisting of the Deputy Minister of Health, who shall be chairman, the chief executive officer of the provincial Department or Board of Health of each province, and such other persons, not to exceed three in number, as may be appointed by the Governor in Council, who shall hold office for three years. That would be the medium for cooperation and co-ordination, for you would have the health representatives of all the provincial Governments on that Council conferring together and working out plans to secure the best results for the whole Dominion.

Would their advice be
accepted by the Minister of Public Health?

The Minister of Public
Health must of course be responsible to this House as a member of the Government. He would not be bound to accept their advice; it would be in his discretion to accept or reject it.

Then what is the use of
having both?

I should say there would be great advantage in having both. I should think it would be a good thing for the minister to be in constant touch with the provincial health authorities, and also for the public health service in the different provinces, and I am quite sure that they could render very excellent and helpful advice to the minister. He, of course, must take upon himself the responsibility of finally acting on it or not. Referring again to section 4, we have the conservation of child life and child welfare, on which I have already spoken.
The next subject dealt with is the inspection and medical care of immigrants and seamen, and the administration of marine hospitals;-

That is within federal
jurisdiction undoubtedly.
Yes; and it is a matter of very great importance. The next subject is the supervision, as regards the public health, of railways, boats, ships and all methods of transportation;-
That is within federal jurisdiction.

Unquestionably, and
again a matter of great importance, having regard to the facility with which a contagious disease may be communicated in transportation.
Would the hon. minister apply that to provincial lines as well?
That is a matter I have not considered.
That is very important.
Of course, if it had to be worked out in a way that would keep well within federal jurisdiction.

Reverting to clause (c) the inspection and medical care of immigrants and seamen, and the administration of marine hospitals, would the Act give power to have your inspection made at the ports of embarkation of immigrants from other countries, so that prevention might be undertaken at the right place?

The inspection would be under the Department of Health, but whether here or over there or at both places would be a question to be settled by the Immigration Department.
Then clause (e), the supervision of federal public buildings and offices with re-



gard to the health of the civil servants and other Government employees therein. Obviously there is no question that that is properly within the jurisdiction of the Dominion.
Clause (f) reads:
(g) The administration of the statutes mentions made by the International Joint Commie-sdon, promulgated pursuant to the treaty between the United States of America and His Majesty relating to boundary waters and questions arising between the United States of America and Canada, so far as the same relate to public health;
Clearly that is also a matter of federal jurisdiction. I shall not go into it at the present time, but probably during the discussion my hon. friend the member for Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer) who has given special study to it, will have something to say upon it.
Then clause (g) reads:
(g)	The administration of the statutes mentioned in the (Schedule to this Act, and of Acts amending the same, and also of all orders and regulations passed or maxle under any of the said Acts; and all the duties and powers of any minister of the Crown under either of the said Acts or any of the said orders or regulations, are hereby transferred to and conferred upon the Minister of Health;
-and clause (h) :
(h)	The collection, publication and distribution of information to promote good health, and Improved sanitation;
Assuredly those are matters of federal jurisdiction.
The establishment of a Department of Scientific Research, it seems to me, is more important than any one single-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have to
remind hon. members-and I do not refer specially to the hon. member who is just now' speaking-that the House is not in committee. The hon. President of the Privy Council has been very courteous in allowing and answering questions of all kinds, but hon. members cannot interrupt the hon. minister for the purpose of expressing their respective opinions without violating the rules of the House. I would remind hon. members that all of these questions may be properly asked when the Bill is considered in committee.

Before passing from the subject of the distribution of literature, I may add that the following rather interesting circular letter came to my attention recently. It was addressed by a Medical

Health Officer in Saskatchewan, in view of the influenza epidemic, to the principal of a school:
You will find enclosed copies of literature on influenza sent out for free distribution by the United States Public Health Service. Not only should the information contained in these leaflets help to suppress influenza, but other infectious diseases as well.
Kindly have the teachers carefully explain this literature to each class.
Until such time as Canada has a Dominion Health Department municipalities must continue to beg and use American health literature.
Perhaps he is not correct in ins statement; at any rate that circular was issued. I have a sample of the literature that was sent out to the schools of that particular western city. First, there is a bulletin of the United States Public Health Service for circulation among all families, on Spanish influenza and how to treat it. Then, diagrams and charts were issued by the United States Department of Health on the subject of influenza and were widely distributed. The United States Department of Health carries on a very active propaganda in the interest of public health, spreading the information all over the country.
The Bill does not contemplate adding another minister to the Cabinet; it provides that the Department of Health shall be presided over by such minister as the Governor in Council may determine. While I have no authority to say so, I should think, now that the war is over, that the tendency would be to decrease rather than increase the number of Cabinet Ministers. A Bill was passed last session which permits of the transfer of one branch of the service from one department to another, and I have no doubt that such a rearrangement of the public service can be worked out as will make it possible for a member of the Government to give the necessary time to the work of this important department. I think it deserves the best thought and attention of a member of the Government in order that the public interests may be promoted, as I believe they will be promoted by this Bill.
As I view the matter, and as the Government views it, the Bill is of very great importance. It is not a new departure in the sense of the Federal Parliament legislating on public health; ever since Confederation we have legislated on various aspects of the question. But it is a new departure in the emphasis which it places upon the conservation of the health of the people and upon their social welfare. It

means that in the new day in which we are now living, when the welfare of the masses of the people must become more and more the concern of the whole people, the Government of the country must devote its best thought and attention to the questions which I have suggested, so that here in Canada, with all our natural advantages, with our great opportunities of developing a truly great nation, we shall have a strong, vigorous and healthy people of whom Canada may be proud and who will retain for Canada the magnificent place which her soldiers won for her in the field. I move the second reading of the Bill.

Bowing to your ruling,
Mr. Speaker, may I put a question to the minister? The minister has had in his hands a great deal of literature which was distributed in the United States. Of course he has read these things; I have not had opportunity to read them. Do they recommend, as a good many doctors in Canada recommend, whisky and quinine for the treatment of influenza?
The 'CHAIRMAN:	Order. The question
of a specific remedy or treatment is certainly not one which can be discussed when we are considering the principle of the creation of a Department of Public Health, and I rule the question out of order.
Even with the minister's permission?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Even with the minister's permission.
Mr. 'CHARLES S'HEARD (Toronto South): Mr. Speaker, II have given some little attention to this Bill and some study to the preliminary conditions which led up to its introduction into this House. While I am free to admit that a Federal Public Health Department would afford great opportunities for good in Canada and that' there are great avenues of work through which it can exercise those opportunities for good and attain a great many objects, I am far from being satisfied with the Bill as it has been brought down by the President of the Privy Council (Hon. N. W. Rowell).
If a Federal Department of Public Health is to be of real value to Canada, it must be ancillary to the Provincial Health Departments now operating in the Dominion. It must assist, and not conflict with, the operation of municipal and provincial health boards; and we must be absolutely sure that its jurisdiction is constitutional and well-defined.
We need not go very far to prove what are and what will become the limitations
75}
of a Federal Health Department; we in ay simply refer to the British North America Act. True, the British North America Act makes but a slight reference to health matr ters per se, but it does make very specific reference to the machinery by which health matters are administered. If we are going into child welfare, if we are going into work to administer the machinery connected with hospitals and dispensaries, we are certainly trading upon the rights of the provinces and the municipalities. Section 92 of the British North America Act defines the exclusive powers of the Provincial Legislatures and subsections 6, 7 and 8 clearly state that the establishment, maintenance and management of public reformatories, prisons in and for the province, and the establishment, maintenance and management of hospitals, asylums, charities and eleemosynary institutions are within provincial jurisdiction. Therefore, outside of hospitals maintained as marine hospitals and quarantine hospital stations at the ports of entry, all the hospital machinery of the country is reserved for adminstration under provincial law.
I shall probably have a number of amendments to move to this 'Bill when it gets into committee, so that I shall not do more now than utter a word of warning. In my judgment the Bill has been framed not altogether with the idea, I fear, of co-operating with the provincial and municipal health departments, but rather with the idea of establishing a Federal department which may exercise such authority as will be gubernatorial so far as the administration of health matters in Canada are concerned.
But, Sir, I am going to support the Bill, -although not in its present shape,-because I believe it affords an opportunity to legislate at the present time on a matter which concerns the best interests of our country.
My first suggestion is one which has already been referred to in the question put by the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon), who asked if a bureau of scientific research was to be established for the administration and co-ordination of this work. I understood the President of the Council to say that it all depended upon the amount of money which this Parliament placed at the disposal of the department. I hope the bureau will be supplied with a substantial sum for this purpose, because every department of public health in a country which has in any way created it as a national feature, has pivoted around its laboratory work. Nay,

more, I will say that laboratory work is the very foundation of health considera-' tions, and you can no more move in a health organization without laboratory equipment, without research work, without devotion to laboratory effort, than you can move a train without its motive power. All I have to do is to refer to the great start made in health work in 1872 by the studies of one of the most illustrious of all distinguished scientific Frenchmen, who in his discussions and researches and experiments in reference to fermentation, electrified the scientific world, and to-day we have amongst the saints of sanitation, that patron saint in medical discovery, the revered and illustrious Pasteur. What had Pasteur been doing? He had been combatting in his laboratory, quietly and alone, the theory of Liebig. Liebig advanced the theory that the processes of fermentation were essentially dependent upon temperature, and that you could have no fermentative processes apart from regulation of temperature and cell development. But Pasteur took a distinct line to analyse that theory, and he showed that there were other organisms which when introduced into the animal kingdom combatted the organisms which produced disease, arid he astonished in particular the British Isles by taking a hundred sheep and inoculating them with a specially prepared serum, which prevented the virulent form of anthrax which was ravaging the sheep flocks in the form of foot-and-mouth disease in the Southern counties of England. That single experiment of Pasteur, the result of his laboratory work, practically abolished the foot-and-mouth disease in Europe and, to a large extent, in this country. That was immediately prior to 1872, and from that date bacteriology and its allied sciences took a new development based upon laboratory work exclusively. Sanitation became a science and had infused into it a new life, vigour and application, through scientific laboratory research work by specialists.
The United States has made considerable advancement as regards sanitary matters. It has it Bureau of Animal Industries, and its Bureau of Scientific Research. It has not only its statistical department, but its advanced experimental stations, and we find, when we investigate the administration of these matters at Washington, that they have a Federal Health Department which is almost wholly and entirely scientific and laboratorial in its efforts. There are four great departments of active workers in sanitary science-there are the great depart-

merit of bacteriology, the great department of pathology, the great department of chemistry, with separate laboratory equipment and departments for each, and the separate department of pharmacology. That is how the Washington Federal Health Department is arranged at the present time. That, however, may be so much Greek to those who do not know the technique and the bearings of those various departments of a Federal Health Department. Take, for instance, the great study of pollution of water supplies. In this Bill there is a special proviso, and a very proper one, which this Government must take cognizance of to regulate the international waterways :-
(b) The enforcement of any rules or regulations made by the International Joint Commission, promulgated pursuant to the treaty between the United States of America and Plis Majesty relating to boundary waters and questions arising between the United States of America and Canada, so far as the same relate to public health.
In other words, that refers to the degree of sewage contamination which may be produced, for instance, at Buffalo in Lake Erie, and the Niagara river, and which may contaminate Lake Ontario and thus breed typhoid and other water-borne diseases along the shores of Lake Ontario. That bacteriological department is one which to a very large extent will be occupied in determining the degree of water contamination. It will also study the actual diseases, the causes of communicable diseases, and what serums can he developed in order to counteract them. And this information can be spread broadcast throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion with great benefit, not only to the local and provincial health departments of the country, but to the agriculturists, yes, and to the manufacturers everywhere. And it can do the same as was done in the United States when they made their great investigations into and studies of hookworm and Pelagra, and practically removed that scourge from the transmontane states of California and Oregon. They discovered not only the cause of the disease-and it was one which affected cattle and men-but the remedy by which it could be cured. May I mention that, as an illustration of how a department of bacteriology could be operated as a federal health department, which would in no respect conflict with either the spirit or the application of provincial laws and provincial rights as they relate to health matters, but which would he enormously beneficial in yielding results which would

save the lives of men and the herds and stocks of the agricultural community?
Let me take the next department, the department of pathology. Hon. members may say: What in the world is pathology? Pathology, technically speaking, is a discourse on disease, but it has also to do with the careful investigations oi the diseases of man and animals, diseases which are communicable from animals to man.
For instance, such diseases as hog cholera and hog measles originate in animals, and when the liesh of one of these diseased animals is eaten by man, the disease may be communicated. In that way the disease is spread, and sometimes causes death. It is the business of the Pathological Department to examine in a pathological way these diseased tissues. You could not find a better example of the work that department is doing than at the laboratory of the stock yards in eastern Buffalo. This laboratory is maintained by the Department of Federal Health at Washington, and it is the duty of a body of trained examiners to examine microscopically samples of every slaughtered animal. If a sample is affected with trichinosis, tuberculosis or anthrax the disease will be detected at once. The examiners have no interest in the stockyards or in the property of the animals, but they have every interest in seeing that the meat is wholesome and entirely fit to eat.
Next we come to the great department of chemistry, which is operated under the Federal Health Department at Washington. This is a department we should certainly have in this country. It attends to all forms of adulteration of food, the glazing of tea, and a hundred other things in respect of which it is necessary to see there is no adulteration or that the proper percentage of nutritive value is contained. This provides an excellent check on fraud and deficiency in the trade and commerce of the country.
As to the Department of Pharmacology, which is a separate department in Washington. It is a department which we should have here, but no mention is made of it in the Bill, unless in the schedule, where it would come, I suppose-, in connection with the Proprietary and Patent Medicines' Act. The Pharmaceutical Department at Washington requires, first of all, to know the contents ,of every patent medicine. Patent medicines are being sold in this country which are supposed to cure every variety and form of ill. They may be frauds; you cannot tell what they contain; there is no department of the Government, so far as I am aware, that is responsible for
stating that they have any efficacy at all. Any one can make up a little colored water, put it in a bottle, advertise it well as a cure for delirium tremens or something else, and make millions on an article that may be nothing but a hollow fraud. We have no one in Canada to investigate and report that these patent medicines are what they profess to be, and whether they have any virtue at all.
Then we come to the proprietary medicines. The difference between a proprietary and a patent medicine is that the formula of a proprietary medicine is published, while the formula of a patent medicine is supposed to be a secret, and as no reputable physician has any secrets, he does not care to endorse the so-called patent medicines. He does, however, use proprietary medicines to show his breadth of mind, and for the good they will do his patients,, perhaps. It is the business of the Pharmaceutical Department to see that the proprietary medicines are made up precisely as represented in the formula.
These are simply suggestions as to what, in my judgment, a Federal Health Department should primarily aim at. The suggestion made by the hon. member for Mus-koka (Mr. McGibbon) was a splendid one, and I should like to see it embodied in the Bill, and made effective. .That is the first suggestion I have to offer. My hon. friend says it is not necessary to embody it in the Bill; that all we have to do is to bring down the necessary estimate. If the deputy minister thinks it is all right-and I can clearly see that the Minister of the Department of Health will have no knowledge of the matter at all-if the deputy minister has ambition enough to initiate a new development along these lines, and thinks it feasible and not too much work, he may agree to it, but there is no statutory obligation on him to do this particular kind of work. I should like to see a clause inserted-and I shall move, accordingly, when the Bill is in committee-that will set forth the metes and bounds of this new department.
We come next to the conservation of child life and the matter of child welfare. I would strongly urge upon the House to strike that out, as there is no possibility of doing any work along that line without encroaching upon the authority and rights and operations of the provincial health departments, except it be in the matter of preparing statistics and giving information of the work that is being done in other countries. In my judgment, the federal work

along this line should be confined purely to statistics, and I have reason for saying so. Wherever the benefits of child welfare work have been observed, the benefits have always been achieved through hospital effort. I should like to quote some statistics from a report of the medical officer of the Local Government Board of England, for the year 1917-18. A speeial chapter of that report deals with child welfare. The death rate of infants is dwelt upon, and it is pointed out that one-third of all the deaths in infancy occur in the first month, and one-fifth in the first week after birth. The decreasing death rate after that period'shows how much saving in life is possible. A table is given which shows that in a thousand births, 20.2 deaths occur among the children of medical practitioners, while 47.1 occur in the families and houses of general labourers. In a women's hospital in New York where there were 8,318 infants born, .15 died on the first day, .10 within the next six days, and .6 in the second week. Amongst the causes of death in children, the English statistics show that 6 per cent were due to acute infectious diseases, 3 per cent to tuberculosis, 18 per cent to diarrhoeal affections, and 7 per cent to pneumonia and lung affections. Genital disabilities carry off a certain percentage. I quote these figures to show that in cases where the women are housed in hospitals and the children have the benefit of hospital care for the first two or three weeks of their lives, infantile mortality is materially reduced. This would seem to indicate that the greatest field for beneficial work in this particular respect is in the maternity and similar hospitals in the country, which institutions are, under the British North America Act, entirely within the jurisdiction of the provinces.
This Bill has been urged chiefly by reason of the achievements of Dr. Anderson in England. But conditions here are entirely different than were those under which he worked. We can have no opportunity of doing what he did, because we are altogether differently constituted. Dr. Anderson's work embraced the incorporation of all the local government boards operative in England. These local government boards were practically separate boards of research. They were not endowed by the country, but were largely connected with the scientific institutions which officially did work for them. The Public Health Bill in England abolished all these and placed them under a central board of administration, a bureau of scientific research, such as that for which I am arguing to-day as a necessity in Canada.

But they also embraced the administration of the Poor Law system, a system inaugurated since the days of Elizabeth. The Poor Law administration, the administration of old age pensions, and charities, were all included under the Health Act; and there were many other features which had to be remodeled,-features that do not exist in this country. The provincial boards of health have done the greatest amount of work, and in health matters we are to-day far in advance of the British Isles, notwithstanding the statistics that have been submitted concerning child welfare. Ontario, I think, is abreast, and probably ahead, of any other place in the world in matters of health,-certainly better off than any state in the Union. Some of the Western Provinces have an equally good record, and in view of the splendid way in which the provinces have administered public health in the past we should be very careful not to encroach in the slightest degree upon their particular work. However, I can perceive much good in the Public Health Department if it will provide a certain amount of money to take care of patients that are transferred from one province to another. Take a case of contagious disease that passes a port of entry unobserved, and goes, say, from Montreal to Toronto, where it is discovered. Who is to take care of that case, and who pays the bill? Clearly it does not come under the responsibility of the province of Ontario, and the Federal Health Department should make some financial arrangement for the maintenance, care, and treatment in the public interests of all migratory cases that occur. In the case of venereal disease, I think a thorough and rigid inspection at the port of entry should be made. There are many cases of syphilitic infection which ordinary medical men can detect without a very careful scrutiny. These cases have in the past been frequently admitted without restraint and have gone on for a year or two, communicating that condition to others besides a long progeny of mentally defective, and, in some cases, epileptic persons, with the necessary entailment of cost. In my opinion, therefore, the greatest work in connection with the Public Health Department is a rigid system of quarantine and inspection in connection with the Immigration Department, 200 per cent better than it has been in the past, to preclude the possibility of these cases escaping detection. A certain number of infectious diseases may be brought to this country by returning troops. The care of them is clearly not the legacy of any particular province, and the Federal

Department ol Health should make arrangements to look after them. If there is space to accommodate them in marine hospitals, well and good; if not, there should be an arrangement by which the provinces might take care of them and isolate them as long as necessary, and be paid through the order of the Federal Department of Health. Over and above all that, there should be provision for the careful study of epidemics as they appear in various foreign countries. We know how this country has suffered in the past from imported epidemics, very little attention having been given them, even by scientific men, until they begian to develop in this country, when they were studied more closely because they then came under the immediate notice of the proper authorities.
If we had a paid department maintained by the Federal Government for the specific purpose of studying these epidemics, distributing literature, studying modes of infection, getting into touch with those who had charge of cases before they landed on our shores, a very considerable benefit would accrue and the work would prove profitable.
As I shall probably have a good deal to say by way of amendment when the Bill comes into committee, 1 shall now conclude; but before taking my seat I would say that if the energies of the Bill are properly and well directed, if the influences behind it are those of pure scientific minds emulating the highest ideals which have distinguished and characterized the medical profession throughout the whole civilized wrorld, then I can see no greater force developed in this great Canada of ours for the betterment of humanity and for the relief of the sufferings to which Canadians may be exposed, and I can see no better investment than a well equipped, well endowed well supported Federal Health Department.

speakeroldname: Mr. ROBERT JAMES MAXIOX (Fort William and Rainy River):
speechtext:
I shall not take up very much time in speaking on this question. First, I should like to congratulate the President of the Privy Council (Hon. N. W. Rowell) on the honour which he has had of introducing this Bill, and also on the exceedingly able manner in which he has put forward the reasons for it. His explanation of the causes that led to the introduction of the Bill was so exhaustive as to leave little for the ordinary medical man to say on the matter.
In dealing with a question like this we should bear in mind that health is the greatest and most vital national problem with which any country has to deal. Some
Bills affect only some of the people, but this affects all the people for in it is vitally bound up the welfare of every citizen. Before I, discuss briefly the objects of the Bill and give my opinion of those objects,
I desire to refer to the criticism that has been levelled at medical men in some portions of the press of this country in connection with this Bill. The medical men have been described in some of the newspapers as political doctors who are looking for a portfolio or something to that effect.
I do not believe that criticism is fair because if you look over the history of the medical profession, if you look over the history of health matters throughout the world, you will find that there has been no advance in sanitation or public health that medical men were not foremost in helping forward. One point in this connection that is worth making is that the effect of this very Bill will be to take away a part of the occupation of the medical men themselves. It would be to the interest of the medical men to oppose the bringing in of a Bill such as this. I consider that the medical men are taking the same high minded stand on this matter that they usually take on public questions. If you will look over the history of the different branches of medicine you will find that practically all the great advances we have had in scientific medicine have been made by medical men. You will remember that it was the German, Koch, who discovered the tubercle bacillus which was one of the greatest discoveries in medical science. You will also remember that it was the great French scientist, Pasteur, who discovered the methods for preventing hydrophobia. That discovery has been dealt with much more oratorically and fluently than I could possibly deal with it by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Sheard). I have the happy recollection, one day a number of years ago now, and some time before the outbreak of war, of standing in the Pasteur Institute in Paris and seeing a mother and father come hurrying into the institute with a little child which had been bitten by a mad dog in order to take advantage of the blessing that Pasteur had given to the world. His discovery was another of the great advances in medical science for which we are indebted to a medical man. Then, we have the discovery of chloroform and ether. Ether was discovered, if I remember correctly, some time in 1846 by Dr. Morton of Boston and chloroform was discovered by Sir James Simpson of that fine old Scotch University of Edinburgh in 1847.
Perhaps Borneo.

Perhaps so. When I got inside I found to my horror a woman with a head about as large as my fist, a woman who was just an ordinary congenital idiot-idiocy is congenital-and she was being exhibited there for ten or fifteen cents. I consider that that was a disgraceful condition of affairs. That woman was no more to blame for having been born with such a small head than you or I, Mr. Speaker, are to be credited for inheriting heads of nearly normal size. In any properly civilized country such an exhibition would not be tolerated; the poor woman would have been put in a proper institution and carefully looked after. Those are some of the subjects which came to my mind while I was considering this Bill, and the Bill itself has suggested to me the following further points:
First: This Bill will bring about united co-operation , and we all know what united co-operation did for us in the war that has just closed. Second: It will bring about a general supervision of the health of our people. The purpose of the Department of Health will be to gather statistics and information of all kinds. The insurance companies of this country are loaded up with the very finest statistics bearing on the public health, but they have no central information bureau such as would be established under this Bill. Third: I think generally it. will educate the country. Fourth: It will also take cognizance of the immigration policy of the country, covering such subjects as mental defectives, trachoma,- which is a very easily contracted disease and very difficult of eradication,-and other diseases. Fifth: International waters-the hon. minister dealt with that, and I need not enlarge on it. Sixth: It should do a great deal preparing young women for

motherhood. I do not think this Bill should interfere in our private life, but I do not believe it will. Its purpose is to educate. Education is a thing you can take or leave, but you cannot take it unless it is offered to you, and this organization should go a long way towards educating young women at a time when they require that education. Seventh: Also it can take up the question of mothers' pensions, which I believe is a very live question and one very worthy of consideration. I should like to emphasize what the hon. members from Muskoka and Toronto mentioned in regard to establishing a research branch. I sincerely hope that a research branch will be instituted in this Department of Public Health. The questions of better housing conditions and child welfare, and better labouring conditions for the workers of this country, also should be considered.
I should like to make a couple of suggestions. In the first place, it should be the object of this department to get the very best man as the deputy minister. I do not think politics should have any interfering power whatever in this matter. There are a number of very able men in Canada to-day who have made a special study of public health, for this is a special department of knowledge and one with which	the ordinary	medical	practitionerhas not full acquaintance, his purpose being to cure, while the purpose of public	health is	to prevent sickness.There	are several	eminent	specialists,among	them Dr.	Starkey	of McGill
University, Dr. Amyot of Toronto, and Dr. Hill, who is now, I believe, in the state oi Minnesota, but who is a Canadian by birth -formerly medical officer of health of London-and stands among the highest of medical health specialists on the North American continent. I do not know any of these men personally; I have no interest in them, but I think we should endeavour to secure the services of a man of their high standing in the science of public health. In the second place, if this department is ultimately given to a minister to handle alone -which the hon. minister (Mr. Rowell) states is not going to be done-I do not think that minister need be a medical man. I believe in the old saying, that a little knowledge is a dangerous thing, and the ordinary medical man has limited knowledge of public health matters. Of course, that remark does not apply to the member for Toronto (Dr. ISheard), because he has made it a specialty for years. But the ordinary medical man has little knowledge of this branch of preventive medicine.

For these various reasons, Mr. Speaker, I shall very strongly support this Bill.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read a second time.

On section 2-Department:

Is it necessary to have another
minister?

So far as I am aware,
no. Under existing legislation the work of departments may be re-arranged; a minister may be head of more than one department.

What minister of the
Crown will be in charge of this department?

I am not able to give
any information as to that. I assume that will have to await the return of the Prime Minister.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-deputy minister, etc.

How will the Civil Service Act affect scientific men, bachelors of science, say, of the university of Toronto, or graduates in medicine, some of whom, I assume will be engaged in this department? Will it be necessary for the Civil Service Commission to re-examine gentlemen who have attained scholastic distinction and who hold degrees from recognized universities?

There is a special provision in the Act for appointing men possessing special professional or technical qualifications without requiring the ordinary Civil Service examination.
Mr. iSHEARD: Will the deputy minister make those appointments?

I assume that they would follow their usual procedure in cases where persons having special qualifications are required for a particular position; they would ascertain the best man qualified for the office.
How would they do that?

I have never discussed
the matter with them; therefore I am not

in a position to tell my hon. friend just how they go about it.

That is the point where
the Civil Service Commission is carried beyond all reason. I cannot conceive of any health department doing any work that is worth while unless in the hub and centre of the organization are a number of trained, expert, and eminent scientific men.
I agree.

To ask 'them to go before a Civil Service Commission is a very questionable proceeding to my mind, but to expect that commission, who do not know the character, the standing or the qualifications necessary, to make a recommendation of fitness for a particular scientific position where the work must be of the highest order-well, I cannot think that that is reasonable or practicable.

The point my hon. friend raises refers more particularly to the Civil Service Act than to this Bill. The Bill refers to the Civil Service Commission only in so far as regards the transfer of men from some existing departments the work of which is taken over by this Department of Health. The general Civil Service Act applies to all new appointments; the reference here is to transfers.
Will all new appointments be made by the Civil Service Commission?
All new appointments are made at present by the Civil Service Commission.

The point of the member for Toronto South (Mr. Sheard) is well taken. It is absolutely impossible for three Civil Service commissioners to select a scientific man for a position of such responsibility as this. If it is left to them, the chances are that in nine cases out of ten they will not get the best man, because they have no way of judging. It is a very questionable proceeding to ask trained scientific men to accept an appointment by examination from three Civil Service commissioners.

Section 21 of the Civil Service Act, which provides for just such cases as this, has often been discussed in this House, but for a different reason: it was too much used by the present Government for questionable purposes. The section provides that when a scientific man is required for the Civil Service he_
shall not be subjected to a special examination, but shall be taken on his merits and on his record; the Governor in Council may override the Civil Service Act and make the appointment direct. The present Government, however, utilized that provision for the purpose of getting their friends appointed who should not be appointed at all. For instance, when a man who was over age wanted to get into the service, the game was to call him some kind of an expert. In that way he was put into the position under section 21. A couple of years ago, I took occasion to look into this matter, and in answer to a question that I asked in the House it was discovered that no less than seventy-five experts had been appointed by the present Government, although not half a dozen real experts had been appointed during that period.

If my hon. friend will
look at the Act passed at the last session of Parliament, he will find that section 21 is repealed and that the principle of section 21 is no longer to be found in the Act.

Then
every appointment has to be made after examination by the Civil Service Commission?

Absolutely.
Mr. (SINCLAIR (Guysborough): Then I think the point is very well taken that the Act ought to be amended, because if that be the case, it will be impossible to get an eminent man to submit himself to examination by the commission.

I think the section to
which my hon. friend referred is not in the Civil Service Act in the form he mentions, but my recollection is that the present Act provides for the appointment of experts, highly qualified professional men, by the Civil Service Commission, without the necessity of the regular examination which the ordinary civil servant must take, and they would ascertain the qualifications of a highly qualified technical expert the same as, under the old system, any minister of the Crown would ascertain them and select from the sources which would be available, the best man who could be secured for a position requiring such high qualifications.

I just want to enter my protest against this method of procedure, because in my opinion it wall fail. I do not think three Civil Service commissioners are qualified to pass judgment on men of that class, and it should be left to the administrative head of that
i

department to choose his own assistants. If that privilege is not given to him the whole thing will be a failure.
Mr. PROU'LX: The practice of the Civil Service Commission has been to appoint committees to look into the qualifications of experts. In this case the commission could appoint a committee of medical men to choose the officers.

The question that has just been raised is a very important one. I at first thought that possibly there was no necessity for creating a health department of the Government to deal with this matter, but I have realized, after hearing the arguments that have been advanced, that I may have been mistaken in my views. Section 2 of the Act provides that the department shall be presided over by a minister of the Crown. The President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) says that it may be necessary to appoint the most eminent men that can be found in order to make a success of the work, and that the Civil Service Commission will ascertain the qualifications of these men as would any minister of the Crown under the old system. The minister who will preside over this department will be responsible for its success or failure, and I would not like to see it possible for him to escape from some of the responsibility for the administration of that department by unloading that responsibility upon the Civil Service Commission. I do not believe that to be in keeping with responsible government. The minister, the head of the department, must be held responsible, and should be free to exercise his judgment in making selections of officers to administer the work.
Section 3 agreed to.
On section 4-duties and powers of minister :
I have several amendments to move to this section as it contains the crux of the whole situation, and I hope the committee will be able to take it up clause by clause.

On section 2-interpretation:
Perhaps the leader of the Government will tell us something about this Bill.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
So far as the Government is concerned, there is no objection to this Bill. It provides for the creation and issue of perpetual consolidated debenture stock. While negotiations are proceeding with the company, as I intimated yesterday, there does not appear to be any good reason why the company should not be permitted to issue debenture stock for its purposes. If the company should be taken over later by the Dominion Government, the power would remain in the company and might be exercised for the benefit of the system, just as the power to issue securities by the Canadian Northern Railway Company is exercised to-day. In other words, a corporation taken over by the Dominion Government, either through the acquisition of its stock or by rental of its system, is still a corporation, and it is desirable that it should have the proper powers to enable it to issue securities from time to time, if thought desirable by its pror netcis. In connection with the financing of the Canadian Northern Railway Company today, all the stock of which is owned by the Dominion Government, instead of the Dominion Government making direct loans to the company, the company is encouraged to issue its own securities in London and New York, and thus finance itself. In

other words, it is still a corporation, although the sole shareholder is the Government of Canada.

There is this difference, however, that if this stock should he sold it will become an obligation or liability, so to speak, of the company. The stock is not likely to sell now for the price it would bring if the railway was really owned by the Government. For instance, if the company sells this stock it might have to sell it below par, whereas if the credit of Canada was behind it, it would be a very much better security and would sell at a higher price. If negotiations are under way with the company, and there is strong probability of the road becoming the property of the Canadian people, some provision should be made so that this stock will not sell at a price that would not be so much to the advantage of the Canadian people as if sold after the transfer of the road had taken place.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think there is some merit in what my hon. friend has put forward. On the other hand, I think, it would be unwise for the Dominion Government to refuse the power to issue securities which may enable the company to carry on pending negotiations. These securities might be temporarily borrowed against, instead of being sold in the market. I think we can control the situation in the Dominion interest, but. I do not like to take the position that, pending negotiations with a company like the Grand Trunk, we should refuse them the power to issue securities which are required at the present time to enable them to borrow money to meet certain pressing obligations.
I have no objection to the legislation, so long as the Prime Minister appreciates my point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I fully appreciate my, hon. friend's point.

This
section provides that the stock shall rank equally with the consolidated - debenture stock. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not understand that the debenture stock of the Grand Trunk is secured upon its assets.
