House again in Committee on Bill No. 27, respecting the Department of Health. Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 4-duties and powers of minister:
I would move that section 4 be taken up clause by clause, as this is a very important part of the measure.
What is meant by " social welfare "?

The first part of this section seems to me to be somewhat ambiguous and might permit of more or less conflict in these departments of public health. I therefore beg to move, in order to make it absolutely clear, that all the. words after

the word " jurisdiction " be struck out, and the following substituted therefor:
Provided that nothing- in this Act shall authorize any officer or authority created by or appointed under the authority of this Act or under any regulation made hereunder to exercise any jurisdiction or control over any provincial Health Officer or any Provincial or Municipal Board of Health or other authority operating under the laws of any province.

My hon. friend from
South Toronto (Mr. Sheard) altogether misapprehends the object of the Bill if he thinks there is any intention of exercising jurisdiction or authority over provincial or municipal health officers. That is not part of the plan or policy of the Bill, and to insert such a provision as he proposes would imply that it was. The majority of the subjects enumerated in the portion of the section which the hon. gentleman's amendment would strike out are matters of great importance which are now covered: by some other statute, and the object of this section is to consolidate them under this one department. It would be not only unnecessary but undesirable to insert such a provision as is proposed.

I might ask the minister what is meant by inserting in this clause the following words: " and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, particularly the following matters and subjects." These are the words I intended my amendment to- affect, not the subsection that follows, il seek to make it absolutely clear that what the new department is to do in these matters shall be ancillary to the work of the provincial and municipal health authorities. Would the minister explain what is meant by these words: " and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, particularly the following matters and subjects."

While the general clause is larger and embraces more than these particular matters specified below, these particular matters specified belpw are to be taken charge of by this department. It particularly emphasizes them, so to speak. The Bill would be sufficient, so far as the enumeration of powers is concerned, if we stopped at the word " jurisdiction." Everything that is enumerated could be done under the broad, general paragraph quoted. It is in order that attention may be focussed on these particular matters which are of importance, and some of which are under other departments, that they are enumerated as being subjects which should come under this department. Clause 4 is 
broad enough to cover the establishment of a research laboratory if the Government is in a position to make an appropriation for it and decides that it would be in the public interest to establish it. It is desirable, if the department is to have the largest scope within federal jurisdiction to conserve public health and social welfare, that we should not cut its powers down unnecessarily.

The fact of the President of the Privy Council stating what his intention is will not be a sufficient guarantee as to the construction to be put upon the Act. I have no doubt the President of the Council understands it in the way he has stated, but he will not be an exhibit of this Bill when it comes into operation. The question is one of the construction that the ordinary legal, or judicial, mind would put upon it. There can be no very great objection to the amendment of the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Sheard), but I would suggest to him that he is not putting his amendment in the best place. In my judgment section 4 is pretty good, and inserting his amendment where he suggests would rather disarrange it. The purpose would be better served by getting his amendment in at the end of section 5, where it says:-
The Governor in Council shall have power to make such regulations as may be necessary to give effect to and carry out the objects of this Act, and to impose penalties for any violation of such regulations.
I would be perfectly willing to accept that suggestion.
This would be the natural place for it.

Let it stand until we
come to section 5 and I will consider it.
Mr. TRAHAiN: I see by the fourth line of section 4 that the department will have to deal with questions relating not only to health but also to social welfare. I would like to know what subjects will come under this general term " social welfare."

il suppose that " social
welfare " means just what the name suggests-the welfare of society as contrasted with the individual, the welfare of the mass of the people. Health is at the foundation of social welfare but " social welfare " has perhaps a little broader meaning than simply the word " health." The labour organizations were very strongly in favour of having a little broader term than the one "health" used. We felt that "social welfare " would have a broader signification. They suggested that instead of calling it a

Health Department it should be called the Department of Public Welfare. Their view was that housing, in so far as it was a matter of federal jurisdiction, would be a proper matter to come under this department as as it was very intimately connected with the social welfare of the people. I think that when this department is created it will very properly call for the administration of the housing plans of the Government which are now being carried out by a committee of the Cabinet and which should he transferred to this department for administration. Matters of that class relating to the welfare of the community and which the department might take up in the public interest would be covered by such a clause as this.
Mr. TRAHAiN: The illustration given by the minister suggests that perhaps the Government might encroach upon civil rights and provincial autonomy. The housing problem is a very large and interesting one. It relates to social welfare in general, but the proposition made by the Government has only reference to granting subsidies to provincial governments or municipalities to help housing in the various provinces and municipalities. The term " social welfare " is very general, and this measure might lead to abuses if that term is not well defined. Generally in connection with legislation, when general terms are used, there is a definition to limit the interpretation to be given to the Act, but here we have a general term which may be applied to many large questions and it is not limited at all. Believing as I do that these words should be struck out of the Bill, I propose to amend this paragraph by moving that the words " social welfare " in the fourth line of the section 4 be struck out.

I cannot accept the
amendment proposed by the hon. member for Nicolet (Mr. Trahan), because I think it would strike out of the Bill a very important feature, which the working men of this country arc deeply interested in. Let me take the illustration that I gave to the House. My hon. friend said that all the Government did was to loan money to the provinces in order that the provinces might loan it to the municipalities. But the Government is doing more than that, it is laying down certain conditions which control the expenditure of that money in order to accomplish the object it had in view. That object was to improve the housing conditions throughout Canada, to insure that the working men should be able to get houses at a moderate price, at cost,
and it was particularly to assist workingmen who had been at the front; and it is important that those houses should be constructed upon the most improved sanitary principles in order to promote the health and welfare of their occupants. It was further desired that such houses should be constructed in localities and under conditions where, if a new area was being opened up, it could be laid out on the most improved Town-planning lines, so that you would set a standard for workingmen's houses which would be a stimulus to the erection of a similar class of houses in all the important centres of Canada. Let me point out the conditions upon which the loan has been proposed and upon which the provinces are accepting it:
Each province shall prepare and submit to the ' Federal Government for approval, a general housing scheme; setting out the standards and conditions to he complied with in connection with local housing schemes. The general scheme of each province shall include a schedule of minimum standards in regard to grouping of houses, provision of open spaces, sizes and heights of houses, sizes and heights of rooms: provision of light and ventilation, heating, lighting, character of materials, etc., which it is proposed should he enforced os the minimum requirements for health, comfort and convenience.
Then it provides for the maximum cost of dwellings:
The object of the Federal Government being to facilitate the erection of dwellings at a moderate cost suitable for working men, particularly returned' soldiers, it is necessary to place a maximum on tne amount which may he loaned per dwelling, and1 the following maximum-

What is my
honourable friend reading from now ?

The regulations governing the Government's housing policy, approved by Order in Council and published.
-the following maximum has been fixed having regard to the conditions existing in the different provinces:-
Then it sets out what is the maximum which may be loaned on any house having regard to its size and character. The next clause deals with the ownership of the land:
Public money may be advanced for building houses on sites owned by:-
(a) The Provincial Government or Municipality.
(lb) Housing societies or companies comprising grouips of citizens associated to promote good housing, supplied with proper improvements; such societies or companies to have not more than a statutory liimitation of dividends payable on stock of 6 per cent.
(c) Owners of lots for the purpose of erecting houses for their own occupancy.

I have merely read those provisions, Mr. Chairman, to show that the Federal Government has a definite object in view in its housing programme. These regulations have been submitted to all the provinces, and Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia have already passed the necessary legislation, and I think New Brunswick has it under consideration. Those are the matters which would come within the heading "Social welfare," and the administration of that policy might properly be entrusted to a. Department such as this. That is what is meant by "social welfare."

The phrase "social welfare" is very general. It may mean the moral as well as the physical welfare of the people. It may mean the shaping of a moral standard for the people in all kinds of subjects-for instance, prohibition. If my hon. friend does not care to amend the section, why not define the phrase social welfare" so there will be no misconception about it, I think that would meet the idea of my hon. friend (Mr. Trahan).

As the hon. Minister has announced the policy of the Government and the interpretation it puts upon the term "social welfare", with all due respect I submit that it proposes to occupy ground absolutely covered by municipal and provincial rights. If the Federal Government intends to exercise supervision and direction over the construction of dwelling houses, it must necessarily conform to the by-laws operative in the municipalities in which those houses and buildings are being constructed. I cannot conceive of any process of carrying out the law as suggested . by the hon. minister, unless some degree of supervision is going to be exercised in connection with the powers authorized by this Act, and if a Federal officer, for instance, is to come to the city of Toronto to supervise, or to direct, or to make suggestions regarding the construction of such houses, under the terms of the interpretation of social welfare as given in this Act, as far as I understand the hon. minister's explanation, I really think that there is at the start a considerable danger of conflicting authority between him and the municipal and even the provincial officers.

Mr. Chairman, I evidently have not made myself quite clear to my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Sheard). What I pointed out was that these clauses require provincial Governments to submit a general housing scheme to be 
approved by the Federal Government. It does not follow that the Federal Government is going to send in a man to supervise the housing policy of any province. For example, the Government of the province of Ontario have already submitted their housing scheme to the Federal Government under the provisions of that clause, and that housing scheme has been approved. In that housing scheme the provincial Government specify the standard and type of house they propose to build; that is perfectly satisfactory to the Federal Government; we approve it, and that ends it. Then the provincial Government enact their own laws in accordance with the scheme which has already been approved by us.

How is the Federal Government to know that the plans submitted have been adhered to and the buildings constructed in accordance with them unless they exercise their right of inspection and supervision?

We assume, Mr. Chairman, good faith on the part of the provinces, and if they submit a scheme to us which they say they are going to follow out, I think we have the right to assume that they will, spend the federal money in pursuance of the provisions of that scheme. That is the line upon which we are proceeding, and I think it is a safe one. All we wish is to secure improved housing conditions, and so far no province has offered any objection to the regulations.

I do not understand what the hon. minister is doing. Does he wish to convey to the committee that the local government of some province has already submitted a housing scheme to the Federal Government?
It has.
Under what Act of the Federal Government?
Under the Order in Council which set aside the $25,000,000. That money was set aside on condition that the provincial governments should submit a housing scheme before they were granted a loan.
But is the advancing of that money not contingent upon legislation which this House still has to consider?

The spending of the money is contingent upon the legislation.

The vote is in the estimates and the House will have to pass it before the money is expended.
Will not the Housing Bill also have to pass the House first?

So far as the advancing of the money is concerned the matter is in the hands of the Minister of Finance, but my impression is that it does not require any legislative Act. The item in the estimates sets apart the sum of $25,000,000 to be expended pursuant to the provisions of a certain Order in Council which defines the general policy.
Will the money be distributed among the provinces?

Yes, it goes to the
provinces. I introduced the subject of housing only to illustrate what might be included in social welfare.
The Government is simply becoming a badly managed loan society.

I fear that we are departing from the discussion of the Bill relating to the Department of Health and entering upon a discussion of the housing scheme. If we get back to the amendment to strike out the words "social welfare", perhaps we shall make greater progress. I am sure that the Department of Health will not exercise any jurisdiction in the matter of the housing scheme unless Dominion legislation gives them authority to do so.
'Social welfare is, in most parts of the country, a well understood term in these days and is becoming more popular and of much greater interest to the people generally. Probably Lloyd George gave to social welfare the important place it occupies today. He brought social questions to the front; he emphasized to the people of the world the fact that social questions and the social welfare of the people of every land must receive more attention than they have received in the past. I do not suppose that the elimination or the inclusion of the term "social welfare" would modify the operation of the Department of Health. But its inclusion in the Bill does give to proposed legislation a wider significance and, I understand, meets the views of the labour element. No section.of Canada to-day is more interested in social questions than the labourpeople. When we consider that sickness is probably the greatest cause of poverty, particularly in the ranks of the labouring people, we see very clearly how closely allied health and
social welfare are. Mr. Stapleford, General Secretary of the Neighbourhood Workers' Association in Toronto, made the statement recently that the most important cause of poverty in Toronto, as in other cities, is-undoubtedly sickness. It is therefore very necessary that we should give attention to social welfare work as well as health work, in order that what this department will accomplish will at least relieve our labouring classes from the greatest cause of poverty, sickness.
I gave some statistics on a previous occasion in this House, which I should like to repeat to-night, to show what an immense loss comes to the labouring people through sickness. We have in Canada a million and a quarter labouring men. It is estimated by the United States authorities- and perhaps the same will apply in Canada -that every working man loses an average of nine days every year on account of sickness. In Canada that would mean a loss of 11,250,000 days to the working people, which, at a very moderate wage, would come to at least $35,000,000 a year. Any Federal department which directs its efforts towards relieving our working classes of that tremendous burden is doing something which, I am sure, will have the hearty support and co-operation of the labouring people, as of others.
It should be the object of this department to establish what, after all, is the best democracy we can have-that is, a democracy that gives all men an equal opportunity. A child that is born in a tubercular condition, or of syphilitic parents, or in unsanitary surroundings, in a home full of filth, has not the same opportunity in the world as a child born in sanitary surroundings of healthy parents. If, therefore, you want to establish a true democracy in this country, give every child a chance to be born of healthy parents and amid healthful surroundings. It will be toe aim of this department, I know, to produce these surroundings and to put our people in such a condition that they will be healthy parents.
With these healthful conditions established-which they can be, not in one year, but through time-we shall bring about in Canada an industrial efficiency such as we have never known. Some years ago industrial efficiency was supposed to depend on the individual corporation and every effort was made to organize corporations in such a way as to produce efficiency Then it was found that even improved methods of organization



were not producing the desired ofBciency, and the era of amalgamation of corporations arrived. We saw some years ago a great epidemic, so to speak, of corporation amalgamations. Many thought that these amalgamations had an improper purpose in view. Perhaps some of them had, but they brought about greater efficiency in industrial life. Now that era is passing and an ora of the conservation of the health and strength of employees has arrived. It is known to-day that efficiency in the truest sense must begin with the conservation of the health and strength of the individual. We are placing a higher estimate on the individual working man and on the value of the human machine, realizing that a man is greater than a mill and the producer more important than the product, and that that which reduces the value of the man lessens also the value of the machinery. Anything, therefore, that this department can do to improve the conditions of the labouring man may properly be considered as participation in social welfare work._

I must say
that the member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) has cut a tolerable swath, considering that he rose to charge some of us with getting away from the subject under discussion. Mr. Lloyd George's social reforms are well known to those who have carefully followed politics in the Old Country, but I do not think Mr. Lloyd George legislated under the phrase "social welfare." When he brought in an insurance scheme, he brought in an insurance scheme. His object was social welfare but his scheme was embodied in a concrete manner in an Act of Parliament.
Mr. Lloyd George did not have to contend with the difficulties we have of a dual legislative authority. There is in Great Britain only the one authority.
My hon. friend has plenty of time to speak when he wants to make his jokes. I am well aware of my limitations, but I should like to make my own speeches, lame though they may be.
I was trying to help my hon. friend.

Mr. Lloyd George introduced old age pensions for the purpose of doing something for social welfare, but he embodied the scheme in an Act of Parliament. We are dealing with a concrete matter, namely, to establish a department of health, that is, a department
[Mr. Steele. 1
which, in all countries in which they have such a thing, has certain well defined limitations which are proper to an Act of Parliament. The phrase " social welfare " has no such limitations. We have had a splendid illustration of that in the speech of the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele). It was a beautiful speech, full of splendid sentiments, and everybody in the committee agreed with him, but it cannot be put into an Act of Parliament just as it was spoken, and I accept my hon. friend's rebuke in wanting to draw the committee's attention to the fact that we are engaged in considering a Bill for the establishment of a health department. I do not think the minister has been successful in meeting the objection hinted at by the hon. member for GuySborough (Mr. Sinclair) and put into shape by an amendment of the hon. member for Nicolet (Mr. Trahan). If that amendment is pushed to a division, I shall vote for it, unless further explanations of the minister are more successful in clarifying my understanding of the matter than his previous ones have been. Either the minister is very much mixed, or I am, and if it be true that he is very much mixed, I may be as mixed before he is finished with me.
I do not see that what he said about housing establishes a need-for these words in the Public Health Bill. What he said about housing was a very great surprise to me. I understood that the policy of the Government in regard to housing was still to be discussed in the shape of a Bill which was mentioned in the Speech from the Throne, but it appears that the policy has been not only settled but put into operation by an Order in Council. I have been pretty patient with Orders in Council,-my hon. friends opposite perhaps think too much so,

but this is a method of procedure which, if I understand it correctly, I should advise the minister to look into very carefully. I am amazed,-I am the subject of consternation,-if I have correctly learned that the Government, by an Order in Council, is actually consulting about a policy which is yet to be debated and decided upon in this House. I leave that matter at that point for the moment, but I cannot see what purpose the words "social welfare" have in this Bill. We are all in favour of social welfare, and every Act of Parliament is meant to promote social welfare. Social welfare is the welfare of society; society includes all the
9 p.m. people in the country, and, of course, however little Parliament

may have succeeded, Parliament is always trying to move, even though stumbling, in the direction of doing something for social welfare. So these words might be put into any Act that is brought before the House. But I think, to say the least, they will be out of place in every Act on a different subject that comes before the House; and unless some specific meaning is given to them I do not see what they are doing in this Bill.
With regard to housing. If I understood the minister's explanations correctly, he wanted us to understand that the Public Health Department will consult with the local governments upon the question of housing and social welfare as it is advanced by this scheme of housing.

The Government has already consulted with the local governments in reference to housing and certain regulations have been agreed upon, and what I suggested was that this department would be an appropriate one to administer them. Perhaps I might answer what my hon. friend said, if he wishes me to, with reference to the Orders in Council to which he refers. The situation is this. Under the Order in Council passed on 3rd December, 19X8, following the Inter-Provincial Conference held here, the Government set aside $25,000,000 for housing purposes. That Order in Council provides that advances be made as soon as a general scheme of housing shall have been agreed upon, between the Government of Canada and the Government of the province applying for the loan. That Order in Council was passed pursuant to the provisions of the War Measures Act, and there was power to make the proposed advance to each province so soon as a housing scheme was agreed upon. Following that Order in Council there was a consultation with the provinces by means of communications sent to each one of them outlining what the Government thought should be contained in any housing scheme of the provinces. Suggestions were asked, and some of the provinces made suggestions, ail of which we considered and then finally certain lines of policy were adopted, the ones I have already read to the House. Pursuant to that policy, the province of Ontario submitted its housing scheme which was approved by an Order in Council passed subsequent to that date, and I think two or three of the provinces have passed legislation dealing with the matter.

I should just like to say in reply that what the minister says astonishes me very much, and as one member of the House, I am bound to add an opinion for what it is worth that it would have been very much better for the Government if they had called Parliament together in December, 1918, and submitted housing legislation to this House before they took a course which practically amounted to legislating as a Government by Order in Council for the Dominion of Canada upon a purely domestic affair in consultation with the provincial Governments. That is practically what, we are told by a minister, was done last December. And then a housing scheme is brought down to this House in the month of February and the House of Commons is expected to sanction it and to set up a Health Department in so far as it relates to this scheme, or to carry out legislation practically settled by previous consultation between the Federal Government and the local governments. That is a most extraordinary method of conducting the federal business of this country, and where we shall land, if there is more of that sort oi thing, I do not think one can really imagine. [DOT] I can scarcely believe my own ears as thdse statements are made to this committee. I do not want to say more on that subject at the present time, but if the Government have made a mistake-and I am sure they have in setting about their housing scheme in that way-then it would be a bad thing for us to follow up that mistake by even appearing to sanction it by letting this phrase "social welfare" remain in the Bill. I, for one, if the amendment is pressed, shall vote for it.

My objection to the expression is that it is altogether too general. It may mean anything. We have undertaken to regulate so many things of late in the life of the people that there is a certain uneasiness throughout the country over these encroachments. I am in favour of a Department of Health. I am also in favour of housing accommodation being provided. Although, if the minister will allow me to say so I do not think that the Government's- housing' scheme amounts to very much. It is simply a scheme of lending money to the provincial governments at five per cent interest. Now the provincial governments can borrow money pretty nearly as favourably as the Dominion Government, and personally, if I Werje lending my money, I -would just as soon lend it on the bonds of the province

of Nova Scotia as on the bonds of the Federal Government, because I think the security just as good, and the interest is five .per cent. The provincial governments would have to pay that rate if they went into the open market to borrow money. The scheme therefore, is of very little advantage to the provincial governments, and it should not be made an excuse for encroaching upon their rights. We all admit that housing is a matter altogether within the juridiction of the provincial governments, and I think it would be far better to leave the provincial governments alone and let them work out their own housing schemes, borrowing money in the open market, rather than tie them up to the Government housing scheme, and then [DOT]follow that up by encroaching on their rights. This legislation is a further encroachment on provincial rights. Why should the Federal Government undertake to control the houses after they are built?
We do not do that.

I do not yet understand what the minister seeks to attain by this Bill. The word "health" covers all the things the minister should want, to deal with in connection with these Ijouses, even if this Government does lend the money to build them. Surely he does not want to look after the plumbing of the houses or supervise in detail the matters which the municipalities look after. What then does he want? If he is concerned only about housing, why not substitute the word "housing" for "social welfare"? The working man has been mentioned. I do not think the working man waijts too much of these regulations. He wants personal freedom. But by this legislation, if the Department of Public Health undertook so to construe the Act. he would not be allowed to smoke a pipe or have a tea party,-for is not that "social"? He would not be allowed to have even a bean supper,-is not that "social"? When you say you are going to deal with the "social welfare" of the people of Canada, the expression is so broad that it would give the min. ister power to control the people in all kinds of ways. I object very strongly to the expression and I shall vote for the amendment, unless the minister suggests a better expression.

I do not think we have yet had from the Government an explanation of exactly what was intended tq be included in the phrase "social welfare." The hon. member for South Perth (Mr. TMr. J. H. Sinclair.]
Steele) suggests that it means matters pertaining to the health of the working man. Now, the preceding words of the section give the Government that power. It might also be inferred from what my hon. friend said that "social welfare" related to the conditions under which the working men of Canada carry on their work; for instance, the sanitary conditions of a building in which workmen are employed, the hours of labour, the age at which minors can begin to work, the minimum wage, etc. All these are matters which deal directly with the social welfare of the workmen of the Dominion of Canada at the present time. There are other factors which might be included. For instance, we have social welfare leagues throughout the Dominion, and they are carrying on a campaign now against cigarette smoking and the use of tobacco of all kinds. Then there are prohibition leagues. It has been decided that this Government has jurisdiction over the question of prohibition. If the phrase "social welfare" is allowed to stand, it will enlarge the power of this Government in a manner which has been severely criticised during the last two or three years. It will enable them to legislate for the country at large by means ol order-in-council embodying the regulations enacted under this section. I further Submit that if the Government are going to deal with questions of labour under this legislation, they may come into conflict with the various statutes which have been passed in at least one province of the Dominion. In the province of' Alberta we have what is known as the Factory Act, which deals directly with questions ot social welfare, in the strictest sense of the word, and more particularly with the social welfare of the workers. It empowers the Government to regulate the hours ot employment, the age at which minors may begin work, the minimum wage, and the sanitary condition of the buildings :ti which workmen are employed. I think that the less we interfere or appear to interfere with the jurisdiction of the provinces the less trouble Ave shall have in the operation of the Act.
Then again, in regard to matters of health, I think that the constitution itself is not very clear on the question of jurisdiction, and when this legislation passes, great care should be exercised by the minister or the officers who will be responsible for the administration of the Act. The province of Alberta, under the jflon. A. G. Mackay, who is at present Minister of Municipalities,

is inaugurating what I believe to be the most progressive health legislation which exists in any province of the Dominion.
Except Saskatchewan.

I will not even except Saskatchewan. We should be careful not to arrogate to ourselves here any authority which will in any way hinder the provinces from carrying out the legislation which they have placed on the statute books this year or in preceding years. It may be said that some of the provinces are backward in their health legislation. If that is so, it is the duty of the people who reside in those provinces to furnish themselves through their own legislatures with up-to-date health legislation. I think the application of this Act should be confined as closely as possible to those matters over which the Dominion Government has exclusive jurisdiction. The Government might, for instance, supplement the work of the provinces by establishing laboratories. If any conflict arose between Dominion and provincial jurisdiction, I do not think the Dominion Government should for one minute undertake to interfere with the legislation enacted by the provinces.

When I was speaking on the Address some weeks ago and referring to this legislation which was forecast, I anticipated then the very difficulties which the minister finds himself compelled to deal with to-night. Many of the members treated my observations rather lightly at that time and evidently thought that there was not much in them, but it is some satisfaction to me to see that they now find that there was some good reason for what I said on that occasion, that it was difficult and dangerous to encroach upon the jurisdiction of the provinces. To-night, when the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) was speaking he made allusion to legislation introduced in the English Parliament, or to something that Mr. Lloyd George may have said about legislation, and I observed that Mr. Lloyd George is never confronted with the difficulty that we have to contend with. In the Parliament of Great Britain they have one sweeping jurisdiction, and have not to exercise any care to see that one piece of legislation does not encroach upon another. The hon. member for Red Deer thought I was joking; I was doing nothing of the kind; on the contrary, I was talking very seriously on a constitutional question that we have to deal with nearly every day, but which they are never called upon to consider in the Mother Parliament. I think one of two things should happen in relation
to this Bill. The words at the end of the main part of section 4 should come out, or " social welfare " should be deleted. If the operations of section 4 are confined exclusively to the matters enumerated I have no particular quarrel with the words " social welfare," but if the following words are retained, " and, without restricting the generality pf the foregoing, particularly the following matters and subjects," then I think " social welfare " should be struck out. If the minister adopts my suggestion the section will read:-
The duties and powers of the minister administering the Department of Health shall extend to and include all matters and questions relating to the promotion or preservation of the health and social welfare of the people of Canada over which the Parliament of Canada has jurisdiction; that is, (a) co-operation with the provincial, territorial and other health authoritiesand so on. If that would be satisfactory to the committee I think it would confine the scope of this enactment entirely to the matters enumerated.

I am very glad to have the suggestions which have been made. Needless to say, the words " social welfare " do not contemplate any interference with the social life of the people, and, as I think I intimated before, they were inserted merely in deference to representations made in the interests of labour, that there might perhaps he a broader meaning to the word "health" that some people were disposed'to put upon it, although I agree with my friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) that the word is broad enough to cover what is in view in the particular use of "sooial welfare" in this section. I would make a suggestion, which has been made to me and which possibly may be preferable to the one made by the leader of the Opposition, that we insert the words in the preamble. We might strike out the words "social welfare" used in Clause 4 and insert a preamble in this form:
Whereas, it is advisable for the promotion of the social welfare of the people of Canada that a Department of Public Health he established in the Dominion

Before the next clause is taken up 1 would move an amendment. It seems to me that the very heart and life of this Bill has been left out. I do not know of a department of public health in the world that has not a bureau of scientific research and I cannot see what permanent results will ensue fot the benefit of the people without such an institution. I would therefore move, that

section 4 be amended by inserting before subsection (a) the following words:
The establishment of a bureau of scientific research with hygienic laboratories including special departments of bacteriology, ipathology, chemistry and pharmacology which shall investigate matters relating to public health.
If we incorporate such a provision in the Bill we shall have a source of great good to this country. I should regret to see a Bill of this kind go through the Parliament of Canada without such a clause, for in the eyes of every scientific man it would appear ridiculous.

The subject matter of
establishing a laboratory for scientific research, as mentioned this afternoon, is a matter which I am satisfied is already fully covered by section 4. In fact, it was eon-sidered, but the parliamentary counsel advised that it was unnecessary to put in any further provision as clause 4 already fully covered it and the only thing that would be necessary would be that the Government should bring down an appropriation to provide for the building of such a laboratory. I have no objection to the insertion of suitable words that would indicate that this department is the department to have charge of such a matter although I think it is already covered. I am not sure that the way the matter is suggested here is the best way to put it. but I shall be glad to take the matter into consideration. If we can go on and dispose of the other clauses ithe Bill need not go out of committee and we can consider what is the best form in which to put this. I suggest that the amendment stand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Amendment stands.
On paragraph (a) of section 4-co-operation with the provincial, territorial and other health authorities with a view to the c -ordination of the efforts proposed or made for preserving and improving the public health:
Mr. WcKENZIE:	Perhaps it would be
difficult for the minister to give some general idea of what is meant by co-operation with the provincial authorities. What would that include?
Mr. It 0W ELL: As I mentioned this afternoon, my hon. friend will see under section 6 we provide for
a Dominion Council of Health consisting of the Deputy Minister of Health, who shall he chairman, the chief executive officer of the provincial department or hoard of health of each province, and such other persons-
The idea is that the health authorities of all the provinces shall be
,
brought together periodically, with the chief officers of the department at Ottawa, in order that they may confer together over matters of common interest, such matters as were mentioned this afternoon. Take the question of the war against tuberculosis and venereal diseases. In all these contagious and very virulent forms of disease, it is exceedingly desirable that there should be as much co-operation as possible between the different provinces in order that the good that is done in one province should not be lost by failure of action in another. It is in order to secure general eo-operation throughout the whole country that this provision is made. This meets the suggestion which the hon. gentleman has made with regard to a divided jurisdiction. It is to get the whole country moving together in combating these forms of disease and in promoting the public health.
Supposing an epidemic of smallpox broke out in Toronto to-day, that would be entirely a matter for the provincial authorities to deal with?
Quite so.
Supposing the same thing happened after this Act went into operation, would the conditions be changed in any way or would the authorities under this Act interfere with that condition?
I should say not; it would make no difference.

I think this clause is one of the best in the whole Bill and I strongly support it because it embodies the idea of co-operation. If the Federal Health Department is going to be of any service at all it can only be of service to the Dominion generally by co-operating with the local authorities. I do not think that we can too strongly emphasize and urge that such methods be adopted. Certain provincial and municipal officers would be brought together by the provincial health authorities for the purpose of consultation and discussion of various methods operative in the various provinces so that there might be concerted action throughout the Dominion, and so that they might discuss advanced methods which have been found to be successful in various provinces. The unanimity of operation and progress necessary to make this Health Act effective could be secured. I would strongly support the clause and I think no objection should be offered to it.

Mr. Chairman, I am very much impressed with the clause in

reference to the co-operation of the Federal, provincial and municipal departments. I know that in the past there has been no attention paid to the water supply of the different cities and towns of the Dominion. Some may say this is entirely a matter for the local board of health. But we know that during past years there have been *epidemics of typhoid in the city of Ottawa and in different cities throughout the Dominion. The local boards of health have not been impressed with the necessity of looking after the watersheds in connection with the water supply of towns and cities.
I would like to ask the minister if it is the intention of the health board to take a general oversight of the water supplies of the different cities. My suggestion would be that when these laboratories have been *established in the city of Ottawa under the jurisdiction of this board, the different cities and towns throughout the Dominion be compelled at certain times in the year, monthly or quarterly as the case may be, to submit samples of the water they are using to this board for analysis and Teport, in order that precautions may be taken to see that the water is pure and proper for human use. The epidemics which have swept over certain parts of Canada have certainly taught us a lesson. In the city of Ottawa, instead of using the water that comes from the lakes or rivers, or wherever it comes from, we are supplied with water from different springs around the city. If proper precautions were taken by the Federal Health department, or by this bbard, that would not happen because the water would be treated in a proper way and we would be absolutely sure of the water we were using. In addition to this, the sewage system of the different cities and towns should be inspected and proper precautions taken with respect to them.
I realise that this would put a very large amount of work upon the department, but there is no reason under the sun why, with the co-operation of the provincial governments and municipal authorities, we should not reduce the death rate in the Dominion to a very large extent. In the different cities over which these epidemics have swept a great many deaths have been caused entirely by the laxness of the several health departments both municipal and provincial.
In the province of New Brunswick we have organized a Health Department with a very efficient man in charge and I think with the co-operation of the Federal department there will he a great improvement
throughout the province. Is it the intention of the Government to take up the matter of water supply and sewage pollution with the different provincial and municipal authorities?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Wigmore) has brought up a subject that has been under consideration by the Governments of this country and the United States. In 1912 an inquiry was started in Washington in regard to the pollution of the Great Lakes, the sources of the water supply of a large number of our cities and towns. That inquiry took in the river St. Clair, lake St. Clair, the lower end of lake Erie, the river Detroit, the Niagara river, a portion of lake Ontario, and the St. Lawrence river, and it developed that those waters had been polluted by the cities and towns bordering thereon. As a result of that inquiry the Governments of Canada and the United States made an appropriation of $50,000 to investigate the whole matter scientifically, and the International Joint Commission has been conducting that investigation for a couple of years. What I am saying now is probably a little out of order, but it is relevant to an explanation of the clause in question. By paragraph 4 of the treaty between Great Britain and the United States, it will be observed that:
It is further agTeed that the waters herein defined as boundary waters and water flowing across the boundary shall not be polluted on either side to the injury of health or property on the other.
Therefore we have pledged our word with the United States, and they with us, that that pollution shall cease. The two Governments, through the International Joint Commission, have been investigating what should be done, and the Governments of the United States and Canada have referred to the commission two questions, which are rather interesting, and which are quoted in the report:
To what extent, by what causes, and in what localities have the boundary waters been polluted?
What is the best method of remedying it? The facts disclosed, for instance, that in the water-borne traffic of the Great Lakes something like 2,600 vessels pass through the Detroit river every year, and that three times more tonnage goes through the Soo canal annually than through the Suez canal. It is estimated that 15,000,000 people travel upon the Great Lakes annually, irrespective of the pollution from the cities and .towns bordering on the Great Lakes. These facts were SO' startling that the commission

investigated how best to remedy the consequent pollution, and they have made a progress report, and a further report is coming in; for that reason it was deemed necessary to empower the Federal Government to carry out any recommendations that the International Joint Commission may make to prevent the turning of the Great Lakes into cesspools.
I think the hon. gentleman is discussing conditions under subsection (f), dealing with the International Joint Commission regulations.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. I asked permission to do so. I admit it is out of order, but, as following the remarks of the previous speaker, it may not be necessary to explain this section again. The co-operation dealt with in clause (a) tliat we are now discussing will therefore be most essential in the carrying out of those recommendations. Supposing, for instance, the International Joint Commission should compel cities and towns to treat their sewage, it will throw a very .serious expenditure upon such cities as Buffalo and Toronto. It is therefore very desirable to have co-operation and co-ordination in the views of the different authorities on the .subject, yet it is wholly and solely a Federal matter. That is the reason why I dealt with it. If any objection is made to the question of child life and child welfare, I would like to be heard thereon but perhaps I had better not touch on it now, as I should be out of order again.
Mr. WIGM.ORE: I think I am absolutely in order on co-operation. It seems to me that the Joint Commission is to be congratulated on the amount of work they have done and the conclusions they have come to. I would like to see some legislation enacted by this new board to protect the water supplies of our cities and towns where they are getting it from a distance, for we all know that along the route of such water supplies there are farm houses and other sources of possible pollution, and there should be some protective legislation enacted by this board.
In Ontario the towns and cities can send samples of their water, and they do send them, to the provincial Board of Health at Toronto to be examined.
That is only optional.
Yes; but I imagine that if you made it compulsory it might be thought to be interfering with the powers of the province.

Any matter within the province would have to be dealt with by the provincial health authorities. Under the new Minister of Health in New Brunswick I should think these matters would be taken up in the ordinary course by the provincial authorities.

Subsection agreed to.
On sub-section (b)-the conservation of child life and child welfare.

I wish to move, Mr. Chairman, that this be struck out, but in doing so I do not want to be understood as being opposed to the work of child welfare. It is probably, of all the departments of health, one of the most important. The reason why I think it is out of place here is because I cannot see that under our Constitution it can do any effective service at all, as all the machinery for carrying out the strict work of child welfare is in the hands of the provinces under the British North America Act. Let me preface my statement by reading to you a section of a report made by the chief medical officer of the Local Government Board of England and Wales of 1917-18, in order that we may clearly see what child welfare proposes. He sets this forth in speaking of child welfare:
It can only be secured by improving the welfare of every mother. What is being done to this end in England is: first, it is being made possible that medical attention be given to every mother by the state supplying for the wife and for every insured person 60 shillings, it is being made possible to obtain priority for milk supply.
But further than this the Government is supplying money for home nursing and "home helps." As maternity hospitals are not generally available, the Government is encouraging in a practical way by financial aid their establishment in the various municipalities. In London where such institutions are numerous the death rate is proportionately low.
But as might be expected from what has already been said with regard to vital processes the aid to maternity cases ought to be applied during the ante-natal period. Child welfare stations are gradually being organized for this purpose. Statistics of work done in such cities as Edinburgh show that though it is not always possible to save the infants of sick mothers, yet almost no death of the mother occurs where such have been under previous observation and treatment. Where maternity homes are not provided, the extension of nursing oversight from Child Welfare Centres is being constantly extended, even to the point of having several beds in such centres where sick mothers and children from unsanitary homes can be taken in emergencies.
Child welfare, therefore, embraces the establishment, ithe operation, and the management of eleemosynary institutions. Under the British North America Act the

specific and exclusive powers of the provincial legislatures in this connection are set forth. Section 92, subsection 6, provides that the provinces shall have exclusive jurisdiction in the matter of the establishment, maintenance and management of public and reformatory prisons in and for the province and (section 7) the establishment, maintenance and management of hospitals, asylums, charities and eleemosynary institutions in and for the province, other than marine hospitals. So that it is ultra vires of the Dominion Parliament to deal with these matters which are specifically reserved for the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities. Moreover, if we take this matter up there will be no great tendency on the part of the provinces to act. This is a very large and a growing question; it is yet in its infancy in this country. Many municipalities and provinces would be only too glad to offer as an excuse for not making any further progress in the matter the fact that the Federal Government by their recent enactment have undertaken to carry on the work.
I venture the opinion that the Dominion, under the conditions which prevail, would not be able to do it. The provinces and the municipalities are doing it now and they are doing it well in some cases. I hope that they will do it still better and that this great work of child welfare will expand and advance systematically and scientifically. While I cannot speak too highly of the object which is aimed at in introducing child welfare into this legislation, I think that to include it here is simply to do something which is entirely in contravention of the provisions of the British North America Act, and for that reason I think it is out of place.

I differ as sharply as it
is possible for me to differ from the member for South Toronto (Mr. Sheard). It is said that when a great man goes wrong he goes very badly wrong; my. hon. friend is so very far wrong that I think he must be a very great man. As a matter of fact, he has given all the evidence needed to prove that it is absolutely necessary for us to do this. He says that in some of the provinces this work is already being done very well; the inference is that in some of the other provinces it is not being done at all, or certainly not so well. The whole purpose of this Bill, so far as child welfare is concerned, is to educate the parents so that they will, through their provincial legislatures or otherwise, give such attention to the child as is absolutely necessary for
its welfare. The ignorance of the people with regard to their own, health is simply appalling; some of them do not give it the slightest attention. Many people who have pigs or cows on their premises study carefully methods of conserving the health of these animals, but give little attention to that of themselves and their children. Children are kept in much better physical condition by educated parents than by ignorant parents. I am surprised at the lack of interests in some sections of the country in the matter of health and of social and child welfare. In the section of the country in which I live this subject has during the past few years become one of the most important with which we deal. For several years past an annual babies' welfare week has been held in our city. The first one I saw on the fifth floor of a department store, which had been cleared out because it was not in use owing to a slacking up of business at the beginning of the war. Here were hundreds of mothers-their children were taken care of in another part of the store-and here were medical men giving free lectures, telling these mothers what they should do to give their children better health, how to bring them up, how to feed them, how to clothe them, how to give them proper environment. Environment has just, as much to do with the health of a child as clean water and good food, as good housing and proper sanitation. If there is one thing in Canada that I am ashamed of, it is the lack of proper ventilation in our homes. Even this building is unfit to work in. But there we had these mothers meeting together and getting this instruction and education. The next year I saw them in the city hall, which was given up for a whole week to that purpose. The same thing is going on all over Saskatchewan. Does the provincial government do this? Well, the provincial government as-sits, I understand, by making a certain financial grant; the rest is supplied voluntarily. Several times I went to our provincial government when the public mind was not so well educated as it is at present and solicited their interest in this work, but found it exceedingly difficult to get any money to carry the work on. However, when the public had been so educated that they realized the work to be necessary and advisable, the government came over very quickly.
The hon. gentleman says that some provinces have not a very good organization. If this Health Department will do the

necessary publicity work it will create such a sentiment throughout the country that every provincial government and every municipality will be compelled to give the necessary grants to carry on this work properly. Educating the public in this way is not interfering with provincial education. I agree that the education of the child in the school is a provincial matter, but does education stop with the school, the high school or the collegiate institute? No; education continues long after a young man or a young woman leaves school. This is the kind of education they want; it is to their advantage to receive it, and we should give it to them. If we are going to limit the education to the schools, then we must deny our newspapers, for instance, the right to circulate beyond their provincial boundaries. Such a thing is so absurd that it is hardly worth mentioning. Therefore, this Government has a distinct field in that class of education, and it is, in my opinion, absolutely necessary that this work should be done. The results in my part of the country have been simply amazing. I have not the figures here, but I know that infant mortality, by reason of this campaign of education which has been conducted, has been reduced very considerably in the past few years. And if we go to other parts of the world, for instance, New Zealand, we find that as a result of the educational campaign which is being carried on, the death rate amongst children has dropped very considerably. Let me quote:
Taking the seven years from 1900 to 1907 the average death rate among children under one year in Dunedin and suburbs was eight per cent. For the last five years the average has been 6.5 per cent; for the last three years 6 per cent; for the last two years, 5 per cent; and for the last year (1911), 4 per cent.
How did that come about? Doctor Truby King says it was because of education. He says that a-
-generally diffused knowledge and recognition of infant requirements and maternal duties would save the community one life per diem, and would correspondingly increase the strength and vitality of the rising generation.
If that be the result of education in child welfare, then, for goodness sake, let us proceed with the necessary education to produce that result in Canada. That result is being achieved in my section of the country, and those provinces which are so backward in this respect should come to the Federal- Government for a little direction and assistance which are all that is contemplated in this Bill. I, for one, would not think of interfering with the provinces

or their duties, but can you have interference with provincial rights and cooperation at the same time? This Bill distinctly says to co-operate in all of these matters, and it seems to me as if the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Sheard), producing as he has, the British North America Act to prove that this is an interference with provincial rights, has at the same time given denial to the Bill that he himself has so strongly supported in its vital points. I cannot see why we cannot have co-operation in the matter of child welfare just as we can have co-operation in the matter of adult welfare. What is the difference? Surely the provinces or the Dominion can agree over a child just as they can over anything else. Therefore, I think, because of the tremendous benefit that this will be, it is one of the most important clauses, and I certainly ask that it be left as it is.

I intend to confine my remarks to the clause under discussion, and will leave the legal aspect to the lawyers in the committee. I believe that the legal adviser of the Government would not put this clause in the Bill if the Government did not have jurisdiction. While I am quite in accord with the clause, I think it does not go forward enough, and I would, therefore, move that it be amended by adding the words "and the welfare of needy mothers." If you wish to look after the child, it is essential that you should look after the mother, particularly in the early years of the child, as it is well known that infant mortality is greatest in the early days of its life and is in direct proportion to the poverty of the parents. Consequently we should look after the mother
10 p.m. and see that she is provided with the necessaries of life; that if she is in financial difficulties, she be assisted in such a way that she can rear her children so that they will come up to adult life in good condition. I think, therefore, my amendment would be quite in order and would improve the clause under discussion.

The hon. member for South Toronto (IMr. Sheard) says that the paragraph as it reads is unconstitutional. I agree with him in that, but there is a way of wording it so that it will become quite constitutional. If, instead of leaving . the paragraph as it is:-
The conservation of child life and child welfare.
he used the words:-

which, after all, is largely, if not entirely, provincial work,-I am referring to the administrative side of it. If paragraph (b) is added to paragraph (a) the point raised by the hon. member for South Toronto will be settled.

I move to amend paragraphs (a) and (b) by striking out paragraph (b) and combining paragraph (b) with paragraph (a) so that it will now read:

Co-operation with the provincial, territorial, and other health authorities with a view to the co-ordination of the efforts proposed or made for preserving- and improving the public health and the conservation of child life and child welfare.

Would it meet the views of the hon. member for South Toronto if, instead of having the subject referred to in paragraph (b) as a distinct paragraph . by itself, it was simply added to paragraph (a)? Paragraph (a) would then read:-
Co-operation with the provincial, territorial, and other health authorities with a view to the co-ordination of the efforts proposed or made for preserving and improving the public health and the conservation of child life and child welfare.
That would mean simply that the department would endeavour to secure the cooperation of the various provinces in promoting public health and child welfare. I understand the difficulty of the committee is simply this, that there is a fear that the Federal Government will enter upon what is purely provincial work, and I quite agree with the committee in that respect. It is not the intention of the Bill that the Federal Department should become an administrative department, as regards these matters of public health and child welfare, but that rather the department should be in a position to gather information from authoritative sources, to distribute that information, to educate the people, as the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Cowan) has said, and to co-operate with the various provincial authorities with a view to securing those ends. I am inclined to take the view that the point raised by the hon. member for South Toronto is a very important one, and that if the section is left as it is there is a danger that the provincial authorities will take it for granted that the Federal Government is going to undertake this work,

In view of the suggestion of the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Cal-der) that the sub-clause as it now reads might mean an encroachment on provincial rights, I would remind the committee that the first paragraph of this section removes any danger of that. Its terms are very general. It declares that this Department of Health can deal only with matters over which the Parliament of Canada has jurisdiction. Our powers are defined by th? British North America Act. Sub-paragraph (b) must be read in conjunction with the opening paragraph of section 4, which says that we must keep within our own jurisdiction.

There is this point:	I
would presume that the Parliament of Canada, if it wished to do so, might establish and operate a hospital somewhere in Canada. I do not think that would be unconstitutional. We already have hospitals for our soldiers, and marine hospitals, and 1 dare say we might have hospitals of various kinds if we wished to do so. It seems to me this Bill should be so drafted that there will be no doubt on the part of the provinces as to its intention. I am strongly inclined to the view that the actual work itself is provincial work, and that drafting of the Bill should clearly indicate that to the provinces, so as to give them no excuse for asking us to undertake work which is purely of a local character. It is in order that there shall be no misunderstanding of the intention of the Bill that the amendment has been suggested.

jl respectfully submit
that the conservation of child life and child welfare is included in "matters relating to the promotion or preservation of public health," and therefore I think sub-paragraph (b) should be struck out as it is only a repetition of the opening paragraph. The objection I have is to the phrase "child welfare." I have the same objection to that as I have to the phrase "social welfare". "'Child welfare" is a very broad expression. As a child's welfare cannot be looked after properly without giving him an education, some good lawyer might argue that this legislation confers powers on this Government to interfere with the education of a child. It was for these reasons I was prepared to support the first amendment proposed by my hon. friend from South Toronto, which to my mind was expressed in the most suitable terms. The phrase " child welfare " is ambiguous, and might lead to abuses in its interpretation. If the committee want to be logical, having accepted the amendment regarding " social welfare," it must accept an amendment removing the words " child welfare." I think the Government would do well to strike out subparagraph (b).

My hon. friend is quite
in error in his view that the use of these words-would authorize any interference in the matter of education. The hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) has clearly pointed out that all these subclauses are governed by the opening paragraph of section 4, which says that the powers of the minister shall extend to matters over which the Parliament of Canada has jurisdiction. Now the Parliament of Canada has no jurisdiction in matters of education, except under the peculiar conditions mentioned . in the British North America Act which would have no application here.

I think that the words
" over which the Parliament of Canada has jurisdiction" refer to "the people of Canada " and not to the word " matters."

I .think the suggestion
made by the Minister of Immigration and Colonization is a good one and should be accepted by the committee. I would have felt inclined at first to believe also that subparagraph (b) relating to the conservation of child life and child welfare, if it had been adopted as it stood at first, might have clashed somewhat with the interpretation my hon. friend rightly put upon the British North America Act. But by adding subparagraph (b) to subparagraph (a) it affects [Mir, Ciald<er. ]
somewhat the meaning and the purpose of it all. Now the Parliament of Canada has no jurisdiction over education so we can leave that to one side. What is then the object this Bill has in view? It is, mainly, co-operation with the provinces. Reverting to section 3 of the Bill for a moment, that section gives the Governor in Council power to appoint such other officers as are necessary for the proper conduct of the business of the department. I wish to draw the attention of the committee to the question of marine hospitals.
I think the person who drafted the Bill could not have read the existing law in relation to this matter. We have an elaborate law relating to the care of sick seamen. We are now asked to adopt a clause which places marine hospitals and sick seamen under the management of the 'Minister of Health. We will have two statutes then conflicting with one another in regard to sick seamen. These clauses provide for the way in which sick seamen are to be attended to. Ships when they enter a port pay what is known as the sick mariners' dues. This money is placed in the hands of the receiver general to pay for the cost of managing these hospitals and attending to the seamen when they are sick. This provision is under the control of the Marine Department, and there is no reference at all in the schedule to'this Act to the Marine Department. The law is not repealed, and we will have two statutes about the same matter and two ministers in control if we pass this section.

speechtext:
The introduction of the word "interprovincial" might take away the benefit of the Act. If a boat plying between Prescott and Brockville in the province of Ontario was without proper equipment as regards its closets, and so

The hon. member for

The question of navigation is a matter of federal control. The ships are all registered and I do not think we need fear anything on that score.

I have in my constituency a railway known as the Quebec Central. It is operating under a provincial charter. Under this paragraph would the Government have any jurisdiction over a railway of that kind?
Provincial roads under certain conditions prescribed in the law become subject to federal jurisdiction, and in that case I should think it would come under this law.

If we read this paragraph with the words contained in section 4, we have the safeguard that these powers shall apply only to the subjects over which the Parliament of Canada has jurisdiction. That provision is to be read with the subclause.

Before we pass to paragraph (e) I have another subsection to introduce, and I think it would come in here. I want to introduce a section to provide for the control of the spread of venereal diseases, and I want to have it specifically set forth. I would suggest that the section to be here introduced be as follows :
To control as far as practical the spread of venereal diseases and to quarantine infected cases thereof so as to prevent interprovincial communication and the importation into the Dominion of Canada of those infected with constitutional syphilis.
The reason why I ask for the mention of veneral disease, with particular reference to syphilis is that it is probably the most chronic of all infectious diseases and that not only does it not limit its infection to those who may come into contact but it spreads to those who may descend from the parents of those infected.
We have had many instances of congenital syphilis which showed little or no

manifestations until a later period in life. These eases could be admitted into the country, and have been undoubtedly, in very large numbers through what I am afraid amounts to more or less neglect in the medical inspection of immigrants. I well Temember one case in the city (of Toronto which came under my notice where the father and mother were both subjects of the disease in a very chronic form. They had a girl of eighteen years of age who suffered from keratitis, or inflammation of the eyes, from which she became almost blind afterwards, although the disease did not show itself until very near puberty; and there were two other children, a baby that had congenital syphilis, and a child of five ot six years of age which also showed evidence of this disease. The chronicity of the malady makes it imperative that some special responsibility shall attach to those responsible, to avoid the admission of such cases into the Dominion of Canada; and it must be the particular duty of the Federal Government to take the necessary precautions because of the insidious character of the infection. It is often carried from one large centre to another. For instance, a diseased person may be in Montreal; he may take train to Toronto and travel through to the coast, sowing his infection as he goes, and it is a case where it does not belong altogether to the authority of any one province. What I have in mind is to exercise two efforts for its control. Of course, no wholesale inspection can be attempted by a series of examinations for such cases, but as they become known to the proper health authorities they should come under the control of a central authority ; or they can be recognized by a thorough and regular inspection at the port of entry. I think some specific reference ought 'to be made to that matter before we take up Federal buildings, international commissions, and so on, and I think this is the proper place to introduce it if we are to have any regard at all for the symmetry of the Act.

I quite ' agree with my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Sheard) to the effect that such inspection might be practical at the port of entry from overseas, but I cannot quite follow him when he states that in moving from one province to another an inspection would be possible, because these cases would be known or that there would be some system of inspection at the port of entry. I cannot conceive of the possibility of stopping a
train, say, on the border between Quebec and Ontario, and having an inspection of the passengers.
No.
Nor can I conceive of the police of Montreal wiring to an agent at the border and saying that such and such a passenger has an infectious disease.
I wish to assure the hon. gentleman, Mr. Chairman, that I had no such thought in my mind.
