speechtext:
The amendment reads as follows:
Mr. Sheard moves to amend clause 4 by inserting as subclause (d) the following words " to control as far as practicable the spread of venereal diseases and to quarantine infected cases thereof so as to prevent inter-provincial communication and the importation into the Dominion of Canada of those infected with constitutional syphilis."

Mr. Chairman, with regard to immigrants, it seems to me the matter is covered by subsection (c), the inspection and medical care of immigrants and seamen. Under the Immigration Act the immigration authorities have power to refuse admission of any person infected with venereal or infectious diseases.

The hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx) has anticipated me. If at the port of entry some man or woman should be found suffering with syphilis, there is no reason why this country should admit and take care of such a case. The main objection I have to 'the motion of the member for South Toronto is that when you get away from the port of entry and attempt to deal with syphilis in the provinces you are encroaching on provincial jurisdiction, just as much as if you attempt to deal with scarlet fever or any similar disease. As the hon. member appears to be very anxious to protect the rights of the provinces, I think he is overstepping his own mark.

tl might point out to the hon. members and to my hon. professional [DOT]colleague from Fort William (Mr. Manion) that constitutional syphilis is an incurable disease and absolutely in a category by itself. It is a disease which I have seen active for ten years, and a disease where I have seen the progeny affected constitutionally down through two generations. It is a disease which can stay in an infectious stage without giving the slightest inconvenience very often, and without even being noticed by the community and without being treated by a medical man. Many of these cases are in their worst form

treated by druggists or others who dispense quack nostrums. For those reasons I think it is incumbent upon the Federal Health Department to use the very best medical knowledge and science in endeavouring to control this peculiar and infectious disease which is distinguished by its chronicity and insidiousness and by the destructive work which it does in those who are in no way exposed to the disease except by their nativity, and which is not communicated as is scarlet fever, smallpox, diphtheria, measles and the ordinary infectious diseases. It is a travelling and ambulatory .disease par excellence, and I think some particular mention ought to be made of it in this Act so as to give the central Federal authority jurisdiction over it.
In reference to the point which has been mentioned, and which the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) says I am contradicting myself upon, I do not agree with him. I am referring to ambulatory cases that wander about from one province to another, that travel from the Atlantic to the Pacific, sowing infection and coming back again, a condition which probably does not apply to any other infectious disease known to medical science except tuberculosis, and this disease is more easily transmitted and communicated than tuberculosis because of its chronicity and the insidious manner in which it works upon the human system. It is for that reason that il think a special clause ought to be embodied in this Bill. If the hon. minister wants to consider the advisability of introducing such a clause, I am not prepared to press the matter very strongly, but I certainly think that the public at this particular juncture expect ithe question to be dealt with and taken ;up by the provinces.

There can be no difference of opinion, I should judge, among members of the committee as to the importance and seriousness of the disease to which my hon. friend has referred, but I think ample provision has been made for dealing with it in the Bill as now drafted. As a matter of fact, in the first draft of this Bill it was specifically mentioned, as were three or four of these worst diseases, including tuberculosis, but they were struck out of the Bill for the reason that the provinces might think, if they were specified, that we were undertaking to relieve them of further responsibility, although our jurisdiction was expressly limited by section
4.	It was thought better, on the whole, not to enumerate these diseases, because we have full power under section 4, subsection (a), in co-operation with the provinces, to

deal with them. But if it is the view of the committee that these diseases should be more specifically referred to in the Bill, I have no objection.

I agree with the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Sheard) that these diseases are the greatest curse of Canada -to-day. There is no denying the fact that with the troops returning we shall have a great increase of these diseases, and that increase will no doubt be spread over every province in the Dominion. So that the Government, through this department, should take practical steps at once to deal with this matter. It is no use shutting our eyes to it, or, as the minister said this afternoon, talking of it with bated breath. We have to meet it by open discussion, by dissemination of knowledge, and above all, by training the people to look after themselves. After all, it is not always a question of knowledge. In treating tuberculous cases we tried to educate the people, so to speak; but we found that it was necessary also to train them to look after their own health. Conditions twelve months hence will no doubt be much worse than they are to-day; therefore, this question should be dealt with at once in a scientific manner.

I do not agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. McGibbon, Muskoka), that with the home coming of the soldiers venereal diseases will increase. As a result of the Work that the medical officers have been doing in the army, the percentage of venereal disease in the army has been very considerably reduced.	You
will find a greater percentage in the civilian population than you will find in the army. We have heard a great deal about trying to make this world fit for democracy; I believe we have a great duty to perform in making democracy fit for the world. This venereal disease problem is veiled in mystery, as is illustrated by the cripples and defectives which follow in the wake of the disease. If we refer to it specifically in the Bill, I suggest that it be mentioned in subsection (i). I suggest that the feeble-minded as well as those afflicted with venereal disease, gonorrhea and syphilis, be referred to there, and, if it be in order, Mr. Chairman, that the matter be left over until we come to that subsection.

I had [DOT]in mind, if I had been in my place, to suggest that the paragraph read:
The collection, publication and distribution through provincial and municipal health officers and local boards of health, of information to promote good health and improved sanitation.
So that the information would come through official channels, I can understand an over-zealous and over-officious officer connected with this Federal Health Department giving an interview to some newspaper reporters, setting forth the details of certain epidemics and their ravages in certain parts of Canada, to the direct injury of the health officers operating in that particular part. In order to avoid that I would suggest that all this distribution shall be done through official channels, and then the local officers of the province and the provincial officers shall undertake the distribution through their particular section. In that way the information always travels through legitimate provincial channels, and that is better on matters of public health than the indiscriminate distribution of statements, publications, criticisms and the like which might be made public through the ordinary channels of the daily press.

My objection to the inclusion of the phrase "social welfare" is that it is so difficult in a country like ours to establish a standard of social welfare. It is all very well to collect, publish and distribute information with regard to social welfare, but the information distributed to people whose ideas are of one kind will not be suitable for those whose ideas are of another. Shall we have propaganda tending to help the socialistic ideas of social welfare; or, as the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) would be willing to say, the Bolshevik ideas of social welfare; or shall we have the Methodist, Presbyterian or Catholic ideas of social welfare? That would depend entirely upon the deputy minister or the minister who administers the department. In a question of such great importance as this we cannot leave the determination of this in the hands of any one man. Under the circumstances, since we have already declared in principle that the words "social welfare" cover too many things, they ought to be dropped even from this paragraph. While I have been a member of this House I have had more than enough pamphlets on the various questions of the day put into my post office box. Every day since this session started' I have received "uplift" literature of all kinds, with a great deal of which I do not agree, although I am in favour of a certain amount of "uplift" in-the right direction. ;If we are to be bombarded from day to day with propaganda with which we do not agree the lives of members of Parliament will be made burdensome.
I hope the minister will not press the amendment.

If there is any particular objection to it, I shall not press it. I think everything that is necessary can be done under the section as it stands. My hon. friend has an entirely different idea of social welfare from what was in view in its introduction in the Bill and its use here. It related particularly to such questions as were of interest to the workingman, such as the question of good housing, the question of social insurance, the facts in connection with unemployment where it exists.
Does not that all appear in the Labour Gazette?

Not in relation to public health. It is intended to have statistics and information as to social insurance and how that operates, in order that the public

might become fully seized as to the results of these measures in other countries.

Hon. J. A. CALDER (Minister of Immigration and Colonization) moved for

leave to introduce Bill No. 52 to amend the Immigration Act.
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, as the title of the Bill indicates, its purpose is to amend the law governing immigration. The Bill is a fairly lengthy one. A good many of the amendments are of a minor character and I think can be best explained and considered when we reach the committee stage. There are, however, a number of amendments of considerable importance to which I might make a brief reference at the present time. I will mention them in the order in which they appear in the Bill.
In the first place, the Bill provides for the extension of time during which persons who enter Canada as immigrants may be deported. Under the law as it now stands, the period is three years-we are proposing to exend that to five years. In other words if any person enters Canada whom we find to come within the prohibited classes under the law, such person may be deported at any time within a period of five years. There is a provision in the law as it now stands casting upon transportation companies certain duties and responsibilities in reference to the carrying of immigrants to Canada. It is proposed to extend the term " transportation company " so as to make it applicable to the Federal Government and the Provincial Governments which have transportation systems. Officials in charge of the Canadian National railways or officials who may be in charge of Government boats or vessels, will be responsible for carrying out the law in the same way as officials of an ordinary transportation company. Under the law as it now stands there are certain prohibited classes; certain people are prevented from entering Canada on account of their being mentally or physically unfit or for some other reason. It is proposed to extend the provision of the law in so far as these prohibited classes are concerned and at this stage I shall merely mention what the proposed new provisions of the law are: (I) It is proposed to include within the prohibited classes persons who are suffering from chronic alcoholism; (2) Those coming within the class of what is called constitutional psychopathic inferiority-probably the doctors in the House will explain a little more clearly than I can just what the effect of these words are. Then, it is suggested that we should carry into our law a provision to the effect that all persons who are either mentally or physically in such a condition as that they are not likely to 77i	.	. t
be able to earn a living should be excluded. It is also suggested that we should set up a literary test and that persons should be included in the prohibited classes who are not able to read. That provision has not been in our law as yet. The Bill also provides that we should include in the prohibited classes persons who believe in, or advocate, the overthrow of constituted Government by force or violence or who advocate the unlawful destruction of property; also persons guilty of conspiracy against His Majesty; enemy aliens who have been interned and also enemy aliens who have been deported from Canada, or from British countries, for any cause. The Bill itself will explain just what is meant there a little more fully.
The Bill also provides that we should take authority to provide for the medical examination of immigrants in the country of their origin or on board ship. There are several sections of the Bill dealing with the duties and responsibilities of transportation companies. In the law as it now stands there is a provision of this kind but we propose to add to and extend this provision so as to throw greater responsibility upon transportation companies that bring immigrants to Canada. We are also imposing upon them more severe penalties for failure to carry out the law. The Bill also contains provision for the examination of seamen when such seamen land in Canada for any cause. Then, there is one other section, probably the most important section in the Bill. It is in the law now as section 38 (c) and under that section the Government has power by Order in Council to prohibit persons from entering Canada for either a stated period or permanently for any reason which may be deemed advisable. It is proposed to extend the provision of that section so as to give the Government greater powers in so far as that feature of our work is concerned. These are the chief provisions of the Bill.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: THE LATE MR. JOSEPH READ, M.P.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE LATE MR. JOSEPH READ, M.P.
speechtext:
Since the last sitting of the House death has again touched our circle, and has removed one of its members. I confess that when I read in the press this morning of the sudden and unexpected death of Captain Read, the late member foT Prince, Prince Edward Island, I experienced a feeling of very deep emotion. Nothing could more forcibly bring home to us the truth of the saying: In the midst of life we are in death. It is inexpressibly sad to me, as I am sure it is to all members on both sides of the House, to reflect that this good and kindly man, who, during the short term in which he had been a member of this House, had won a place in all our hearts and who but yesterday was among us, is now no more. We all liked him, Mr. Speaker. We liked to see him in his place; we liked to hear him speak; we liked to converse with him in the corridors and elsewhere in social intercourse. I think we liked him most because of his strong individuality, his originality of thought, his homely philosophy, his shrewd knowledge of men and affairs, and the humour which illuminated all his speeches.
The late member for Prince came of fighting stock. Both his paternal and maternal grandfathers were connected with the Imperial Military and Naval Service. While a young man he followed the sea as his calling, and having taken a course in a nautical academy at Liverpool, he became entitled to an Imperial Master Mariner's Certificate. Later he entered commercial life in the province of Prince Edward Island, in which, I understand, he made a signal success. He was held in much respect in the commercial community, having been for a considerable time president of the Maritime Boards of Trade. He was keenly interested in public affairs
before coming to this Parliament, having been for three terms a member of the Provincial Legislature. In 1917, at the last election, he was returned to this House. He took a keen interest in all affairs which came before the House from time to time, and as he had a wide knowledge of affairs, was listened to with interest and respect. Personally, and on behalf of all on this side of the House, I desire to express our very deep regret and sorrow at his death, and to extend to those of his family circle our most sincere sympathy in their bereavement.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: THE LATE MR. JOSEPH READ, M.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of members on this side of the House who sat. with the late member, I wish to thank the' leader of the Government (Sir Thomas. White) for his kindly words in respect to our departed friend, Captain Joseph Read, who represented the constituency of Prince, P. E. I. I am sure that we all have much pleasure in taking to ourselves and representing as our own what has been so truly said by the leader of the Government with respect to Captain Read.
Captain Read was a splendid, strong, rugged type of that Canadian citizenship of which we are all so proud. He was a man of strong personal opinions, of honesty of purpose, of honesty of conviction. There was never any mistake as to where he stood on any question; this good, old, honest, sturdy mariner always made his position clear on the floor of this House with regard to any question in which he took part or interest. The leader of the Government has said that he was a master mariner; so he was. We have many master mariners in this country, but not so very many who hold the high position that Captain Read did. He passed the severe test to which men in that calling are subjected by the Imperial Board of Trade; he was a first class seaman and a splendid navigator. He carried that reputation all over the world. Moreover, he had the reputation of being good and kind to the men who served under him, all of whom regarded him as a gentleman and a hero.
The leader of the Government spoke ol Captain Read having been in business. I should like to mention an event in his business life which was regarded as not common to very many men. At one time Captain Read failed in business, and what he had was not sufficient to pay all his creditors. He went back to sea and made money, and although under the laws of this country he was not obliged to pay his old debts, it stands to his credit that he paid every cent of these

old bills which he had not been able to pay when he was obliged to enter the Insolvency Court of Prince Edward Island. Few in the world have done that, and that circumstance reveals such an excellent trait of his character and stands so well in line with what we know of Captain Bead that I think it is well to mention it. We are sad and sorrowful at his departure. He has served his country well; he lived to a respectable old age. We can only bow to the will of Him who does all things wisely and well.

On motion of Mr. H. B. Morphy (North Perth) for the third reading of Bill No. 13, respecting the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada:

This Bill was allowed to go through the Railway Committee at the request of the Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Reid). He said that he had conferred with the Acting Prime Minister, who had suggested that there would be no harm in letting the Bill go through, as it would be explained in the House. The Bill is to enable the Grand Trunk Railway Company to raise additional funds. The record of that company in the way of financing and raising money has been so remarkable that a great deal of opposition arose to the Bill in committee. 1 suppose it passed the Committee of the Whole; unfortunately, I was not here. The member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) says that he did not know about it either; he was one of the members who opposed the Bill in the Railway Committee. If I am not trenching upon the rules of the House, 1 should like to ask an explanation from the Government as to the necessity for this Bill. If popular rumour is correct and the Grand Trunk is to fall into the hands of the country, there is no necessity for this Bill. If the Grand Trunk is not going to fall into the hands of the country it will be most unfortunate to permit this country to do any more of the wild-cat financing that it has been doing for the last number of years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I expressed the opinion of the

Government in regard to this Bill oil Friday evening when it was in the committee stage on the second reading. I stated that the object of the legislation was to authorize the Grand Trunk to issue debentures for the purpose of its financing. I said that it was not thought wise for the Government to prevent the company from obtaining authority to issue these securities, pending negotiations which the Government is having with the company. The company has many pressing obligations and will require to finance. I pointed out also that if the Government took over the Grand Trunk Railway Company they would take it over, as the Canadian Northern Railway Company was taken over, as a corporation. Power to issue debentures will be required by the Grand Trunk Railway Company as a corporation if taken over by the Government, because as a corporation it would be its object to finance itself as much as possible. That is the policy we have adopted with regard to the Canadian Northern Railway Company. Instead of advancing that company money from time to time, we entourage it to make issue of its own securities as a corporation in New York and in London, Some of those securities are guaranteed by the Dominion Government and some are not, but the point I make is that whether the Grand Trunk continues as a corporation or, as we expect, comes into the possession of the Government, it will still be a corporation with power to issue securities when necessary.
Another point is this. Pending the negotiations to withhold this power might have very serious consequences, consequences that I do not think any of us would like to see with respect to the Grand Trunk, and I have not been able to reach the conclusion that it would be fair or just for us to withhold power that is necessary for the temporary financing of the company. That is the general position which I indicated last Friday night when the matter was under consideration. I stated also that the Government was in a position though this legislation is passed, to control the issue in such a manner as to protect the public interest, and that, I take it,, is all that the House is concerned with.
If no negotiations were pending and the Grand Trunk required authority from this Parliament to issue debenture stock such as it has issued in the past, I suppose no difficulty would be raised, because the proceeds of the debentures so issued would be devoted to the purposes of the company, namely, to take care of deficits or to provide

for betterments or improvements or extensions. That, in general, was the attitude which I adopted on Friday last. I have given the matter careful consideration, because I appreciate the point of view of my hon. friend and also what was put forward by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) when the Bill was in the second reading stage. But the Government has reached the conclusion that this legislation authorizing the Grand Trunk to issue securities should not be withheld.
Mr. iMACKIE (East Edmonton): 1 would like to point out that the statement made by the Acting Prime Minister has not been heard by at least twenty-five members sitting behind him. It is an unfortunate thing that this occurs in the House, but it is also an unfortunate thing that the members of the Government do not exert themselves so as to be heard. It is not fair that members on the back benches should have to wait until the publication of Hansard to find out what the Acting Prime Minister has stated.
I would like the members on the front benches to keep that in mind so that they may let the members on the back benches know exactly what they are saying.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the third time.
