Lt.-General Sir SAM HUGHES moved:
That, in the opinion of this Ho<use, in view of the statements made public in relation to the Guelph Novitiate during the month of June, 1918, and the circumstanoes and facts concerning those and other similar charges concerning the evasion by young men and the oonnivance of others to defeat the ends and aims of the Military Service Act and other Acts and Orders relating to the upbuilding of the Military Forces of Canada, it is advisable that a Select Committee of this House be appointed to inquire into the matter with full authority to examine witnesses under oath, to pay necessary expenses and to report to this House.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion concerns the practical claim to sovereignty on the part of the Jesuit Novitiate at Guelph, and the practical recognition of such claim by the Government of the Dominion of Canada. This charge may he laid not against this Government alone, but to my certain knowledge against practically every government that has preceded it for a great many years.
The Novitiate is a farm situated about two miles beyond the city limits of Guelph. About one year ago, in the spring of 1918, between forty and fifty people were said to be employed on this farm, and a number of these were reported liable for military service under the law. The military representative at Guelph at that time was a very reputable gentleman named W-e-s-t-o-b-y; I spell the name out because there has been some confusion over it. The military representative of the district was Colonel White, formerly in command of the 30th Wellington Rifles, and a gentleman of the highest standing in the city of Guelph. The assistant provost marshal was a young officer who had served with distinction at the front and had been wounded and invalided home, leaving his two brothers still in service at the front. This man's name was Captain Macauley, with then headquarters at London, Ontario. The Novitiate failed at the outset to report their men for medical examination under the Military Service Act; they failed to report their men for any purpose under the Military Service Act; they failed to report them under the military order relating to the 20-23 years of age class. The Novitiate, though repeatedly asked, refused

to give any names or any facts, or to recognize in any way the authority of the Government.
It was repeatedly requested to give information by Westoby, White and Macauley. Westoby on the 30th of November, 1917, wrote to the Novitiate and the letter is undisputed. The Novitiate resisted Macauley's actions on June 7, the time of the so-called raid, and the law was defied here, while the military police were everywhere else arresting people. No one was arrested at the Novitiate either for failure to register or to report, or for harbouring those who ought to have reported. I may say that some of the complaints concerning this Novitiate first came from those who were favourable to its religious persuasion. They felt ashamed to think that their sons at the front were doing their bit fearlessly in the cause, while here could be seen, from the roadside any day, forty or fifty of these men, all seemingly able-bodied husky fellows not reporting and practically defying the law-a condition of affairs which is fatal to the institutions under which we live. The Ministerial Association of Guelph has been brought into this matter to a considerable degree, with the object of trying to draw a herring across the trail. This association, in common with all ministerial associations throughout Canada, had been, at the request of the Government, long active in recruiting and had done yeoman service. Many congregations in Canada, before conscription was enacted, had scarcely one able-bodied man of military age who was not in the service. With one or two exceptions this was true of Guelph. Every one had clamoured for a solution of the Novitiate scandal. After the so-called raid an
4	p.m. attempt was made to inflame a portion of the public against the Ministerial Association, who had been assisting recruiting at the request of the Government, and incidentally assisting in the elections to return the Union Government. And on the failure of the raid and the suppression of the press, and also the humiliation of Macauley, the association smashed the press censorship and issued the following statement:
1.	That our attitude is not one of religious intolerance.
2.	The issues involved are issues of universal interest, and consequently of universal obligation.
3.	The association has not initiated this matter nor is it inspired by gossip.
4.	The association makes no charges, but
seeks investigation of charges made by the authorities.	,
5.	If the Military Service Act hold any one responsible who shields a defaulter, an institution charged with harbouring 22 should also be held responsible.
6.	We, as pastors, refuse to be regarded as a class who have no right to interfere with such matters, or of being incompetent or incapable of being leaders in the community, or in the charges to which we have been called for such purpose.
The Ministerial Association's assistance had been sought and freely given from the beginning, both in recruiting and in the elections. After the elections the Rev. Mr. Palmer, Presbyterian minister of Guelph, and a member of the Ministerial Association, spoke to a member of this Government, the Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie), by whom he was assured that justice would be done. On his return from Ottawa, however, Mr. Guthrie told Mr. Palmer, in these colloquial terms, " Doherty says they are all right and are to be left alone." On another occasion Mr. Palmer again spoke to Mr. Guthrie, whereupon Mr. Guthrie returned to Ottawa and sent him Hansard of July 13, 1917, with pages 3498 to 3503, and of July 19, 1917, pages 3702 to 3717 marked, bearing on the case and showing clearly that these gentlemen in the Novitiate were amenable to the law.
There are further reports to which I shall now make passing reference in case the matter may be brought up in any tribunal. There is a report that there was a very important telegram sent by the Solicitor General to his law partner Mr. Kirwin, who, I understand, was the lawyer for the Novitiate. One can readily understand how excitement grew in this matter, and the circumstances connected with the incident had been a public scandal all over the country. London had repeatedly requested that action be taken; the officers were talking the matter over; the people were discussing it, and a rumour became current that these men, not only twenty-two of them but all of them were put there in hiding. Added to this was the story that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) had a son there. I have not had the privilege of seeing this gentleman for a number of years, but several years ago -he was a lad of 17 or 18 then-he certainly was not, in my opinion, a fit subject for military service. But the story got around that he was there in hiding, and one can easily conceive the intense excitement that these rumours engendered. Instead of doing what they should have done, namely, calling Westoby, Macauley and White and saying: "Here are the boys, come and inspect them and take those who should go,"

there was an attempt from start to finish to disregard the law, and they acted as if they considered that they were not amenable to the laws of Canada and would not recognize any authority. Further, there was a rumour of bad feeling between the Department of Justice and the Militia Department, and 'there was a report that the Militia Department, to its eternal credit, ordered the thing to be cleaned up. If that order was issued, then I congratulate the Minister of Militia (Major-General Mewburn). Following this, on June 7th, 1918, a train from London arrived at Guelph at 7.35 p.m., and in order to obviate any tittle-tattle, and with a view to precision, I am giving the dates. Now Macauley had eleven men in mufti. He wore the chevron on his arm showing his authority, but he and his men were in mufti, because he did not want to go into Guelph with a body of troops and create any excitement on, his way to the Novitiate. He came and made inquiries at the drill hall, got a cenveyance and drove quietly to the Novitiate, arriving there before nine o'clock at night. He took only three men to the door, and a member of the Novitiate refused to give any information, but telephoned ;to Judge Hayes and to Lawyer Kirwin. The latter came to the Novitiate and Macauley informed him that he had decided to take three of the students in order that he might have a test case. On the wall there was a long list which he glanced over, the list evidently containing the names of the people in the Novitiate. Not one occupant of the institution had, any document exempting him from service. The Novitiate repudiated Macauley's authority and refused to accede to any request of his for information. They communicated with the Department of Justice at Ottawa-J understand with the Minister of Justice himself-and the department communicated with Macauley, who, however, being a military officer, very properly declined to take orders from any other department than the Militia. The Department of Justice then evidently communicated with the Militia Department, and in the absence of the Minister of Militia some of the officers, after midnight that night, telephoned Macauley, ordering him to leave the Novitiate the same night. An opportunity was thus given for any men who cared to do so to escape. Macauley returned the next day, however, to obtain the names of the occupants, but the list was gone. The Department of Justice that night,-that is the night of the raid-in order to entirely suppress the matter, ordered the press not to publish a word 
in connection with it. That order came from the Department of Justice and can be traced directly to the Minister of Justice himself. The Minister of Militia later sent an apology. Then, Colonel Godson-Godson, Provost Marshal, followed. But the serious thing, so far as Colonel Godson-Godson is concerned, is that he visited London, and that letters on the subject either by him or his followers were taken from the files there. Macauley was sent to Winnipeg. There was a second press censorship issued, but the people of Guelph had been excited to such a pitch that they would not be bound by this censorship any longer, and the pulpits and some of the press, ignoring the censorship, published the facts of the case; but when the Rev. Mr. Palmer went to the Northwest on a lecturing tour he found that his' addresses were not allowed to be published.
The matter was brought to the attention of the Dominion Government and they took the stand, possibly very properly-I think they were perfectly justified in demanding specific charges-that they would decline to go into the matter unless specific charges were given them. These have been furnished them by the Bev. Mr. Palmer and they are:
1.	The Department of Justice at Ottawa interfered with the Military Board at Guelph in their efforts to obtain information as to the status of the inmates of the Guelph Novitiate.
2.	That in doing so, the department extended special- privileges to an institution which should have been treated like any'other institution.
3.	That the Hon. C. J. Doherty interfered with Captain A. C. Macauley on the night of June 7th, while he, Capt. Macauley, was carrying out the instructions of his superior officers."
4.	That the Department of Justice, through its minister, prevented the placing in military service of young men of military age residing in the institution.
5.	That the press censorship instigated by a minister of the Crown intensified the feeling that special protection was being given to the institution at Guelph.
. I hereby state that the above charges are made by me in good faith, believing them to be true and fully borne out by evidence which can be produced.
Kennedy H. Palmer.
When the matter was brought to the attention of the Government, as I say, they declined to act unless specific charges were made involving the Government. Formal charges were made by the Kev. Mr. Palmer and are, to my mind, specific, but lest there should be any misunderstanding, I will, from my place in this House, assume the responsibility of enumerating some of the charges or rather statements, which are made for the purpose, not of attacking the

Government, but of challenging this pretended sovereignty of any organization or its assumption of superiority to the State. These statements are as follows:
1.	That the Government improperly failed to make the occaipants of the Novitiate register for medical examination or for service under the M.S.A., and the Government also failed to punish those harbouring defaulters in the Novitiate.
2.	A member of the Government (Mr. Guthrie) informed a member of the Ministerial Association that " Doherty says they are all right and they are to be left alone."
This is improper interference.
3.	The Militia Department order London to take action and Macauley took it.
This was proper.
4.	The Novitiate communicated with the Justice Department.
That was perfectly constitutional.
5.	The Justice Department improperly communicated with Macauley.
6.	The Justice Department communicated with the Militia Department.
That was perfectly proper.
7.	After midnight the Militia Department communicated with Macauley and improperly ordered him to retire from the Novitiate.
S.	The Justice Department improperly ordered the press censorship.
9.	The Minister of Militia apologized to the Principal of the Novitiate, and indirectly censured Macauley when the order should have been to the Principal to observe the law.
10.	Col. Godson-Godson, Provost Marshal for the Militia Department, visited the Novitiate and it is claimed, further apologized.
That is a matter of no importance whatever.
11.	Godson-Godson visited London and it is claimed improperly and surreptitiously had certain letters removed from the Military files there.
That is a matter of small account but it can be readily explained, I understand.
1>2. Macauley was improperly removed to Winnipeg by the Militia Department.
I need not comment upon these facts- they speak for themselves-but they do not carry out the principle that we should have equal rights, equal laws for all and special privileges for none. This Novitiate has arrogated to itself the right to be regarded as a sovereign power. I understand that Colonel Street, of Ottawa, himself a member of that community, who was acting in a military capacity, was refused and that he had the very same experience as Colonel Macauley at Guelph and London and as others had throughout the Dominion. If these institutions are to be superior to and override the law, I do not regard that as a proper condition of affairs and I certainly do not purpose consenting to having
a sovereign body within a sovereign body in the Dominion of Canada. The State must be supreme and all organizations and corporations must bow to its will.
I remember once in an election case in Victoria county objecting to seven or eight names being put upon the list. The members of a corporation that owned a little building sought to get their names upon the list as voters. They had sworn a few months before that the building was only worth $250 and yet they came forward and wanted to get tneir names on the nst as joint owners of this building. I objected on the ground that there was not sufficient property to qualify the members of a corporation of that kind and that their names should not go cn. Judge Deacon who was presiding, said that these corporations were seeking to override the laws of the country, that they had neither sterns to kick nor souls to save and he held that the members of that corporation could not go on as voters. Others must do the same as Judge Deacon did if these corporations are to observe the law.
I might point out that serious complaints reached me regarding this Novitiate at Guelph, and they came from those of the same creed as the members of the novitiate themselves. They felt ashamed that	any one should undertake to
evade the law as was done in this instance. I might point out another instance, and there are many of them, to the credit of the ecclesiastics of that church, where a young man was called out by the Militia Department. He immediately ran to the leading ecclesiastic of his district and sought to get influence to have him exempted. The ecclesiastic looked him up and down, heard his case and said: " Get into a uniform; you are the type of man that should be fighting; why are you asking to be exempted?" That, young man got into his uniform, but he finally got out of it in spite of his ecclesiastical friend. I could give instance after instance where people in that community have been humiliated to find that, because behind the scenes work was going on where young men have been improperly exempted from going to the front while others have been taken. There is nothing that has spread the spirit of rebellion in this Dominion, nothing that has created a feeling so strong against the Government, as the fact that the Military Service Act has not been administered in the spirit of equity throughout Canada. That has spread a bitter feeling. People have seen their sons taken and sent to the front while their neighbour's sons have been allowed to remain and have not been inter-

fered with. The military officers, who got $10 a head, could not be induced to touch certain young men, whereas they would go in and grab other young fellow's under age, or close to the age, in order to take them away. It has bred that spirit of rebellion which injustice always breeds, and a particularly strong feeling characterizes this community around Guelph.
There is no intention of being intolerant. All the intolerance has been on the part of the Novitiate. Almost a year elapsed after the passing of the Military Service Act before any action was taken. Tolerance! The Militia and Defence people were more than tolerant. It was more than three months before they acted, and the Novitiate still defied them. I will read this definition of tolerance:
It is first the recognition of the rights of private judgment in matters of faith and worship ; it is also the liberty granted by the governing power of a state to every individual to hold, or publicly teach and defend his religious opinions and to worship whom, how and when he pleases provided that he does not thereby violate the rights of others or infringe laws designed for the protection of decency, morality, and good order or for the security of the governing power.
What was then to be done? Our men were being driven back from St. Quentin, and the whole civilized world was feeling that there was a possibility of the Allies meeting a defeat. These men were called out, and they failed to respond and defied the law. If even intolerance was displayed, it was displayed, under this definition, by the Novitiate at Guelph. If ever tolerance was displayed, it was displayed by the department- in not taking prompt action before they did. Then there is the fact of recognition by the State of the right which every person has

Will the hon. gentleman
allow me to ask him a question?
Yes, a dozen.
Is the hon. gentleman prepared to give the House any information as to the percentage of Catholics and Protestants that fought in the Allied armies?
I am not concerned as to whether a man was a Roman Catholic-

I know you are.
Sir'SAM HUGHES:-or a Protestant, one way or the other. I am not going to deal with that aspect of the case at present. On a proper occasion I will be prepared to take up that phase of the matter, but it has nothing whatever to do with what I am arguing here

I might say that I am very glad indeed, now the hon. gentleman has mentioned the matter, to state that Roman Catholics throughout my constituency-English and French, British and other nationalities, in fact all the Roman Catholics in the district-have spoken to me again and again about my action in having this matter placed on a proper basis.
Now to resume my speech:	Third, the
fact of recognition by the State of the right-
Perhaps the hon. gentleman would allow me to ask another question?
With pleasure, anything to satisfy my hon. friend.
Were there not more Catholics fighting in the Allied armies than there were Protestants?	.

I really could not
say. I have never asked a man what his religious faith was. In my life time-

I can tell you now that
there were.

I have followed the motto of Talleyrand. He was asked at one time, " What is your religion?" Talleyrand replied, " My religion is that of every wise man." He was asked, " What is the religion of every wise man?" To this he replied, " A wise man never tells his religion."
I will now make a third attempt to continue my speech:	Third:	the fact of recognition by the -State of the right which every person has to enjoy the benefit of all the laws and all social privileges without any regard to difference of religion. That is all I have to say on the question. I merely desire -to present the facts of the case without comment. I might say that since putting this motion on the Order Paper, in consultation with a number of my friends, they think that if the Government would consider the matter and refer it to a judge, or a commission, or some tribunal of that kind, other than to the individual members of the House, it might possibly be a quieter way of solving the trouble, and might get at the facts much more readily, and with less circumlocution. Bearing that in mind I will accept any proper solution the Government may have to offer with respect to the matter.
Major-General MEWBURN (Minister of Militia and Defence): I have listened to the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) with a great deal of interest, and while the specific charges that he wishes to have investigated do not materially affect the Department of Militia and Defence, yet

I feel that that department has been referred to and it does, in connection with this matter, touch very closely the Department of Justice in the operation of the Military Service Act. The hon. member stated that great criticism was levelled at us for our not looking into this matter at an earlier stage, and I do not wish to cast the responsibility on any other department, or, according to a slang military term, " pass the buck." I am prepared to take the responsibility for my department to the fullest possible extent. Up to some time in April the Department of Justice, as is well known, was charged with the apprehension of all men liable for military service. The Department of Militia and Defence had nothing to do with apprehending men for military service until such time as we were notified by the registrars under the Justice Department that any individual man was not entitled. to exemption, and had been ordered to report to one. of the depot units. If that man failed to report then he became a deserter and the duty devolved upon the Militia Department of apprehending him. Towards the end of April an Order in Council was passed releasing the Dominion police from duty in connection with this work, and the Militia Department was then charged with the work of apprehension, so that from a period of the end of April until some time in May, which is not a very long time, passed before we could assume control of this work after having received the necessary information.
I would like to explain to the House at the outset that as far as my department is concerned, I have always felt, since publicity has been given to this unfortunate matter, that we would welcome any investigation. We are not afraid for the light of day to shine on any of our work, and I will be willing, and be only too glad, speaking personally, to have any investigation that the Government may decide to grant. But I wish to state my position regarding this matter, and will first refer to the instructions I gave regarding an investigation at the Novitiate, because the first instructions emanated from me. Secondly, I desire to-read the apology that I sent to the rector of this institution I am not ashamed of that apology, and I think any hon. gentleman when he knows the facts will agree that it was the only manly course to take. I say without hesitation that I would take that action again were I to be put in the same position.
Throughout the whole of this unfortunate affair, and throughout the operation of the
78 i
Military Service Act, I regret to say, there has been too much talk indulged in through the country, and too much questioning as to whether a man was a Roman Catholic or a Protestant-as to whether he was a Roman Catholic, or a Presbyterian, or a Methodist, or an Anglican, or a French-Canadian. I say that all the men that enlisted were Canadian soldiers and should be treated as such. If that had been the spirit which prevailed throughout there would have been considerably less heartburning and greater unity in the country.
Now, Sir, on the 31st day of May, 1918, I was informed by a very reliable party that there were several men in the Jesuit College at Guelph who were evading military service. The names of two young men were given to me specifically, and the name of a third young man in Guelph, who had nothing to do with the Novitiate, was mentioned. I immediately sent a minute to Captain Tyndale, who was acting as secretary of a sub-committee of the Militia Department which was looking after the operation of the Military Service Act, and keeping closely in touch with the Department of Justice to whom the whole operation of this Act had been entrusted. That sub-committee was meeting every afternoon considering matters that arose in connection with the Military Service Act, keeping closely in touch with the Department of Justice, as I have said, and carrying out any instructions that might be given. I will now read the instructions that I issued, and these are the only instructions that I ever gave relating to this matter. I shall read from a true and correct copy of the Minute of Instructions given by me. The original of this document was sent to Captain Tyndale.
Of London?

No, Captain Tyndale of Ottawa, who was secretary of the sub-committee in my department. He in his turn passed the original on to the Provost Marshal, by whom it was forwarded to London where it was filed. When this matter came up the statement was made, publicly and otherwise, that I had given definite instructions different from what I actually did give, and I requested that -the original document be returned to the Headquarters file in Ottawa, from which it should never have 'gone. The document was returned from London. The statement made that the Provost Marshal went to London and took certain documents

off the files there was not true. The instructions given were:
Memo to Captain Tyndale:
I am informed through a very reliable source that there are several men at the Jesuit College, Guelph; particularly men by the name of Newman and Craig, who are escaping military service. Steps should be taken to get after these men. There is also another very glaring case, and that is James Alexander, son of A. W. Alexander, Guelph. Can you have these cases followed up? Probably the Provost Marshal would help you.
(Signed) S. C. Mewburn.
I do not think it is necessary to refer here to the Alexander case, because very shortly after that the young man in question joined the forces and went overseas. That is a copy of the original and it is the only document that I ever issued in connection with this matter, except the apology which I have referred to.
I would like to give the House the benefit of what followed, as far as my department is concerned: Captain Tyndale immediately transmitted that document to the Provost Marshal, who in turn sent it to London and gave instructions to the Deputy Assistant Provost Marshal there to look into the matter.
Captain Macauley proceeded to Guelph on the night of the 7th of June, and that night called at the Novitiate. At midnight on June 7 the Adjutant General received a telephone communication from the Minister of Justice (Hon. C. J. Doherty) stating that Captain Macauley had arrived at the Novitiate at 9 p.m. and proposed to make certain arrests of men who were not, in fact, liable for military service. In view of the representations of the Minister of Justice the Adjutant General gave instructions to Captain Macauley by long distance telephone to suspend action tor the night, but to revisit the college in the morning and obtain full information.
Briefly, this is what appears to have occurred on the evening in question. Captain Macauley reached the Novitiate about 9.20 p.m., accompanied by nine military policemen whom he posted about the building. Entering in plain clothes and not producing any written authority from the General Officer Commanding the District or from the Provost Marshal or the Assistant Provost Marshal, as is required by the Order in Council of 30th April, 1918, he demanded as an alternative to an immediate search of the whole premises that all the men of military age in the Novitiate should be assembled in the dining room for interrogation. During the interval Captain
[Major-General Mewburn.]
Hingston, a chaplain who had served for some years overseas and who was on leave and happened to be visiting the Novitiate, asked him for his authority.

Father Hingston is
himself a member of the order.
Major-General MEWBURN: He was visiting there; he had been a chaplain overseas.

He is a member of the order.
Major-General MEWBURN:	He may
have been. He was on leave and was there for a few days, I understand.
To that request his reply was a demand to know who Captain Hingston was and why he was wearing uniform with captain's badges. Captain Hingston protested against the illegality of Captain Macauley's proceeding, but the assembling of the men of military age was conceded in the face of Captain Macauley's reiterated statement of his intention to search the house forthwith. The men were assembled accordingly and their interrogation proceeded. While this was going on the rector, or Father Hingston, got into telephone communication with a solicitor and through him with the Minister of Justice, who hin>
self reached Captain Macauley by telephone at about the time that he had decided that he would remove in custody three of the men of the Novitiate. Captain Macauley refused to take any order from the Minister of Justice-I do not blame him in that-but complied with the order subsequently given by the Adjutant General at the latter's request. That confirms, I think, what the hon. member referred to in this regard.
A letter from the rector of the Novitiate protesting against the illegality and irregularity of Captain Macauley's conduct was received by me, and a letter of apology for the mode in which the inquiry had been carried out sent in reply. In order that the House may have full information and see just exactly what the feeling was with regard to this' matter, I wish to read the letter from the rector of the Novitiate to the Minister of Militia, written from St. Stanislaus' Novitiate, Guelph, dated June 8, 1918. I was out of the city at the time, and I had no knowledge of this until I returned the following day. The letter is as follows:
The Honourable Major-General Mewburn, Minister of Militia and Defence,
Ottawa.
Sir,-I beg to lodge a most emphatic protest against the conduct of certain military author-

ities of Military District 1, at St. Stanislaus' Novitiate, Guelph, Ont.
Last evening at 9.35 three men in plain clothes, one of whom said he was a Deputy Provost Marshal, called at this house, and demanded that all the members of this community be paraded before him within the delay of five minutes.
When I asked him for his authority for a proceeding so unusual and at such an unseemly hour he produced from his pocket a brassard with the letters D.P.M., which he said was his authority, and added that if I did not summon the community at once, he would proceed to search the house for deserters and defaulters under the Military Service Act.
I went to the telephone to consult our lawyer as to the legality of the proceedings, and asked Father Hingston, who was but three weeks back from service overseas as military chaplain, to interview these military gentlemen. To Father Kingston's questions the leader of the party said that his name was Macauley, that he was a captain and a D.P.M., in proof whereof he again produced the brassard from his pocket. As the possession of a brassard was not thought to be of itself sufficient proof, the gentleman in grey tweeds, who said he was Captain Macauley, exhibited a typewritten copy of instructions which he proceeded to read. The passage which seemed relevant and on which he based his right of search was substantially as follows: "Any officer or N.C.O. acting under written authorization of G.O.C. or O.C. of a military district or area, if he has good grounds for believing that deserters or defaulters under the M.S.A. are being harboured and concealed, after reasonable demand of entrance and refusal thereof, and upon producing the aforesaid written authorization, may forcibly enter and search the premises, etc. . . Asked for the written authority mentioned in the instructions, the gentleman could produce none, but insisted nevertheless on his right of search.
Meanwhile, about an hour and a half went by, during which time various telephone messages were sent to three different lawyers, and Captain Macauley himself tried to have another automobile sent out from the city. The community, which rises at a very early hour, had long since gone to bed.
Finally, Captain Macauley, who had grown impatient at my reluctance to submit to the indignity of a search, especially on the part of persons who could not show proper authorization for so doing, this delay, moreover, being attributed by one of his party to quibbling and a desire to gain time for concealment, declared his intention of proceeding forthwith to search the house. Two outside witnesses had been summoned by me, Thomas Bedford, a neighbour and a J.P., and Joseph O'Leary. In their presence Father Hingston reiterated his formal request for the production of some written authorization, and as this was not forthcoming, he registered a formal protest against the search without proper authorization, and warned Captain Macauley that he must take the responsibility for his illegal act. Captain Macauley declared his intention of searching the house-without further ado, and taking out his note-book began by asking the names of the four persons then in the room.
Just then one of the legal gentlemen consulted telephoned, and after hearing the circumstances advised me to overlook any irregularity there might be in the proceedings
and to do all I could to facilitate the obtaining of all the information required. I did so, and offered Captain Macauley either that he himself should visit the bedrooms and dormitories or that I should have all the members of the community wakened and summoned to the refectory. He chose the latter alternative. Meanwhile, it appeared that the three men with whom we had been dealing up till now were not alone, but had all along been accompanied by a force of deputy police, some of whom, if not all, were armed, who had formed a cordon about the house, and could be seen, some peering in at the windows, others standing guard at various intervals or pacing their beat on all sides of the house. Of these as many as eleven were counted, and when later on our lawyer arrived, for we found the actual presence of a lawyer absolutely necessary, he found the front gate closed and guarded, which, however, was opened for him.
The interrogatory began about eleven o'clock and lasted about an hour and a quarter. Three members of my community were seized as deserters and placed under close arrest. They were told to make ready to leave for the barracks and were conducted under escort to the dormitories to make the necessary changes in their clothing. None of these young men, as I understand, come within the scope of the Military Service Act, or of any subsequent Order in Council, our order being moreover strictly and exclusively a religious order. A telephone message was sent to the Hon. Minister of Justice at Ottawa. Thereupon he communicated with the A.A.G. who stayed the unjustifiable proceedings. After much telephoning to London and to Ottawa Captain Macauley and his party left our house at 1.40 a.m.
I now beg to protest as strongly as I can against this outrageous conduct. If the Militia Department of Ottawa needs any information about the Novitiate at Guelph, I will do all in my power to furnish it. If the Military authorities of this district wish to ascertain for themselves the status of this house and of its members, I will give them every facility for so doing. But I will not submit without protest to the.wholesale indignity of having my house invaded at night, of having the gates of the grounds closed and a guard set over them, and of having a cordon of police on patrol around the buildings, as was done last night. I will not accept in silence the base imputation that this religious community is in league with deserters to evade the law, nor can I tolerate in the least degree that such an odious impression be made on the public mind as undoubtedly must be made by such a preposterous display of force. For the only inference that can be drawn from such special treatment, from the unwarranted and high handed manner of the whole proceedings, which we regard as an insult not merely to ourselves but to the Catholics of the Dominion and to all decent men, is that we must indeed be what ignorant and often confuted factions have made us out to be, double-dealing, dangerous men, who can be made to obey the just law of the land only at the point of the bayonet.
This morning when Captain Macauley called he seemed at pains to minimize the events of last night. He excused himself for the number of men he had brought with him from London on the plea that he did not know what violence he might have to contend with. This is almost on a par with the disappointed credulity of those searchers who poked into the

alcoves of the dormitories and even into the latrines, and were amazed to And only bareness and simplicity where they hoped to raise startling mysteries.
Captain Macauley assured the A.G. that there had been no friction of any kind. This is true in the sense that on our part he met throughout with unfailing courtesy; that the delay caused in the beginning, due to his failure to show proper written authorization, was qualified by the assurance of our readiness to comply under proper procedure; that we even gave refreshments to all his party, most of whom had spent several hours in the cold. But it is not true in the sense that we did not most deeply feel and resent the opprobrious treatment to which we were so unjustly and unjustifiably subjected.
It is not for me to say who is to blame for such an unprecedented manner of acting, but this I will say, that it would be. hard to devise a clumsier or more exasperating manner of extorting Information which a polite letter or visit would have readily elicited, than that of bringing a posse of armed men from London to Guelph to a peaceable religious house.
It is thanks to the Hon. Minister of Justice and to the prompt and courteous intervention of Major General Ashton that a very painful situation was somewhat softened and a much more oritical situation averted. A repetition of such an indignity would be bad for the country at large. Is it too much to hope that those .who have such large discretionary powers as those enjoyed by the Provost Marshal should be possessed of at least ordinary consideration and tact, and not permit themselves to become in any way the instruments of bigotry?
It is not the intention that this letter should be published. The same motives that promoted us to endure with patience what we considered unjust and high-handed treatment rather than to create a scene, prompt us now to withhold from the press anything of a nature to excite public opinion. If, however, untrue and defamatory accounts of the events complained of should be circulated, it may become necessary to publish this letter, adding, if need be, some further details.
Incidents of this nature become known very rapidly and so strange a proceeding could soon be reported not only in Canada but also in the United States and elsewhere, causing a great deal of ill-feeling and possibly religious strife, which at all times is most deplorable, but especially when the exigencies of war demand a closely united people.
I am, Sir,
Your very respectfully,
(Sgd.) H. Bourque, Reotor of St. Stanislaus' Novitiate, Guelph, Ontario.
The instructions contained in the Order in Council regarding the right of search were advisedly made very explicit and were well defined, so that a man could not make a search in any place without first receiving proper written instructions from a superior authority. Everybody in my department has been warned that in connection with any action taken under the Military Service Act they must use the greatest possible discretion and courtesy. When I received that
[Major-General Mewburn.]
letter I was horrified at the manner in which this officer had performed his duty.
Did the minister consult Captain Macauley and get his version of the case?
Had the students in the Novitiate presented themselves for registration and received certificates of exemption?

I understand from the report received after this took place, that the Novitiate had failed in its duty to give the names of those who were in the institution. I did not see any certificates of exemption.
Has the minister a record of the number of times that Westoby, Macauley, and the London office asked the Novitiate for the very information which he is prepared to produce to-day?

I am speaking only from memory, but I understand that upon at least two occasions the Novitiate were asked by the registrar under the Military Service Act for a list of the names and they failed to furnish it.

They were asked
twenty times.

Seeing that one account of this raid, so to speak, has been laid before the House, would it not be well for us to have the other side of the matter, that is, Captain Macauley's account of it. We would then be in a position to judge the matter better.

I could give the House the benefit of all the information I have including the names of all in the Novitiate, but I wish to carry out as far as possible the wishes of the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes), and I inferred that there would be an investigation when all the original documents would be produced.
I just wish to touch on one more point, because the hon. member (Sir Sam Hughes) referred to it. He spoke in regard to the son of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) who, I deeply regret, is not here to-day, because this touches him personally and through his department. I was aware that the son of the Minister of Justice was in the Novitiate, and long before this raid took place we were informed that he was not of military age, that he was medically unfit, and that there were medical certificates from three military medical officers in Montreal stating that he was unfit.
A private board.
I know there were three medical officers examined him.

I notice that the hon.
member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) denies that. I have a personal information as to that fact myself.

If I may be permitted to say so, I have defended Judge Doherty's son. I do not think he was entitled to go at all; I never did; but he had not a certificate from a military medical board; though he had certificates from private doctors.

He was turned down by
the board.

speakeroldname: Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Acting Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The subject covered by
the motion of the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) and referred to by the Minister of Militia (Major-General Mewburn), has in one form or another been before the Government for many months, and has absorbed throughout the country a degree of attention which I humbly venture to suggest is out of proportion to its importance.
When the question first came up in June, 1918, I personally, being overseas, had no knowledge whatever of the circumstances, but on my assumption of the duties of Acting Minister of Justice in November, 1918, the subject very soon came to my attention. I think it was toward the end of that month that a deputation headed by the reverend gentleman the hon. member for Victoria has referred to, the Rev. Mr. Palmer, waited upon certain members of the Government to make a plea for an investigation into what they called the Novitiate affair in Guelph. That deputation was composed of other reverend gentlemen besides the Rev. Mr. Palmer, and accompanying it were certain members of Parliament. The subject at the time was carefully reviewed in the presence of the Acting Prime Minister, of the Minister of Militia, and of myself; possibly other ministers .were present as well. A statement was then read before the ministers. which statement, how'ever, appeared to be for the most part a recital of reports, and contained nothing in the way of definite allegations and nothing, in our judgment, upon which the investigation which they sought could with any propriety be hung. The Acting Prime Minister at that time made it very clear to those present that if anything in the nature of charges of impropriety were brought by responsible persons to the attention of the Government -anything in the nature of specific allegations of fact that constituted wrong-doing on the part either of members of the Gov-

eminent or of officers of the Government, or of any one under the Government's control-necessarily an appropriate investigation would have to take place, and that the Government stood prepared, when that was done, to deal with the matter as such matters are properly dealt with by a government. Should those charges when so made involve the integrity and public conduct of a minister of the Crown, it would, of course, become necessary that they should be communicated to the Prime Minister, and the Prime Minister would then take into consideration the proper course to pursue.
I understood from the members of that delegation that they would proceed to formulate charges of that character. I knew or heard nothing further about the matter for some time thereafter, when I noticed in the press a statement to the effect that these charges would not be formulated or presented. Later on, however, and indeed very recently, I was informed that such charges were to be formulated, and we then stood prepared, as we had stood prepared all along, to recommend the appointment of a commission or some appropriate tribunal to investigate anything that could be said in such definite and meaningful language that a commission could address itself to the task of ascertaining the truth or falsity of the charges made. On last Thursday night, I think it was, there was communicated to the Acting Prime Minister a document signed by the Rev. Kennedy H. Palmer which the hon. member for Victoria reads to-day. I rather understand the hon. member endorses this schedule of charges and follows it by certain allegations which for convenience he summarizes towards the close of his remarks but which had not been brought to my attention until I heard them from his lips this afternoon. Consequently, as to these latter it will be impossible for me to deal with them with that degree of care and consideration which such a matter demands. However, I wish to make some reference in the House to the document presented by a responsible citizen, the Rev. Mr. Palmer, last Thursday night.
The first charge reads as follows:
The Department of Justice at Ottawa interfered with the Military . Board at Guelph in their efforts to obtain information as to the status of the inmates of the Guelph Novitiate.
In this connection it is proper, I think, to remark that among the duties of the Department of Justice is a supervision, from the legal standpoint, of all the de-

partments of government, to the end that the activities of every department may be conducted within their proper legal limitations. Consequently, it might be quite the fact that the Department of Justice would interfere with some specific act of another department, and provided that act were not within the limits of the law, the Department of Justice might be justified in so doing, if the circumstances of the moment made interference necessary in the public interest. There might, therefore, be such a thing as interference on the part of the Department of Justice of the nature alleged in the first charge, which interference would not necessarily be improper. On the other hand, there might be interference which would be wholly improper. Consequently, to constitute the first allegation something in the nature of a charge of improper or wrongful conduct on t'he part of either of a member of the Government or of any officer of the department, the word "improper" or some word to that effect should be read into the first sentence.
The second charge is to this effect:
That in doing so, the department extended special privileges to an institution which should have been treated like any other institution.
I would be the last to intimate to the House that any institution in this country should be treated differently from any other, and if any action of the Department of Justice resulted in discrimination in favour of or against any institution, then that action was ipso facto an improper action.
The third charge is to this effect:
That the Hon. C. J. Doherty interfered with Captain A. C. Macauley on the night of June 7th, while he, Captain Macauley was carrying out the instructions of his superior officers.
The remarks which I made bearing on the first allegation apply just as clearly and with equal force to the third. The fourth allegation is this:
That the Department of Justice, through its minister, prevented the placing in military service of young men of military age residing in the institution.
It will be very apparent to you, Mr. Speaker, and to every hon. member of this House that the Department of Justice might have done exactly what is stated in clause 4, and have been acting only in the discharge of its duties. There were thousands of young men of military age in this country, who under the Military Service Act, were exempt for various reasons, and one of the duties of the Department of Justice in the enforcement of the Act was

to see that such exemptions were duly exempted. Consequently it is manifest, beyond the possibility of question, that some allegation of impropriety would require to be inserted in clause 4 of this document before there would be anything which, if it were established before an investigation board, would constitute an offence or a wrong-doing on the part of the administrative authorities. The fifth reads:
That the press censorship instituted hy a minister of the Crown intensified the feeling that special protection was being given to the institution at Guelph.
I do not think that this could have been worded as intended by the draftsman of the document-tha,t the press censorship, instituted by v, minister, intensified feeling. The press censorship may have been wrong or it may have been right; it may or it may not have intensified feeling. But the question whether or not it intensified feeling is not at all dependent on whether it was right or wrong, and for the life of me,
I can see nothing in clause 5, in its present wording, to constitute anything
5 p.m. that could be inquired into and which, if it were found to be true, would necessarily involve either a minister or an officer in any wrong-doing or malfeasance.
Such is the document that was then presented; and, generally speaking, I think it is about as wide as the summary presented by the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) to-day.
In what I have to say as to the recommendation I shall make in regard to the charges of Mr. Palmer, I wish to be understood as applying as well to any additional matter in the way of a specific charge as to this affair that may be included in the entire address of the hon. member for Victoria this afternoon.
As to the attitude of the Department of Justice at 'the present time, the position in which I find myself is not by any means one that is free from difficulty. I am in the position of Acting Minister of Justice, and am of course responsible for the department and for all that is done in it while I hold that position. At the same time I speak in this Parliament as well on behalf of the minister. By the supplementary words that I think must be taken $s implied in the charges made by Mr. Palmer, the minister himself-assuming those words to be implied or inserted is charged with something that can be properly denominated an impropriety, something at all events in the nature of malfeasance
of office. Were the minister present in person he might take the course which I think I would take if my name were substituted for his in this document, namely, to review in detail all the circumstances connected with 'the transaction, as, for example, to, take the name of each individual who was within the institution at the time in question and to make an argument in full in defence, accompanied by the presentation of evidence, precisely as might be done in 'the final investigation itself. That, I think, is the course I would pursue. But as representing the minister, and without direct authority from him, I do not feel I would be justified in anticipating judicial investigation, and in disclosing the evidence that would necessarily have to be brought to the attention of the tribunal of inquiry. I think, rather, it is my duty to enter a statement of the final conclusions which the Department oi Justice desires to be recorded as its conclusion, and to place on record as well a statement which I have received from the Minister of Justice as.to the allegations contained in this document. Before doing so, however, I feel bound to say that after examination of all the fadts brought before the department, the Deputy Minister of Justice. has furnished me with a document which, if it is correct-and all this may be inquired into-would go to show that not one single novice or individual in the institution at the time of the raid or, I think, at any subsequent time, was liable for military service.
In this connection I wish to bring to the attention of the House a distinction which some hon. members seem to have overlooked. The Military Service Act, as drafted, established certain qualifications which would entitle an applicant to exemption under that Act. If he was entitled to exemption his business was to prove his right to it and to obtain a certificate. There was another feature. The Act under section 2 stated that all men described therein came under its operation, with the exception oi those mentioned in the schedule at the end of the Act. Now, the schedule was one of exceptions and not of grounds of exemption at all; and any one coming within the four corners of this schedule of exemptions was not within the operation of the Act. In this respect the Act followed the principle adopted by the British Act and I think, by t'he American Act as well. Included in these exceptions are, first, men who hold certificates granted under this Act, and

That question as to whether these students did come under that classification or not was still a question of doubt that had not been settled by the Government at the time of this so-called raid.

The report of the Deputy Minister of Justice which we have on file, and rvhich I will read to the House if desired, was to the effect that on the facts submitted there were none of the members liable except three as to whom there might be doubt. The names of the three were given and as to them further inquiry was suggested. Now I see no reason why I should not make as plain as I can to hon. members here what constitutes, at all events, one of the points which has aroused confusion and doubt and which has created very much of the difficulty that has arisen over this institution. The wording of the exception is this:

I do not know whether J have made myself clear but that was what the discussion was about at the time and the minister I think said something to the effect that one year, or perhaps more than one year, would be required to put in by a student before he received the tonsure.
As to that, of course, I do not make myself responsible; the debate will have to speak for itself, and the minister will answer for himself and for what he said at that time.
Now, I have outlined what has been presented to me as one of the matters in dispute, and it occurs to me that it would be well that the subjects referred for investigation should be so wide, and the tribunal oi such a character, that a reference might be made of that question, so that at all events the opinion of the commission may be obtained. On the other hand, the opinion of the Department of Justice in this regard has not been something in the nature of a fortress that no man could overthrow. There was an appeal. This question could have been taken at any time before a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada, who acted as Central Appeal Judge under the Military Service Act. I am not sure, I have not made inquiries, but possibly this very point has come before Mr. Justice Duff, in the discharge of his duties as Senior Appeal Judge. So that if the ruling of the department on that point of law was believed to be wrong, there was always a door open

through which appeal could be taken and a final determination of the subject gained.
I will say only this: That having reviewed the record, in so far as it is now in the Department of Justice, and having received from the Minister of Justice a full account of his connection with the subject, in June, 1918, and since, I have no reason at all to come to any other conclusion than that his whole relation to the affair, and his conduct throughout, was only what would become a conscientious and competent minister of the Crown and a gentleman. I have received from him to-day a specific denial of the allegations contained in Mr. Palmer's statement, and that denial he asked me to read to Parliament, and in it he says: The imputations made with regard to his action, and that of the Department of Justice in respect to the Guelph Novitiate are entirely baseless. The facts as ascertained by the Militia Department fully establish this. He will welcome any inquiry by which, in the judgment of his colleagues, the public interests may be served.
It would seem to me, in view of the nature of the problem that now confronts the House, and of the nature of the investigation that will be most useful and most appropriate, that the commission that is to so investigate, should be composed of a judge, or judges. And I believe,- assuming that Mr. Palmer will agree,-that where in the points I mention, allegations do not amount to a charge of wrong-doing, there should be inserted or agreed to be implied therein, some word of the nature of " improper." Assuming that he will agree to that, so that there really may be wrong-doing alleged, and something to investigate, I propose to recommend that a Royal Commission issue for the investigation of these charges, and that the powers of the commission shall be wide so as to embrace anything of a specific charge of impropriety affecting the same matter that can be gathered from the remarks of the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) this afternoon, and so ample in scope that the whole matter can be searched to the bottom.
There is nothing to conceal on the part of the Department of Militia-of that I am quite certain from the minister-and I beg to assure the House that on the part of the Department of Justice there is equally nothing to conceal. The Minister of Justice at present is several thousand miles from here, but it is our hope that it will not be long before he returns. I am sure that the member for Victoria would be the last to [iMr. Meigrhen.]
suggest that proceedings should be taken by way of this motion until he does return and has full opportunity to put in his defence. Consequently, with the intimation that the commission shall be able to act as soon as the minister returns-at all events that it shall be appointed upon his return-and that it shall be ample and wide enough to cover the charges alleged, I ask leave to suggest that such be the form of investigation, and that in the meantime the motion standing in the name of the hon. member for inquiry of another kind be withdrawn.

I have listened with a great deal of attention to the speeches which have been delivered this afternoon on the motion made by my hon. friend from Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes). I now gather from the remarks of the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen! that a Royal Commission will issue so that a thorough investigation may take place of the hon. gentleman's charges. As to the resolution itself, it is thus worded:
That, in the opinion of this House, in view of the statements made public in relation to the Guelph Novitiate during the month of June, 1918, and the circumstances and facts concerning those and other similar charges concerning the evasion by young men and the connivance of others to defeat the ends and aims of the Military Service Act and other Acts and Orders relating to the upbuilding of the military forces of Canada, it is advisable that a select committee of this House be appointed to inquire into the matter with full authority to examine witnesses under oath, to pay necessary - expenses and to report to this House.
Mr. Speaker, 1 daresay, although I hold no brief for the Jesuit Order, that the reverend gentlemen from Guelph, and the members of that Order generally in Canada, will welcome any investigation that may be ordered by the Government under that resolution. But the Acting Minister of Justice will notice that this is a very broad resolution because the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) proposes to inquire into:
" other similar charges concerning the evasion by young men and the connivance by others to defeat the ends and aims of the Military Service Act."
The proposed inquiry would therefore apply to other charges as well as to those which affect the Guelph institution.
Mr. ME.IGHEN: The investigation would be upon the charges, as stated by me, contained in the Rev. Mr. Palmer's statement, and anything else relating to the same matter that can be gathered from the speech of the hon. member for Victoria.

If the Government intended to have such a wide investigation through a Royal Commission, I would say that those Cabinet ministers who instigated the exemptions for fanners' sons in the province of Ontario should he brought before it. Because I find, Mr. Speaker, that during the election of 1917 very wily cir- _ culars were issued, especially in the province of Ontario, by means of which the farmers were invited specifically to disregard the Military Service Act. In these circulars the farmers were told not to mind the consequences, their sons would remain on the farm and not be called upon to bear arms. I am very positive in my statement because I have one of those very circulars under my hand, and which reads as follows :
The Farmers Will Be Protected.
Union Ministers Issue Statement.
Ottawa, December 3, 1917. General Mewburn, Minister of Militia, states : Farmers coming within Class A called out for military service, who are actually employed upon a farm in the production of foodstuffs for Canada and her Allies, and whose services are necessary in the work of such farm, will be exempted from military service.
If their claim for exemption is not allowed by the tribunal, an immediate appeal should be made. Arrangements are being made to extend the time for such appeals. The Minister of Miliita further states that if the farmer so called out for military service who is now honestly employed in the production of foodstuffs should be drafted into the army. General Mewburn feels it will be his duty to relieve hem from millitary service on the condition that he returns to the farm and Continues to be so employed.
Then, we have a long letter written by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. J. D. Reid) to some candidates in Ontario, telling them in effect "Do not mind; you can restore the waning faith of the farmers. Tell them not to he afraid; we have taken all the necessary precautions to ensure that these farmers' sons will not be called to arms."
I regret indeed that the scope of the investigation twill not permit such evidence to be adduced as I mentioned a moment ago. Evidently a very crafty appeal was made to the electors of rural Ontario. First, the Minister of Militia and Defence-he is such an honest minister that I think he did not devise this scheme himself. In fact, I am told that the master of the administration, the man who owned the Government at that time, Sir Clifford Sifton, is the man who initiated this proceeding; it is said that he came hurriedly back to Ottawa after a survey of the constituencies
and told the Government that the dictum of the Minister of Militia and Defence would not be sufficient and that a test case should be taken at once before Mr. Justice Duff, the Central Appeal Judge, to whom my hon. friend a moment ago referred. So the test case came before Mr. Justice Duff, and, of course, the promise made by my good friend the Minister of Militia and Defence was thus implemented in time, and the elections were won. As the member for Victoria says, there was then "evasion by young men and the connivance of others to defeat the ends and aims of the Military Service Act." I would like to have that charge fully and thoroughly investigated, so that the good farmers of Ontario and the members of the Ministerial Association of that province may see clearly how they were doped during that election and what a fraud and a sham was the administration of the Military Service Act. Any fair-minded citizen, any broadminded member of the House of Commons, whether he be Roman Catholic or Protestant, will admit with me that the raid organized against the Guelph Novitiate in the dead of night on the 7th of June last spells humiliation, spells indignity, bitterness and disunion in Canada. Sir, we live in a British country, and any British country can claim to be a free country; but it cannot be a Dee country if a religious minority is not respected.
I must thank the Minister of Militia and Defence for the very frank statement he made to the House this afternoon. He read from the beginning to end the dignified protest he received from the rector of the Novitiate at Guelph. He acted the part of a man of honour when he sent that apology to the Novitiate after he had received the protest from the rector in June last. Now, what, briefly stated, are the facts?
One thing that I remember in my practice of law is a dictum of Mr. Justice Johnston, one of the brightest judges who ever sat on the bench in the district of Montreal. He once said to a jury: "Gentlemen of the jury, when I was a young man I read a book the suggestive title of which was: 'Put yourself in his place.' You are now about to pass judgment on the prisoner at the bar; your duty is to put yourself in his place." Mr. Speaker, in relating briefly the facts concerning the raid on the Guelph Novitiate on the 7th of June last, I ask every fair-minded Protestant to put himself in the place of the rector of that Catholic institution.
On the 7th of June-not at noon, not at three o'clock in the afternoon, not even at

six o'clock, but at 9.30 at night-three men appear suddenly in the parlour of the institution, wearing plain clothes, and, without any parleying with the rector of the Novitiate, give a general order to parade all the members of the Novitiate within five minutes.
The first thing that the rector asked of the gentlemen who appeared to lead the other two was to produce the authority with which he was vested. The member for Victoria said a moment ago that his authority was his brassard. But Captain Macauley did not wear his brassard; he had it in his pocket, and when he was asked by the rector to produce his authority he took this brassard from his pocket and said: "Here is my authority."
Let me point out to the member for Victoria that the Guelph Novitiate is not a farm; it is a college.
Then the rector went to the telephone to consult the counsel of the institution. Then Father Hingston appeared. Father Kingston is a Jesuit, son of the late Sir William Hingston, who was a member of the Senate and one of the leading physicians of Canada-indeed, of America. Father Hingston, as I insisted on a moment ago, was just back from the front where he had served as a member of the Canadian Expeditionary Force-here he was under military garb in that institution. So that the gentlemen from London and from Guelph who were so nervous at that moment lest the institution would shelter evaders and slackers could well have confided their consciences to Father Hingston, then Captain Hingston, a gentleman who had served his King and his country, and who had lost his younger brother on the battlefield of Flanders. It was only at the moment that Father Hingston appeared that Captain Macauley gave his name and produced his brassard as the symbol of his authority, and then, on being further questioned, produced a typewritten letter which purported to give his authority.
Mr. MURPHY; A copy.

A copy of a letter purporting to give him the necessary authority. The passage which seemed relevant and on which he based his right of search was substantially as follows:
Any officer or non-commissioned officer, acting under written authorization
