of G.O.C. or O.C. of a military district or area, if he has good grounds for believing that deserters or defaulters under the Military Service Act are being harboured or concealed after 	-
reasonable demand of entrance and refusal thereof, and upon producing the aforesaid written authorization, may forcibly enter and search the premises. -
When Captain Macauley was asked for the written authority mentioned in the instructions, he could produce none, and yet he insisted on having the whole order paraded before him at that late hour. Moreover he threatened, lie was not going to listen to any parleying, and he began putting questions to three or four members of the Order who were present in the parlour. Then Captain Hingston registered a last protest against a search without proper authorization. Overlooking the irregularity of the proceedings, the Rector invited Captain Macauley to visit the bedrooms or dormitories, or if he preferred, offered to summon all the members of the Novitiate to the refectory. Captain Macauley chose this latter alternative. While he appeared to have come there with only three men, as a matter of fact-and I wish to impress this on the House-he had come within the precincts of the Novitiate with three men, but there was a cordon of eleven other men around tne premises anu the gates of the institution were closed and guarded by one of the eleven.

I know the hon.
member does not want to mislead the House. Captain Macauley took three men into the house with him, as is admitted by all parties, and there were eight more outside.

Between my hon. friend and the Rector of the Novitiate my heart is in the balance, but I have the words of the Rector that there were three men with Captain Macauley and eleven around the building, fourteen in all.
There were eleven altogether.

The interrorgatory began about eleven o'clock and lasted about an hour and a quarter. Three members of the community were seized as deserters and placed under close arrest. They were told to make ready to leave for the barracks and were conducted under escort to the dormitories to make the necessary changes in their clothing. None of these' young men were within the scope of the Military Service Act, or of any of the subsequent Orders in Council, as has been clearly established by the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen). They all come within the exceptions under the Schedule to the Military Service Act.
6. Clergy, including members of any recognized order of an exclusively religious character,

and ministers of all religious denominations existing in Canada at the date of the passing of this Act.
The three men were about to follow Captain Macauley as far as the barracks when a telephone message from the Adjutant General at Ottawa was received, staying the unjustifiable proceedings, and after much telephoning between London and Ottawa, when one of the officers from Guelph reminded Captain Macauley that he was not acting within the military law, Captain Macauley left and returned at 12.40 in the morning, after having accepted the courtesies of the Order and partaken of the delicacies offered by them. All this occurred in the refectory at a late hour, and to show how those sinister Jesuits are. they who are supposed to eat at least one Protestant a day, the members of the Order placed before them the delicacies of the refectory, and the officers and men all left well pleased with the hospitality they had received. The action that was taken was most unwarranted; it was a high-handed way of dealing with the citizens of a free country like Canada, It is true that next morning Captain Macauley went and excused himself; but The "heather was afire," the harm was done, because the news had been telegraphed to all parts of the Dominion, and possibly to Europe. ' The Press and pulpit denounced the double dealing of those sinister Jesuits. The rector addressed a dignified protest to the Minister of Militia and Defence, and the latter answered in the same manly way that he has spoken this afternoon. This is the letter sent by the minister to the rector of the Novitiate on the 11th June from Ottawa:
M.y dear Sir,-I am just in receipt of youi letter of the 8th instant on my return to Ottawa, and iwords cannot express to you my deep regret of the action taken toy the Deputy Provost Marshal, Captain Maoauley, on the evening of the 7th instant.
My attention was called to the matter on my arrival in Ottawa this morning and I And that my Adjutant General has taken immediate action for a most thorough investigation, and if the facts are as stated in your letter-which of course I do not doubt-1 can assure you that the error in judgment committed by this officer will he dealt with in a proper way, as I will not tolerate any such action on the part of any military officer as far as the operation of the Military Service Act goes.
As I have already stated, I deeply regret this occurrence and I thank you for your frank letter.
The question of the liability for military service of any of your students is a matter that is now being considered by the Department of Justice.
Believe me.
Tours faithfully, (Sgd.) S. C. Mewburn.
This apology having boon made, every one thought the matter would remain at rest, but the agitators throughout Ontario began pouring accusation upon accusation upon the Guelph Novitiate, and they, in self defence, although there was a special censorship for this special case, insisted that the facts should be made known to the people of Canada.
Later on, on June 22nd, a statement was issued by the Department of Militia and Defence as follows:-
A list of the members of the Novitiate of
military age, together with the dates on which they entered the order, has been furnished by the adjutant-general, the ages being stated as accurately as is possible without the production of official certificates.
From this it appears that there are now in the community thirty-five men of military age, of whom twenty-five entered the order before the first proclamation under the Military Service Act, on October 13, 1917, the greater number of them having entered during the year of 1915-16, or earlier.
It seems clear on the information available that there can be no question hut that all the young men, except the two named, are free from liability to military service by virtue of the fifth exception in the schedule to the Military Service Act, which exoepts all members of an order of an exclusively religious character, which the St. Stanislaus' Novitiate undoubtedly is. The same exception applies to men affected by the order in Council of April 20, 1918.
It appears that the son of the Minister of Justice entered the order on March 30. 1918, when he was under no liability under the Military Service Act. Before taking this step he presented himself for a medical examination before physicians, of whom two were members of -the Medical Board of Review in Montreal, and their finding was that his condition was such that it would be necessary to place him in Category E, which would make it impossible for him to undertake military service.
The result of the investigation indicates that the inquiries instituted were justified, and the Department of Militia will take steps to insure that any members of the Novitiate liable under the Military Service Act will be required to serve.
In this statement it is said that there were two members of the order liable at that time. These two members were John Holland and John O'Halloran. It was found later that John Holland came under the fifth exception in the schedule to the Military Service Act, as he became a cleric on September 9, 1917. A copy of certificate of his ordination is now in the possession of the Department of Militia and Defence, Ottawa. John O'Halloran was found to be an American citizen, and therefore not liable under the Act. His birth certificate and certificate of his father's naturalization as an American are also in the hands of the department. So, not one of those who were

Mr. Speaker, I am led to support the resolution moved by my hon. friend from Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) because of the circumstances surrounding this incident in connection with the Jesuit Novitiate at Guelph. The facts have been stated so fully both by the hon. member for Victoria and by the hon. the Minister of Militia and Defence (Major-General Mewburn) that it is unnecesary for me to go over them again. But the very fact that the authorities of this institution resisted an investigation by the military authorities was bound to lead to a good deal of dissatisfaction in that neighbourhood and, as the news spread, throughout the whole of Ontario and the other provinces. The members of the Ministerial Association of Guelph only took the matter up when it had been pressed upon them from several different sources. The first parties to raise an objection to what was being done at the Novitiate were the members of the Reman Catholic faith in the city of Guelph. They saw their boys being drafted, and some of them enlisting, and then they saw their neighbour's sons of the same faith going into the Novitiate and escaping service. They learned from the statements of the military authorities that the
rector, and those in charge of the college, were refusing to give the information that the military authorities required and which they were bound to give under the Act. That tended to further excite feeling in the city of Guelph.
il believe that every impartial man, no matter what his faith may be, will agree that the circumstances surrounding this case ought to be investigated judicially. At least I can quote one man in my own city, the Rev. Father Minehan, who stated publicly that after what had been said in connection with this institution he was of the opinion that there should be an investigation. This is a matter affecting not one particular class of the people only, but, I believe, that every person having a knowledge of the facts, and a knowledge of the rumours and reports which were going around, was anxious to have an investigation.
Perhaps he was one of the conspirators.

If he was one of the conspirators I do not think he was conspiring to the injury of the rector of the institution or any person connected with it. The conduct of the Ministerial Association of Guelph was admirable. These men had gone to their own congregations and urged all their young men to enlist. One Presbyterian minister went so far as to report a young man in his congregation who was eligible and who was trying to escape. By reporting that young man to the authorities, he drove the young man's family from his congregation. They resented his action but I am glad of what he did because it shows you that the men who went after the Novitiate and asked for >an investigation in this case had done everything in their power to get every person they could influence to do his duty under the Military Service Act. You have a group of men acting in that way and, under those circumstances, is it any wonder that they should resent what they saw and what the military authorities told them was going on in the Novitiate?
It was not only the citizens of Guelph that came to them and told them what was going on, buo the men who were charged with the enforcement of the Military Service Act in Guelph reported to the Ministerial Association that they had tried over and over again to get the information that it was necessary for them to get from the authorities of that institution and that they had been refused. [DOT]



Up to the time that Captain Macauley made his visit to the institution, very many attempts had been made to avoid anything like a raid, to avoid force, 'to avoid anything that complaint might be made about and to get the information in as reasonable and easy a way as the authorities of the college could give it. Is it any wonder that in the city, as well as over the whole countryside, there should be a great deal of excitement? Is it any wonder that the press censorship and the fact that the daily papers in Guelph and Toronto were notified that nothing was to be said about this institution, or about the visits of Captain Macauley and his officers to it, should have increased the excitement and intensified the resentment that the people felt over this oase? The rector and those in authority acting with him were responsible for this excitement. If they had observed the law they would have reported all the men who were there at least for registration. If the rector had been willing to give the names to Captain Westoby when asked for them instead of putting obstacles in the way, and if, when he had been called upon, 'he had thrown open all the doors and said, " Come in, and see what is here, and whom you think you have a right to take," this trouble would have been avoided. That is what the chancellors and the rectors of all the other universities and colleges up our way did. There was no military raid at Victoria, Knox, Wycliffe or Trinity colleges. In none of these colleges would you find a man who was of military age. But Captain Macauley apparently thrust the case upon the authorities in Ottawa and he got instructions to visit the institution and, because he could not get in by their leave/ he went in by force, as he had a right to do.
I am entirely in agreement with the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) when he says that the very method that Captain Macauley took to get in there was designed to allay excitement and to prevent anything like a disturbance. If he had marched through the city of Guelph, as he might have done, with a force of men, there would have been a group of people following him and if a crowd from Guelph had gone out that night there might have been much more serious consequences than happened. Whether he violated some military red tape or not, I do not know, but in my judgment he acted wisely and he adopted the course that enabled him to accomplish his purpose without trouble. This visit

w'as made in a wray to which objection cannot be taken. It certainly is not at all to be compared in violence with the method that was adopted in the city of Toronto by the head of the military police there who went into social functions, the Y.M.C.A., and all kinds of institutions to drag young men out. He would go where a dance was being held as he did one night to the Knights of Columbus Hall. He would not give these young men time to go home and get their exemption papers, some of them having been exempted; he took them away. He went down to the boat when the ball games were on and every man who did not have his paper he apprehended. That is the way the law was enforced in Toronto, and if that is not a good deal rougher an 1 more inconsiderate than anything that happened in Guelph, I am very much mistaken. When that kind of thing was going on in Toronto, Hamilton, and Guelph itself, is it surprising that a great deal of excitement and dissatisfaction existed when this institution refused to open its doors and show who were there? That in itself is the cause of the trouble that has arisen. I am inclined to think, Sir, that the Superior of the order which is represented in Guelph at St. Stanislaus College shares in the opinion that I hold myself that the rector of that institution acted very unwisely because we find that immediately after the raid took place the rector was removed to some other sphere of action. He may have been promoted, or he may have been removed for some other cause, but we know that he did not enhance the reputation of his institution by the course that he pursued because he brought upon it a great deal of criticism that was entirely unnecessary and would never have been levelled against it if he had acted in a different way.
Now my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) talks about the respect that is due a religious minority. Mr. Speaker, I have respect for every man's religious beliefs ; I have respect for a religious minority. I think that in a matter of a man's religious belief, whether he be a Mohammedan, a Hindu, or anything else, if he honestly believes in those religious opinions, he has a right to practise them and he ought to be protected in practising them, and as I understand the law of the country and the sentiment of the people he will be protected. But a religious minority should not be exempted from performing its duty at a crisis such as we were in at that time. A

man cannot claim that because he is a member of a small sect he should receive special consideration as a citizen. First and foremost, in time of war a citizen of Canada has to obey the military laws of the country. He cannot be exempted on that ground, and he should not ask for any special privileges because he is a member of a minority. I think that to advance arguments of that kind shows how remarkably weak the case is. The chancellors in Toronto colleges did not feel humiliated, and did not take it as an insult when the military police visited their institutions to ascertain whether they contained any men fit to go on service. That being so why should the rector of this institution feel humiliated? Yet that was the whole case made out by the hon. member for Maison-neuve; that this was a humiliation to the Guelph institution and those in charge of it, and that they were insulted by the military police going there. I do not think they had any reason to feel insulted. The head of any other institution of the same kind, that I know of, would not have regarded it as an insult. On the contrary he would have assisted in the investigation, and would have been glad to provide all the information that was in his power. 1 think such a pleads only drawing a red herring across the trail, and if that is the best excuse that the Rector of the Guelph institution has to offer I think he has very little indeed. It was no time for any man, whether the head of a college, or a bank, or a'factory, to be standing upon his dignity. Dignity is all right in its place, but when a man stands upon his dignity and resents the admission of properly constituted officers to examine whether the men in his place are fit and eligible for service, I think he is straining his regard for his own dignity, and I do not think it will have very much effect in that way. Then hon. gentlemen will notice the fact that there was a list of all the inmates in the college displayed the night that Captain Macauley visited the institution, but when he went back next day that list had been taken down and could not be found. Why remove those names unless there was some cause for it?
The Minister of Militia said he was not disposed to go into the Alexander case. "I do not think it is necessary to refer-here to the Alexander case," he said. I think that it is necessary, Mr. Speaker, to refer to it. I will put the Alexander case alongside of the Noonan case, and this is what happened. Alexander and Noonan were
both reported to the Militia Department. Alexander was employed by his father in the manufacture of war material. He asked for exemption, but was refused and was placed in khaki.

He volunteered.
Major-General MEWBURN:	He came
forward afterwards.

I thought he had been drafted. At any rate he was engaged in making munitions. Now place his case against that of Noonan. Noonan was playing baseball on a Guelph team, and when these proceedings arose he entered the Novitiate. In the one case a man was engaged in the manufacture of war materials and he was taken. In the other case a man was engaged in playing baseball and goes into the Novitiate and escapes service. IHow is it possible that the people of Guelph should not resent such unequal treatment given to two different young men in the same place? That kind of thing stirred the people up, and it is the reason for all the dissatisfaction and trouble that has occurred.
My hon. friend from Maisonneuve gave a long list of Jesuits who had served in the war. I have not got a list of ministers who went to the war, but I know scores of them who volunteered as privates and went out and did their work in the trenches, so that this service in the war was not all on one side. I think the ministers are entitled to the same consideration as any person else.
Now the Acting Minister of Justice tells us that these young men are not liable for service, and if I understood him aright the Deputy Minister of Justice is responsible for an opinion to that effect. If that is the case the members of this House who passed the Act certainly did so under very serious misapprehension. They passed the Act after having received an opinion from the Minister of Justice that warranted them in believing it was impossible for any man to hide in a college in the way complained of. This is the statement made by the Minister of Justice.-
On what page of Hansard is it to be found?

The statement which I am about to quote was made on July 19. 1917, and is to be found at page 3,568 of the revised Hansard. The minister was replying to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the then leader of the Opposition. He said:

The right hon. leader of the Opposition will recognize that the theological student, from the moment he gets his tonsure, or minor orders, which he does at the end of his first year-or, at all events, that is the general practice-enters and forms part of the clergy.
My right hon. friend shakes his head? I am not making that statement without having verified it on the very best authority. I have satisfied myself beyond peradventure on that subject. So that that leaves, under the class to be covered as divinity students, so far as the Catholic colleges are concerned, only the young men just coming in, before they have got any orders.
Now, Mr. Speaker, these young men who went into the college-
Would the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him one question? My hon. friend has been speaking now' for a considerable length of time. Will he give one figure?	-
What figure would the hon. gentleman like?
I have just put it to the hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

I do not see that that question has any bearing on what I am quoting. Now I have quoted from the statement made by the Minister of Justice, on which this House voted. The members of the House at that time had the right to believe that the Minister of Justice was able properly to interpret the practice, and state it as accurately as any man here, because he himself was brought up in a college of the same order, and therefore one would suppose he would know the rules of that order. That is what the Minister of Justice said at that time, and that is what led this House to believe that it was impossible for a young man to enter a college and be exempted from military service simply by getting in there. Further, the rector of the institution is authority for the statement that any young man entering the institution could leave at any time within three years and change his whole course of life. Instead of remaining and preparing himself to be a member of that order, he could leave and become a physician or an engineer, or enter any profession. So that no young man entering that order is bound by any vows, he cannot be classed, I do not see how he can be, as a member of the clergy. And when we have regard to the way this Act was enforced against the clergy of other denominations, the proceedings in this case will appear most strange. Up at Sault Ste. Marie I knew a young man who had been for two years

preaching as a Methodist. He was a clergyman lacking but one thing-the single act of ordination. He had gone through all his studies, he had been on probation in the field, he had had charge of different congregations, and all he lacked of being a clergyman was that which is conferred by the ceremony of ordination, yet he was drafted under the Military Service Act. Notwithstanding that it is -claimed, I understand, by the Deputy Minister of Justice that the minute a young man went into this college he was exempt from military service. There is an inequality, an unfairness about that, which impresses anyone who does not understand the remarkably fine distinctions of the particular order concerned in this investigation. I submit, therefore, that the Government is justified in submitting this case, with all its attendant circumstances-the things that went before it and the things that followed after it-to a judicial inquiry to bring out the facts and let us see whether it was possible under the Act for a young man to go in there and immediately become immune from serving the country as our other young men had to serve the country. The matter will have to be established beyond peradventure in order to satisfy the people, because no good citizen wants to shirk his duty; every man objects and has a right to object to inequalities of service as between different classes of citizens. That there have been inequalities is a matter that does not admit of discussion. They have been so obtrusive and so extensive that it is not at all surprising that the people of Ontario in the neighbourhood of Guelph should be extremely excited about it and should demand an investigation into all the facts.

Mr. Speaker, if there is anything really disagreeable to me it is to take part in a discussion of this kind. I come from a province in which racial and religious questions are absolutely unknown; where a man, provided he is honest, is considered as a man and as a British citizen, no matter whether he is English or French, or Irish or any other nationality; no matter whether he is an Orangeman, a Catholic or a Protestant. We do not mind about these things in the province of Quebec. I regret to have to take part in a discussion of this kind, because after all that had been said on the other side of the House since the beginning of the session we were entitled to hope and believe that we are getting rid of all these questions, as to their being brought up in

tlie manner in which they have, the rules of the House do not permit me to qualify that at 'this moment.
Sir, we are discussing a question which affects the Jesuits. I do not wish to boast about my province, but to show you what is our mentality in the province of Quebec let me remind you of something that happened in 1888. Long years before, the Jesuits had been deprived of the properties of which they were the owners in the province of Quebec, properties worth millions of dollars at that time. Several times the Government of that province had been asked to settle the question of the Jesuits' properties, and when the Hon. Mr. Mercier was Premier of Quebec he decided to settle the question. The whole case was investigated and the Legislative Assembly of Quebec decided to vote $400,000 for the benefit of the Jesuits. But it was contended by some in the Legislative Assembly that a part of the population of the province of Quebec was Protestant; that this money was to be taken from the public funds and that, therefore, money of the Protestants was being taken to satisfy the Jesuits. Hon. Mr. Mercier then decided-he was supported by the whole Government-to give to the . Protestants of Quebec an amount of the $400,000 in -proportion to the English Protestant population. Accordingly, $60,000 was distributed to the Protestants of that province to dispose of as they wished; the balance was given to the Catholic bishops to dispose of as they saw fit. That is the kind of mentality we have in the province of Quebec; that is why you never hear such outrageous questions discussed there as the one which has been brought up to-day by the hon. gentleman.
The member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) declared a moment ago that nothing extraordinary was done at the Guelph Novitiate. He says that the same thing was done at the Toronto University; the same thing has been done in all the Protestant Universities and nobody was scandalized. But will he tell us whether the officers of the Department of Militia went to those universities to make investigations at 9.30 at night? If they had gone to the Guelph Novitiate in the day time no one would have had anything to say, but they 'thought that when everybody was in bed was the ' proper time to disturb and create trouble in that institution.
We are told by the member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) and by the member for Maisonneuve (Hon. Mr. Lemieux) that a cordon of soldiers was placed around the
building. The member for Victoria said that the order came from Ottawa to leave the Novitiate alone at night, thereby giving a chance to the Jesuits to. evade the law and escape their duty. As to that I shall answer later on; but I want to point out that I am not surprised at what has been said. 1 heard something more wonderful than that when I was a student at the Jesuits' college in Montreal. We were told-I was then a young man-'that there was a tunnel connecting the Jesuits' college with l'Hotel-Dieu, a hospital where nurses are tending the poor and the sick-and there were stupid asses who came to see if that was true. So, Sir, we need not be surprised at what we hear to-day.
My intention, Sir, is not to give any special attention to this Guelph business; it has been disposed of this afternoon in a most noble and generous way by the Minister of Militia (Major-General Mewburn), the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Meighen), and the member for Maisonneuve (Hon. Mr. Lemieux).
If the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) thinks for a moment that the Jesuits are trying to evade their responsibilities and to shirk their duties as citizens of Canada and of the British Empire, he does not understand the Jesuits at all. Let me give an illustration to show that he is absolutely in error, and-I trust he will take this in the right sense-that he does not know what he is speaking about. Much has been said this afternoon concerning Rev. Father Hingston, whom I know personally. It has been said that he has done service overseas. He has done more than that and credit must be given to him as well as to any other man who has done his bit for his country. Father Hingston was the promoter and the first recruiting officer of the Irish Rangers in Montreal. He was their chaplain, accompanying them to England and France, and when later on he was called back to this country, he did not think that he was through, but he went to the United States and delivered addresses wherever he had an opportunity of doing so for the benefit of the Allies.
Shirking their duties! Let me give another illustration. Rev. Father Arcand, Rector of St. Mary's College, when war was declared in 1914, asked the hon. Mr. Pate-naude, who was then a minister of the Cabinet, to send instructors to the college to drill the students. What was the answer given by the Government at that time? The answer was that they could not do that as it would be too expensive. Imagine

the Government becoming thrifty at that time. The Government also stated that St. Mary's College was the first college to make such a demand. Later on, this same Father Arcand came to Ottawa and asked the Government for permission to form a corjf? of students for overseas service. That permission was refused and I can give as authorities to support my statement, Judge Delorimier, Mr. O. S. Perreault, a most distinguished member of the Chambre de Commerce of Montreal and Mr. Laberge, a very distinguished architect of Montreal. This same Father Arcand came to Ottawa in order to get precise information as to what young boys of the college could do to help in producing foodstuffs. He addressed himself to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) who referred him to the Minister of Agriculture but no practical result ensued. May I add that the Jesuits of St. Mary's College were the first to relieve their students from attendance at school so as to permit them to fulfil their duties towards their country? I can go further to show my hon. friend that he is certainly ill-informed and absolutely wrong, and that he is, I have no doubt, unwittingly misleading the House when he tries to make the House believe that those Jesuits are endeavouring to shirk their duty and to save their students from fulfilling their duty.

I think the hon.
member is unintentionally doing me an injustice. I never in my lifetime referred to St. Mary's College. I could have referred to Mont St. Louis College which did its duty splendidly. It is the hon. member who is in error.

I have just this to answer to my hon. friend, that all the colleges of the community of Jesuits are, in solidarity, responsible one for the other, just as certain members of certain lodges are responsible for all the lodges.
Then I shall be only too glad to hold the whole Order of Jesuits responsible for the misconduct at Guelph.
Certainly you would.
Just one head, one general, one black coat.

It was in the afternoon on a Sunday in the month of May, 1918, that the students of St. Mary's College who were called to the colours, were convened in the sanctuary of the chapel. After the blessing of the Holy Sacrament, the rector, Rev. Father Arcand, addressed the boys as fol-
[Mr. Gladu.)
lows, and I must give credit to the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville (Mr. Gauthier) for having given me a copy of the speech:
Dear boys, the hour of departure has come for you. I have only this sentence to utter: Do your duty-do your duty to yourself, to your family, to your race, to your Alma Mater and to your country. We have done all that we could to give you the very best of education. You will hear that conscription is a bad law; that it is a curse. Do not listen to such expressions. It is the law of your country, and you owe it obedience. We will not let you go alone; two of our priests will follow you to the barracks and even on the firing line. They will be your comrades; they will do their duty as you will do yours.
But before entering into your new career, you have a last sacrifice to submit to. Go and bid good-bye to your mother. This task will cause you sorrow, but stand up like men, buckle your belt, conceal the tears in your eye, and let a smile be on your lips, so that your mother will not realize the enormity of the sacrifice imposed on you by your country.
I ask any fair-minded man in this House, no matter on what side he sits, if this is the language of a man who is endeavouring to shirk his duty and to teach his students that they should not fulfil theirs.
Let me give my hon. friend the name of another Jesuit who did something that was certainly worthy of notice. The patients in the pest house at St. Johns, in the province of Quebec, to which those suffering from contagious diseases are sent, asked for a chaplain to attend them. There -was a man who could not go overseas, not being of military age or fit for service at the front, but who was ready to face death in another form. He offered his services as chaplain at this pest house, and was locked in with all those sick people, and for months and months he has been facing death through breathing the poisoned breath of those poor soldiers. His name is Rev. Father George Lebel. Nobody in the outside world knows his name; his work at the pest house has received no recognition, but he has the satisfaction of having done his duty. He has done his duty, not as a soldier, not as an honorary colonel who needs a major-general to defend him; he was not a John Wesley Allison, but merely a Jesuit who offered his services without any remuneration whatever.
There is another Jesuit whom I will name -the Rev. Father Sigouin. He was unable to go to the front, but he was able to serve in other ways. He is giving all his time to re-education. The Jesuits have never refused to give chaplains; they have supplied as many as were requested.

Let me give another example. I have known for years the Rev. Father Cadot; in fact, he was my professor at college. He is now a missionary amongst the Indians at Cape Croker in Ontario. Not one of those Indians could have been compelled to enlist as they were exempt under the law, but Father Cadot, appreciating his duties as a citizen of this country, appealed to the Indians, and 63 out of a total of 67 of military age offered their services. Fifty-seven were accepted, and fifty-three have gone to England, the other four being turned down as unfit for military service at London, Ontario. Forty-eight of these Indians got as far as France; five were sent back to Canada on reaching England. Of the forty-eight who went to France, twenty-two were wounded, and six were killed. I have said that sixty-three enlisted out of sixty-seven. The other four never enlisted for the very good reason that Father Cadot had no influence or authority whatever over them, because they were not Catholics. To sum it up, the sixty-three Catholics enlisted, and the four who were not Catholics did not endist.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) spoke this afternoon of Loyola college, Montreal. This college is not yet twenty-five years old, but at least 287 of her boys were in active service, and 34 of them were killed, amongst whom I might mention the only son of the hon. member for Maisonneuve, also the brother of Rev. Father Hingston. These boys won 20 Victoria Crosses and other distinctions. St. Mary's college, also in Montreal, has furnished at least double the number Loyola college did-double in enlisted men, double in wounded, and double in killed.
Turning to the West, I am in a position to state that all the pupils at St. Boniface College, in the province of Manitoba, who were fit and of military age enlisted right from the beginning of the war to the end. The hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) has been Minister of Militia in this country, and knows that there is a hospital at St. Cloud in France, but what he does not know is the fact that 75 per cent of the doctors who are giving their services at that hospital were educated by the Jesuits in Montreal, mostly at Loyola and St. Mary's colleges. The same is true of the Laval hospital. Many of the doctors at that hospital were students at St. Mary's or Loyola college.
Surveying the Jesuit order in general, I find that over 700 Jesuits have enlisted, over 160 of whom have given their all.
They have won decorations as follows: Legion of Honour, 39; Military Medals, 36; Croix de Guerre, 303; Citations, 519; and other decorations, 30.
Shall I say something about the Jesuits in France? Does my hon. friend know that Marshal Foch, the glorious and immortal Marshal Fooh, was educated by the Jesuits? Does he know that as far back as 1872 the General's professor of mathematics predicted his future greatness when he told him that he would one day be the man who would bring down the German flag which was then floating on the fortress of Metz? Foch, who was educated by the Jesuits, was the man who achieved this glorious success, and he is undobutedly the most brilliant student ever educated by the Jesuits. My hon. friend has probably heard of another distinguished man, General Mangin, and I am sure the name of General de Castelnau, who gave four sons to the cause of the Allies and. civilization, is also familiar to him. A large number of the Generals of the French army were educated by the Jesuits, and in England over 2,000 students of Jesuit colleges volunteered before conscription went into force. Of these students 400 have laid down their lives for their country, and the great Jesuit college of Stoneyhurst has the distinction of having contributed over 160 of her students to the ranks. These figures may probably be of little interest to many hon. members, but as it has pleased the hon. gentleman to create an impression and a feeling that it was the spirit of the Jesuits to shirk their duty and evade their responsibilities,
I think it is only right to put before the House and the country facts showing the splendid work which the Jesuits have done, in this war, and proving that the hon. gentleman, had no grounds whatever for the statements which he made.
We are told, Sir, that those who are accused of shirking their duty are disloyal to the Empire. How many times have we not heard that during the last two or three years? May I state certain facts, which probably are of no great interest to my hon. friend but which will certainly prove of considerable importance to others. The hon. member is no doubt ignorant of the fact that every day during the war 15,000 Jesuits prayed for the success of the Allies, and he is probably also unaware that since the signing of the armistice every Jesuit in the world has been ordered to offer a special prayer that the Allies may obtain a just and substantial peace. Does he know that in our Catholic churches the Jesuits

every day pray for the King? If the House will bear with me 1 will repeat this prayer.
We beseech Thee Almighty God, that Thy servant George who hath received from Thy mercy the reins of power, may receive also an increase of all virtues so that, adorned with these, he may graciously arrive unto Thee who art the way, the truth and the life. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
I observe that my hon. friend (Sir Sam Hughes) is laughing. Let me ask him a question. There are thousands of Jesuits praying daily for the King. Will he state frankly whether he has gone to church once a year for the express purpose of praying for His Majesty? The Jesuits offer another prayer, for the Royal Family. Is that an indication of disloyalty? They say:
Oh Lord save Our King George,
And hear uis in the day we call upon Thee.
We beseech Thee Almighty God, that Thy servant George, who by Thy divine mercy hath taken upon himself the government of this realm, may receive an increase of all virtues, wherewith, being becomingly adorned, he may turn aside from what is evil and foul, may overcome his enemies, and being made pleasing in Thy sight, together with the Queen Consort and Royal Family, may he happily come unto Thee who art the way, the truth, and the life. Through Christ Our Lord. Amen.
I am sure the hon. gentleman has never said half as much as that for the Royal Family. It does not do simply to boast of your loyalty; you must prove it, and the men who have been offering their lives upon the altar , of sacrifice have been proving their loyalty in a far greater way than many of those who are traducing them to-day. Sir, it is true that in this country there are disloyal men; but those who are disloyal are not the ones that are sometimes attacked for disloyalty. They are neither the Catholics nor the French Canadians; they are not the majority of those who sit on this side of the House. No. They are the very few men who, on the other side of the House are always ready and eager to sling mud and heap censure on those who do not share their views.

Mr. (SPEAKER: The hon. gentleman's language is certainly not parliamentary.

I abide by your ruling, Mr. Speaker, but I deeply regret at this moment my unfortunate unfamiliarity with the English language. It would afford me an opportunity of saying about the same thing in other words. What I want to say, however, is simply this: Those who are disloyal

to the Empire are not those who are attacked to-day, hut rather those who seize every opportunity that presents itself to spread dissension and create disunion in this country. They are the disloyal men. There are, I think, but few hon. gentlemen in this House who hold the conviction that the British flag is not wide enough to afford shelter and protection to every British subject in this country. What is the ambition of those who are always attacked? Our ambition is very simply stated.
Our aim is to create a great country in Canada; we have no other ambition. We want to respect the convictions of others and we pray those who do not share our convictions to be kind and generous enough not to attack at any moment without any reason whatever.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to occupy the time of the House ' for a , very few minutes only and in doing so I wish to say in agreement with the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Gladu), that discussions and statements which have to deal with religious dissentions are very disagreeable to me. It is not my intention to enter into a discussion of that kind to-night or to follow the hon. member through the more or less rambling remarks that he made. 1 would also like to say that I do not belong to either of those orders to which he made reference at the beginning, but I want to make these few remarks as one who belongs to the soldiers of this country, and in doing so I want to remind hon. members that the resolution before the House deals with what purported to be an evasion of the Military Service Act. I do not say that these charges are true or that they are not true, but I do say that when we ask for an investigation into the truth of these matters we are doing a kindness to that institution if the remarks of those who speak for it are correct. This is not an outrageous question or one which should not have come before the people or Parliament of this country. The impression has gone forth that the facts as alleged are true, and it is the duty of every honest man who has the good of his country at heart to have the truth of this matter cleared up, no matter who is injured in the clearing up of it.
I want also to state that these charges go a little farther than that; they involve a minister of the Crown. We have had read on the floor of this House to-day what I take to be a denial by the hon. the Minister

of Justice (Mr. Doherty) that he had any part in this affair. I fully believe that not one shadow of suspicion will eventually rest upon any one in authority here. I cannot believe, for example, that the Minister of Militia and Defence (Major-General Mewburn) would have been for one second a party to allowing any body of men to violate the spirit or the letter of the Military Service Act.
That brings me to the point that I rose to-night to make. We must be very guarded about interference in these affairs by any one in authority. Some of us fought the election a year ago on the Military Service Act or conscription. We did so because we thought that equality of service was the basis of all democracy and that we should get more equal service under that Act. We might have been wrong. Hon. members in this House may differ with me honestly on that question, but I do not believe that any man will differ from me when I say that a greater injustice could not exist in any country than that conscription having been adopted you could take the poor man s boy and let the rich man's boy get off free, or that any one with authority or influence could keep his hoy or some of his friends from coming under the working of the Act. Because we tried to enforce this Act with an honesty and fairness worthy of a democratic people, I rose to make these few remarks and I say that the Government did right when they placed this matter for investigation in the hands of one of the judges of the country. Every one interested will profit by it. The Novitiate itself has every reason to profit by it if the statements of its representatives are true. The minister involved stands to profit by it because there is no denying the fact that there is suspicion abroad. It is the duty of the country and of Parliament to remove the stigma which has been cast on the good name of Canada and in doing this let us be honest and fair.

Mr. Speaker, living in an adjoining county to the county of Wellington, in which the Novitiate is situated, I think it is proper that I should represent the sentiment which exists in my county. I want to mention a few things in regard to which we have had a lot of trouble. In the town of Orangeville, the county town, there were half a dozen young men arrested for not having their exemption papers with them, in some cases young married men. These young men were not allowed to go aboard the train with their wives and children. They were held there until they got their exemption papers sent
from their homes. These were cases of young men who were really exempted under the Order in Council of the 20th April last year hut it was weeks and weeks before they could be got off. We tried to explain this to the people. I wrote to the Minister of Militia (Major General Mewburn) in several cases and said that these people did not come under the Military Service Act but the reply to my letter was that "This is out of our hands; the officer commanding at the headquarters of the district is the one to apply to.'-' We could get very little satisfaction in some cases. In the midst of it this trouble came about at the Novitiate. I do not wish to say a word about this Novitiate because it is a Catholic institution and I was very sorry to hear the last speaker on the Opposition side of the House (Mr. Gladu) get up with the anger that he did because there was religion in this question. Then he started to repeat some very fine prayer and wound up with desperate anger again. I really thought when he was reading that prayer that he represented quite a number of people in Canada who thought it was far safer to be behind a solid stone wall praying than to be facing the mouth of a cannon. You can understand our feelings when we found that inside twenty-four hours orders were given exempting those in that one institution, whether these men were exempt under the law or not, and that these orders came direct from Ottawa, not from Toronto or London, instructing the officers at Guelph that proceedings were to be called off and an apology made. If the Minister of Militia undertakes to apologize for every young man who was unlawfully taken against the Military Service Act it will take him at least six months to write these apologies. There were young men in the county of Dufferin that I wrote to Ottawa about and each one of them got exemption only after from three to six weeks' hard work. I do not think there was any need of that. In many cases the law went to extremes. I honestly believe in the resolution before the House to-day if the Government is honest in dealing with it. I believe it is in the interest of all churches and of all classes represented in this House. If I believed that an institution or class with which I was connected had done wrong I would be the first to try to have the stigma removed from them; I would be the man that would be asking for an investigation. Why should not the parties interested in this matter feel the same way? It has 'been admitted to-day, I think by the Minister of Militia', that the

men concerned in this case had not their discharge papers, nor any papers that would set them free. Under the circumstances I think they should have been held for military service just as any other young man was.	'
Now let me deal for a moment with what the Acting Minister of Justice has told us to-day. I will frankly admit that when this Military Service Bill was being brought down I was one of a few members that went to the Minister of Justice and asked that the divinity student clause be stricken out, and I will tell hon. gentlemen why I did so. I know boys that were raised right beside where I live, who had gone to college and been there for from two to three years ready to be ordained. Did they wait for exemption when the call came for their services? No, as soon as the war started they heard the call, they volunteered to go to the front, and the universities and colleges of Ontario were consequently almost stripped of men. Afterwards the Bill was introduced containing the divinity student clause to exempt all the young men that were in college. Was that a fair thing to do? Is there a man to-day in this country who will stand up and say that it was honest and fair to the rest of Canada? I deplore the fact that Protestantism and Catholicism have been made an issue in this matter to-day. Some of the very best friends I have in the county of Dufferin to-day are Catholics. There are Catholic friends of mine in that county that had two sons and a daughter go overseas. I know of hon. gentlemen sitting on the opposite side of the House whose only sons have fallen in the war. Those men deserve credit, but why should we-because somebody has done wrong, or is supposed to have done wrong, no matter what church they belong to-shut our eyes to what is alleged to be an evasion of the law? T was somewhat surprised when the Acting Minister of Justice told us to-day that there was a provision in the Act to the effect that so long as young men had got into a college or university they were free from the operation of the Act. I cannot understand that. We could well have left in the divinity student clause if we had understood that we were going to be misled in that way. What was told us, and what was distinctly understood, in this House, was that unless a young man had been in a college for two, three, or four years-I do not remember the exact period now-and was about to be ordained, that he would be liable under the Military Service Act.

Why should fault be found with some hon. members in this House in asking that there should be a fair and honest investigation? For my part I cannot see why there should not be such an inquiry. I do not think that the investigation that has so far been held can be so designated. The Minister of Militia told us to-day that he inquired as well as he could. But he heard only one side of the story, and, of course, it was denied. I am not saying whether that was, or was not, right, but I do say that when men such as the members of this Ministerial Association, men who did their utmost to help the Militia Department of Canada, and to help Canada, to get all the young men they could for service overseas, are asking for a fair and honest investigation, I cannot see why it should not be granted? I hope that when the investigation is granted that it will take place with open doors, that there will be nothing covered up, and that nothing will be done but what is just and right. If the people who are now accused are exonerated they should have every reason to feel satisfied. I tell hon. gentlemen plainly that no member of this House will feel more satisfied than I if I can go to those who have complained to me that justice is not being done and tell them, " The complaint was only hearsay, it was only a report. A fair and honest investigation has been held into the conduct of the persons charged, and it has been found that they did not do wrong, but did their duty."

This afternoon I had no intention of making any remarks in connection with the matter now engaging the attention of the House. I have not had the opportunity of reading the file in this case, and for that reason do not propose to enter upon a discussion of the various matters involved, but I happen to have in my possession a copy of a report made by Captain Macauley to his superior officer, dated London, June 10, 1918. I mentioned the matter to the Minister of Militia to ascertain if there was any objection to placing that report on the pages of Hansard, and he replied there was none whatever. It did seem to me, as the debate progressed, that as Captain Macauley was not here to make a statement himself, and as he had been severely censured for what he had done, it was only fair that the House should know what he has to say regarding this matter. It is true that the case will be investigated by a royal commission, but that will not result in the report being printed in Hansard unless it is placed there during the

course of this debate, at all events, not in all probability. I therefore rise merely for the purpose of reading the report to which I have referred.
What is the document? Is it a report?

It is headed " Investigation and Report re Bedford Farm, Guelph, Ontario." I understand it is the same institution that is under discussion here. The report is from Captain A. C. Macauley to Major J. Hirsch, his senior officer, as I understand:-
Sir:-Acting under your instructions I proceeded to Guelph on the 7 th inst., and on arrival made arrangements to visit the marginally noted farm. I arrived there about 8.20 p.m.-[DOT][DOT] Bedford Farm time," they do not adhere to the daylight saving time-accompanied by Inspector Minard, C.S.B., Sergt.-Major Garner, C.M.P.C., one Sergeant C.S.B., and six constables. I took the precaution to place (3) three men at points that would enable them to see if any one left the buildings while the investigation was being made. I asked for someone in authority and was informed that the rector would be down in a moment. The rector came and I introduced myself, informing him of the object of the visit. I asked to see all the men of military age who were stopping at the farm, and after satisfying him that I had the authority to request same, he agreed to liave them all assemble in the dining room, which was the only room large enough for the purpose. About this time a Father Hinkson appeared on the scene and asked again for my authority. I asked him who he was and why he was wearing military uniform with the rank of captain. He stated that he had been to France, attached to the 5th Art. Division as chaplain. He tried to prevent any investigation being made, although he admitted being only a guest at the farm. However, he phoned a lawyer by the name of Kerwin, and a Judge Hayes. The latter advised him not to put any obstacles in my way and asked if I would speak to him, Judge Hayes, over the phone. During the conversation Judge Hayes told me that he had advised Father Hinkson that it would be wiser to help rather than hinder me, in carrying out my instructions, if he was satisfied that I was Captain Macauley as I represented myself to be. I might state here that Father Hinkson told Judge Hayes that he had no reason whatever to doubt my identity.
After all this delay the previous arrangement was carried out and all were assembled in the dining room. During the time that the men were assembling, two tried, unsuccessfully, to leave the building by a window. The men assembled were questioned by Inspector Min-ard and myself. Three of the men I examined I had detained for further examination, as they appeared to me to be defaulters under the Act.
About this time I was informed that Mr. Doherty of Ottawa, father of one of the guests at the farm, wished to speak to me. During the conversation, Mr. Doherty stated that he was the Minister of Justice and ordered me to stop all action, saying I had no right to be in Bedford Farm making any investigation. As I was acting under instructions from my C.O., I told Mr. Doherty that I could not take any
instructions from him that would in any way interfere with the carrying out of my instructions. He them asked me if I would at least suspend further action until he communicated with General Mewburn, the Minister of Militia. This request I complied with. Sometime later I received a phone call from General Ashton, Adjutant General, Ottawa, instructing me to suspend any further action other than to make a thorough investigation, and forward to him a complete report, and that he was informing the A.P.M. London, that such instructions had been given me. This was confirmed later by a wire from A.P.M., M.D. No. 1.
I am attaching a list of names of men of military age, who are living at Bedford Farm, together with their ages and the dates that they became guests at the farm, not one of them registered under the M.S.A. I am firmly convinced that the majority of these men are defaulters under the Act, and in support of my belief, I submit for your consideration the following information I gleaned from the "Rector" himself.
1.	Any young man may enter the place providing he is in good health and has his matriculation.
2.	He pays no fees and receives no salary for any work he does on the farm.
3.	He signs no agreements whatever and is under no obligation of any kind.
I have since learned that parapraph 3 is not altogether accurate; that an obligation is taken which compels the young man in question to renounce home, so to speak, and remain with the institution. It is only fair to state that. The letter continues :
4.	He may stay any length of time or he can leave any time he chooses at his own discretion.
5.	He may take certain studies, which would eventually admit him to the priesthood after fifteen years.
6.	He would not necessarily be ordained a priest though he lived there a lifetime.
In view of this information, I contend that these people do not come within the meaning of Para. 6, Schedule of Exemptions on page 26,-
I think he means "exceptions" when he says that.
-Red Book of Instructions dealing -with Deserters and Absentees without leave. Should my interpretation of this paragraph be wrong, I beg to draw your attention to the fact that all young men of military age could avail themselves of the opportunities thus presented by institution of this kind, for the express purpose of evading military service. It seems to me Sir, that it is of vital importance that a ruling regarding this case be obtained without delay.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Tour obedient servent,
A. C. Maoauley,
Captain.
