Air. JOHN H. SINCLAIR (Antigonish and Guysborough): Mr. Speaker, I do not profess to he able to add anything of value to this discussion, but I desire as a Protestant to express my sincere sorrow that the Ministerial Association of Guelph found it necessary to meddle in this regrettable affair. I suppose that the Alinisterial Association is composed of Protestant Ministers, and I should like to feel that they were engaged in spreading the gospel of peace rather than doing police and detective work in connection with the Alilitary Service Act. I cannot for the life of me understand why an association of clergymen would want to interfere with the administration of the Military Service Act when the country was filled with officers of all descriptions whose duty it was to attend to that duty.

Suppose we put the boot on the other foot. Suppose an Association of Roman Catholic clergymen-Jesuits, if you like, but Roman Catholic clergymen-held a meeting at some point and passed a resolution inviting the military officers to make a raid on some Protestant theological institution, Presbyterian, Methodist or Baptist. You can imagine the wild scene that would follow in the office of the Orange Sentinel and the speeches that would be made in the school houses and lodges throughout Ontario.
The member for Dufferin (Mr. Best! expressed regret that the Minister of Militia (Major General Mewburn) had apologized for this unjustifiable raid. In my judgment, the Minister of Militia did just what any gentleman would do. I regret that the member for Dufferin does not himself see it in that way. What else could the Minister of Militia do? We must all admit that what was done was certainly very roughly done. Captain Alacauley the officer in charge acted with unusual and unnecesssary severity, and it was right

that the Minister of Militia should frankly and promptly express his regret.
I wish to be permitted to assure my Catholic fellow citizens, both in this House and out of it, that the spirit which instigated this raid is, I hope peculiar to the district around the town of Guelph and to certain places in the province of Ontario. Thank God it does not exist generally throughout Canada, and I ana certain that it does not exist at all in the province from which I come. Speaking for the Protestants of my province, I wish to say that they desire to accord to our Catholic fellow citizens the same respect and freedom that they claim for themselves. I was pleased to learn from the acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) that after a careful and thorough investigation the charges against the Jesuit college at Guelph were found to be unfounded, and that there was not in the institution a single man who was liable for military service.
If that be the case,-and no hon. member has any just reason to doubt it-one wonders why, this investigation is asked for and why it is granted. I trust this step is not being taken for the purpose of giving further annoyance to those worthy citizens who have already been very badly used. After hearing the sneeches of the -.Minister of Militia (Mr. Mewburn) and the Acting Minister of Justice, both of whom assured the House that there was nothing to investigate, I was disappointed that they should end up by saying that they had decided to grant a Royal Commission. I understand, however, there is no objection on the part of the Jesuit Order to have a full and thorough investigation and that they are quite ready to meet it. What justification, let me ask, can there be for the insulting manner in which this raid was carried out? Can any fair minded man justify it? Why was it necessary to go there in the night time? Why did the officer not go there in a manly and soldierly way in the daytime and ask the principal of the college for the names and ages of the boys and of the other residents of the institution? Surely that would have been the proper and decent manner in which to carry out his duties as a military officer. The whole proceedings are to my mind contemptible. It was pointed out by the hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux) that on that particular night the only man in the Novitiate fit for military duty was a returned soldier who had a good record at the front and who had lost a brother on the battlefield. One can
imagine the feelings of this mgji at the treatment his associates were receiving at the hands of the Government that he had served with so much courage and at such a sacrifice! The hon member for Maisonneuve also referred to the splendid record that the students of the various Jesuit Colleges throughout Canada had made in this war. Hon. gentlemen will remember that at the time of the last election an unfortunate slander was spread throughout the country that the clergy, that were expelled, from France during recent years and that had come to Canada, were instigating people to resist the Military Service Act and that they were not loyal and were not doing their duty as good citizens of this country. I have the honour of having a monastery in the county which I represent. Most of the Brothers in that monastery were men who had left France for the reason I have mentioned and who had been residents of Canada for some years, but as soon as war broke out, every one of those men of military age started for Halifax in order to take passage to France and join the colours, and some of them I am told made the supreme sacrifice. I am not familiar with the clergy in other institutions of that kind, but I know what happened in my own constituency and there is in that constituency no class of men whom I have more reason to be proud of than the fathers and brothers belonging to the monastery at Tracadie. The hon. member for Maisonneuve has also told us that 35 students of one of those very Jesuit institutions laid down their lives on the battlefields of France and (Flanders, amongst them being his own brave son. Surely that ought to satisfy hon. gentlemen opposite who are pressing for this investigation. I regret that my hon. friend the hon. member for Victoria (iSir Sam Hughes) deemed it necessary to make this motion, and all I wish to say is that this discussion if it will do nothing else, will serve to vindicate the character of those worthy men whose only fault is that they belong to a different faith from that of spme hon. gentlemen opposite.

I am very pleased to learn that the Government are going to have an investigation. T have listened very carefully to the speeches that have been delivered, this afternoon, and the whole trend of some of them has been to shelter a certain number of men in the town of Guelph. It was asserted that Ontario had promised to raise a certain number

The hon. member for Cape Breton South says that he sees in this debate nothing more or less than a difference between Roman Catholic and Protestant. All I have to say with regard to that remark is that I think his eyesight is very bad. I regreit it, because 1 have a kindly feeling for my hon. friend, and I should like to think his physical condition was of the best.

I have no glasses on, you
will notice.

I would suggest that
he put glasses on before he make a statement of that kind. The speech of the hon. member for Yamaska (Mr. Gladu) reminded me of a story I heard once about an old Scotch preacher who took for his text: The devil goeth about like a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour." The preacher divided his subject under three heads. He said: "We will ask, first, who the devil he was; secondly, where the devil he was going, and thirdly, what the devil he was roaring about." As I listened to my hon. friend from Yamaska I thought I might very well ask him what he was roaring about, and whom he was seeking to devour. It did not seem to me that this discussion should have aroused in him such an ebullition of youthful! feeling as he exhibited here to-night. He has spoken of this institution and that college, and carried us to practically every Jesuit institution in the country from the Atlantic to the Pacific, giving us the name of the person in charge and reciting some of the prayers which are said for the King and the Royal Family. The hon. gentleman said that prayers alone were not enough, that loyalty must be proved by acts as well as words. I was glad to hear him say that because I think when the enlistment figures from certain parts of this country came to His Majesty's ears he might be excused for asking for something more substantial than prayers. The hon. member himself is entitled to special consideration, because he is a very great friend of the soldiers. He has told us so himself, and I am not disposed to'dispute his statement; in fact, I think the figures bear him out. Why, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was so popular with the soldiers at fch*

last election that he received every soldier vote that was polled in his county, and there are not many members here who can make that boast. The polling of those votes indicated, to a certain degree at all events, what the county of Yamaska did in backing up its prayers by acts. I have said the hon. member received all the soldier votes that were cast in his riding, the total number was eight.
Referring to one of the Jesuit institutions in the province of Quebec, I think at Montreal, he said that before some of the students attending that Jesuit college started for overseas the reverend head of the college called the students together and made a brief addresss. I caught a few words which my hon. friend quoted from that address. He said that the reverend' head said to the boys: "You have heard that conscription is a bad law, that it is a curse; do not listen to such words." I should like to ask my hon. friend where the students of that particular college could possibly have heard words like those. Were they carried down from the province of Ontario? Who made use of such words? If they were made use of, it must have been by some person whom the head of the college thought the boys would listen to and be influenced by. I think I am justified in asking my hon. friend to tell us who made use of those words.

Certainly. The words were used by those who were the anti-British champions in 1910 and 1911, and who since that date have become, with their friends, ministers of the Crown. They breathed in 1917 the same spirit throughout the province of Quebec as they breathed in 1911.
Hear, hear.

I was very glad to see hon. members opposite endorse the answer given by the hon. gentleman. He said that persons who made use of these expressions were people of anti-British tendencies in the province of Quebec.
I do not understand the hon. gentleman.

My hon. friend said that the persons who had declared the conscription law to be a bad law were antiBritish people. Well, we shall see how this statement applies. I desire to read a few words which were uttered by Archbishop Begin, the senior archbisholp of the Roman Catholic Church of Quebec, and published broadcast throughout that province as the expression of his opinion of
the conscription law. My hon. friend says that those who deemed conscription a bad thing were the anti-British. I shall now read what the senior archbishop of the province of Quebec said concerning the law.
Will my hon. friend pardon me. I;-
I knew my hon. friend would squirm.
I never said that.

My hon. friend sees
the necessity for a disclaimer, but he committed himself before I undertook to read this. IHe is like many boys and youthful members; he is rather prone to say what he does not mean. He allowed himself to be carried away by the vehem-10 p.m. ence of his own eloquence, and said things that he will find it rather difficult to back up, even in Quebec. Now may I be permitted to place on Hansard the statement of the senior archbishop of the piovince of Quebec in regard to the conscription law. He said:
This conscription law is a menace which causes the Canadian clergy the worst apprehensions.
This military service, as it is proposed, or at least as we are enabled to judge from the speeches and statements its discussions have provoked, is not only a serious Wow to the rights of the Church of Christ, independent in its domain, and whose laws and practice exempt the clergy and that class of the society which that name designates from the service under arms1.
Is it signed?
Certainly.
By whom is it signed?
The senior archbishop of Quebec.
What paper is the hon. member quoting from? Is it the Sentinel?

I am not sure whether it was printed in the Sentinel or not, but it is not taken from the Sentinel. The paper from which I took it was the Kingston Standard. Let me quote some more.
The clause as It is written might lose some of its ill if it were interpreted in the spirit of the Church. But what guarantees have we that the members of the special tribunals will be all Catholics, enlightened and good-willed, capable of pronouncing with sincerity and knowledge on a question of its importance?
If we judge by the very crude knowledge revealed by certain speeches made in the Commons, one may, indeed, fear that some legisla-

tors, so little ill-willed, may not make a choice that we would approve, and here is what legitimatizes all the fears.
I have given you the words of the senior archbishop of Quebec, in regard to conscription. Do my hon. friends opposite deny that he made use of those words? Does any hon. gentleman opposite say that he did not issue a statement to the press of this country? Now, notwithstanding those remarks of the archbishop, I am not prepared to go as far as the hon. member for Yamaska (Mr. Gladu) who characterized as anti-British every one that was opposed to this law and regarded it as a had law; but I do say that the utterances of a man in the high position of the archbishop in question in regard to the conscription law-such utterances as I have read, and similar assertions by other dignitaries' of the Roman Catholic Church in this country-are to a certain extent responsible for the doubts that existed in the minds of Canadians in regard to the situation in the Guelph Novitiate. That cannot be gainsaid. The hon. member for Mai-sonneuve (Mr. Lemieux)
For what?
Maisonneuve.
What?

I shall take another constituency the name of which is more easily pronounced. The hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux), I will say. To one who has not the advantage of being able to speak the French language with the accuracy and the fluency with which I would like to speak it, it is exceedingly convenient to refer to a member who represents two or three constituencies, for it gives him a choice in names. I will therefore refer to my hon. friend as the member for Gaspe. He gave expression to his usual wail in regard to the Military Service. Act and the usual condemnation of the Minister of Militia for the message he sent to the farmers of the country. It strikes me as coming with extremely bad grace from any hon. gentleman on the opposite side from the province of Quebec or any of the Maritime Provinces to refer to the Military Service Act. Under the Act about 85,000 men were obtained. If the province of Quebec had done its duty and had supplied by voluntary enlistment its share in proportion to population as Ontario and the Western Provinces did, there would not have been any Military Service Act for it would have been unnecessary.
It is very well for the hon. member for Gaspe or some other hon. member from the 
province of Quebec to refer to the matter of conscripting farmers in Ontario and the Western Provinces, but Ontario had sent overseas thousands of farmers to take the place of farmers who stayed at home in Quebec and who were advised to do so by persons who should have siiown a different disposition. I am not saying for one moment that the hon. member for Gaspe advised men to stay at home, but I do say that there were persons who gave expressions to opinions such as those of the senior archbishop of the province of Quebec which I have read and which induced or influenced thousands of young men in that province to stay at home and thereby accentuated the farming difficulties in Ontario and the Western Provinces. _
The hon. member for Gaspe pleads for the minority. Well, I suppose that every church you could mention- in Canada is a minority, whether it is Roman Catholic, Presbyterian, Baptist, Anglican, Methodist, or whatever it may be. But I would like it to sink deeply into his heart that there are duties and responsibilities devolving upon minorities just as much as upon majorities.
I do not think that any person who has read and studied the history of this country can claim that harshness has characterized everything that has been done towards the minority. They have been treated with generosity. There is no desire on the part of any person to persecute the people connected with the Guelph Novitiate.
What is the situation? Captain Macauley has come in for a great deal of criticism. He did not use tact, it is said; he did not use good judgment, and so on. His lack of tact or judgment has not been specially mentioned. He went there not at the dead of night. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) should travel a little, should come further west. He will And out that in June it is not dark at eight or nine * o'clock in the evening. Captain Macauley went to this institution in daylight, in civilian clothes, as he says, so as not to attrapt special attention to the carrying out of his orders. He did not go of his own accord. He went because he was ordered to go, and the Minister of Militia told us this afternoon that he had information from what he considered a most reliable source that there were men in the institution who were liable to military service. Acting upon that information, I presume, he or some other person, ordered that investigation as he had a perfect right to do. It does seem to me that all the trouble could have been avoided on the evening on which Captain Macauley

made his visit if, when he made known, the reason for his visit, the head of the institution had called the students together at once and said: "Here they are; if there are any men liable for military service, I am not aware of the fact; question them for yourself." That would have been the simple and proper course for him to have taken.
Why was there any holding back? I fail to see the reason why. Will any person tell me that because a student happens to be an inmate of a certain institution he is exempted, or should be exempted, because of that fact? That is something I am sure no person will attempt to argue in cool blood. It is something I am not prepared to accept.
I	do not see any reason why hon. gentlemen opposite should profess such annoyance because of the investigation of the institution. The Minister of Militia understood from a reliable source that there were men there who were liable to military service and the order was given to make an investigation. Captain Macauley goes up to make that investigation. The wires are set to work and he is told to leave the in-stution and let the fellows stay there.
The Minister of Militia, in his letter of June 11,-I think it was-to the head of the institution shortly after the so-called raid, said: that the whole question of the liability of these students was being given consideration by the Justice Department. If there was doubt in regard to the liability of the men in this institution to service, why was an investigation ordered until that doubt was cleared up? Why is it when the matter was in doubt and being investigated by the Justice Department that the so-called raid was made? It seems to me that if it was a matter which had not been definitely settled as to whether the students were liable or not there should not have been any orders given for an investigation until the doubt was cleared away. There was not only a matter of doubt then, but there appears to be a matter of doubt now, as to whether these young men were liable for service or not.
I am glad that the Government intimated its entire willingness to have an investigation. I am glad for two particular reasons. If you like, there are two classes in the country concerned. If you like, there is a difference of . opinion between Roman Catholics on the one side and Protestants on the other. Certainly, there are some people who think there has been favouritism shown to certain ones in that institution and I think it advisable that that impression should be dispelled. The statement has been made here that none in this institution were liable to military service. I think that is another reason why there should be an investigation. It is decidedly in the interest, not only of this particular institution but of general harmony in the country, that there should be a full, fair and complete investigation which will remove any doubts that may exist in any person's mind as to whether any favouritism has been shown in regard to the students in this institution or not. That is the reason why I commend the action of the Government in granting an investigation. I think they have taken the proper course in withholding this investigation until the return of the Minister of Justice who is particularly concerned. I do not think anybody will object to that for a moment. That is only fair play, and it is fair play that wins in the long run.
Mr. 0. TURGEON (Gloucester):	Mr. Speaker, it had been my firm intention not to take any part in this debate. I now rise simply for the purpose of correcting, for the public benefit, a statement which has just been made by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) with reference to the hierarchy and Cardinal Begin of Quebec. My hon. friend is certainly not aware of the very commendable manner in which Cardinal Begin acted at the beginning of the recent great war. I have no authority to speak on behalf of Cardinal Begin, but we happen to be very closely related, being the sons of sisters, and knowing the Cardinal's sentiments with respect to the great war, I feel that I would not be doing my duty if I were to allow the hon. member for Frontenac's remarks with respect to the Cardinal to pass unchallenged. Mly hon. friend has stated what Cardinal Begin is supposed to have said with respect to the clause affecting students of the church in Canada. The clause in question was one which had been inserted by the Prime Minister in the original Bill exempting clerical students from military service, and which was adopted in modified form by the Prime Minister at the instigation of some hon. members on this side. It was while that clause was under discussion that Cardinal Begin gave expression to his opinions with respect to its possible effects in relation to divinity students. But my hon. friend has not seen fit to direct the attention of the House, or of the country, to what Cardinal Begin had done since the outbreak of hostilities to induce the young men of his province and of his diocese to make the necessary sacrifice in order to enlist



and rally to the support of the British Empire and of the Allies in Belgium and France. Had my hon. friend put the matter at issue honestly and squarely before the House I would not have intervened in these proceedings. I have only done so in order to give this explanation and in order that Cardinal Begin might not rest under the imputation of being opposed to Canada's participation in the war and of not having done his full duty, not only as a British subject, but as a prince of the church in Canada. My object is to make the point clear and unmistakable for the benefit of the people of Canada, and more particularly the people of Ontario, so that the friends of those hon. gentlemen who brought forward this motion cannot plead that the dignitaries of the Roman Catholic Church in Quebec, or other Catholic dioceses, have not done their duty in that regard; when it is the fact that their addresses to their people should be yet fresh in the memory of every member of the House and of the people of Canada as well.

I have listened with considerable interest to this whole debate. At times I doubted whether I should take part in it, and at other moments I felt the impulse to say a few words. To my mind, and I know that hon. gentlemen upon'the opposite side who do not agree with all the sentiments that have been expressed this afternoon will also say so, the debate has been somewhat rambling.
The hon. member for Frontenac who spoke a few moments ago has an unhappy way of saying things. It is not so much what he says, but the manner in which he says it, that is particularly displeasing to hon. members from the province of Quebec.
I would like to tell the hon. gentleman- and we have perhaps had a tilt or two in the last twelve years-that I have given up all hope of him. If I had any influence in the right quarter, I would ask that the prayers that were read this afternoon might be somewhat amended, so that not only would we pray for His Majesty the King, the Queen Consort, and the Royal Family, but that -we might also add a prayer for the hon. member foT Frontenac.
I suppose it would do me about as much good as it does the Royal Family?

I suppose even prayers would not have any weight with the hon. gentleman, much less words. The resolution that was introduced this afternoon by

the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, in view of the statements made public in relation to the Guelph Novitiate during the month of June, 1918, and the circumstances and facts concerning those and other similar charges concerning the evasion by young men and the connivance of others to defeat the ends and aims of the Military Service Act and other Acts and Orders relating to the upbuilding of the military forces of Canada, it is advisable that a select committee of this House be appointed to inquire into the matter with full authority to examine witnesses under oath, to pay necessary expenses and to report to this House.
In connection with this resolution the hon. member for Frontenac succeeded an making a speech dealing with the soldiers, with the archbishops and bishops of the Catholic church, and succeeded in getting in his customary attacks upon the province of Quebec, and went on to dilate upon the subject in his own inimitable style. My thoughts were running along a different line. As I read the resolution I saw more in it than an attack upon the Guelph Novitiate. I saw also these words:
and the connivance of others to defeat the ends and aims of the Military Service Act and other Acts and Orders relating to the up-building of the military forces in Canada.
I do not know if it is the intention of the Government to allow my hon. friend from Victoria to go to the extent of his resolution, but I find that in glancing over an address which he delivered to his constituents there is this passage;
More than one year ago an agitation was begun on the question of labour. We were recruiting " too many regiments " ; we were " taking too many men away from work "; " munitions manufacturers and others would be at a standstill "; " farmers could not put in their crops "; and " Canada has already done her full duty," were daily recited. They, unfortunately, had an effect upon the Prime Minister. The result was that I was asked in March, 1916, not to press recruiting, and recruiting to-day is, and has been, dead in Canada for fighting purposes. " Safety First," or the useful and well paid, but not dangerous jobs are readily filled ; but for the gallant boys in the trenches there is little or no backing.
That, to the casual observer at least, will tally exactly with what the hon. member for Victoria means by " other Acts and Orders relating to the upbuilding of the Military Forces of Canada." Knowing the resourcefulness of my hon. friend from Victoria I just wonder how far he will go with this investigation. Will he, for instance, be allowed the opportunity to investigate the conduct of the leader of the Government?

Will he be allowed to investigate the conduct of my hon. friend who is one of the two Presidents of the Privy Council for Canada? I say "one of the two" Presidents of the Privy Council, not that I mean any disrespect, but because I find by the Auditor General's Report that Canada is graced to-day with two Presidents of the Privy Council, one in his seat in this House, the other abroad, in the person of the Prime Minister. Will he investigate the conduct of one of these? He may wish to investigate the conduct of several othei ministers; does the Government intend to give him that latitude? He asks for it in the resolution. Will the member for Victoria be allowed to inquire into the conduct of the farmers of Ontario and the farmers of Canada who protested against theii sons being taken? The member for Victoria asks for that. Or, forsooth, will the Government simply say: eliminate everything else and we will give you the right to investigate what the member for West Toronto and the member for Frontenac ask -the conduct of the Guelph Novitiate? Sir, does it seem just, does it seem fair, that every other influence or element that worked against the upbuilding of the military force of Canada should not have its conduct investigated, but that attention should be given solely to this poor little Novitiate in Guelph? I ask in all sincerity; is it because this little Novitiate belongs to the religious minority of this country that theii conduct alone should be investigated, not the conduct of every man who tried to prevent the upbuilding of Canada's military force? Surely the Government will allow the member for Victoria to have a thorough and full investigation; surely he, aided 1 hope by members on both sides of this House, will have a right to go before that Court of Inquiry and examine into the conduct of this one and that one, great or small-because there must be no class difference; all men must be upon the same footing.
Sir, I am not charged by the Jesuit Order of Canada to interfere with an investigation into their conduct. I listened with great pleasure to the member for Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair), who does not belong to the same church as the Jesuits, speaking about the pettiness of this investigation into the affairs of one small Novitiate. The voice of the hon. member was pleasing to my ears, for here was one man who, though not belonging to the faith of the minority, urged that all this pettiness be
80J
put aside. Time after time the greatest and most eminent statesmen of this country have advocated that these questions be not approached from the standpoint of parish politics, and that all differences between races and creeds be put aside. Would you, Mr. Speaker, not be surprised if I, belonging to the religion of the minority, should ask that the conduct of some particular sect or faith other than my own should be investigated? Hon. gentlemen opposite are of too large mind not to be heartily sick of these petty little attacks against certain people of this country solely because they belong to the religious minority.
We have heard it said to-day that in the province of Quebec, to which most of us on this side belong, we do not understand these petty little attacks. We have there, living in close community and in the very best of good-fellowship, members of different religious beliefs. Never do you hear one gentleman of the province of Quebec make attacks upon the religious minority of the province. The member for West Toronto, I think it was-it may have been the member for Frontenac-said very truthfully that there should be no minority or class of people in this country with privileges that are not extended to others. Make no mistake about it: we advocate that on this side of the House. We ask for no privileges; what we insist upon and what we mean to hold are the rights and the privileges that have been granted to us, not by certain hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, but by the British North America Act of 1867. We do not plead for more extended privileges; we do not plead for any particular rights. We want the constitution protected. We are asked to live upon the rock of the constitution. Sir, we will not try by any means whatever to evade the working of the British North America Act, nor will we brook any interference with the rights that we have under that Act. I say this so that once and for all what is understood by the " Quebec question " may be grasped by even the most ignorant man in the country. That is the Quebec question; it is absolutely nothing more than that.
Occasionally, through the kindness, I assume, of the member for West Toronto, I get a copy of the Orange Sentinel. I read it with great care. I have other friends in the country who send me pamphlets bearing the " no popery " cry; others are kind enough to send me circulars about the damnation of the church to which I belong. I sometimes marvel how it is that I have so many kind friends throughout the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Acting Minister of Justice has clearly and accurately stated the position of the Government with reference to this resolution. That position is precisely the same as that which it took when the matter was first formally presented to us in December last by Rev. Mr. Palmer and some other members of the Guelph Ministerial Association and some hon. members who have spoken here to-day. We stated at that time the attitude of the Government towards all charges involving allegations of impropriety or wrong-doing to be that these charges should be investigated; that if a charge was preferred against a minister, the matter should be drawn to the attention of the Prime Minister whose duty it would be to take such action as he deemed expedient; that if allegations were made respecting departmental administration, then appropriate inquiry should be had in such a case. In other words, the attitude of the Government was that, upon all charges definitely formulated by responsible parties, appropriate investigation should follow. We therefore stated to the members of the Ministerial Association and the others who were present with the deputation on the occasion referred to, that if charges were formulated the Government would take action by way of having a proper investigation made. It was necessary, we thought, that there should he a formulation of charges, first, in order to justify the Government in taking action, and secondly, as affording the foundation of allegation upon which a commission could be based. No specific charges were formulated following that interview, but on Thursday night last I received the charges signed by the Rev. Mr. Palmer which were presented here to-day by the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes), and I at once cabled them to the Prime Minister. The acting Minister of Justice has read to the House the reply received from the Minister of Justice, that he would welcome any inquiry by which, in the opinion of his colleagues, the public interest would be served. He stated further, as was read by the acting
Minister of Justice, that the imputations made with respect to his action and that of the Department of Justice in respect of the Guelph Novitiate, are entirely baseless. That is the position of the Minister of Justice.
The Minister of Militia and Defence has stated that he also desires an inquiry, and in view of the fact that these charges, or like charges, have attained wide publicity and that there has been a good deal of public discussion of the affair in question, the Government has reached the conclusion that a full investigation should be had through a commission, as stated to-day by the Acting Minister of Justice. That is all I desire to say with reference to the matter, except this: That the hon. member for Victoria, who was obliged to leave for Toronto to-night, asked me before leaving the House to state on his behalf that he accepted the statement of the Acting Minister of Justice, and authorized me to withdraw on his behalf the resolution; which I now beg leave to do.

speakeroldname: Air. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: I had no intention of saying anything upon this very sensitive question that is now before the House, nor do I propose to say very much at this stage. I think it is very regrettable that questions of this character should be brought up in the House of Commons. Questions of a religious character are bound to divide the House along those lines, and it is very regrettable that they should be introduced into this House if they can be otherwise settled. I think the Government is more or less to blame in this connection, in view of the explanation they have given. It is very clear that the resolution put upon the Order Paper by the hon. member for Victoria contains a great many charges, and if one of those charges is to be investigated by the Government every one of them should be investigated. The Government, of course, is responsible for the character of every motion that goes upon the Order Paper and is allowed to come before the House. I am long enough in the House of Commons to know that no motion can get on the Order Paper without going through a certain routine, and if it contains anything objectionable it should not get on the Order Paper. Surely, if there is not enough machinery now to prevent questions of a questionable character appearing on the Order Paper there ought to be some censorship of them. If it is desirable to have censorship of the mails and newspapers and public speakers,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. member not recall that at the close of my remarks I suggested to the hon. member for Victoria that his resolution be withdrawn, and also that at the close of the remarks of the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) he did withdraw the resolution?

If the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) suggested to the hon. member for Victoria to withdraw the resolution and it was withdrawn, I would like to know what we have been discussing. What has been before the Chair? The whole thing is wrong and irregular.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The only time it was withdrawn was when the Acting Prime Minister spoke.
I was absent in the early part of the evening, but three or four hon. members have spoken since I came in and I never heard of any other motion.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It was not withdrawn
before. I simply suggested its withdrawal but the suggestion was not taken up.

Then it seems to be a sort of imaginary withdrawal. The minister says it was withdrawn, and still discussion continued. It had no right to be discussed and the whole proceeding was irregular, if the hon. member is correct in saying that he suggests the withdrawal and it was withdrawn.
Mr. 'MEIGHEN:	No withdrawal took
place until immediately before the hon. gentleman himself rose.

There had been a great deal of discussion before I rose. I understand the question was discussed the whole evening on this motion, which I say should have been withdrawn the very moment the Acting Minister of Justice announced the mode by which he intended it should be dealt with. This acrimonious discussion could have been avoided and the investigation of the matter approached in a more proper frame of mind than is possible after the country has been influenced by the discussion that has taken place this evening.
Why did the hon. gentleman not take his objection at a more appropriate time than now?

I did not think that all the wisdom of the House was centered in me, and more than that, I was not here. I was keeping exceedingly quiet until I found that the leader of the Government (Sir Thomas White) had something to say. I told him I was not going to speak and I thought he would follow suit and say nothing. However, I simply point out what would have been the proper course, and I must say that I have not heard any great argument in support of this investigation.
I take the same ground as I took on the resolution with reference to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, that I will take my law from the Acting Minister of Justice in matters of the kind. He has not given any good reason, or any reason that satisfies himself, that there is very much to investigate in this matter. He said he would give permission to Mr. Palmer to reconstruct these charges and possibly put something in them that would hold water, but, as they stood, I understood him to say, there was not much in them. He gave a certificate of character to the Minister of Justice, and expressed the opinion that everything in connection with the matter was satisfactory. Nevertheless he thinks that something should be
done to placate the mob, like the judge of old who allowed the populace to choose Barabbas. That, I think, is largely the frame of mind of the minister. There is nothing in it, he says; I find no fault in this man; my hands are clean; let his blood be upon you and your children.
I hope that if the investigation takes place it will be such a one as will do ample justice to all concerned and that the tribunal will be of such a character as to be entirely above the slightest suspicion, and that cleanout justice and fair play will be meted out to all parties.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It would not be amiss to inform the House that there has been no withdrawal of the motion. The question would have to be put from the Chair and then a withdrawal could only be made with the consent of the House.
The Acting Minister of Justice is wrong then.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Strictly speaking, a
motion can only be withdrawn at the request of the mover, but I think I may take it for granted, from the statement of the Acting Prime Minister, that he speaks for the hon. member for Victoria I therefore put the question as to whether the hon. gentleman shall have leave to withdraw his motion.
Motion withdrawn.

On the Orders of the Day:

I would like to ask if the Government has received any protests regarding the immigration into Western Canada of Hutterites and Men-nonites from the United States; and, if so, what action, if any, has been taken by the Government to meet the situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. Minister of Immigration (Mr. J. A. Calder) is out of town and he has asked me to answer this question, notice of which had been given previously. This is his answer:
The answer to the first part of the question is "Yes." A large number of protests has been received from various parts of Western Canada objecting to the settlement of Mennonites, Hutterites, and other conscientious objectors arriving from the United States.
The protests are based mainly on the following grounds:
(1)	That these people are conscientious objectors and as a consequence, will in future claim exemption from military service or endeavour to evade same if called upon;
(2)	That they claim special school and language privileges for their children and that they will resist the enforcement of the school laws of the several provinces in which they reside;
(3)	That they live in communities and are a detriment to other settlers residing in the same neighbourhood.
As regards these settlers and the action taken or proposed to be taken to deal with the situation, I desire upon behalf of the Government to state:
(1)	The great majority of these settlers are citizens of the United States. They are seeking homes in Canada as all American citizens have a right to do under existing laws and regulations.
(2)	The Government is not encouraging this particular movement of settlers to Canada.
(3)	The Government has not granted to these settlers any special privileges as regards schools or language.
(4)	Under the provisions of an Order in Council (P.C. No. 2622), dated October 25,

1918, all Mennonites entering Canada are subject to military service, as provided by existing laws for all residents or citizens of Canada. Such immigrants are not now and never have been entitled to the special privileges granted to Mennonites who settled in Western Canada under the provisions of an Order in Council dated August 13, 1873.
(5)	Under the provisions of an Order in
Council (P.C.	1676), dated August 12,
1899, Hutterites who entered Canada as settlers any time thereafter were given the fullest assurance of absolute immunity from military service. This Order in Council has been cancelled as regards Hutterites entering Canada in future.
(6)	The Government proposes to submit to Parliament at an early date a Bill, the provisions of which will debar all immigrants entering Canada in future to claim exemption from military service on conscientious grounds.
On the Orders of the Day:

Mr. Speaker, the creation of a Commission on Industrial Relations has been announced by the Minister of Labour, and the gentlemen mentioned by the papers as commissioners are Chief Justice Mathers, Senator White, Mr. Tom Moore, Mr. Riordon and Mr. John Bruce. May I ask the Acting Prime Minister if it is the intention of the Government to nominate a French-Canadian member to this commission? I would suggest as a matter of justice, the province of Quebec being the second largest industrial province of the Dominion, and 90 per cent of the labourers in the factories there being French-Cana-dians, that it would only be fair to have at least one French-speaking member of the commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

The member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) a few days ago inquired if the United States had refused coasting trade privileges to Canadian shippers in American waters. In response to an inquiry upon the subject I have received from
Ai'KIL 8, 1919
Washington a message to the following effect:
Advices from our representative for Lakes District indicates apparent scarcity business on Lakes for American ships for this season. Coastwise permits are now almost invariably declined on Atlantic and Pacific coasts only exceptional situation warranting departure from this policy.	_
By Order in Council the Minister of Customs is permitted to grant coasting privileges to American shipping in Canadian waters. The Order in Council, which is dated the 5th February, 1918, provides:
During the period of the war, until otherwise ordered the Minister of Customs may, under conditions specified by him, authorize collectors of customs to issue licenses permitting vessels of the United States of America to engage in the Coasting Trade of Canada.
Inasmuch as the United States now declines to confer the privilege upon Canadian vessels engaged in their coasting trade, it is contemplated that no further licenses be granted to American shipping for coasting trade in Canadian waters except under very exceptional circumstances. This will place our policy in this regard on a parity with that of the United States.
Is the hon. minister aware that a number of armed American vessels are on the Great Lakes at the present time?
I am not aware of there being any armed vessels on the Great Lakes at the present time. I shall make inquiries and let my hon. friend know to-morrow.
Sir THOMAS WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved that Bill No. 28, to confirm two Orders of the Governor General in Council respecting the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway System be read a third time.

Air. Speaker, in addition to the remarks that I had the honour to make recently when this Bill was before the House, I think it is also my duty to draw the attention of the Government to the grave situation which arises by the fact that the Government instead of proceeding amicably with the company has proceeded by way of what is virtually expropriation. If the Government had been a little more prudent probably it might have come to an amicable arrangement with the Grand Trunk Railway Company. By proceeding as it has done it has
absolutely no control over the Grand Trunk Railway Company or the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. Tne only thing the Government can do is to take over whatever property is actually situated in Canada. It cannot attach or seize the holdings of the company; these are kept in London.
It cannot attach or seize whatever railway connections are held by the Grand Trunk or by the Grand Trunk Pacific outside Canadian territory. This shows in what an awkward situation the Government will be. The Government will have no control whatever of the connections of the Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk Pacific in the States. Deprived of their American railway connections the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific are more a burden to this country than an advantage. By proceeding by way of expropriation, or by way of Order in Council under the War Measures Act, which is absolutely the same thing, the Government will find themselves in the position of having whatever railway property is situated in Canada, but they will be deprived of all the other holdings which the Grand Trunk Railway Company possess. The Government will not be able to bring about a liquidation of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company or the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Those two companies have their head offices in London, and if the Government want to press for payment of the bonds for which the Grand Trunk Railway Company may be held responsible, that company will enter into a long drawn out litigation with the Government and probably the ultimate result will be that very grave danger which I pointed out during the last discussion which took place in this House, namely, that the Grand Trunk Railway Company will win out in court. The Government advised us that they had taken all precautions in regard to the legal aspect of the question and that there was no danger whatever that, by the Government's acting as they did, by way of Order in Council, the Grand Trunk Railway Company would ipso facto be relieved of their obligations in connection with the bonds which they have guaranteed. I have consulted on this point with two oi the most prominent lawyers in Canada, one in Toronto and the other in Alontreal, and both of them are of opinion that the Government having failed to live up to the terms of the agreement of 1903, cannot compel the Grand Trunk Railway Company or the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company also to live up to that agreement. The Government, of course, may say that on any legal question wise men may differ, and

it is possible that my opinion., which is in accord with the legal opinion of these two prominent lawyers, may not be the one which the court may accept, but it is possible that it may. On questions of such importance the members of the highest tribunal often hold divergent views, and it is very imprudent on the part of the Government of this country to risk the whole matter on a question of ligitation. I do not anticipate that the Government will, on account of any argument that I may put forward, change their opinion on this point but if I might venture to offer the Government some advice, it would be not to force the matter to ligitation, but to come to an amicable arrangement with the Grand Trunk Railway Company or the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, because if the Government fail to reach an agreement, it will be a very dangerous question on which the highest tribunal might differ, and even if they compel the Grand Trunk Railway Company to live up to their obligations and pay the bonds which they have guaranteed, I am very much afraid that the only thing the Government will have to sustain such a recourse wdll be the property which lies in Canada, deprived of all its foreign connections, particularly its American connections, and deprived of all the other holdings that these companies keep in London and which are not attachable by any action which the Government might take. This,
I believe, will exemplify to the House the advisability of a careful study before committing the country to such a course; and, what a regrettable step the Government have taken in proceeding as they have done without defining their railway policy, and without making a further attempt to reach an agreement with the company. If the Government decide to force this matter to litigation and not come to an amicable arrangement with the company, they will be left only with the rails and rolling stock, and these, the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) described to us as a huge heap of scrap, or at least fifty per cent of it. This is what the Government will have in its possession to guarantee the immense indebtedness which their imprudent procedure has placed upon our shoulders, thereby relieving the Grand Trunk Railway Company.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the third time.

What is the explanation of the increases and decreases?

The first is an increase of $1,000 in the salary of the deputy minister; it has been decided as a matter of policy to increase the salaries of deputy ministers from $5,000 to $6,000. Then, the salary of the assistant deputy minister, Mr. St. Laurent, who is one of the most efficient men in the service, has been increased from $4,000 to $4,500. There is provision for 350 officials, but there are not that many in the department; in fact, the number is much less. Last year there were not 16 employees in the First Division, Subdivision A, although provision was made for that number. This year I am not sure whether there are 16 or not, but certain officials are to be advanced, largely through their annual increases, and brought up to the First Division, Subdivision A; we therefore estimate that it will take $9,000 more to pay the salaries of this class of clerks than it did last year- The same applies to the Second Division, Subdivision A: there were only 60 last year, and we are making provision for 80 this year, although I do not think there will be that number of clerks in that class. In the Second Division, Subdivision B, there was a decrease in the number of employees, from 88 to 65. That simply means that a number will be promoted from Subdivision B to Subdivision A of the Second Division. The same applies to Third Division, Subdivision A; there is an increase from 63 to 70, due not to an increase in the number of clerks, but to promotions. The total expected increase is about $600, but as all the positions may not be filled it is hard for me to tell the committee what the actual increase will be. In fact, there may be no increase at all.
During the past year very little work was done by the engineering branch of the department-such as dredging, the building of vrharves and breakwaters and so on. I think I am safe in saying that not nearly as much has been done as hon. members would like to see done. Not nearly as much has been done as I myself would like to see. If there is one thing that I think the country should look after, it is the transportation around our sea coasts. The ordinary trade of the country cannot be carried on unless we provide the necessary means of handling transportation; unless we do certain dredging and build wharves and breakwaters. I am sorry that I have

not been able to put in the Estimates anything like as much as I would like to have put in for these works-and it is not because I do not realize their importance.
There has been some decrease in the engineering staff; not merely as much, perhaps, as there should have been. About a year ago all building operations carried on by the Government were put under the Public Works Department. Previously the different departments had carried on extensive building programmes of their own. The Militia Department had a building programme and a building staff. The Military Hospitals Commission had quite a programme and quite a large staff. The Marine and Fisheries Department did considerable building. Now this work is all done by the Public Works Department and that means quite an increase to our architectural staff. No department of the Government during the past year has been busier or has rendered more efficient service to the country than has the architectural branch of the Public Works Department. We have constructed all the military buildings that have been found necessary throughout the country; we are constructing all the buildings required by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and the Department of Marine and Fisheries -although of the latter there are but few. Our energies during the past year have been devoted chiefly to the construction of military buildings and buildings for the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment Department.
Is this work done through contractors or by the department?

We prepare the plans
and specifications. In practically all cases we call for tenders and the work is done by contract, which is invariably given to the lowest tenderer. During the past year only two works were not done by tender and contract. These were in Nova Scotia, one at North Sydney and the other at Dartmouth, opposite Halifax, and were in connection with the aerial service of the Naval Department.
During the latter part of the summer it became necessary to protect our coasts against submarine raids. The United States Government desired to assist us and very generously offered to send men and equipment to Canada, and the Naval Department of Canada was asked to provide accommodation. We realized that it was impossible to prepare plans and specifications, call for tenders and have the work completed before the ground froze, and
therefore two works were let to local contractors-at least, one was a local contractor and the other a contractor now of Ottawa,-on the cost plus basis.
What was the amount involved, roughly speaking?
The estimated amount of the North Sydney and Dartmouth works was around $115,000 and $120,000. The work would have cost more than that had it been pushed to completion.
Was it in connection with the war?
Yes, absolutely. It wa3 for the housing of the United States aerial forces.
What will be done with those works now?
I am afraid there will not be much use for them in the future.
They were not completed?

No. In addition to the work at North Sydney and Dartmouth, extensive works were also necessary for the hydroplanes, which involved very extensive concrete structure running down into the sea, so that the planes could glide down and fly from the water Not very much of this work had been started. The buildings were in process of completion when the armistice was signed, and it was then a question what should be done with them. There were a number of buildings constructed of wood which were in an unfinished condition; and rightly or wrongly, after serious consideration, not by the department but by the Government as a whole, it was decided to complete the buildings that were then under construction. There was one place in which certain concrete foundations were about two-thirds built, and we finished the work because it was considered that possibly some use might be made of the buildings. Speaking generally, however, work ceased the moment the armistice was signed. The buildings in the two places cost around $300,000. The North Sydney buildings were used to some extent for the housing of troops and will probably be used for the accommodation of Newfoundlanders returning home. Personally, I do not think there will be very much use for these buildings in the future and we must charge the cost up to the war. With these exceptions every building that has been erected in Canada has been built by public tender, contract

being let to the lowest tenderer, and a great many million dollars have been involved. There has been some fault finding, and criticisms may as well be disposed of at once. In one or two places we were criticised for exercising too much precaution. It was said that we lost valuable time in preparing the plans and specifications and in calling for tenders, but we kept pretty well in touch with the situation and had an idea how many wounded returned soldiers there would be-I am speaking more of the hospitals now than anything else-and there were always at least three Deds for every two returned wounded men, while in many places there were two beds for each soldier.
Did you build the Ste. Anne's hospital?
The Ste. Anne's hospital was under construction when this work was handed over to our department.
Was the Militia Department building it?
No, the Military Hospitals Commission. They had given contracts amounting to about $300,000, and we have gone on and let various contracts aggregating over a million dollars.
Have the hospitals been built partly by the Hospitals Commission and partly by the Public Works Department?

Before April, 1918, it was called the Military Hospitals Commission, but we can treat it as the same organization as Sir James Lougheed's department. They were constructing hospitals for their department in many parts of Canada and the buildings were in course of construction when we took over the work. We carried out what arrangements they had made and if additional work was required it was done exclusively by the Public Works Department, and we are satisfied that we have saved the country money.
These buildings are now all under the Public Works Department?
No.
I mean the erection oi them.

They are built by the
Public Works Department. There are military hospitals administered by the Militia Department-one at Halifax, one at Fredericton and there will be a large work at Kingston, and the St. Andrew's Hospital at Toronto, formerly St. Andrew's School.

There is an Orthopaedic hospital in Toronto which is complete and up to date in every respect. These will be administered by the Militia Department until the soldiers are handed over to the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment Department. After that, I presume that the great majority of the buildings will be handed over to the Civil Re-establishment Department. If I had had my way from the beginning, I think a very large amount of money expended in the erection of military hospitals would have been spent in making additions to various city and municipal hospitals in different places. Then, when they were not required by the Militia Department they could go over to the municipalities and public organizations and be of some economic value. But as to the buildings which we have erected, if they cannot be used by the Soldiers Civil Re-establishment Department I do not know that they will be of much use to the people of Canada generally.

As my hon. friend is referring to the buildings in connection with the aerial service at Dartmouth and North Sydney, may I express regret that the splendid buildings and equipment which we had at Toronto have been sold by the Imperial Munitions Board to an American gentleman or an American firm.
I do not know what my hon. friend intends to do with the buildings that have been erected at Dartmouth and North Sydney but at all events, there is this to be considered : I believe in the future of the aerial service. We know what wonderful discoveries were made during the last years and what extraordinary help was rendered to the cause of the Allies by the aerial service. The response to the call by young Canadian aviators has been most remarkable during the war and I really believe that there is a splendid career opening up to our young men in that new service. It is a matter of every day occurrence that in Europe, for instance, the passenger service is performed to a limited extent, it is true, by the aeroplane. The postal service already exists in several countries through the air service. Contracts have been given by the Washington Government at some of the large centres in the United States for the transportation of mails from one point to another, and I believe that within a very limited period of time the aerial service will be a matter of course and will revolutionize the transportation system.
As we had an excellent groundwork for this aerial service in Canada, I was surprised to see that the Imperial Munitions

Board had sold that magnificent equipment which had been provided in Toronto.
I hope that my hon. friend, before disposing of those buildings in the Maritime Provinces, will consult with his colleagues and ponder over this matter because I sincerely believe there is a great future for the aerial service.

We have no intention whatever of disposing of those buildings until we have more light upon the whole question than we have at the present time. The buildings there are for the hydroaerial service consisting of hydroplanes which rise from the water. I cannot just say whether the buildings in Nova Scotia will be of much value from the aeroplane standpoint, but my hon. friend can rest assured that the buildings will be taken care of and that nothing will be done until the matter has been very thoroughly considered. I think he is a little in error in his remark about the buildings in Toronto having been disposed of. We have not disposed of any buildings which could be used, in any general sense, for the aeroplane service. Of course, the Government of Canada, as such, had nothing to do with any of these. They were built and owned by the Imperial Munitions Board. The Government purchased practically all the buildings which the Imperial Munitions Board had at Camp Borden, and that was really the centre of their activities. There was a building in North Toronto owned by the Canadian Aeroplanes Limited. It was put up to the Government to see if we would not buy it. Our department had a very careful investigation made by appraisers, but considering the structure and everything else together with the amount they required, we did not think it was good business to purchase it. It was a building in which they constructed aeroplanes, and it had nothing to do with the flying 4 p.m. of the machines themselves. The Imperial Munitions Board got a price which was more attractive to them, and the building was sold to a gentleman who purchased a great many of the aeroplanes. We have retained twenty of the aeroplanes at Camp Borden. A staff of engineers and mechanics has been kept there to look after them, and I can assure my hon. friend that, in so far as this will be of any benefit to the aerial business in Canada we have not lost touch with it. My hon. friend must realize that the aeroplanes that have been built by the Imperial Munitions Board have been built for a special purpose. They only carry one or
possibly two men. They were all right enough for the purpose for which they were constructed, but they were of practically no use from the commercial standpoint or for the carrying of mails. They would, however, be of very great value from the educational standpoint, for teaching men to handle them and imparting instructions along the general lines of aerial business. We have kept twenty of those, we have the whole plant at Camp Borden, but we did not consider that it was good business to spend money on the building at North Toronto when somebody else was willing to buy it, especially as it did not appear that it would be of very great advantage to the country as a whole.
My point is that this had developed into a very efficient Canadian industry, and now it has gone into the hands of a foreigner who has control of everything.

I am old enough to remember that at one time the ambition of my life was to own and drive an automobile and I thought that possibly I could reach that point some day. I do not know but that possibly I may be able some day to own and manage an aeroplane. But I think it will be some time before the Dominion of Canada will be justified in going into the business of manufacturing aeroplanes. The only object in getting that building would be to go into the business of manufacturing aeroplanes. I do not think the time has arrived when we would be justified in going into that particular form of Government ownership.

My hon. friend does not want to be up in the air.
Mr. CARVELL- Not in that particular sense. For that reason I think we pursued good business methods in allowing that particular establishment to be sold elsewhere. But I think we exercised good judgment too in maintaining the plant, and the aeroplane buildings at Camp Borden. We have there the nucleus of a Canadian service, not that these machines will be of very much value from a commerical standpoint but they can be used for educational purposes.

Does the minister not
know anything about the large number of aeroplanes that were assembled at North Sydney and as I am told, passed over to the Government of Canada? Has the Department of Public Works had anything to do with that?

We had nothing to do
with that. I understand that some were

assembled and are there yet. That did not go through my department but I know the American Government were very generous, that they have donated some of these machines to the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
My hon. friends will realize that those were hydroplanes, and are used purely for coast defence purposes. We have the buildings and plant, and some machines, forming the nucleus of a hydro service from an educational standpoint. To what extent we can avail ourselves of that plant later on I do not know; I can only hope that in the future it will be of some service to Canada.

The minister is asking for about a thousand dollars more than last year. He will remember that when he took charge of the Public Works Department he announced that he found that department terribly overloaded, and intimated that he was going to use the broad-axe very freely, and going to cut out all unnecessary expense and unnecessary help. I am surprised to find, after that promise of the minister, that his Estimates have been increased and not reduced. Speaking with one of the employees of the Department of Public Works last summer, with whom I am on very friendly terms, I asked him was he very busy. He replied, no, that he was staying at home just as much as he could.
I said to him, " If you have nothing to do I should think you would be frequenting some of the places of amusement" He replied, " If I did that too many people would be asking the same question as your are, and wanting to know what I am doing; I think the best way to avoid embarrassment is for me to remain at home and keep out of sight." I would like to know from the minister how many men he has in the service who are keeping out of sight and drawing their pay?

I am afraid my hon.
friend was not present earlier in the sitting when I spoke about the number of clerks for whose salaries I am asking a vote. I then said we had not got the number of clerks in our department that is mentioned here, and we do not expect to have them. Without doubt, in the Public Works Department in Ottawa to-day a great number of clerks who are not required and who are giving very little value for the money they are receiving
Put them out.

-I will explain to my hon. friend the situation in which I find myself. These are mostly old men, and 
some old women, who have been very long in the service, and would probably be objects of charity if we turned them out. Unfortunately there is no provision in the law to-day for the superannuation of people of this class. I have no means of providing for these old people, if I turn them out* except by giving them two months' salary. Probably there is no man who wants to cut the expenses of his department down any more than I do, but I have not reached the point 'where I can discharge people of sixty, sixty-five, seventy, and seventy-five years of age, and leave them dependent upon charity and upon their friends for sustenance. A year ago legislation was brought down to provide a fund by which we could retire very many people in this class in Ottawa. For some reason or other that Bill did not pass and the result is that I find myself unable to get rid of these people except by the method I have described. I do not want to do it, I don't think it is right, and I do not think my hon. friend would do it if he were in my position. However, we hope to bring in legislation this year enabling us to retire on something like a competence which will keep them from becoming objects of charity, those old servants who have been efficient in their day, but now on account of old age, are not able to render efficient service, and I believe the House will grant that legislation willingly. There are something like twenty-four such employees in our department, and we are asking the Civil Service Commission to make some provision by which we can accomplish their retirement without letting them feel that the country is kicking them out into the cold. That is true of the Inside Service. Naturally, in the case of a staff of two hundred or two hundred and fifty, a great many changes take place annually; girls get married and people die off. I am satisfied there must have been twelve or fifteen of such cases last year, but not a single addition has been made to the staff as a result of those changes. Nevertheless we are carrying on the work quite efficiently, and I do not think it will take very many years, if we succeed in getting the legislation for which we are asking, before we get our staff down to a real business basis, and so long as I remain at the head of this department it is my intention to aim at that standard.
So far as the Outside Service in concerned, I must confess that I am hot on nearly as solid ground. There are a great many in the Outside Service of the Public

Works Department during the past year who have not given very much value for the salaries they are drawing. That, however, is not the fault of the officials; we were not able to provide work on account of the war. We have not been spending money in the engineering branches, and hence there was not the same amount of work available for the outside employees as usual. I believe that some of these offices are overloaded, and I have already got rid of some employees, although not nearly as many as I should like to. But again let me say that I have a little humanity about me, and it is a pretty hard thing to take a person who occupies a Government position, who is willing to perform all the services you ask of him and wants to be an efficient servant, practically by the throat and say: Go and find a job elsewhere. I have done that in some cases, and it is not a pleasant occupation. I would have done it to a greater extent had it not been that a little less than a year ago legislation was passed by which the burden was thrown upon the Civil Service Commission of classifying and reporting upon the whole service of the country, which report is now practically ready.
We were promised that report two months ago, but I realize the tremendous amount of labour which that commission is carrying on and I am finding no fault at its not being ready. When that report comes down it will contain certain recommendations for the re-organization of the different services. And rest assured, that if the Civil Service Commission report that at any place there are officials who are not earning their money, or whose services should be dispensed with, then notwithstanding my dislike of taking positions away from people, I shall carry out the recommendations of the commission. I may tell my hon. friend frankly that in the Engineering Department of the Outside Service there are a good many who are not working very hard at the present time and whose services I think could be dispensed with without any serious detriment to the country, and just as soon as the classification report is in my hands I shall act on it. Maybe I will have to go further than I have indicated, but I cannot say until I get the report.
1 want my hon. friend to realize that I have not changed my views at all on the Civil Service of Canada. I have not tried to give to our Civil Servants more than I think they are entitled to, but I have tried to use them fairly as far as my department is concerned.
Who is making that Teport?

The Civil Service Commission. That was the burden cast upon them by the legislation passed here less
than a year ago.
I saw by the newspapers that some American firm was classifying the Civil Service. Will the hon. minister tell us if that is the case,, and what that firm is doing?

Yes. I do not know that I can give very much information. Mr. Myers, who has been employed by the Civil Service Commission, is simply acting as one of their employees for the purpose of assisting them in making a classification of the Service. There are two other gentlemen engaged with him, but I do not remember their names. Mr. Myers comes from Chicago. Those gentlemen are not making the classification any more than the Civil Service Commission are, but they are simply a part of the machinery by which the commission are trying to arrive at a real business basis for the Service. We have had the Civil Service Commission and some of these gentlemen before us in Council and have discussed a great many questions of policy and the lines upon which they are attempting to work out their report, and I think if my hon. friend could have listened to those gentlemen he would have come to the conclusion that they are men who know their business.. They are taking a standard for everything. They say that certain people performing a certain grade of work requiring certain qualifications and abilities should receive a certain salary, and then they are putting all the staff in the different departments in appropriate classifications. There is no getting away from the fact that our Civil Service has been a very unbusi-_ nesslike organization ever since Confedera-" tion. We are all sinners; perhaps some of the new members are not, but most of the hon. gentlemen facing me are sinners, and I confess I am one as well, for in the past we have asked particular Governments to place particular men in service, simply because those men wanted jobs. It was not a question whether they were particularly fitted for the jobs, or that the department needed their services; it was a question of getting jobs for the applicants, and they got them, with the result that the service has been overloaded-
And glutted.

Yes, and glutted, in
very many cases. But the Civil Service

Commission are honestly endeavouring to arrive at some business basis upon which the service can be reorganized. I may as well state here that they are recommending a scale of salaries on practically a pre-war basis, not a scale based upon the present high cost of living, the latter being taken care of by bonuses. 1 believe, when the report is received, it will be found to be based upon purely business methods. Then it will be a question for the Government of the day to implement, if necessary, the scale of salaries by bonuses until such time as things get back to a normal condition, as we all hope that they will in the very near future. Whether that be a year or two years, the 'Government will have to take care of that interim period just as business men have to take care of the wages paid to their employees.
Are the experts high class men, and how much are they being paid?

I am satisfied that they are high-class men, because I have had an opportunity on a number of occasions of discussing these questions with them. Only a week ago we discussed with them the Printing Bureau-of which we have heard something in this House-and I think they have some job on their hands to get the Bureau down to a business basis.
