We got their views, they got ours, and also the views of the Bureau officials, and the Civil Service Commission are now grappling with that subject. I am not able to answer my hon. friend as to how much these experts are being paid as it is not under my department, but there is no objection to giving the information to the House, and we will get it at the earliest possible moment.
. Mr. SINCLAIR (Guysboro): I understand that my hon. friend is inclined to return to the system of pensions for employees who are past the working age. That is not a new system; it was in force many years ago, and, if I remember rightly, it was abandoned and we went back to the position where civil servants, like other men, had to look after themselves and put something by for old age. For my part I object to any system of pensioning unless it is extended to all old people irrespective of whether they are civil servants or not. Old age pensions is a big 'question and there is a great deal to be said in favour of it, but I cannot see any reason why a man who is working for the Government should be put in a better position than any other good citizen who is working as best he can from 
day to day and in his old age is not able to take care of himself. There is no real distinction between the two .classes, and there cannot be any distinction drawn between the Inside and Outside Service so far as that is concerned. I would like to know from the hon. minister, because that is the impression he left on my mind, if it is the policy of the Government to return to the old plan of pensioning civil servants of the Inside Service?

I never knew that there was a pension law in this country. There was a superannuation law which existed for a great many years and was repealed in 1897 or 1898, but that is very different from the question of pensions. In the case of superannuation, it was based upon the length of service. I think after ten years a man was entitled to superannuation, and after thirty-five years he received thirty-five fiftieths of his average salary for the last three years, but that was the maximum. After he had been thirty-five years in the service he had a right to retire and take his full retiring allowance. That law was repealed. Most of the people who were in the service at that time and were entitled to take advantage of that law have passed away. But that (superannuation law did not apply to all the different clerks in the service because there were those who were classed as temporary, and I do not think it applied to messengers and the lower grades. So the result is we have in all the departments a number of these old people who never would have been entitled to superannuation if the superannuation law had not been repealed.
It is therefore, a question whether we shall continue to keep these people in the Government employ or not. There are, in the service, many people who are able to perform in a perfunctory manner the services which they are called upon to render. For instance, a man may be a little old and perhaps cannot do his work as efficiently as one would like him to, but he will do it, and the question arises: Will you turn that man out into the cold or will you give him some kind of a retiring allowance by the way of pension? There is a great deal in what the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) says as to the distinction between the status of civil servants and that of people in the ordinary avocations of life. But an old man in the Civil Service may say: I want to continue to perform the duties which you impose upon me; and that being the case, the Government is confronted with this proposition:	Shall you keep
in your employ a man who, because of old

age, has become inefficient, or shall you retire him on a small pension? Speaking for my department, I could have the business of my department carried on and save a lot of money to the country, and yet pay these old servants a reasonable pension, because in many cases their services are really not required. *In ordinary commercial life, one can say to a man: You are not fit to run my sawmill and, therefore,
I do not want you any longer. And you can put him out and that is the end of it; his friends or some one else must take care of him if he has not been able to lay up a competence for himself. But the Government of Canada is not the only organization in the world that makes some provision for old and trusted employees. There is a good deal of humanity in the world and many organizations are taking care of their old employees. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company provides a superannuation fund for practically every employee who has reached the age of sixty years, after having been a certain number of years in its service. The superannuation is not very large, but it is something to tide a man over the declining years of his life. The Grand Trunk Railway Company, the Government railways, and the banks have similar superannuation funds. The Bank of Montreal is much more generous to its old employees than is the Government of Canada either in the legislation which we introduced last year or in the legislation which we purpose introducing this year. The method I have advocated of pensioning of these old men is not new; it is practised by practically all the big employers of labour in this country. It seems hardly logical that a man in the employ of the Government should be placed in a better position than a man who earns his living by some other method, but nevertheless I hope the time is coming in this world when a better relation will exist between employers and employees than has existed in the past, and I hope the Government of Canada will not be the first to adopt a policy of casting adrift every old man who has become unable to perform his duties as economically or profitably to his employer as he did when he was younger. This war has, I think, taught us that a better relationship must exist between employers and employees in the future, and the Government would set an example to other employers of labour if it would adopt some scheme of pensions to provide for these people in their declining years.

Has not the Civil Service Commission power to transfer employees from one department to another?
I was under the impression that that was the case, and I am sure, in view of the scarcity of labour in this country, it will be a surprise to many of us to learn that some of the departments have been greatly overmanned while others have been greatly undermanned. The minister told us that in the engineering branch of the Department of Public Works there were many men for whom there was no work. I think the Civil Service Commission have been advertising for men with engineering qualifications to fill certain positions. I would imagine that as 16,000 appointments have been made during the past year by the Civil Service Commission, some of those idle employees in the various departments might have been utilized in some of the other services. I rather thought that, with the power conferred upon the Civil Service Commission, no particular branch of the Government would have exclusive jurisdiction over its employees, but that all would come under the control of the Civil Service Commission.
During the last year or two we have been hearing a great deal about pensions, and for a good reason, namely, that men have given up their health and been crippled and maimed in rendering a great public service to the country, but I do not see that men, who have grown ol'd in the service of the country and who have been protected as well as it is possible to protect any class of the community, should have special rights over the average citizen who is not in the public service. The minister told us that there were in his department about 24 men who were of an age that they were not competent to render efficient service. What is their average age?

It is true that the Civil Service Commission have power to transfer employees from one branch to the other, and it may interest my hon. friend to know that more than a year ago we offered these 24 employees to the Civil Service Commission for disposal, but we did not have any bids, the trouble being that their average age was at least 65 years.
What are their salaries?

As a rule, they would be the lower grades from $1,000 to $1,200, although perhaps some of these men might have more than that. A number of employees in the Department of Public Works have been transferred to another department in which their services are capable of being utilized. My hon. friend must be in



error as to the Civil Service Commission advertising for engineers. I have not been following the advertisements, but I think he will find the advertisements are mostly for architects. I do not know whether we could employ any more architects to-day, but I believe we could. During the past year we have been driven right to the wall for architects. We had to make arrangements with some of our architects to work three nights a week up to eleven o'clock, and we had, of course, to give them additional pay. We had to get public buildings ready for the soldiers. Early in the summer we had to have barracks; then we had to have military hospitals and hospitals for the Soldiers' Civil Ee-establishment Department, and we had to have architectural assistance. There may, of course, have been a case or two of applications for engineers.
If the CSvil Service Commission will apply to me for engineers I shall be happy to furnish tl*em with quite a number of splendid men whose services in the Department of Public Works could be dispensed with. I assume it is correct that the Civil Service Commission handled 14,000 appointments last year, but a large number of these would be temporary appointments. The Civil Service Commission appoint officials in the Customs and Inland Revenue offices all over the country; they appoint caretakers, country postmasters, engineers. They appoint all the officials of the Public Works Department. Since I became Minister of Public Works in October, 1917, I have had something to say about the appointment of a governor, a judge, a senator, and a director of the Canadian National Railways, and that has been the extent of my patronage since that time. I have nothing to say about the appointment of engineers, foremen, or any of the employees connected with the public works of .Canada.
What about your departmental solicitor?

My departmental solicitor was appointed by the Civil Service Commission. They called for applications, of which they received about forty-six. I do not know who formed the committee to decide upon the appointment, but in some way the commission went over the matter and decided upon Mr. T. J. Carter, a barrister of New Brunswick. Mr. Carter has lived in my constituency; he was a lawyer before 1 was. We have had a good many fights, political and professional. He is the best man in Canada for the position. I wanted a man who could attend the Ex-

chequer Court all over Canada when necessary and watch the interests of the Public Works Department in expropriation cases- besides, of course, advising the officials of the department in ordinary matters. As long as I am Minister of Public Works and Mr. Carter is solicitor the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) will not have any more Belanger cases to discuss in the House.

I saved the country
quite a lot.

I saved it before my
hon. friend did.
Who called the minister's attention to it?

I heard about it, anyway. Mr. Carter has had forty or fifty cases in the Exchequer Court during the last five or six years; he has also had arbitration and expropriation cases in New Brunswick. I have been his opponent in nearly every one of them; therefore I am a pretty good judge as to whether he is the proper man for the position. While I had nothing to do with his appointment, I am entirely satisfied with the selection made by the Civil Service Commission.

Is it the intention of the
Government to establish any of these hydroplane stations in British Columbia for the protection of the Pacific coast?
Mr: CARVELL: I am not able to state the policy of the Government on such an important matter. During the war, in conjunction with the United States authorities, it was decided to establish these two stations on the Atlantic coast and they were in course of construction when the armistice was signed. We did not consider that there was any danger at that time on the Pacific coast.

The minister says that
the service is composed of a number of old men, and he is so tender-hearted that he cannot bring himself to dispense with their services. The man I referred to a moment ago is not an old man.
Is he in the Inside or the Outside Service?

I will ask the minister
a question. Is it not a fact that in certain localities the salaries of the men who are supervising certain public works are greater than the amount of money to be expended in the works under supervision?
I could not answer that off-hand. In some cases that would be true; Sault Ste. Marie is one case.

Will my hon. friend get
the information?

I shall be glad to get the information. I have not tried to conceal the fact that in the engineering branch of the outside service there are more officials than are needed under present conditions. On the other hand, if, now that the war is over, we could see our way clear to vote sufficient money to start the works that ought to be started, there would be work enough for practically all these people. I think the leader of the Opposition could put his finger on three or four persons whose services could be dispensed with without any injustice to the country. He knows the position that I am facing. No doubt Sherbrooke is another place where there is not enough work for all employees. We have transferred men from one part of the country to another with a view to overcoming this difficulty. Last month we closed up one of the engineering districts because there was no work for it to do. While I do not say that we could close up many more, there is no doubt that a reduction in the interests of economy could be made and.the service jstill be maintained.
Are you going to remedy that?
As soon as the Civil Service Commision make their report I shall know what to do. I am awaiting that report, and I assure my hon. friend that I intend to act as soon as I get it.

The minister tells us that the Civil Service is practically composed of old people.
Mr. CAR\7ELL: I did not make any such statement. I said that in my department we had 24 old people whoise services could be dispensed with,

I had always thought that the only fossils that were connected with Parliament were in the Senate, but evidently they are in the Civil Service too, and I begin to wonder if they are not in the Government. I am afraid the people will come to think that the Government is composed to some extent of men of that sort unless something is done to remedy matters. If we are going to have an old age pension fund we should have one uniform system, because if every department had a system of its own there would be about twenty different Cabinet ministers 811
all controlling different schemes. I think it would be far better for the Government to establish a Pension Branch for old age which would include every one.

I never intimated that there would be a Pension Branch in the Public Works Department. The Bill that was introduced a year ago covered the whole Civil Service. We are collecting data, and I hope we shall be able to get some such legislation through during the coming year. Every department will, of course, take advantage of the fund in so far as they come within its provisions.
Air. AlcMASTER: It is always difficult to criticise the hon. minister when he is passing his Estimates, because his entire frankness disarms criticism. However, one of the reasons for the somewhat critical attitude of the country towards the Estimates is the fact that the Union Government displayed such a rosy programme before the people. I remember the hon. minister making a speech down in his native province, where he said that something new was going to happen every week, and some fresh step taken in the path of progress. To-day, however, the minister informs us that he has been unable to effect these reforms, and it is evident that the millennium has not yet arrived. When there were new departments being formed almost every day, when the Cabinet was increased from about 14 to about 24, when there was such a demand for help that he was enabled to conveniently place in other departments those for whom he had no use in his own, it is a sad condition of affairs that all the predictions of the minister have not been fulfilled. We never asked that people should be appointed to public office, and I wish to dissociate myself entirely from that school of political thought represented on the other side of the House which would reinstate in Canada the patronage system. We have absolutely no sympathy with that system but I think that this country can progress only on the basis of sincerity. One of our great griefs is that this Government, notwithstanding its pretensions about the elimination of patronage, has not in fact abolished it. The minister said he had nothing to do with appointing engineers or wharfingers, etc., the only appointments he had anything to do with being that of a judge and some other high officials. I contend that since this Government came into power they have appointed practically no one to high and important office who was not one of their supporters; and their pretension that

they eliminated patronage-an announcement which received the blessing of one of the prominent Protestant churches in this country in solemn conclave assembled -has no foundation whatever. We should be sincere, and the minister will find us on this side of the House prepared to cooperate with him in every step that will tend to an efficient and economical administration of the country's affairs. But we do think it would be well for him and 'those associated with him to avoid making "these claims to peculiar and superior political virtue. I cannot help calling to mind the most amazing avowal made by the Minister of Kailways and Canals last year when, in reply to a letter addressed to him by our departed friend, the late member for Prince Edward Island, he wrote that supporters of the Union Government, whether they were Liberal-Unionist, or Conservative-Unionist, would receive the same treatment at the hands of the Government. I submit these remarks merely in the hope that what I have said may tend to greater sincerity in the conduct of public affairs.
If my hon. friend thinks I have not been sincere-

I do not want the hon. minister to misunderstand me. I do not accuse him of any greater insincerity than the whole Unionist party. He is just one of them, and I would not state for a moment that he was personally insincere.

I do not accept that explanation for a moment, and I might as well tell my hon. friend so. I have not played any of the games he has been talking about; I have observed law. I have not dealt in the patronage business, and have never interfered with any one in the appointments to positions except the four I have mentioned.
Mr, McMASTER: Why should these four men be excepted?

If my hon. friend read the law he would know that the Civil Service Commission has not the right to nominate judges, nor governors, nor senators, and therefore the burden is cast upon me to give my recommendation to the Prime Minister. Of course, the hon. member is at liberty to use the word " insincerity " if he thinks fit.

I must make myself
clear. I never inferred for an instant that the Minister of Public Works had interfered with any offices of a subordinate char-

aeter. What I said was, that he and hi3 colleagues in the Union Government made great pretensions that they had abolished the patronage system, w'hen in fact they have not done so. Surely patronage has reference to the appointment of a judge or a governor as much as it has to the appointment of a wharfinger.

Will the hon. member
tell me how in the world a judge can be appointed if the Government does not assume the responsibility of appointing him?
Of course the responsibility is on the Government, but the Government should not make any pretensions-
My hon. friend is talking through his hat.
I do not wear my hat in the House, and I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. gentleman's language is not parliamentary.

I have been trying to speak all evening just for the purpose of putting down all this war of words that has come on. My reason for speaking at all- was that the matter that begun it was a matter appertaining to the particular part of the country from which I come-these aeroplanes, or, as we call them in our country, humming-birds. They were buzzing around our ears last summer. I would like to ask the minister if he would be good enough, at some time in the near future, to lend a little bit of information to this House as to some of the contracts that were let down there with respect to the aeroplane plant on what we call Indian Beach at North Sydney and with respect to hydroplanes on Kelly's Beach, North Sydney.
I will be very glad to give the information now if my hon. friend wants it.
I would like the House to have it.
I shall only be too happy to give it.

I know all about it myself. I would like to know how it was that Captain Dickson, who was an undertaker in Louisburg, got a very large contract on Kelly's Beach for the construction of hydroplanes on force contract. This is what we were told down home-an undertaker building aeroplanes on force contract! I might almost go farther and insinuate that perhaps I might get as much information in regard to this matter from the leader of

the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) as I would from my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works. However, perhaps I might go a little farther and say that Mr. George Kyte might have told us the whole thing about it. I will not speak of the dead; there is one of these who has passed away and 1 hope he is in a better world, but I might have gone a little bit farther and spoken of partners of members of this House knowing something about that areoplane and hydroplane business, if it is required that this House should know a little more about it than appears on the outside. I have had too many of these aeroplanes buzzing around my ears and I would like to know how it was that these things happened. My hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) spoke about patronage. Let me ask the minister how it wras that in connection with this matter in North Sydney we find Captain Dickson, an undertaker, Dan Louis McDonald, Luke Day, Bob Musgrave, George Kyte, Freeman O'Neil, Walter Crowe, not one Tory in the outfit. Patronage? Yes, there was patronage, but I have sent men there for jobs with the ordinary pick and shovel and because they were recommended by Butts they could not get jobs as they were supposed to be Tories.
Does my hon. friend only recommend Tories?
No, but they were supposed to be Tories

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am soiry to be
obliged to interrupt the hon. member.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that you will not decide this is out of order because I want to have the privilege of answering it before we pass on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member. I do not want my remarks to be considered as referring to him particularly because they are addressed to the committee in general. But the debate has wandered very far from the item under consideration. Old age pensions and aeroplane posts both on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts are certainly far from the item under consideration which has to do with salaries in the Inside Service of the Public Works Department.
The discussion about the undertaker is appropriate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member (Mr. Butts) has brought up a matter that the minister desires to answer before this item is adopted. I think that, with the unanimous consent of the committee, the minister should be permitted to answer, but I shall then ask the committee to return to the item under discussion.
I think the hon. member (Air. Butts) has a right to finish his argument if you are going to allow the minister to reply.

I bow in all fullness to your ruling but really it seems to be my misfortune to be always out of order/ Now, when there is some talk about patronage it will surely not be my misfortune to be the only one to be closed off. There was a lot of talk about patronage this afternoon. Is it not true that Allan J. Cameron, a returned soldier, of the village of Arichat, in the county of Richmond, applied for a situation as departmental solicitor and was he not the only lawyer who was a returned soldier who did apply? He went overseas as a private. I am going to ask the minister further: How many flying machines were there at Sydney Harbour; what did each cost; are there any records of any particular flights of any one of these fliers? Last fall when this Kelly's Beach hydroplant station was dismantled a large number of buildings were sold. And the peculiar thing about it-I speak on my own personal responsibility-is that these buildings were sold for $1,100-a five, ten, fifteen cent store price-before they* were advertised, and that George Burchall of the Toronto mine bought them.
How much did they cost?

They must have cost at
least five times that amount.

Speaking to the last point first, it is something I never heard of before. If there were buildings sold I do not know anything about it. If they were sold by the Public Works Department I can easily find out all about it, and I will be only too happy to do so and give the information to my hon. friend. It is the first news that has come to me that any buildings were sold at all. If there were buildings sold I would assume they were possibly buildings that were on the land that was expropriated, because, mind you, we could not buy this land at the price we thought was right, and we therefore went to the Exchequer Court with the case.
As for the number of flights made at Sydney Harbour, I do not know anything about it; I do not even know what the hydroplanes cost. I understand they were

donated by the American Government, but that is a matter entirely with the Marine and Fisheries Department, who will know more about it than does my hon. friend. Although it has nothing to do with my department, I will look the information up for my hon. friend's benefit and give it to him.
As to the departmental solicitor, it may be that Mr. Cameron made application to the Civil Service Commission; I do not know as to that. After the solicitor was appointed, I am not sure, but I think I saw the list. However, my hon. friend does not have to bother me about the matter, because I did not have anything to do with it. Let him go to the Civil Service Commission and he will get all the information he wants. He will get the names of all the men who applied, together with their occupations, and he can find out how many were returned soldiers. I understand there were ten or eleven of them, but I do not know.
I do not know the name of one of them. 1 could not tell my hon. friend the name of a solitary man who applied for the position, only the name of the man who was successful, and another man in my own depart-men whom I happen to know made an application. That is all I know about the matter of the appointment of a departmental solicitor. I want to tell my hon. friend that I have no apologies to make in regard to this matter. I will go further and say that at the Civil Service Commission had not given me a man in whom I had confidence . as a lawyer I would not have accepted him. Because there come times that when you - want a thing you want it, and you don't want something that is no good to you. I uo not say that Mr. Cameron was a good lawyer or a poor lawyer; I do not know anything about him, I never heard a word about him before. But I wanted a lawyer and I have got one. I am quite prepared to stand by everything I did, and if the Civil Service Commission had not given me a lawyer who could go into court and look after the interests of the Public Works Department I would not have accepted him. I want to get back now to the question that is really under discussion, and that is the construction of hydroplane stations. When my hon. friend (Mr. Butts) gets the facts perhaps he will have to revise some of the opinions that he was so willing to give to the House. The whole trouble is that the man who got this contract happens to be a Liberal. That is the explanation of the whole trouble, we may as well have it out now as any other time; he was a man whom I am told now did not vote for the [Hr. Carvefll.]
Union candidates in the last general election.
Mr. MoOREA: He was a wise man.

I did not know anything at the time as to what his politics were. It turns out now that those are the facts of the case. I am prepared for a thorough discussion and we will see whether my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. MoMaster) is right in his statement that we will not give a Liberal anything at all.

Mr. Chairman, may I be allowed to make a contradiction? With all due respect to the minister, I never said anything of the sort. As a mattter of fact the subject of these hydroplane stations was never in my mind at all when I was speaking. I was referring to a much larger question, that of the claim of the Government to have abolished patronage when I believed that the ministers had chosen Very important officials from among their own political friends. I do not want to be accused unjustly, and I know that the minister would not accuse me unjustly.

I would not want to accuse my hon. fri*nd unjustly. The trouble with the hon. gentleman is, is he says himself, that he is a new member, but he talks a good deal and says some things perhaps that he really does not mean. I am going to show the hon. gentleman that he evidently was not well informed or he would not have made the (sweeping statement which he did. I narrated earlier to the committee that sometime in the autumn a demand was made upon the Public Works Department for the construction of two of these seaplane stations. They consisted in each case, as I said before, of a number of buildings. I suppose, perhaps, there would be half a dozen large buildings, and also some sort of a concrete slide which went down into the water, and which latter was a very large affair. The cost of the buildings was estimated at a certain amount, the exact sum I have forgotten. We found, and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was most insistent, that this work must be done at once; no matter how it was done it must be done at once, because the cold weather was coming on and the minister contended, and he was right, that if we resorted to the ordinary course of preparing plans and specifications, calling for tenders, and letting the contract, it would take a month. If a month were to elapse the buildings would not be finished during the autumn, and in that case they could not be finished at all. That is what I was advised.

However, I protested, and probably must have lost four days' time in doing so, and refused to go on by force account because I do not believe in the Government of this country constructing any works by force account unless there are very strong reasons for doing so. Doubtless there are times when work by force account must be re-feorted to. I commenced to look around then for contractors. It was well known around Sydney and North Sydney and in Halifax that this work was going on. A Mr. O'Neil, a man whom I had known before, came here and spoke to me about who was going to do the work at North Sydney and I told him that I had not made up my mind. My hon. friend has mentioned a number of names in this connection. The only man that I ever met in the transaction, until after the contract was drawn, was Mr. O'Neil, and another gentleman who was with him. I do not remember the name of the latter, or that I could say who it was even if the name was recalled to me. He had a letter from Mr. Dickson. I knew Mr. Dickson before, and when the hon. gentleman talks about him being an undertaker he is not giving the House-
He is.

He may be, I axn not
saying lie is not, but he is also a contractor, a wrecker, a man who has done big business on the coast. I say this and I know what I am talking about.
So do I.

I would not make this statement if I did not know what I am talking about. I made inquiry as to who this man was from confidential sources in the province of Nova Scotia before I gave a contract, and I did not ask whether he was a Liberal or a Conservative either- that question never arose at all.
Then there was the matter of the Halifax work. The firm of Bate, McMahon and Company had done some work I believe for the department
Would the minister tell me if this Mr. O'Neil that he refers to was not a former employee of the Public Works Department who was dismissed from his position for offensive partisanship?
I never heard of it.

Was he not employed
in some department?

I tell my hon. friend I
never heard of it.
You have heard of it.

I am going to thrash this matter out, and I am delighted it has come up. I want things like this to be brought forward because I want the House to know how I have run this department during the last year. I knew this matter was coming up because I have heard a great deal about it in the last six or eight months, and I am delighted my hon. friend has taken this opportunity of giving me a chance to explain it. Mr. O'Neil was in the employ of the Government, and came here

Let me tell my hon.
friend he was never in the employ of the Public Works Department.
I can only say that if he was I never knew it.
He never was.

Dickson, who received the contract, was in the service of the Public Works Department and was dismissed for offensive partisanship. O'Neil, who was employed by another department, was also dismissed for offensive partisanship.

I do not know that. I know that he was in uniform and lie told me that he was in the Government service at Sydney-I think in one of the hospitals there. Now, as to Mr. Dickson, if he ever was in the employ of the Government I never knew it. I knew he had been a contractor with the Government.
I am as familiar with Cape Breton county as either of the hon. members, and I never heard of his being in the service of the Government in any shape or form.
I will be glad to give my hon. friend the title of the position he held. He was in the Government telegraph service at Louisburg as general line repairer.

Even if he had been in the employ of the Government, and had been dismissed for partisanship, that is no reason why he should not work for the Government if he works honestly and uprightly. I had the Halifax situation and the North Sydney situation on my hands and time was pressing. I went to Colonel Low to see if he could take the work. He represented Bate, McMahon and Company who were doing work at Sydney and also at Halifax. He said: Yes, he could take on the Halifax work. I gave him the con-

tract for the Halifax work, and I want to tell my hon. friend that I did not do this without taking the whole thing to council where it was thoroughly thrashed out. I canvassed the whole situation with a number of men in the contracting business in the province of New Brunswick, and I could not find a single man who was in a position to take this contract. I know the contractors in my province and I could pick out every man who ordinarily would be in a position to undertake this work, but everybody was busy down there last year. The Valley railway, as we call it, was under construction, and practically every contractor in New Brunswick was employed upon that, as well as some of the principal contractors in Nova Scotia; the Government was carrying on tremendously big works at Halifax and Sydney, and practically every Nova Scotia firm that I knew anything about was engaged there. I want to say here that Mr. George W. Kyte never came to me and I never spoke to him until recently. The leader of the Opposition has been referred to, but I never heard from him, and he had no more to do with the matter than a man in Saskatoon. I inquired of a certain man who happened to be here-and I will give my hon. friend his name in confidence-a large employer of labour in the province of Nova Scotia, probably the largest there, a man who knows every workman in Gape Breton Island, about the situation. He told me that Mr. Dickson was well qualified to carry on the work. I sent for Mr. Dickson, and he convinced me of 'his ability to undertake the work. I gave him the contract on force account, and the work was inspected as no other work was inspected in my deipartment last year because the contract had not been given until my friends had come to me with stories that they had got in Sydney and they said, "You are employing a Grit to do this work," and asked me to rescind the contract. I would not do so and I never yet have done so. I could not believe that because a man happened to be a Liberal he could not work for this department honestly and uprightly, that is no part of my political faith. I have given my hon. friend the facts as I understand them.
Had the hon. minister any inquiries or communications of any kind from any such firms as Rhodes, Currie & Co., or Chappie Bros., Sydney?

I do not think so.
Rhodes, Currie & Co. at that time had just entered into a contract for work at Hali-
[ Mr. Carvell.]
fax to cost half a million dollars, in addition to the Camp Hill hospital, which they had under construction. I have no recollection of ever having heard from Chappie Bros, at all. I do not think I had a solitary application from any person to do that work except from Mr. Dickson. I may be in error about this, but my recollection. is pretty good.
Mr. BUTTS; It was not advertised?

Of course it was not.
That is what I have been telling my hon. friend. It was a matter of such urgency that I could not advertise it. That is why I had to have it done by force account. That contract was only for the construction of cheap wooden buildings. I presume that every hon. member of this committee has seen a similar class of buildings. There is no plastering; I think there is no foundation except some posts, and the buildings are sheathed with shiplap I think it is called-
An hon. MEMBER; Clapboard.
Mr. CARVELL-or tongue and groove material. The inside work is purely of wood with a layer of tar paper between the boards. Even the roofs are not covered with shingles, but with a ready roofing material. It is the cheapest kind of work you could imagine. Any man capable oi handling a saw and hammer could qualify as a carpenter on it. It did not require a man of great ability, it only required a man who could employ men and who would be honest and not pay higher wages or higher prices for material than he should pay, and who would rush the work and get the best out of the men.
This work was carried out under inspection?

Absolutely; not only
under local inspectors, but I utilized the officials of the Engineering Department both from Sydney and Antigonish for the purpose. In addition, Mr. Fuller, the Assistant Chief Architect in this city, made trip after trip to North Sydney and Halifax, and he reported to me personally, not through any of the officials. And I want to tell this committee that there was nothing constructed in the Public Works Department during the past year which I personally investigated and looked after so closely as I did that work at North Sydney. At the time I thought I was carrying on an ordinary business transaction. A man had applied to me, I had found out that he was

well qualified for the work, and I gave him the contract. It was not until same of my colleagues joined me and I got the story, and I saw what I had to face, that I took a personal interest in the construction of that work, and I stand by it from A to Z. If there is anybody wants any investigation I hope he will come on with it.
Was there any interference on the part of some members of Parliament to press the hon. minister to give that contract?
No, not from members of Parliament or members of the Government. I let the contract myself as Minister of Public Works, and I take full responsibility for everything done there.
What was the cost of these works?
Can you tell me the size of the buildings?

There were three large barracks-I suppose they would be a couple of hundred feet long and 40 or 50 feet wide, but I could not state the dimensions exactly. There is no question whatever, Mr. Chairman, that the buildings did not cost any more than they should have cost. That is not the question at issue at all. The question at issue is that I gave the contract to that particular man. Nobody would raise any question as to the character of the work. The contract was carried out to the letter, it was under forced account, and the contractor did as he was told to do.
And when the Minister of Naval Affairs was pressing for it?

Yes, not merely pressing; he was demanding that I go on and do it by force account, and he was violently protesting against taking the time that would be necessary to prepare plans and specifications and call for tenders. It takes a month to do that, and he wanted it done in a day.
Was that work done in conjunction with the United States Government?

No; the next question that came up was as to tlhe construction of these ramps running down into the sea, and that at North Sydney especially was a very serious proposition and a great deal of dredging would have been required. In fact, I have often wondered if it would not have been possible to locate the work at
some other point, because the next part of the contract was going to run into some six or seven hundred thousand dollars before it was completed. There again, I wanted to call for tenders, but the same condition existed. On account of the objections I had had from Nova Scotia, I did not give this other work to Captain Dickson. I did not want to have any trouble over it and I was not sure that Captain Dickson had had the experience in heavy concrete work of that kind. I, therefore, gave that part of the work to Bate, McMahon and Company, and I did not know of any other party I could get and no other person applied to me. Bate, McMahon and Company started the work, and I think the day after the armistice was signed, we stopped the work. It was, of course, an easy mattei to stop the concrete work and what is there speaks for itself. It would have been an absolute waste if we had gone on with the building, so we went on and completed, not all the buildings, but those that were under construction at the time.
I realize this matter does not come up under the Civil Government vote, but as my hon. friends wish it to be threshed out,
I shall be only too happy to give them all the information wanted. The mattei can be brought up in the Public Accounts Committee and Mr. Fuller, the architect, who made it his special business to investigate these matters as they went along, can, if required, be summoned and he will give all the information he can, and all the other officials of the department will be only too glad to give all the information possible. At the time I gave this contract, I had no knowledge as to what relations this man had with any person in Nova Scotia, He did the work well.
He did good work?
Yes, and he did it quickly, and if the war had gone on, the United *States marines would have been properly and comfortably housed during the winter.
Was what is now being criticized a part of war work?
Yes. There is no criticism of the work.

Of the man who did the
work?

The criticism is of the
man who got the contract.
Was the work supervised by an engineer of the department?

Certainly. There was
one man all the time and two men most of the time the work was going on, and in addition to the local men who were supervising the work, I told the committee that 1 sent the assistant chief architect there on three or four occasions to supervise the work personally and see that it was properly done. I do not think there will be any criticism of the cost of the work nor of the manner in which it was carried out. Probably my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) will have to admit that an apology is due.
Mr. iMcMASTER: I must protest against the minister's endeavouring to give the House the impression that any remarks of mine were made in connection with this contract in. Nova 'Scotia. I knew absolutely nothing about it, and my remarks were made without reference to it. I want the minister to understand that, because it is true. [DOT]
Mr. OARVELiL:	I accept that in toto.
iMy hon. friend did state though in pretty plain words that this Government did not purpose giving contracts or anything else to any men except those who had voted for the Government. That is the last thought that has entered into my mind in anything il have done. I can only say in conclusion that this illustrates the wisdom of the Department of Public Works keeping to the tender and contract system, and that when one is expending public money, it is better to expend it in the open, so that any man, no matter who or what he may be, will have an opportunity of tendering on it and the Government will get the best and the cheapest work there is and there will be no cause for criticism.

Under the heading "Contingencies, travelling expenses," the amount last year was $30,000. That is a big amount, but this year it is increased to $44,000, an increase of $14,000. Do some of the officials of the department intend to travel more this year, or what is this for?

Last year we used the whole $30,000. A few minutes ago I gave an illustration cf the North Sydney question to show the committee that sometimes situations arise which are a little different from the ordinary. For instance, I sent the assistant chief architect all the way from Ottawa to North Sydney on three or four occasions to make a personal inspection of a particular work. With the tremendous amount of work we still have under way for hospitals for the Department of Soldiers'' 
Civil Re-establishment and the work we shall have under way for some of the big buildings that are being constructed and all the little harbours, breakwaters and so. on, that are being constructed throughout" Canada, I find that money spent in supervising engineers is a very good investment, and in a great many instances in the last year and a half I find it has paid me to send a man from Ottawa, possibly to British Columbia or any other part of Canada. I have adopted this policy, that whenever I have had any suspicion or any reasonable ground for suspicion, and I think it is foi the benefit of the Department of Public Works to have a man make a personal investigation and report to me personally, to send one. Therefore, I presume it is going to require more money to carry on inspection work during this year than in the past, and for that reason, I am asking for a larger appropriation. If the money is not required, it will not be expended, but if it is necessary to send a man to any part of Canada to supervise any public work, and to come back and report to me personally, I want to have the funds to pay his expenses.
When was the departmental solicitor appointed?
I have not the exact date, but I think some time in February, about five or six weeks-ago.	.
Have all the accounts of Dickson been settled?
No. Some small amount is, I think, still pending.

I do not quite understand this item of $5,000 for a departmental solicitor. Apparently, all the departments of the Government have solicitors of their own. Why not have the legal business of the Government transacted by the Departr ment of Justice? The Minister of Justice is there to advise all the other ministers, and the Minister of Public Works, according to the constitution of this country, if any legal question arises in his department, must refer the matter to the Department of Justice and ask for its opinions. Besides the Minister of Justice, we have, so as to complete the legal machinery of the Government, a Solicitor General. The functions of a Solicitor General, in the Federal Government as in the Imperial Government, are to appear before the courts and represent the interest of the Government, the interest of all the departments. The ministex does not require the services of a departmental solicitor.

When the minister needs a solicitor let him apply to the Department of Justice. He talks about economy; here is an opportunity for him to practise it. The minister says that the solicitor appointed in his department is a good lawyer; let him go back to his practice and let the minister apply to the Department of Justice when he needs legal advice. If each department is to have a special solicitor in cases in which it is interested before the Exchequer Court, what is the use of having a Solicitor General? What is the use of having all the lawyers who are employed in the Department oi Justice? What is the use of having Mr. Newcombe, the deputy minister of that department?

In the first place, the salary is $3,500, not $5,000. But the solicitor for the department can save a good many times $5,000 each year. Everything my hon. friend says is constitutionally true and correct. If I want an opinion upon a matter of law or upon the construction of a contract involving a question of principle in my department, probably I should go to the Justice Department for it; I have been doing that in the past, and I will probably do so in the future. Since this solicitor has been in the department, however, we have kept him busy. Matters come up every day on which we get reports from him, and get them more quickly than we could get them from the Justice Department. I realize thal the Justice Department has every department of the Government to attend to, and I cast no reflection upon it. But my hon. friend has forgotten the distinction that I attempted to draw. The duty of the Justice Department is to pass upon the validity oi contracts, to interpret documents, to advise the departments what the law is on various points that come up. I am not attempting to take away from the Justice Department any of its functions. But' it is not the business of the Justice Department to send its officials all over the country to attend the Exchequer Court when property is being expropriated by the Department of Public Works. Take the Belanger case. A piece of property in my hon. friend's own city was required by the department. The construction of a dam at the mouth of the St. -Charles river would overflow some of the adjacent land; therefore it became necessary to expropriate that land. The department expropriated not only the land that would be overflowed, but also four or five times as much land below the dam that would not be overflowed at all.
Mr. LEMilEUX: Who did that?
The Government.
Which Government?

The Government that
preceded this one. It was done, I think, in 1914-15; I have not the exact date. A local solicitor was asked to represent the Justice Department. Now, I do not know anything about that gentleman and I want to be very careful to say nothing in derogation of him. But I have read the evidence:
I have read the case very carefully, and my judgment is that this gentleman, although a good lawyer, had never had very much experience in the expropriation of land, either for the Government or for the railways. That is a class of litigation all by itself. A man might practise law for twenty-five years and not know much about that particular branch of the law unless he had had the necessary experience. The gentleman who represented the Justice Department in that case considered that if was not his business to hunt around and gel witnesses-he told me so himself when 1 discussed the matter with him, although he said that in the end he had to get them. The witnesses who were brought before the court swore that the land was worth all the way from twenty to twenty-three and twenty-four cents a square foot. One witness said he was not sure; he would put it at from ten to fifteen cents a square foot. That was simply a voluntary statement. The judge of the Exchequer Court accepted the ten cents a square foot as being the value of the land, but stated-I do not think he used these words, but this is the suostance of them-that in his judgment the case had not been properly tried.
He used the word "reluctantly."
He gave that judgment reluctantly, taking the minimum amount mentioned by any witness-and it was mentioned only by one witness. At ten cents a square foot the value came to something like $120,000.

$225,000; and then the ten per cent was added, bringing it up to about $240,000. IHad the Public Works Department been represented in that case by such a counsel as we now have-a man who has had much greater experience in such cases than many men in Canada have had-I do not think we should have had that verdict. Fortunately, we have got around that particular transaction. I know

something about the law of expropriation; I have had a few cases in my experience. We appealed to the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court gave us a new trial. We abandoned practically all the land below the dam.
Did my hon. friend visit the premises?

Yes, and it did not take me long to see the whole thing, either. We have abandoned all the land below the dam which we do not want, and we shall have to settle in some way with the owner of the land for what we have taken. If we cannot settle amicably, we will go to the Exchequer Court, and the departmental solicitor will be there to represent the department. We call him " Departmental Solicitor" but he is really a counsel. His duty is to go over the country and act as counsel for the Public Works Department and for the Government. He takes nothing out of the hands of the Justice Department or of the Solicitor General; he goes before the Exchequer Court representing the department with a waiting brief, or an active brief, if necessary, in order to see that the interests of the department are protected. Let me give the committee another illustration. We have a case in the city of Victoria now involving about $200,000. A firm of contractors have brought action against the Government claiming that they have been improperly dealt with. I knew something about the case before I became minister and as a lawyer I came to the conclusion that this firm had not been unfairly dealt with. Accordingly, I decided to contest this case. I have spent a night and part of a day discussing it with the Department of Justice, the Solicitor General, and the Departmental Solicitor. I have taken many occasions during the last month to go over the evidence with the Departmental Solicitor and I think he knows the case now nearly as well as I do. If it goes to trial he will be there to represent the Public Works Department.
What will be the status of the departmental solicitor before the court?
He will have status in the court. There need be no fear about that, and if he has not we will see that he gets it. Now the Government is expropriating a dry-dock in Halifax.
The minister has not answered my question.

I have told my hon.
friend that the solicitor will have a proper 
status before the court. I am not charged with the conduct of the court and am not the judge; therefore I cannot say exactly what the solicitor will do. But I know he will be there and will have a status and be heard. I was going to say that we are expropriating a dry-dock in Halifax involving $1,250,000. In connection with this, I will go over the whole matter with the departmental solicitor and together we will work up the case so that when he goes before the court he will be possessed of all the knowledge which the Public Works Department can give him. I have no apologies to make for asking for this $3,500 for a departmental solicitor, neither have I any apologies to offer for the gentleman who happens to occupy the position at the present time.

I cannot give the exact figures but I am informed that there are 63 vacancies, or about 287 employees, instead of 350.
I asked for the unexpended balance.
It would be around $60000 to $70,000.

$300,000 unexpended?
Is there over
No, about $60,000 to $70,000. There are 63 clerks with an average of $1,000 each or about $63,000.
Would it not be well to give the unexpended balance for each ,ndi\idual item, so that wre can see the saving there is?

The reason we prepared the estimates this year in the old way is because we have not the report of the Civil Service Commission. Another year if I occupy this position I shall certainly ask Parliament to vote only the amount of money we expect to expend. You cannot always state the number of officials with exact precision because you can never foresee any contingency, such, for instance, as there was last year in the Architectural Branch.
You have provided for that in the Estimates under "sundries."

I do not quite understand the explanation as regards the solicitor. The minister said he wanted to have a man whose special duty it would be to attend the courts whenever the interests of the department might be involved. This officer is either necessary or unnecessary, and if he is necessary it must be because the Department of Justice is not doing its duty as it should. I do not think the minister intends to imply that the Department of Justice is not performing its duty.

The Department of Justice of necessity appoints a man in the locality as their solicitor and entrusts to him the conduct of the case. The department cannot send their man out to Vancouver to argue a case before the Exchequer Court there.

Will it be possible for this solicitor to do it?
Mr.. CARVELL: He will do it.
How can one man do it?
Because the Exchequer only sits in one place at a time.
And can he attend to all these cases?

Certainly. I have given illustrations of cases in different parts oi the country. A man is appointed by the Department of Justice, in Quebec, say. He never comes near the Public Works Department, but takes the file handed him by the department. I want a man who belongs to the department and knows all about it and can discuss matters with the deputy minister, the chief engineer, the chiei architect and myself, so that we may know exactly what we are going to do in court. A man in Levis or Halifax cannot come here to get his information, sitting night after night, and consulting with the minister the same as the departmental solicitor can. No disrespect is intended to the Department of Justice or its solicitors throughout the country, but we want a man who will be in court armed with all the facts.
What becomes of the unexpended balance at the end of the year?
It lapses.

I will be very glad to da so on the very first occasion possible. 1 hope to get into Supply again on Thursday and I shall then be very glad to furnish that information.

generally to the Civil Service. The House again in Committee of Supply. Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Ocean and mail service between Canada and Great Britain, $1,000,000.

['Mr. Speaker, the Bill as presented is self-explanatory, its main oh-', 'jeets being twofold; first, to set aside Armistice day, the second Monday in November each year, as a perpetual memorial of the victorious conclusion of the recent war; second, to establish a set day each year as a permanent day of Thanksgiving. I purpose speaking at greater length on the second reading of the Bill, and I will therefore reserve any further remarks until that time.']
Last year this vote was $400,000. What is the reason for the increase of $600,000?

The smallness of last year's vote was due to knowledge of the fact that we were unable to obtain steamers to carry on the mail service, and the department felt certain that that amount would be ample for any mail service that could be carried out during that fiscal year. Now that the war is over it is hoped that we shall be able to re-establish the former mail service across the Atlantic, and the vote now corresponds to the amount asked for prior to the war. However, it may prove impossible, even during the current year, to obtain the necessary steamships to carry the mail according to the terms of the contract which was in force prior to the war. In that event the full amount will not be expended. We merely wish to have authority to enter into a mail service contract, and we anticipate that the services as a whole will probably require the amount of money asked for. This, of course, is purely a mail service and not a freight service.
Does the minister mean that the steamships do not carry any freight?
They carry freight, but this vote is for a mail service.

In view of the prevailing high freight and passenger rates, which greatly exceed those in force before the war, and of the fact that so many steamers are now being released for ordinary transportation purposes, it seems to me the Government should be able to make contracts with the steamship companies to carry mails at a much lower subsidy than that paid in pre-war times.

The hon. member's suggestion is a proper one, and will be considered; but as a matter of fact I think the steamship companies would rather carry freight than mails, because the compensation is much less remunerative for the carriage of mails.
Is this steamship subvention on a basis of so much per ton of mail carried, or is it given in the form of a subsidy?

The contractors are paid for two round voyages each week, but the service has not been completely performed during the last two years. The subsidy amounts to $5,292 per round* trip, and of course if the voyages are not performed the money is not paid.
Any payment is made irrespective of the amount of mail carried on each voyage?
Yes.
With what steamship line is the contract made?

The contract was with the Canadian Pacific Ocean Services Limited, but during the past two years the Government was obliged to utilize the services of any steamship that was available for this purpose.
Steam service or services between Canada and Newfoundland, $70,000.
What is the nature of this service?

This service is carried on between the port of North Sydney, Nova Scotia, and Port aux Basques, Newfoundland, and is operated by the Reid Newfoundland Railway Company. It calls for one trip each day, excepting Sunday, between the ports mentioned. There is no change whatever in the service.
Mr. CA'HILL: Was the whole of the $70,000 spent on the service last year?

The sum of
$57,000 was expended for the last fiscal year.

This service was very well performed indeed by the Reid Newfoundland Company, but since the war begam they have not been able to give us as good a service as formerly, principally, I presume, because they could not get the steamers. Will the hon. minister be able to give us the names of the steamers for the present season, and state if the company will have the necessary complement of boats to perform the daily service?

So far as the department are advised, the steamers at present in service are the Kyle, the Sagona, and the Glencoe. No contract has been made for the present year, so of course we
do not know at the moment what steamers they will offer for that service, but we assume that those steamers are likely to be offered for the service.
Steam service or services between Canada and the West Indies or South America, or both, $340,666.66.
Does this provide solely for mail service, or is it partially for freight service?
This is principally freight service. However, the contractors are obliged to carry mails.
Is .any provision made in this item for the possible opening up of trade with the Pacific coast ports via the Panama canal?
No, this service would not include that route.

I would like to draw the attention of the hon. minister to the desirability of providing for the promotion of that trade. Only a day or two ago I was advised of a case from the coast where a firm had 1,500 tons of freight to be handled. On the Pacific coast we are importing large quantities of goods from it/he West Indies- spices, coffee, and such like, and a very valuable trade can be developed.

I quite agree with my hon. friend that a service of this kind would be of great benefit to those on the Pacific coast. I had a very interesting conversation this morning with Mr. Robert Dollar, who by the way in his early days lived in Canada, but for the last thirty or forty years has been in the United States. He is known throughout the world for his interest in Pacific coast steamship services. He informed me that he has in mind the opening of a service between Vancouver and New York. I spent a little time trying to induce him to include a Canadian Atlantic port.
Preferably Halifax.

There might be
more unsuitable places. I think Mr. Dollar will establish the service immediately if he can obtain a steamer, and he is at the present moment negotiating in Great Britain for the purchase or construction of one. I have also this to add, that he did not want a steamship subsidy from the Government, and would not take one.

What line is this subsidy
paid to?

This service is
performed by the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company, of London, England. The Canadian termini are St. John and Halifax. The West India Islands called at are Bermuda, St. Kitts, Montserrat, Dominica, St. Lucia, St. Vincent, Barbados, Trinidad, and some others.
How many boats have they in the service?

Four, usually.
Two of them were requisitioned by the British Ministry of Shipping during the war, and were returned to the service only recently.
Are they very good boats?
I think so. The .service has been very satisfactory. I understand.
What is the speed?
Eleven knots.

Did they make
any money last year?
Mr. A. K. .MACLEAN: I think they made a small profit. Of course, as might be expected, they complain that they lost heavily by having two of their steamers requisitioned by the British Ministry of Shipping. At the present moment they are asking for an increase in the passenger and freight rates on the ground that the service is not giving them sufficient revenue. However, I do not mean to say that that statement is correct.

Is the hon. minister
aware that shipmasters and ship owners very seldom admit making any money?

I have discovered that during the last few days.
Mr; DUFF:	The minister informed the
committee that this amount was paid to the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company. I think that part of this amount is paid to that company, but is it not a fact that part of it is paid to Pickford & Black, whose boats ply between Halifax, Jamaica and iCuba?
No, it is all paid to the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company.

Do not the Jamaica boats
get any subsidy?
No.

These boats are loaded to
the hatches every trip and cannot take all the freight that is offered; a lot of freight

is left at Halifax every time the boats leave. If these boats can ply between JTalifax, Jamaica and Cuba without a subsidy, the Royal Mail Steam Packet boats ought to be able to do likewise.

It may be quite true that during the last year or two the contractors were not able to carry all the freight that was offering, but my hon. friend must remember that the sendee was being performed with two steamers only. [DOT]It may be that during certain seasons oi the year when sugar is moving the steamers have quite sufficient freight; but it is also true that at other seasons the boats both in and out are short of cargo. Although the service between Halifax and Jamaica is performed by Messrs Pickford & Black without any subsidy, it must be remembered that they have no passenger accommodation on their boats and those boats would hardly be regarded as sufficient for a subsidized service.

The Jamaica boats carry
passengers.

Not to any extent. Under the arrangement made with the West India Islands at. the time of the tariff arrangement, Canada agreed to establish an improved service, and the contract made with the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company was the result of that agreement.
I notice that this item also calls for service between Canada and South America. What boats perform that service?
The service is continued from the West India Islands down to Georgetown, British Guiana.

The hon. minister seems to be in doubt as to the amount of money this company made during the past year. I regard it as very important that he should insist on a statement of the earnings of these boats, for only so can we have an intelligent idea as to whether we should continue these subsidies or not. They will always take the money from you if you will give it to them, but they are always loath to give you their figures. When we are subsidizing a line which does not carry our mails we ought to be very strict about gettingsuch information. As the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) says, these companies may be able to carry on the services without this assistance, and the only way in w'hich that can be ascertained is by getting a complete and accurate statement of their earnings. T-hat is difficult )to procure; it would take a clever, expert accountant to tell from the books of a

ship-owning company whether they were making money or not. I would ask the minister to look into this question and see if we are not allowing this to drift a little too much, and if, each year before the Estimates come before the House, he could find out the standing of the different companies and what they earned during the previous year.

My hon. friend means that it takes a steamship man to catch a steamship man. Perhaps -his advice may be worth something. The matter of granting subsidies to steamship companies, particularly in connection with services tc other countries, is, I must admit, a very doubtful one, and it may be, in view of the changed conditions brought about by the war, that many of those services which are to-day receiving subsidies might get along very well without them. That is a matter deserving investigation by the Government. And only to-day I have received such a recommendation from some of the officers of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and probably I shall- recommend that some investigation be made as to the necessity of continuing those steamship subsidies. In many cases, we would develop trade much more rapidly by leaving the operation of such services to private parties. There are, however, many cases, particularly of a local nature, where it is, perhaps, quite difficult to avoid granting a subsidy.
As regards the item "steam service between Canadian Atlantic ports and Australia and New Zealand," in answering a question put by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) the other night, I omitted to tell him that this subsidy is paid upon the basis of an export service only. That is, a contract in that particular case is made with a New Zealand or an Australian shipping company which, under the contract, is to perform four trips per month, and not with any specified steamship. When their steamships reach New Zealand they pick up a cargo and proceed to any other part of the world where business may carry them, and the next month the service may be performed by other steamers altogether, but belonging to the same steamship line. Therefore, that particular subsidy is paid towards the development of our export trade with Australia and New Zealand.

If those steamships could pick up a return -cargo the necessity of paying them a subsidy would be obviated, because they would be able to earn freight
rates both going to and coming. If there was not the barrier of protection to get over when they arrived at a Canadian port, no doubt they would be able to obtain sufficient cargo to warrant their returning to Canada, and consequently they would not need the subsidy.
How much money was paid to the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company last year for subsidies?
The amount was $209,640.
How many trips were made?
Sixteen.
What is the reason for the increase in this item?

Last year, as two boats were off the service, it was not necessary to appropriate the full amount as required by the contract. Now that the four steamships are back performing the service under the contract, we can approximate quite accurately what the maximum amount required will be.

If we take the first six items under the heading "Atlantic Ocean," there is an increase of $853,000 over last year. On what does the minister base his estimate of the amount of subsidies that will be earned by the different companies-on the average subsidies granted during the -past three or four years, or on the subsidies granted last year?
Are these annual contracts?

The first contract with the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company covered a period of five years. The contract expired last year, and it was renewed by Order in Council until October next. I suppose, at the end of that time, a new contract will be entered into with the company, or some other arrangements will be made.
Does the Department of Trade and Commerce have anything to do with fixing the freight rates in these services?
In every case where a subsidy is granted to a steamship company the freight rates must be approved by the department before they become effective.
I understand that this year two additional boats are to be put on the service or services between Canada and the West Indies or South America.
They were put on in February of this year.
Last year only two boats were running?
There were only two, although the contract provides for four. Two were requisitioned by the Minister of Shipping for war purposes.
When there is a surplus quantity of freight to be shipped from any Atlantic port to the West Indies, who has control of what freight shall be taken and what freight left?
The steamship companies, I should think. They probably accept the freight as it is offered.

An exporter in my county sent a shipment of hay to one of the Atlantic ports, and six months passed before he could get space for it; in fact, the shipment was taken care of only about ten days ago. During all that time it has been lying at the port-I think it was Halifax,
I am not sure-the steamship companies refusing to accept it. Is there no arrangement under which freight like that can be taken care of?
I assume that the misfortune of this shipper was due to the war. It would be hardly fair to attach all the blame to the steamship company.
The war was pretty well over six months ago.

During the war the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company had only two steamships for the service and were unable to carry all the freight that was moving between the West Indies and Canada. I imagine that during that period a great deal of freight was handled by schooners. A great many of our imports came via New York; sugar was railed from New York to the refineries at St. John and Halifax. I have no explanation to offer as to why this shipment of hay was delayed so long. I imagine 'that the steamers performing the Service would carry the cargo which was deemed to be most essential to the interests of the people of the West

Indies at that time, and possibly hay was not regarded as absolutely essential.

This proposed vote is a large one, and the people would like to know whether they are going to get value for it. When did this vote begin? Have imports and exports increased by reason of the grant of this large sum of money for the encouragement of trade?

I am informed that the case I cited a few moments ago was taken up with the Department of Trade, and Commerce, but that the department appeared to take very little interest in the matter. The department should be willing to give consideration to matters affecting the shipment of freight to be carried by this subsidized steamship service. In view of the fact that freight rates are now very high, is it necessary to subsidize this steamship service as largely now as it was subsidized when freights were low? Owners of steamers or sailing vessels are anxious to get as large a subsidy as possible. The Minister of Trade and Commerce should find out whether the company can make its service sufficiently remunerative as not to require

the payment of these large subsidies by the Government. I am surprised that the minister asks Parliament for an increase of nearly a million dollars in subsidies, in view of the fact that freight rates have been high during the last few years.
