The minister says that the department control the freight rates. I understand they issue schedules. If these schedules are not adhered to what will the department do-for instance, if there is any overcharging?

If a subsidized steamship company charged greater freight rates than those approved of by the department the department would, of course, be obliged to inquire into the matter and, if the offence were very serious and not adequately explained, consider the cancellation of the subsidy.
Is the schedule part of the contract?
No, it is not. '

Then you could not
break the contract?
That is the point.

The contract states that the freight rates shall be subject to the approval of the department. As regards the hay referred to by my hon. friend, I never heard of any complaint about this particular shipment, and am very sorry if the matter has not received attention. I shall look into the question and write my hon. friend.

If Cuba and Porto Rico were included in the call ports of this line, trade with the West Indies would be very much fostered. At the present time shippers of dried' fish require to use the Havana market. They must ship their goods via Boston or New York. If ithe minister will make inquiries he will find that there are considerable imports of codfish into Cuba from the Pacific coast cities of the United States, via Panama canal. It seems to me that the Canadian Atlantic coast is the natural source of supply for that market, but the exporters are handicapped by the fact that there is no steamer sailing from any Canadian port touching at Havana or Porto Rico. One of the boats, I think, calls once a month at Santiago, Cuba. I am not sure whether it is the boat that
m
goes to Jamaica and Georgetown in Dem-erara or the subsidized line. At any rate, a boat calls at Santiago, but it is on the opposite side of the island. I suggest that the minister might take the matter up with the steamship line when the contract is being renewed, as it would be in the interests of the industry as a whole.

At the present time
there is about 35,000,000 pounds of frozen beef that was left on hand when the war closed; in the West the quantity being about 20,000,000 pounds. It has not been possible to secure accommodation on the oceangoing boats. Has the Government undertaken to arrange for space in these ships?

The matter to
which my hon. friend refers is hardly relevant to the subject before the committee,, but it is true that at present there is in Canada about 40,000,000 pounds of frozen: beef which would have been readily marketed were the war still on. This quantity of beef is now in the hands of Canadian packers, not because of any lack of shipping but because there are no purchasers.
If the price were reduced, some might be willing to buy even in this country.

I doubt very
much whether it could be marketed in this country even at a much reduced price. Advices received from the British Government seem to indicate that they will purchase this frozen beef provided they are given leave to sell it in other countries- Greece, Roumania, Italy and one or two other countries, and it seems probable that this large quantity of frozen beef will be marketed very shortly.

Most of this beef was
slaughtered in this country and cured and stored for Great Britain, and at the close of the war they refused to take it. I understand that British and Canadian ships are carrying across frozen beef which was purchased from the United States under contract, with the result that this beef is being left on the hands of the Canadian packers. The British Government have evidently released the ships but have commandeered sixty per cent or seventy per cent of the space in them, and if I am correctly informed they are using the ships to transport supplies from the United States to Great Britain and France instead of providing space for the accommodation of those in this country who produced on the good faith of the Imperial Government.
This item contemplates a service either to the West Indies or South America, or both. I know that the line hitherto has not gone further south than Demerara. Is that still the fact?
It is.

We have therefore no provision for trade with ports further south. In view of this fact, is the Government contemplating the opening up of South American markets? This is a large field, and as our products will no doubt be looking for new markets the matter is an important one. Perhaps it has already engaged the .attention of the department.

There is a shipping firm in Montreal, MacLean, Kennedy and Company, who are now considering the '[DOT]matter of establishing a steamship service 'between Canada and South America. There are many inquiries regarding such a service, and I have no doubt that during the year one will be established.

With reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Northumberland in regard to the service to Cuba, I might say we have between one or two ports in Nova Scotia and Porto Rico a fairly good service that does not cost the people of this country one dollar, and is not performed by steamers. There are a number of clipper ships in Nova Scotia, owned in Lunenburg, sailing each fortnight for Porto Rico from Lunenburg, while ships also sail from Halifax to Havana. These are schooners of about 125 tons. If they can do this business without a subsidy the big steamship companies should do the same.

What the hon. gentleman says is quite true, but that does not convenience the public who, if they want to ship to the ports named, must do so at present via Boston and New York. I quite realize that full cargoes go from Lunenburg but that does not in any way affect the case I am endeavouring to present to the minister. I would like to tell the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) that during the past winter practically all the refrigeration space of the ocean steamers was used for carrying frozen beef to the United Kingdom.

I think these subsidies should be voted with the distinct understanding that the department will ascertain whether it is necessary to grant subsidies or not. I am not very well versed in shipping by water except that, as a shipper, I
fMr. Tweedie.]
have had occasion to note what the rates were before the war and to know something about what they are now. You would be surprised to know that there has been an increase of as much as a thousand per cent over what they were in normal times. I have been shipping some goods to the United Kingdom and the freight has been three times the value of the goods when they left this 'port. If the carrying trade is getting the same rates as it has been getting in the last two years I do not believe it needs any assistance from this Government. The minister should promise this committee that before any of the subsidies are paid he will have a proper accounting made to see what amount of money these ships are making and if they are in need of this money from the Government in order to give the necessary service. Our rates by rail have been increased by about forty per cent, but that is nowhere with the increase in tne water rates. We want these services continued, but we want to know, before the Government is called upon to subsidize a service, whether that subsidy is necessary or not.

I agree with my hon. friend that the Government should not enter into any contract to pay subsidies unless they are assured it is necessary to the performance of the service. The accounts of the steamship companies are always submitted to the department before a contract is entered into. It is true that freight rates have been very much higher in the last two or three years than prior to the war, but it is also true that it costs a great deal more to operate a steamship to-day than it did then. Every day applications are made to-the Department of Trade and Commerce for an increase in the subsidies paid particularly for local services. Pretty nearly all of the steamers engaged in local services in Eastern Canada and on the Pacific coast complain that the subsidy they are receiving does not enable them to earn even dividends upon the money invested in the service.	,

May I mention, in reply to the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. MoCrea), that recently a contract was entered into to carry goods from St. John to the United Kingdom at four and a half cents a pound, and before the goods left this side the rate was reduced to one cent per pound.
What kind of goods?
Boneless codfish.

I wish to draw the attention of the minister to two items of news which reached this country from the Peace Conference and which will affect this year's Budget. We have been told by the newspapers that the German merchant fleet has been surendered to the Allies and that a division of the ships has been made among the different allied nations. We have had expression of views from different members of the Government since the opening of the session to the effect that Chnada at the Peace Conference has to-day the status of a nation. Therefore, as a nation Canada must have received part of that German fleet. I would like to know from the minister the number of ships that Canada has received, if any, and where these ships will be placed. As regards the particular item that we are discussing now-(Steam service between Canada and the West Indies-I have also seen in some of the papers, sent by the official representative of the press at Paris, a statement to the effect that Canada would receive as compensation for her war activities either Greenland or the West Indies. I prefer the West Indies, and if we are to receive the West Indies, would the minister be kind enough to tell us if this subsidy will be discontinued?

I am afraid my
hon. friend (Mr. Cannon) is not contributing very much to the peace of the House and that he wishes to provoke a little discussion.
Not at all; this is quite relevant.

I am unable to inform my hon. friend as to whether or not any distribution of enemy shipping will be made and if so whether any will come to Canada. I understand that the German shipping that is being distributed now is for the purpose of carrying foodstuffs to certain countries, and in that event I would imagine that the shipping would be placed in the hands of some of the powers which are able to handle it. I am unable to apprehend the point of my hon. friend's question as to the West Indies. I would like to remind him that the West India Islands are not owned by Germany, and they cannot hand them over to Canada.

I know that, and I mentioned this because T found this correspondent sending most extraordinary news. I do not know why he is kept there at all.
Steam service between Canada and South Africa, $146,000.
How much of the 873,000 voted last year was spent?
There were only three sailings on this service last year, and the amount spent was $36,000.
Then you contemplate a more extended programme of sailings this year?
Yes, we hope to resume the sailings which were carried on prior to the war.
Who is receiving this subsidy?

The Elder-Demp-ster Company. It is a monthly service and the steamers leave a St. Lawrence port- Montreal, I think-in the summer, and St. John or Halifax, at the option of the contractors, during the winter.
Is this $146,000 the same subsidy that was granted before the war?
Yes.
What class of commodities are sent from Canada to South Africa?

In 1918, Canadian goods to the value of $2,714,000 were transported to South Africa by this service, and the principal items of Canadian origin included flour, agricultural machinery, calcium carbide, binder twine, automobiles, butter, cattle, lumber, wax, cereal goods, egg-fillers, woodenware, wheat and furniture.

The minister states that only one-half of the $73,000 voted last year was expended. Now he is asking for a vote of double that amount. What is the increase due to? Is it because the minister expects to pay bigger subsidies, or does he anticipate having more ships plying between Canada and South Africa? If the latter is the reason, has he made any inquiries to see what ships are available for the service?

As I have already stated, the contractors are to perform a monthly service. Last year, owing to the lack of shipping and the commandeering of vessels by the British Admiralty, only three sailings were carried out. This year it is expected that the contract will be carried out in its entirety, which will mean twelve sailings, and will involve a payment of $146,000 for the year in subsidies. We are assured that the company will be able shortly to fully carry out the contract.
I

Has the subsidy been
increased?
No.

Why should we pay seven per cent of the value of the goods we shipped to South Africa in the way of subsidy in order to get our goods into that market? It seems an extraordinary amount of money to pay for that purpose.
I do not know what my hon. friend means by paying seven per cent.

I gather from the minister's statement that he has not altogether decided in his own mind as to the imperative necessity of these subsidies. If he is not absolutely convinced that they are im-fMr. A. K. Maclean. 1
pcratively necessary, is it right that he should ask for these subsidies to be voted when, according to the figures given by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) the other day, there is an apparent deficit on ordinary account of something like $100,000,000? It seems to me it is not putting the committee in a fair position to ask us to accord our approval and take the responsibility of voting subsidies amounting altogether to about $2,500,000, unless the minister is able either to assure us that they are absolutely necessary, or assure us in the most formal fashion that we are merely voting these subsidies subject to his making the most searching inquiry as to the necessity for them. Because I take it that a most serious financial condition confronts this country unless every possible means are adopted to cut down the expenditure. I would like to impress that fact upon this committee, I think we should all take it to heart, that the financial situation of this country is such as it has never faced before, and the whole of the appropriation for the public service should be regarded in the light of that fact.

I can only repeat that before the contracts are entered into, searching inquiry will be made in each case to ascertain if there is any necessity for the subsidy. There is this to say concerning steamship services to South Africa, Australia and New Zealand during the present year and I think I am perfectly accurate in making the statement-that it would be practically impossible to have an established steamship service between this country and the other Dominions mentioned without a subsidy during the present year. It must also be remembered further, that the freight rates are, or will be, more favourable to those countries from Canada than if we were relying upon free shipping for our service. My hon. friend knows that steamship freight rates to-day are very excessive, in fact a steamship owner can get almost anything in the way of freight rates, although, of course, those rates are not as high as they were two or three years ago. For the time being, however, I think the subsidized steamship service to distant countries like South Africa and Australia is in the interest of Canadian trade. If we are to collect a revenue we must develop our trade, both domestic and foreign, and I do not think that any very substantial objection can be made to the granting of subsidies for the time being. When shipping is freer and trade restrictions are removed, I admit, it will then be

very proper to inquire as to whether or not these subsidies should be continued.

I agree with a good deal of what the hon. minister has just said, but in rapidly glancing through these items I fail to see any reference to a direct service between Canada and France. It may be due to my inadequate knowledge of the Budget, and that possibly elsewhere in the Estimates an amount is provided as a subsidy. Perhaps the hon. minister has some information in this regard, and also as to a direct service between Canada and Belgium, for which country I have naturally a tender spot in my heart. Has any company to the knowledge of the Government undertaken a free service, that is, as far as we aTe concerned as a Government, between the two countries, or has any application been made to the Government for a subsidy for a service between France and Canada, for instance; and, if so, has it been refused; and, if refused, why? France and Belgium at the present moment are going through an era which in my humble opinion is most propitious not only for the resumption of the old trade relations, but for the establishment of a new service. These two countries to-day, at the very moment when peace is about to be signed, are entering a period of virile activity in reconstruction, and they will need not only the raw materials of this country but our manufactured articles in large quantity. I should be indeed very sorry if the Government and this committee were not disposed to subsidize such a service, especially this year.
Mr. A. K. MAjOLEAN:	My hon. friend
will notice that in the Atlantic ocean subsidies there is no provision for a subsidy for any service between Canada and European ports. A great many subsidies formerly were paid for such services, but as during the past four years it was impossible for such services to be performed these items were struck out. (I did not think it was necessary to reinstate them in the Estimates, because I am satisfied that any steamships operating between Europe and Canada during the present year will be able to obtain all the freight they can handle at very satisfactory rates.

Are you not authorized
by statute?

We were authorized to pay $200,000 to steamship services between France and Canada; I think, however, that that statute has lapsed. 'During the later years when it was available, during the war, of course no steamship company applied for the subsidy, and there has been no inquiry this year. I was informed to-day that a steamship service is to be established between France and Montreal.
Is it the Canadian Pacific?

No, La Cie Generate
Transatlantique.

I was approached to-day by some representatives of that company in connection with this proposed service. It is expected that the service will be in operation by the first of May. This is a service we are getting without a subsidy, and I really do not think it is necessary to pay any subsidy between Canada and any European ports during the present year. For instance, if we sell to Belgium under the credits which we give to her $25,000,000 of goods, we are assured that there will be $25,000,000 of goods for ships to carry to that country; and if $50,000,000 worth of credits are extended to France, and she avails herself of those credits, there will be goods of that value to carry to France. So I do not think there will be any necessity at present to subsidize a service between Canada and France or Belgium or any other European ports.
The hon. minister means continental ports?

Yes. However, at a later date, on some other item, I have promised the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) an opportunity of discussing the matter of trade between Canada and France, and when we reach that item I shall be very glad indeed to hear from him in relation to the development of Franco-Canadian trade.

I understood the hon. minister to say that of the $73,000 voted for the Canada-South Africa service last year, there was only $36,000 expended. What becomes of the remaining $37,000? Will it be added to the $146,000 asked this year?
No, that vote lapses.

I wish to corroborate the statement made a moment ago in regard to the service between Canada and France. I think by next month we shall have between Montreal and Havre, and perhaps another French port, a first-class service. La Cie Generale [DOT] Transatlantique is one of the big steamship lines of the world, and it maintains between New

York and some of the French ports a most excellent service. The other day I met M. de la Touche, the president of the company, who was in Montreal as the guest of honour at a luncheon given by some of the business men. He there declared that his company is ready to put in commission two or three, and perhaps four, big steamers between Canada and France; so we shall have an excellent service. However, if there is to be any subsidy paid to any line established between Canada and France, I would say, give it to that company, because you will be sure of getting the ships and the service. They are not claiming any subsidy, but I do not think they would refuse it if offered to them. It is a great pity, however, that this statute should have been allowed to lapse. My hon. friend should reinstate it, because it took so many years before we were in a position to obtain that subsidy from the Government.
The Allan line struggled along for many years with a second-class service, and finally, I think, they succeeded in building up quite a business between Havre and Halifax in winter and Quebec in summer. I would be very sorry to see this item of $200,000 for a subsidy for a steamship service between Canada and France lapse, because it forms part, so to speak, of the Treaty of Commerce which exists between the two countries. I see that that treaty has been denounced by the French Government. That is to say, notice has been given to all nations having treaties with France that she will, after a certain period of time, reconsider those treaties. Now that Canada, France and Great Britain are so closely allied after this great war, and when we are so much interested in the prosperity of France and in bettering the good relations which exist between that country and ours, I sincerely hope that Canada will renew as favourable a treaty as possible with France. Of course, the news has spread throughout France of late that, Canada becoming bone-dry, part of the trade which existed between the two countries in former years will be* cut off. If we do not import the excellent French wines, I do not see what we may well import from France with the exception of masterpieces of painting, sculpture and the arts generally, but a referendum will take place in a few days in Quebec and I am quite sure that province will be favourable to light wines and light beer. And I hope the other provinces of the Dominion will follow suit, and then the Dominion Government will do the sensible thing and give to moderate people an op-

portunity of using in moderation the good French wines and light beer, so that there will be a raison d'etre for the old steamship service which existed in former years between Canada and France.

There is a phase ol
these subsidies which it is our duty to bring to the notice of the Department of Trade and Commerce. The high cost of living in this country is a subject that should receive the attention of that department and of the Government as a whole. The condition of trade and commerce in Canada has to do with articles of food, and I would direct the attention of the minister to the fact that the ordinary consumers should not be called upon to furnish money to send foodstuffs out of Canada while prices are sky-high as they are to-day.
The large masses of the Canadian people who are consumers have to pay enormous prices for butter, beef, fish and other articles that enter largely into our everyday production. The price of butter to-day throughout this country is from 64 to 65 cents per pound, and if those people who have to pay 65 cents per pound for butter are called upon to pay duty on the shoes and clothing that their children wear, iu order to furnish subsidies for steamships to take foodstuffs out of the country to be sold at a cheaper rate in some foreign part of the world, that is not good governmental management. The price of beef in Canada to-day is enormously high. The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Tweedie), very properly in the interest of his constituency and his city, asked about space to carry frozen or chilled beef from Canada across the Atlantic or somewhere else out of this country. Before we grant subsidies for carrying beef out of this country, the home market should be something like normal. There are some things that should be plentiful and cheap in Canada. I can understand the price of tea, or tobacco, or cotton, or other articles which we do not produce ourselves, getting dear in this country, but I never could understand, nor have I any right to understand, why flour or beef should be dear in Canada. Flour and beef should be plentiful in this country because we produce enormous quantities of both. I would point out to the minister and every other member of the Government that the big question of the day is to get back to normal as regards our foodstuffs, because the people cannot, with very high prices which they have to pay, support their families in comfort upon- the wages they

are now getting. Neither the Minister of Trade and Commerce, nor any other minister has a right to go down into the pockets of poor people for millions of dollars to pay subsidies !to boats to enable the producer to charge too much for his product. Far be it from me to say or do anything detrimental to good and natural trade in foodstuffs, and if we produce enough of those articles here, the producer can surely make a fair, honest profit without being bolstered up in this way by the granting of large subsidies to take foodstuffs out of this country, thus enabling the producers to charge prices above normal. Nothing that the Government can do to-day is more important than to give their attention to making living comfortable and reasonable for the people.

Will the minister give me the figures as to the value of goods carried in 1915, 1916, or 1917 by ships which are subsidized? I want to find out in what way there is a benefit to trade between Canada and South Africa by subsidizing ships_ if they are carrying only a small proportion of the trade. What does the minister think would be the outcome if he were not to subsidize those ships? Would that be a detriment to the trade of this country, or shall we still have to pay a premium of seven per cent on goods we are exporting to induce people to buy them, in addition to actually furnishing the purchaser with credit for the whole amount? Are we going to continue to pay part of the freight charged for delivering those goods and yet get nothing back except somebody's note?
My hon. friend goes very far when he says that these subsidized steamship services have done nothing to develop trade in far-off countries.
I did not say any such thing. I was asking the minister what they had done in that direction.

I cannot speak with exactness as to that; I imagine nobody could. I believe that the subsidies paid to these steamship lines plying regularly between Canada and South Africa contribute something to the building up of Canadian trade. There will come a time-perhaps it is fairly reached now-when that trade shall have received sufficient help by way of subsidies from Canada and will operate without Government aid. But I do think that these subsidized services have done a great deal toward the development of trade. The leader of the Opposition
opened up the important subject of the high cost of living. Prices are not normal; shipping is not normal; shipping rates are not normal; the producing countries of the world are not producing in normal quantities. Nothing in this world is normal; we are obliged to face unusual conditions. Canada imports largely, particularly from the United States, and we must have some way of paying for the things we import. We cannot pay for them in money. No country can pay for its imports except by exporting. Therefore it is important that we have an export trade. It is true that the price of flour is very high to-day, but the farmer of the West will tell you that, owing to the increased cost of production, he is not making very much out of the wheat which he is producing. The wheat that we export is our surplus product; that is true of almost everything that we export. However, I do not wish to engage in a discussion of that subject to-night; I am hopeful that some other item in the Estimates will afford a more appropriate opportunity of doing so.

The minister explained that trade with South Africa increased from $2,300,000 in 1911 to over $11,000,000 in 1918. What proportion of the amount carried in this period was carried by non-subsidized lines and what amount by subsidized lines?
In 1912 the value of goods carried by subsidized service to South Africa was $4,000,000, in round figures.
What subsidy was granted that year?

It was $146,000.
In 1913 the value of the goods carried was $5,860,000, and in the following year an amount slightly in excess of $4,000,000.
Was this subsidy the same?
Yes, and in these earlier years I think it was fully earned. In 1915 the value of the goods exported was over $5,000,000; in 1916, nearly $5,000,000, and in 1917 about the same amount.
Was that all carried by subsidized steamers?
Yes.

Can the minister give the
value of the goods carried by non-subsidized lines?

I have given our total exports to South Africa covering the period which I have just mentioned. Prior

to and in the early days of the war the greater part of our trade to South Africa was carried by our subsidized steamers. During the war our exports were abnormal, as is evident from the figures of 1911. Some of these exports, I imagine, found their way to South Africa through American ports. A great deal of our exports during the last two years was carried by sailing ships from -Canadian ports. This is particularly true of lumber.
Can the minister give us the amount carried by non-subsidized lines during the years that he has mentioned?

I have not the
figures at hand.

The minister says that we have subsidized steamship lines to create overseas trade with South Africa and elsewhere and to get rid of our surplus foodstuffs. But we have not sufficient to feed our own people, why should we continue to subsidize these steamers to take away the foodstuffs that we ourselves require? For instance, there is not a sufficient quantity of butter this year to supply our own people.

Outside of flour, not very many foodstuffs were exported to South Africa. Does my hon. friend say that we should prohibit the export of wheat from Canada which we produce in abundance? The other articles exported are agricultural machinery, binder twine, automobiles, paper, lumber, carriage ware, chairs woodenware, furniture.

The things that are shipped by subsidized ships are apparently all manufactured goods, so that the manufacturer is not satisfied to get protective tariff here, and thereby rob the people of the country directly, but he must also have a subsidy to ship his goods out of the country. Is that the position the Government are taking?
Steam services between Halifax, St. John's, Newfoundland, and Liverpool, $20,000.
What steamship line is this?

This is a service that has been subsidized for a number of years, and which was not performed last year. The contractors were Furness IVithy Company who have an office at Halifax. The ports of call are Halifax, fit. John's, Nfld., and Liverpool. It is a service which' the contractors claim, has never paid them. The company, taking their entire shipping, which is widely scattered throughout the 
world, doubtless earned handsome profits, but the representations to the department have always been that this service did not pay.
This service, I understand, is only for freight.
Freight alone.

I will ask the minister not
to request the committee to pass this amount, it is absolutely unnecessary. The company have made large sums of money in the past few years in this and other services, and I would point out that there is no subsidy for a service between St. John's, Nfld., Halifax and New York, which is far more important to the people of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The minister will remember that a few years ago this service was performed by the Bed Cross Line which operated the Stephano which was torpedoed, and the Florizel, which was lost off Cape Bace. After these ships were lost the line did not operate but, to their credit, the business men of Halifax purchased two or three steamers and operated them between St. John's, Nfld., Halifax and New York.

Is -the hon. member advocating a subsidy between Halifax and New York? If so he will give the railroads an excuse for raising their rates as there is competition between the boats and railroads. Across the ocean there is no rail competition. -

I do not say that any money should be voted, but if any amount is granted I do not think it should go to the Furness Withy Company. It is more in the interest of the minister himself and of the country that the subsidy should be granted to the Halifax people operating the line between Halifax, St. John's, Nfld., and New York.

I would not like to drop this item, but I can only say about it what I have said in regard to other items, that inquiry will be made before any contract is entered into. There is a great deal of uncertainty as to what our shipping service will be during the present year, and I simply want to make provision for the subsidies in the event of ships being available and it being deemed advisable to establish the services. I appreciate the remarks of my hon. friend respecting the (Halifax, St. John's, Nfld., and Liverpool ' service, but this particular service is quite a factor in Canadian-Newfoundland trade and it has been deemed desirable to con-

tinue it in the interests not only of Canadian trade but of Newfoundland trade as well. I agree that the matter should be investigated before any contract is made, but I should like the committee to allow the sum to be voted. Our chief exports of Canadian origin, are lumber, box boards, canned apples, canned lobsters, canned beef, fish, seal oil, cod oil,. tallow, oats, cheese, fuTS, machinery, lawn mowers, wire fencing, etc.

I cannot agree with the minister in his statement that the Furness Withy Company has not been remunerative, and I would like him to inform the committee where he got the information. With regard to the trade between Canada and St. John's, Newfoundland, I think we should give the subsidy to our own people, who are constituents of the minister, and his own friends in Halifax who operate a line of boats rather than give the subsidy to the Furness Withy people who are millionaires. I am merely speaking on behalf of the minister's own people as a matter of courtesy and kindness seeing that he can hardly speak for them in this matter himself as he is in charge of the Estimates. If there is any subsidy I think it should go to the concern represented by Mr. J. W. Began, who is not a political friend of mine. This service extends from Halifax to New York as well as St. John's, Newfoundland. It is very important in view of the exchange situation that we should have a service between Nova Scotia and New York. The business men of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick will do more business if they can get connection with New York. Last year when that connection was cut off we were worried a good deal because we could not ship goods to our New York customers. The Government should do everything possible to see that the connection which we now have is continued. I am going to ask the Minister not to make this contract with the Furness Withy and also to submit to us in the Supplementary Estimates a vote for a Halifax-Newfoundland and Halifax-New York service.

This money is not being voted to any particular company. It is open to any person at all. With respect to the matter of a subsidy for a steamship service to New York, all I can say is that the matter shall have the very best consideration. In only one- instance are we paying any subsidy for a service to an American port, and that is for a service from a British Columbia port to a port on the Pacific coast in the United States. I
think that is carried out in pursuance of an agreement made with British Columbia at the time she entered into Confederation. However, I shall be glad to give consideration to my hon. friend's suggestion. I do not think that any application has ever been made for a subsidy for a service to an American port.

This service strikes
three countries-, Canada, Newfoundland and Great Britain. Have either of the other two countries paid any subsidy?

No, I do not
think so.

I see no good reason
why Canada alone should subsidize this service. It is certainly more important to the colony of Newfoundland than to us, because, if this steamer touches at St. John's going direct to the Old Country, she naturally will have a considerable trade between St. John's and Liverpool. If they are not subsidizing her and the English Government are not subsidizing her, why should the Canadian people be called upon to pay $20,000 for this service? The minister says that this is not for any particular company but be will find, on inquiry in his department, that this amount has for years and years gone to the same people.
I remember this item ever since I came to this House quite a long time ago, and the money always goes to the same people. It is a very indifferent sort of -a service. I remember having it up with the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) and it was then exactly as it is to-night just as -a matter of course and nobody saying anything about it. As to granting subsidies to steamers going to American ports, if a subsidy is necessary to get the trade we want in those American ports, I would certainly say grant it. If we can get a good service without a subsidy, all right, but this traffic can be established between Canada and some American port with a good steamship service. There is a tremendous trade growing up between Nova Scotia and New York in fish, and this steamer that my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) speaks about must be very important in that way. If we cannot get a service without a subsidy it would be well spent money to establish such a connection. My hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) talks about the dangers of establishing competition between steamers and railways. Competition is the only salvation that we have in my part of the country. When we have water competition we can always fight the rail-

ways but the moment they find that they have the field entirely to themselves they put up their rates.

Touching the point
raised by the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) as to the desirability of this subsidy being handed to a local company, if the records are examined it will be found that this subsidy was originally given to a local company in Halifax but the service which was established by the Halifax people turned out to be so unsatisfactory that after some years it was turned over to the Furness-Withy Company. It was not until after the local company had had a fair trial that the English company came into it. As to subsidizing a steamship service to New York, if the policy is entered upon of subsidizing steamers on the Atlantic to the United States, and the trade of that region may be considered as largely in that direction, I would remind my hon. friend (Mr. A. K. Maclean) that there are several points on the western shore of Nova Scotia which will be very glad to have assistance in the way of subsidies for a steamer plying between those ports and Portland and Boston. I have an idea that some applications of that kind may reach the minister, and if he decides to give a subsidy to New York I suppose we may then have a definite precedent for asking for one for a service to Portland and Boston.

It would be just as reasonable to subsidize the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company to run their boats on lake Ontario in competition with the Grand Trunk and other railways as to subsidize a line from Halifax to New York.

If subsidies were
necessary to give the people of Ontario a reduced rate I would say they should be given. But it is quite likely they are getting low rates on these boats as it is, because they can carry so much cheaper than the railways.

Exactly.
Steamship service between Baddeck and Iona, $5,825.

This is a service I wish to bring to the notice of the minister. It is in my riding. It is the connection from Victoria county with the Intercolonial railway. It is the only connection we have between the main portion of my riding and the railway system of Canada. The people are threatened with a closing down altogether of the service. Last year and the year before, the owners of the boats did not make
[Mr. McKenzie. 1
a cent, but, on the contrary, lost money, and they told me, and I think they told the minister, that unless something is done for the service they will have to close it, they cannot afford to run a service for the country without making more or less profit. Everything enters into the running of a steamer has gone up in price. They used to get their coal for $3 a ton, but now they have to pay $8 a ton for it. Everything else has gone up in proportion, and yet there has been no increase in the subsidy for steamers. It is nine or ten years I believe since there was any increase in the subsidy for this company. Now it is peculiarly a service in which the Government has an interest, by reason of a connection existing with the Intercolonial. The railway has built a wharf at Iona, where its service ends, and it has also built a wharf at Baddeck Properly speaking the service should be owned by the Government, because the railway takes freight and passengers from all parts of Canada to Baddeck. The railway sells tickets for Baddeck and lands passengers there, but when those passengers get to Iona they have no connection except through the boat operated by this company. If the boat stops the Government will have to provide a conveyance of its own in order to carry out the transportation conditions of the tickets which they sell at points all over the world where they have connections. I am aware that some communications have reached the department from the owners of this steamer with respect to this matter- and I am urging upon the Government-I would like to bring it particularly to the attention of the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) if he were here-to take this service over, to purchase the boat of this company and thus own the connection between the railway and that side of the Bras d Or Lakes. As the Minister of Railways is not present perhaps the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce is in a position to say whether or not the Government will carry out my suggestion. If not, let the Government try and keep the service going. Let it grant some material assistance so that this service can be maintained.

I have just been wondering what the basis of this system of subsidies is. When the previous items relating to subsidies for foreign steamship services were under discussion, I thought possibly those subsidies might be justifiable, but now we have arrived at the point where subsidies are being voted for local steamship services, and I am curious to know how long this policy has been in existence,

and what is the actual reason for adopting it. Those of us -who do not live in the Maritime Provinces, and who have to depend upon railways for transportation, when the railway rates go up have to pay the increase without coming to the Dominion Government for assistance. For my part I do not see why any such discrimination should be practised.
My hon. friend is in the backwoods, like myself.

My hon. friend comes from a section of the country where he cannot go very far without running into a railroad, and, therefore, he cannot quite appreciate the condition of other sections of the country which are not so happily situated. There are sections of Canada which to-day are not blessed with railroads, and where that public convenience does not exist. It is not unreasonable, therefore, that the people of those sections should get the benefit of small aids to steamships. My hon. friend says that in Ontario they do not go to the Government for assistance under such circumstances. There has never yet been a railroad built in Canada which did not apply to the Government for help, and therefore the sections of the country enjoying railway accommodation have been aided by the Government. There is no greater sin in aiding a steamship line than in aiding a line of railway. With respect to the Maritime Provinces, I happen to know the locality referred to by my hon. friend	the leader of the
Opposition. The	county of	Victoria
which he represents, happens to be without a railroad at all, and there are very few counties in the Dominion of which you can say that. In the absence of any railroad, they have steamship communication, and I must say that under the circumstances the reasons for granting aid to a steamship line are just as strong as for subsidizing the construction of a railroad. I cannot see what difference there is.

I do not think the reason advanced by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) is any excuse whatever for the payment of subsidies to these steamship companies. He says, and says truly, that no railroad in Canada has ever been constructed without applying to the Dominion Parliament for aid.

That does not make the
policy any more justifiable.
Not at all. In connection with railways we have pursued the most damnably insane policy that has ever been pursued in any country under the sun.
Oh, oh.

There has been a
decision in the Supreme Court of Canada that "damn" is not a cuss word-at least so I understand-and on the strength of that decision I use the word advisedly. Why, the fool people of Canada have given to the railroad companies about three times the cost of the entire undertakings. Because they have been so foolish as to do that, members get up here and justify the continuation of subsidies in aid of the running of steamships. I am not criticising my good old friend, the member for Queens-Shelburne, for whom I have a sincere respect and admiration, he is merely giving expression to what seems to be in the public mind. For my part, I agree entirely with the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Euler), that it is just about time the people of Canada adopted a policy of right-about-face in regard to this matter of subsidies. The fact that we have continued pouring these subsidies into the maws, the insatiable maws, of railroad companies, and to help little steamships to run between certain ports, for so many years, is no justification for the continuation of that policy now. Indeed, in my judgment, it is a better justification for discarding it. Because we have been insane and foolish, and stupid for thirty, forty, or fifty years, is no reason under God's heaven why we should continue such a policy. Why should not the people of the Maritime Provinces provide their own steamships and look

after their own transportation? I want to say with reference to the Intercolonial Railway that has furnished the people of the Maritime Provinces with transportation for the last forty or fifty years, in fact almost since Confederation, that the rest of Canada has spent tens of millions for the upkeep of this railway in order that the. people down there might have their freight carried at a rate that, f think, in the earlier days, was just about one-third of the rates charged by privately owned railways. It is all very well to talk about giving subsidies to railroads, but that is not done in other countries so far as I know. In the great republic to the south the railroads are built by private enterprise and made to pay by the same agency. But in our country it is the exploiters and the promoters of the railroads that have got all the millions. The people have had to continue to pour in these hundreds of millions into private channels in order to keep the railroads going. Is it not high time we put an effective stop to that kind of thing? If you are going to have privately owned railroads, in God's name let the people concerned build these railroads themselves and pay for them themselves, and not take the money of the country for the purpose, as has been done all these years. By our action we have tangled up the country so that it has involved Canada in a loss of from a billion to two billions of dollars. The Canadian Pacific Railway, as I told the House the other night, received in cash, lands, exemptions from taxation, and exemptions from duty, amounts that would suffice to build the road two or three times over. The syndicate and the men who were behind the construction of that road made their tens of millions out of the enterprise and went away to the Old Land to spend it, and we, the people, have been obliged to pay the piper. I thank you, Mr. Chairman, for not calling me to time, but my indignation is aroused when I see all these petty subsidies being voted from year to year simply because it has been the policy pursued in the past. It is now time that we ended it.
Mr. Chairman, I have to correct the member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) when he would give the House to understand that railroads in the United States were built without subsidies.
Generally speaking.
Not generally speaking.

As I understand it, all the Pacific roads in the United States were

very heavily subsidized with grants of public land. That is merely by way of introduction, Mr. Chairman. What I would very earnestly commend to this committee is that we should have a clearly defined policy on this question of subsidies as well as on other questions which are now before the Canadian people. In order that we may vote money intelligently we should have a clearly defined statement from the Government-

May I ask the hon. gentleman whether it would not be a good idea for us to have a clearly defined policy from the Opposition, especially as the great majority of the hon. gentlemen apposite are at complete variance with the policy of their leader?	.
I would merely point out to the hon. member for-
Jerusalem.

I would merely suggest to him that it is for the Government to place before the people clearly defined policies, and it is for the Opposition to criticize those policies, and, if thought best, to advance alternative policies. We are voting large sums of money to-night without any declared statement of the Government that these subsidies are required. It is interesting to note, Mr. Chairman, how, when the province of Nova Scotia is-I won't say attacked; no one would attack such an amiable province-but if any of the rights of Nova Scotia-any of the perquisites which Nova Scotia has be.en enjoying for many years-
" Perquisites " is a better word than " rights."

If they are merely approached we have from both sides of the House Nova Scotians rising to defend those perquisites with great enthusiasm. Now, I feel that there is a great deal 'to be said in favour of the proposition of the member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler). If we are going to try and adjust what benefits one part of the country rather than another from the public purse, we shall enter upon a long and difficult subject of inquiry. There are those in Eastern Canada who might suggest that the West has benefited very largely by the tremendous expeiidi-ture of public money on the railway systems through that country; and that might possibly be offset against the very considerable amount of public money expended upon the Intercolonial Railway and the cheap rates which the Nova Scotians, New Brunswickers

and others have enjoyed in shipping their goods to the West. I am not sure -whether that would he ait all a profitable subject for inquiry, but I do think that we might very properly investigate the question as to whether these subsidies should be granted at all, and it seems to me it is incumbent upon the Government of the day, on whom primarily the responsibility of direciting the affairs of this country rests, to place their policy clearly and distinctly before the people. We all desire to do what is right and just and fair to all parts of the Dominion, but there is something to be said for those who feel that public money should not be placed in the hands of private interests without a very clear policy on the question, and without knowing as far as possible what public benefit is to result from such expenditure.

These squalls do not touch me at all, Mr. Chairman. This is a public service of splendid merit and one that has been in existence for the last thirty years, and although I have been in this House nearly fifteen years I have never heard it attacked before. I do not see why there should be any opposition to it to-night. It is the policy of this Government, as it was the policy of every previous Government, to render public service. And if the earnings of the Intercolonial Railway by reason of this connection were before the House to-night, and it were found that large passenger and freight earnings had come to the Intercolonial and, through it, into the coffers of this country because of this connection, I do not think there would be any further criticism. I am sure that the benefit so derived more than pays the interest on any little subsidy that is given in this way, and I venture to say that it is a fairly profitable proposition for the Government, because the company that is receiving this subsidy has only a short haul of eleven miles, the Intercolonial gets the long haul on all freight, and the Intercolonial can afford to carry that freight, but it could not afford to carry it at all if it could not get it to its destination. This boat takes the traffic alongside the railway at Iona, the company have only an eleven-mile haul, and can not charge passengers more than a small sum for going across. It is necessary in the interests of the country that we should continue this connection.
I saw an item a few days ago in Maclean's Magazine suggesting satirically that when we came to talk about a cent we all
got enthusiastic because that was within our financial conception. I observe that $1,000,000 was voted to-night and there was not a word said. But it appears that this item got within the financial grasp of some gentlemen and they woke up to discuss it.

It is hardly fair to charge these votes all to the province of Nova Scotia. The local service votes altogether amount to $240,000, and three or four of them exhaust more than one-half of that sum. There is the steamship service between the island of Grand Manan and the mainland of New Brunswick. I do not know what the population is, but I should think about two or three thousand. Perhaps my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Copp) will tell me?
Twenty-five hundred.

I would think that was an instance where we might very well sustain the service by voting this grant of money, particularly if the service is not self-supporting, and it is claimed that it is not self-supporting in this 'case. As a matter of fact, I would imagine that 90 per cent of all these steamship- services never earn a dividend. There is another item of $10,000 for a service between Halifax and Newfoundland. That is not a provincial service. Then I notice one very small item for subsidizing a service between Pelee island and the mainland. I think that is in Ontario, and I am glad there is one item here chargeable to that province. Then, there is an appropriation of $70,000 for a steamship service between Montreal, river St. Lawrence points, Magdalen islands, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, which service is of interest to Ontario, Prince Edward Island and Quebec. There are other services of that nature, and hon. members, if they go through all the items, will observe that more than one-half of them are for steamship services which are not provincial. The same defence may be urged on behalf of all these items as was offered for the unbidden child, namely, it is very small, and the objection, therefore, is quite small. I wish I could say that it was my judgment that these subsidies did not perform a public service, and I really wish they could all be dropped. I hope they will be in a few years or in a very short time, and it may be true that some of them should be dropped now.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend from Manitoba can hardly appreciate the situation unless he knows the province of Nova Scotia. I have in mind a service for which a subsidy is to be voted in the county of the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair). Guysborough is practically without a mile of railway, the chief towns and seaports being accessible only by a steamship service betwen a point on the railway on the strait of Canso from which the particular points are served by subsidized boats.
What is the subsidy given?

It is $5,500. I
do not think it would be possible to maintain a service without some subsidy. Most of the local services are also subsidized by the Provincial Government and even now they contend that the subsidies granted by both Governments are, taken together, not sufficient, and requests have this year been made for additional subsidies. The operating accounts of these services are submitted to the department, and in hardly any case can it be shown that the companies have earned a dividend, and in a few cases we are informed that this year unless increased subsidies are given, the services will be abandoned. As the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) said, many of these services should be subsidized by the railways as they really operate as feeders to the railways. To hon. gentlemen who are interested in the applications of any of their constituents for increased subsidies, I can only say that these matters are now being considered by the department, and the Government will, some time during the present week, have to take action in the matter one way or the other. So far as the Main Estimates are concerned, no increases whatever in local subsidies have been granted. There is an apparent increase of $70,000 in item No. 173, but that is really a consolidation of several services which were performed separately in the past, and I do not think it represents any increase.
What are the services which were given before and which the minister says are consolidated in this item?

I understand it means first the service which was in existence for some years between Montreal, Quebec and Gaspe, ports on the river St. Lawrence as far as Gaspe basin. The other, I think, is the service between Pictou, Prince Edward Island and Magdalen islands. I understand there was a third service between Sydney 
and some other ports, I forget which, but I would like to know from the minister if this service does not include the first two I have mentioned.

It includes the
service on the north side of the river St. Lawrence, ports on the south side of the river St. Lawrence and Magdalen islands.
I understand a reputable company have made arrangements with the department to perform this service, and have found steamers suitable for this service.
I understand they have at last secured steamers suitable for the service.

During the course of last year, in fact, since the beginning of the war, the services between Montreal and Gaspe and between Pictou and Magdalen islands have been very poor. The boats which were assigned to those routes previously were good boats, but at the beginning of the war they were sold to the Admiralty or to the Imperial Munitions Board, and the service suffered in consequence. Last year the service between Pictou and the Magdalen islands was very poor, the boats being not at all suitable for the service. The company had chartered a tug called the Enterprise, from Halifax, and the people of Magdalen islands complained very loudly about the inferior service which they obtained. Exporters to Magdalen islands and exporters to Gaspe were not satisfied with the service, and there was no passenger accommodation on either of the boats. This year, the Government has, I am informed, found a company which is backed by very large capital and they have found that they can secure the Lady Evelyn, which formerly was the mail packet at Rimouski, to perform the service between Pictou, Prince Edward Island and the Magdalen islands, and they have secured another excellent boat which was built at the Davey shipyard at Levis for Spain. That boat will perform the service between Montreal, Quebec and Gaspe ports. I understand the same company have obtained a subsidy for a service between Montreal and Newfoundland and they will also perform a service between Quebec and the north shore of the St. Lawrence where there is an excellent trade to look after.
What is the nature of the trade between Gaspe and Magdalen islands?

Between Pictou and
Magdalen islands there is a good and pay-
APRiL 8, 1919
ing service in fish, flour and provisions generally, and timber. The people of the Magdalen islands are badly in need of this service and besides the Magdalen islands are isolated for several months of the year. The population of Magdalen islands is 7,000 people. The service between Montreal, Quebec and Gaspe is an excellent one because all those ports on the coast ship their fish to the large centres.
We must by all means give them the necessary transportation facilities, because more and more the people of central Canada will require fish. The department has been very generous in supplementing that service and I am pleased to know that a responsible company will perform it this year.
Steam service between Froude's Point and Lockeport, N.S., $600.

If the minister will look up and down the column and see the items running from $1,000,000 down to this vote of $600, he will want to apologize for the smallness of this item. It is for a service to connect the town of Lockeport with the nearest railway point. I want to assure the member from Brome (Mr. McMaster) that this subsidy is not going to make anybody rich, let alone any private corporation. The little steamer is operated very cheaply by the town of Lockeport. I think the town clerk is the purser; I do not know what other official is the master. At all events, they are trying to keep body and soul together, and the thing is losing money. Lockeport is one of the most important fishing settlements in Nova Scotia, and as it has not the good fortune to be on the main line of railway this little service is the means of communication between the railway station and that large growing town. I want to ask the minister, when he is considering the supplementary estimates, to see if he cannot make an addition to the subsidy to that little service. I give him the guarantee that it will not make anybody rich and that the subsidy will not go into the hands of a private corporation.

That is one of the items which is now having consideration.
Steam service between Grand Manan and the mainland, $10,000.

I would urge on the minister the absolute necessity of increasing this subsidy in the Supplementary Estimates. I am familiar with the Tunning of this steamship and I know that for a number of years the company have not declared a dividend. During the last four or five years they have not written anything off for
depreciation. It is not possible to get in touch with Grand Manan and Deer islands except by means of this boat. Moreover, this line touches St. Andrews, St. Stephen and other places. The company have been offered $50,000 for the steamer that is running on that rcute, the Grand Manan, and unless some additional assistance is given to this line I am afraid that it will have to go out of business.
how many trips a day does this steamer make between Grand Manan and the mainland?

She visits Grand Manan, Deer Island, Eastport, Campo Bello, St. Andrews and St. Stephen on alternate days. She makes three trips a week to St. John in the summer and one trip a week in the winter, visiting the different islands in the meantime.
Is more than one steamer employed in that service?
Only one.
Who is the owner?

She is owned by the Grand Manan Steamboat Company, of Grand Manan, N.B. As the member for St. John has said, this boat serves quite a number of places. The company have asked for an increase of subsidy for the present fiscal year to the extent of $5,000. The matter is being considered; a decision will be made, favourably or otherwise, in the course of a few days.

I hope that the decision will be favourable, because I know that these men have not made one dollar. Their statement of receipts and expenditures for the different years they have been in operation shows that they have gone behind every year.
Steam service between Halifax and West Coast Cape Breton, calling at way ports, $4,000.
What are the ports of call ?

Halifax, Port
Mulgrave, Port Hawkesbury, Port Hastings, Port Hood, Mabou, Margaree, Grand Etang, Cheticamp, and Eastern Harbour, calling once every two weeks at Havre au Bouche, Cape George and Pleasant Bay, and calling at Inverness, Broadcove Marsh and Margaree Island whenever there is a reasonable quantity of freight or number of passengers to be landed or embarked, weather permitting.
What is the name of the boat?
Strathlorne.

It is claimed by the company that there is not sufficient water to enable them to enter Margaree Harbour. I do not think that is correct; I believe that the boat can call there if the owners so desire. I would ask the minister to see to it that when the contract is being renewed the company be compelled to go into Margaree. The harbour has been considerably improved during the last two years, and I am sure that a boat can go in there. There may be a little trouble in doing so, but it is important and necessary that the boat should call at Margaree, because that would dispense with the necessity of lightering goods at that port. There is 13 feet of water in the harbour.
The matter is now being investigated by the Marine Department, who will make a report on the matter of the sufficiency of water in the harbour.

A request comes from my constituency that this boat call at Ballantyne's Cove on the last trip of each year. This steamer sails from Halifax and goes through the state of Canso, and it involves the traversing of only a short distance to cross Bay St. George and reach the port of Ballantyne's Cove. They say it would be a great advantage to them to have one trip, and they would prefer the last trip of the season. The people in that village are some twenty miles away from railway communication and are served altogether by water, and that is about the only opportunity they would have for the transportation of goods in the winter.
I shall look into the matter.

There are two services between Mulgrave and Canso, and between Mulgrave and Guysborough, which should be performed by the Intercolonial railway. I trust the minister will bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of Railways. These services are really feeders to the Intercolonial railway, of which they are extensions. They collect freight for the Intercolonial railway, chiefly fish, and the trade has grown considerably. Several years ago, when these boats were first put on, there was no fresh fish industry in that vicinity. The people were com-

pelled to cure their fish and sell it salt, but the opportunity of getting their fish shipped opened up the trade in fresh fish. I have obtained from the station agent at Mulgrave figures showing how the trade has grown. In 1898 the number of tons shipped was 1,415 the value being $99,050. The railway freight paid on these shipments amounted to $11,312. In 1908 the shipments had grown to 3,372 tons of the value of $235,900, and the amount paid to the railway for freight was $31,644.03. Last year, 1918, the number of tons was 13,000 of the value of $1,560,000, and the amount paid to the railway for forwarding that fish was $158,986.35. In addition to this large amount of freight these vessels have delivered thousands of passengers to the Intercolonial railway at Mulgrave. This is of great importance to the Government railway. The question may be asked if it is doing so well, [DOT]why is the subsidy continued to be paid? The reason is that it is very difficult to keep these vessels in operation all the year round. The ice in the Strait of Canso is very heavy at present, and if you went to Mulgrave you would probably not see any clear water as far as the eye can reach down the Strait. These vessels during the winter months have to force their way through the ice, and no owner will put his vessel to that kind of work unless there is money in it. If you left it to the ordinary shipowner he would run his vessel in the summer and autumn but would not continue in the winter season. There would be no connection between these points and the railway at Mulgrave during that period unless we had these subsidized boats. I think the Railway Department should furnish good boats capable of going through the ice and making connection with the town of Canso and these places. There are over 2,000 people living at Canso and they are sixty miles from the railroad. It is the most important service in my county. This is about the only money paid in my constituency. Consult the items spent on public works for the present year, and you will not find $2,000 expended in the whole constituency of Guysborough. On 150 miles of coast you will find practically no expenditure by any department. I want to impress on the minister the fact that it would be a great deal better if the Railway Department took charge of this service and put suitable boats on the line. I am confident the result would be very satisfactory and would pay very well, because the trade would bring considerable business; and a small subsidy like this is very little com-

pared with the large amount of money the railway makes out of the traffic when it reaches Mulgrave.

I am well acquainted with the locality served by the steamship services to which my hon. friend refers, and I agree with him that it is essential that that part of the country should have this or some other steamship service, as otherwise they would have no access to the railways, inasmuch as the whole coast line of Guysborough county is without railways. I have always been impressed with the view which my hon. friend puts forward, that at certain points these services might well be performed by the Intercolonial railway, and in the particular case to which he has just been- referring I think a strong argument could be made for the adoption of such a policy. I assume my hon. friend has discussed the matter with the Railway Department at one time or another; but whether he has or not, I shall be very pleased to urge it upon the minister.
Steam service between Newcastle, Neguac and Escuminac, calling at intermediate points on the Miramichi River and Miramichi Bay, $2,500.

I have not had my attention called to this matter before. I understand the hon, gentleman to say that the service has not been performed, or not properly performed. Last year I think the steamer was injured by fire and for some time was not available for the service. I understand now she has been restored and will be on the service again, or has been on the service recently. However, I shall be very glad to look into the remarks of my hon. friend, which I shall see in Hansard, and the matter will be made clearer to me by reading them there as I was not able to follow my hon. friend very closely. Before a contract is made with any particular company, the service will be carefully investigated. We must see that a proper steamer receives the contract.
Have any steamers called at any Nova Scotia ports that are not receiving subsidies?

Yes, quite a number; very few are receiving subsidies.

Is there any inspection or
report made to the department w'hether these subsidized steamers have fulfilled their contracts and made regular calls at the different ports?
Mr. Tupper, the inspector of subsidized steamers, makes a report on every service to the department stating how the contracts are carried out.

Does he go to the different
places to see how the services are performed?

I think he visits the boats every year.
Steam service between Pictou and Montague, calling at Murray Harbour and Georgetown, 15,000.

This amount of $5,000 is too small and those who have been performing the service find it very difficult to continue. Things have changed. The price of coal and wages are so much higher that they say it is impossible to carry on the service for this amount. It is an important service for those portions of Prince Edward , Island, Montague, Georgetown and Murray Harbour, which are not touched by other steamship services. I should be extremely pleased if the minister could find it possible to make provision for an increase in this subsidy in the Supplementary. Estimates, because it will be a great advantage to the entire community concerned.
Schooner service between Pictou, New Glasgow, Antigonish County ports and Mulgrave, $1,000.

The vessel which performs this service is improperly designated in the item as a "schooner," whereas it is an auxiliary boat with gasoline engines. I would like to have the word "schooner" struck out and a more suitable term substituted. I would also remind the minister that the department has received an application for an increase in the subsidy, all the details being set forth in the petition that came from the locality interested. There is a proposal that this boat shall collect some traffic at Pictou, coming from Prince Edward Island, which will make this an interprovincial service and a very important one to all that section of the coast. There are six or seven small ports on that coast where an ordinary steamer cannot call because the water is too shallow; there has to be a special type of boat in order to enter those places. The community interested engage in farming and fishing but are quite distant from any railway communication. This service Is important as it enables the people to get their supplies in the spring, especially fertilizer which they require for the land, and to send away their fish and other produce to New Glasgow and Sydney. I do not think, however, that it can be carried out for the sum of $1,000. If the minister will refer to the correspondence and the petitions that have been received by the department he will find that a strong case has been made out for an increase in the subsidy, and I hope the matter will receive due attention.
I am aware that the contractors have applied for an increase of $500, the matter having come before me personally.
I believe the increase asked for is $1,500.
I think the committee should rise after having passed this item. We are anxious to help the minister out, but it looks as if we shall be here until one o'clock if wh go on as we are now doing.

I suggest that we pass the next two items.
Steam service from the opening to the closing of navigation in 1919 between Pictou, Mulgrave and Cheticamp. $7,500.

I would suggest to the minister that the same observations which I made with respect to the service from Halifax to the west of Cape Breton Island would apply here also, as regards the service from Margaree Harbour.
Does it relate to the same harbour?
The same harbour but there are two different services.
What is the reason for the wording of this and the next item wherein reference is made "to the closing of navigation in 1919"?

The next item,
has reference to ports on the Bras d'Or lakes, which in the winter season are closed.
We have passed items relating to other ports which are also closed during the winter season, but the same phraseology was not followed.
I think the explanation is that the service referred to is limited by winter conditions.

I quite agree, but what the minister says would be equally true of the
steamship service between Newcastle, Neguac and Escuminac.
I will not undertake to say how the difference in phraseology occurred, it may cover a period extending back for a great number of years, but I do not think it is of importance.

The change in phraseology
would not affect the subsidy?

No.
Steam service from the opening to the closing of navigation in 1919, between Port Mulgrave, St. Peter's, Irish Cove and Marble Moun-

tain, and other ports on the Bras d'Or Lakes, 56,500.

Why has the vote for
this purpose been reduced from what it was last year?

It was increased last year on account of special services which will not be- necessary this year. Part of the service will be performed by another steamer, which will be explained when we reach a later item.
The other service will take up the ports of call of this service?

Yes.
