speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: UNIFORMITY OF ADMINISTRATION AND OF PENALTIES.
speechtext:
The pleasure would be greater if I could have first heard the motion supported by the mover himself.
The terms of the resolution are to the effect that the House shall declare that a uniform system of administering the law with uniform penalties in relation to defaulters, deserters, slackers, evaders and others amenable is essential to the wellbeing and good government of the country and is due to the soldiers who went to the front and fought so well in the great cause of human liberty.
The first comment I have to make is that in essence the resolution calls merely for a uniform system of administering law. Fundamentally, under the constitution, the administration of law is in the provinces, not in the Dominion. The Dominion has jurisdiction in the matter of the framing of the law, the passing of statutes within the purview of its powers under the British North America Act, but the administering of the law is wholly for the Provinces. As my hon. friend (Sir Sam Hughes) probably knows more intimately than I do, there is a measure of administration of punishments in the army which is under military law and carried out by courts martial. To that extent, of course, the administration of law may be said to be Federal, but I do not apprehend that the mover of the motion has reference to the sphere of jurisdiction exercised under military law. What he refers to rather is the area of legal administration which is in the hands of superior and district court judges and of magistrates, and in so far as it is a matter of administration, a matter of procedure and organization for carrying it out, it is for the provinces alone. It may be, however, that what the hon. member means is that by statute, wherein we enact the law, we also provide that the penalties open to magistrates and courts shall be in every case uniform, and tnat that uniformity shall extend to the punishment of all defaulters, slackers, evaders and others amenable. If I am right in my estimate of what the hon. member has in mind I fear that the resolution is too wide to commend itself to the favourable consideration of Parliament. If what the hon. gentleman intends to affirm is, that enacting legislation, whether adopted in this Parliament originally and now, or by Order in Council based on legislation passed by this Parliament, must provide that all penalties applicable to offenders of the classes named shall be alike, shall be uniform, I repeat that I do not think the resolution will commend itself to the good judgment of Parliament.
In the first place, the words " others amenable " would refer, of course, to all offenders of every oharacter whatsoever. However, I have no doubt that the mover of the resolution has in mind merely offenders against the Military Act. But it could not be affirmed with any hope of success that Parliament, or the Government acting on the authority of Parliament, should adopt the policy of providing that all penalties must be alike for all offenders, whether the offence be of a serious or of a minor character or whether it be accompanied by mitigating circumstances or not. In all the history of our jurisprudence, legislation providing penalties provides at the same time a minimum and a maximum-at all events, a maximum-penalty. Within the orbit of these two extremes those administering the law are empowered to go, and the purpose and principle of such enactment is that in proportion to the grossness of the offence shall the punishment be. That is the principle which pervades the Military Service Act. It is the principle which actuated Parliament in affording latitude to magistrates in imposing punishments under that Act. In a word, it is the very same principle which pervades the whole Criminal Code, and which pervades many other statutes establishing penalties passed by this Parliament, as well as statutes establishing offences passed by provincial legislatures.
It will no doubt be complained by some that in the actual working out of this Act. as, indeed, is the case in the actual working out of all penal legislation, there has been a very great lack of uniformity in the disposition of individual cases by magistrates and judges. There can be no question that a survey of the operation of the Military Service Act would disclose tha1 different attitudes were assumed by different magistrates, and that even judges differed widely, and some of them almost incomprehensibly, in their estimation of the degree of offence perpetrated by one who had violated the Military Service Act. But that is a phenomenon in no way singular to the operation of the Military Service Act; it is to be found in the history of the every day administration of law. Any one who has to do particularly with the administration of clemency under the Criminal Code,

which is vested, of course, in the Department of Justice, will be struck every houi of every day by the wide diversity of views, and the consequent wide diversity and lack of uniformity in punishment imposed by the various magistrates and judges of the land. That, to some degree, is taken care of by the exercise of clemency on the part of the Department of Justice-taken care of only by the mitigation of punishment, and never by an increase in the punishment of those who are let off lightly by the courts. The latter sphere of jurisdiction the Department of Justice does not have, the department's function being merely in clemency, and not in original punishment. This function of the Department of Justice operates, of course, in relation to the punishments inflicted under the Military Service Act, as in relation to all other punishments. In so far as its exercise is concerned, if it is intended that any complaint be levelled against it, that complaint would more properly be answered by the Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) who from the commencement of the operation of the Act, has had that sphere within his jurisdiction.
It is true that there did occur instances of the apprehension of defaulters under the Military Service Act, where there was some shock to the public conscience by very minor penalties being inflicted. Those were in the main, if I mistake not, punishments inflicted on what were known as Group 3 defaulters; that is to say, defaulters who though they had registered and had not failed to report for medical examination, had nevertheless failed to report for duty. That class of defaulters was a very large one, and the regulations passed under the authority of the Military Service Act itself did not provide any option on the part of the magistrates or judges to impose merely a fine as a penalty for that offence. However, in various parts of Canada magistrates did exercise an option which they did not have of imposing fines. In some cases very large and appropriate fines were imposed and in others very small, trivial and inadequate fines. It was felt that it was not desirable to have these dispositions of cases by magistrates in every case open to be called in question in the courts of the country. For example, in cases where the magistrate had risen to a sense of his duty and had imposed a penalty commensurate with the offence, it was not desirable that that conviction should be open to be upset after the fine had been paid and the offender was free. Those were cases where the offender had suffered something not, at all events, incommensurate with the offence he 
had committed. Consequently, within the powers vested in the Governor in Council, an order was passed which ratified and confirmed convictions that had been followed by a fine where the fine was fixed at not less than $250 nor more than $5,000. That left other convictions where smaller fines had been imposed upon Group 3 defaulters open to be upset, and indeed, not recognized at all by the Department of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: UNIFORMITY OF ADMINISTRATION AND OF PENALTIES.
speechtext:
Those who failed to
register were known as Group 1 defaulters; those who, though they registered, failed to report for medical examination when ordered, were known as Group 2 defaulters; those who, though they did not fail in either of these two respects, failed to report for duty were known as Group 3 defaulters, and that is the large class to which the remarks I have just been making apply. As to the first two classes, those who failed to report, and those who, though they did not fail to register, failed to report for medical examination, my understanding is that the regulations provided under the authority of the Military Service Act enabled a fine to be imposed, but I think in each case a minimum and a maximum fine was fixed.
As to Group 3, the legislation did not, nor did the orders passed under the authority of the legislation, provide any option on the part of magistrates to impose a fine at all; but notwithstanding this, magistrates, some of them at all events believing they had that option, did impose a fine; and now by Order in Council these fines have been ratified provided the fine was not belcw a minimum of $250 nor above a maximum of $5,000.
Group 4 defaulters were those who, having reported for duty and donned the uniform, deserted. Group 5 defaulters were soldiers defaulting on the conditions of their leave of absence by failing to return at the required time. Group 6 defaulters were the nineteen- year old class who failed to report for registration. I am not discussing the first two or the latter three classes at the present time.
I was making some remarks in regard to the experience of the department in the lack of uniformity of sentences imposed on Group 3 defaulters and the action taken by the department to ensure that where convictions were obtained in those cases the

punishment should be adequate and fair. However, what I wish to impress upon the House is the fact that the administration of the law is essentially in the hands of provincial officials, that is to say, magistrates who are provincial officials, and, from them, judges, who, in the ordinary sense, are not provincial officials hut exercise a function which is within the jurisdiction of the Provincial Legislatures as to procedure. There is another feature that I may refer to.
In the treatment of Group 3 defaulters it was discovered there were magistrates who persistently failed to appreciate the spirit and intent of the Military Service Act, and before whom men who had been found and apprehended, after a great deal of expense and trouble, would either be not convicted at all or, owing to a failure on the part of the magistrates to appreciate the magnitude of the offence, would have a very light penalty inflicted on them. In these cases the policy of the department was to instruct the officers in charge-that is, in so far as this work has been under the Department of Justice-to take no more apprehended men before such magistrates. That policy has been pursued consistently and the course adopted was to deliver such men to the military authorities to be tried by court martial. So that wherever magistrates were found who failed in this respect to appreciate their duties, and to act in pursuance of the letter and spirit of the Military Service Act, we took the only course open to us, and would bring no more offenders before them, instructing our officers, as I have said, to turn them over to the military authorities for trial by court martial. From January, I think, to the end of April, 1918, the police work under the Military Service Act was administered by the Military Service Branch of the Department of Justice; and from the end of April until about the middle or the first of January of this year, 1919, that work was taken over and administered by the Militia Department under the Provost Marshal. After the termination of actual war, and about the first Of January, the work was again resumed by the Department of Justice and is now in charge of the Dominion Police. I believe that the principles which I have defined as actuating us in the administration of the duties of apprehension under the Act were virtually the same while under the Militia Department as under the Department of Justice. We have under consideration at the present time-but not sufficiently advanced to enable us to make any statement
to Parliament-the question as to the entire disposition of this subject of the treatment of deserters and defaulters; but at present the administration of the law is just as I have defined. So far as we have it within our power to bring about some degree of uniformity in the treatment of offenders we have done so, but our power in this regard is necessarily limited by the constitutional restrictions to which I have briefly referred.

subsubtopic: UNIFORMITY OF ADMINISTRATION AND OF PENALTIES.
speechtext: I would like to ask a question of the Acting Minister of Justice. Were not instructions issued by the Department of Justice to the magistrates or justices of the peace-instructions published in booklet form- advising them to be very lenient with the men brought before them?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: UNIFORMITY OF ADMINISTRATION AND OF PENALTIES.
speechtext:
No such instructions
were ever issued. Booklets were given to our own officers for their own guidance, but the Department of Justice has never presumed to give instructions or even advice to magistrates or judges, who are in no sense officers of the Department of Justice; nor can I understand the attitude of mind of any magistrate or judge who could think that he was subject to instructions or advice from the Department of Justice. Justice is best administered by the department when it refrains from attempting any jurisdiction in that regard over magistrates or judges. The hon. gentleman has reference, I think, to a statement issued by a magistrate in the city of Quebec-I think he is a magistrate, but he is generally known as Judge Langelier- to the effect that he received instructions from the department. Such is not, and never was the case; and nothing was further from the mind of the department than to attempt to instruct magistrates in Quebec or in any other province. It appears that an officer of the department, Colonel Whitehead, according to his report to us, in going over his papers in a case read a paper which be had prepared on his own authority, which did not come from the Department of Justice and was merely for the guidance of his officers as he himself said. He was requested by the judge for a copy, and having received it the judge proceeded afterwards to proclaim that he had been instructed in such an such a manner by the Department of Justice. I do not think I need say anything further. I have heard the matter referred to in the House on previous occasions, but the whole point is answered when I say that no instructions

of any kind were ever issued to judges or magistrates.

I gathered from the
remarks of the minister that he referred to [DOT]rhat had taken place before the -court presided over by Mr. Justice Langelier in Quebec. I have followed that discussion in the press. I know Mr. Justice Langelier-an ex-member of this House-and he is a man who enjoys the confidence and respect of the bar and of the public of Quebec. He has always been a faithful and impartial administrator of justice. Some months ago when the deserters were brought before his court he received instructions from Colonel Whitehead, a Dominion Police officer, in which he was presumably authorized, to act leniently towards the men brought before him. However, the Department of Justice, through Mr. Newcombe, said that he should not be satisfied with very small fines but should be more severe towards the deserters and evaders.
Mr. Justice Langelier was somewhat shocked when he received that news not personally but through the public press. He at once wrote back to the officer in the Justice Department, I think Mr. Newcombe, the deputy minister, that he had received his instructions from the Government. A discussion arose and finally Mr. Justice Langelier published those instructions verbatim. If I am well informed, and I think my memory does not fail me, an apology came from the Department of Justice. -I think it was sent by Mr. Newcombe himself when it was proven that Mr. Justice Langelier had received through the regular channel his directions from the authorities to act leniently with deserters. I have seen the correspondence which has been published in the press. I only rose because, in the remarks of the Acting Minister of Justice, I detected the tendency to put the blame upon Mr. Justice Langelier. As I have read that correspondence and as I understand it, I think I am justified in stating that Mr. Justice LangelieT did his duty fearlessly and that he acted under the directions which he had received from the authorities in Ottawa.

After that we had the famous Order in Council which imposed a fine of $250 minimum and now young men unable to pay are obliged to go to jail.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the quality of mercy will not be unduly strained if the Department of Justice will try and define more clearly the different penalties under the Act for the guidance of magistrates in the province of Ontario at least. I know that even in Ontario there is a wide range of opinion as to the degrees of punishment that should obtain for various groups of defaulters. For instance in the western part of Ontario, surrounding the city of London, I am informed on authority that I do not desire to question, that defaulters are being allowed off with a penalty of two months' guard duty in the barracks. For men of the same class in eastern Ontario the minimum penalty in Ottawa is a fine of $500 or twelve months in jail. I have appealed to the Department of Justice in vain for a modification of that penalty. I have endeavoured to the best of my ability as a representative of my constituency, to find in the constituency certain instances which will qualify for the minimum penalty without success. There must be something wrong with the administration of justice in the police courts

of Ontario when men of average intelligence will vary to such an extent in imposing penalties for offences of this kind. The groups are so well defined that the variations cannot exist to such an extent as will justify magistrates in varying their decisions so widely as they do. I claim that it is the duty of the Department ol Justice to interfere in the decisions arrived at. I understand that there is a disposition on the part of the department to interfere with the penalty of imprisonment but not with that of a fine. I would like to know why it is that if they are disposed to interfere with one class of penalties they are not disposed to interfere with the other also. If a prisoner is entitled to consideration in the matter of imprisonment I think he is also entitled to consideration as to the amount of the money penalty inflicted. I know of a case where a young man had reported twice voluntarily for service and was turned down by the military authorities as physically unfit because he had the fingers of one hand amputated. That .young man, having been turned down when he volunteered twice, was ordered to report for service and, possibly owing to lack of intelligence, he may have figured that having been turned down when he volunteered there must be some mistake in ordering him to report for service. Sometime during the last two weeks he was arrested and brought before a magistrate who figured that he was justified in inflicting the minimum penalty $250. That man having shown his willingness twice to serve his country notwithstanding his deformities, and having been refused twice by the military authorities, should have been entitled to the minimum penalty, or should have been discharged immediately.
Now, Sir, the position taken by the Department of Justice at the present time amounts to this: That notwithstanding the fact that this young man should be entitled to consideration, he cannot now obtain redress from that department because he has been fined and has paid the penalty of $250. As I said before, I have endeavoured to find a case that in my judgment should qualify for the minimum fine, but it is utterly impossible. I find that even for the same offence two magistrates will each mete out a different degree of penalty. In the North riding of Renfrew men are being penalized with six months' imprisonment or $250 fine. In the South riding '.they are being (penalized tq the extent of $500, or twelve months' imprisonment. Now, I submit that there should be some attempt made towards uniformity
in these judgments, and if such a disparity obtains in the imposition of sentences 3uch as I have explained; then I claim that the Minister of Justice should intervene. I understand that he has already stated on the floor of the House to-day that in cases where magistrates impose too light a penalty, the convicted persons instantly become offenders before a court martial for trial. If it is held that there is a right to interfere in one class of cases connected with the administration of justice, in my opinion interference should also be permitted in such cases as I have called attention to.

subsubtopic: UNIFORMITY OF ADMINISTRATION AND OF PENALTIES.
speechtext:
The motion ot the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) is a very important one, and deals with a very important subject. I quite agree with the Minister of Justice that we have no right to ask any court to mete out uniform penalties. On the other hand, I agree with the wording of the resolution in saying that we should have as much as possible a uniform system of administration of the law. It is highly desirable in dealing with a question of this kind,-having reference to the military system which is uniform all over Canada, the service being as much as possible uniform and the men called out being of uniform class and qualifications,-when we come to deal with deserters or defaulters, that some court which has a general and proper conception of all the circumstances relating to the matter to be tried, should have jurisdiction to deal with the case as far as that can possibly be done. I have no desire to reflect in the slightest upon any magistrates. It is marvellous to me how well magistrates do in the matter of the administration of justice; and if we apply the duties that we impose upon magistrates in another way we will better understand, perhaps, the difficulties that they have to contend with. Supposing for a moment we asked laymen to start the practice of medicine, and said to half a dozen in every town, " You are doctors, go out and treat the people of this district; prescribe medicine, treat surgical cases, and do all that pertains thereto." Hon. members can readily understand what an awfully murderous condition of things would exist if such men were let loose to engage in the practice of medicine in this country. Well, we who are lawyers claim that the profession of law is just as scientific as the profession of medicine, and that it is just as necessary to have a scientific knowledge of law as it is to have a scien-

tific knowledge of medicine. When we ask laymen who have not a scientific knowledge of the law to administer a complicated statute of the kind in question here, together with a number of Orders in Council that have to be interpreted in connection therewith, it is marvellous that these men are doing as well as they are doing. But when that condition of things can be , avoided, when we have courts in this country composed of first class judges, when we have capable lawyers to whom the necessary duties can be assigned, I think the mover of this resolution is quite right, and has given us a subject of the highest importance to deal with, when he says that there should be uniformity in the administration of justice. I hope that that phase of the matter, at all events, will receive consideration from the Department of Justice.
I do not know what saintly men you may have in Ontario as magistrates, but in the province that I come from any constable who goes round with a batch of informations in his pocket, looking for a magistrate to prosecute, can always find the sort of man that he wants. A man of that type will just convict as that officer suggests to him, and will mete out the kind of sentence that the officer wants. This may be a reflection on the good people of my province, but I must tell the truth, and I know that there are such magistrates. I am not saying whether you have such justices in the province oi Ontario or not, but we have them, and we have them pretty much all over the country, and it does not take an officer who is engaged upon the business to
3	p.m. which I referred long to find out where that sort of magistrate is. The magistrate in Nova iScotia is paid by the fees he derives from these magisterial proceedings, and the constable is also paid out of the fees. That, of course, to the ordinary individual is an inducement for securing heavy fines and getting heavy fees. So much for the necessity of lifting this matter above the ordinary petty courts of this class, and putting it on a footing where it will he given the, serious consideration that such important proceedings merit.
I wish further to bring to the notice of the Minister of Justice, and more, especially to the notice of the Acting Prime Minister, that the condition existing in Canada to-day of, I suppose, thousands of young men being liable to be called up for punishment, is a condition of things that should continue only for the shortest possible time. This country of ours was not used to the business of war. It had no training by rea-

son of ancestral heredity in military matters. In this country we were timid in the matter of this military business, and many of our young men who were absolutely honest-thousands of them in fact-did not have the nerve to go up against it. Consequently, they are not criminals at all; it was simply that many of them did not have the real fibre necessary in such a crisis. Now our old law books, and our best authorities on criminal law, tell us, and we believe it, that before there is a criminal action there must be a criminal intent. If you apply that test of criminal intent to many of these poor fellows, who were really afraid, who were timid in this matter, it is obvious that they did not contemplate committing any wrong, but now they find themselves in their present condition. I think we should bring this nightmare, which has followed the war, to an end as quickly as possible. The House will readily understand the feelings of fathers and mothers in this country having sons in such a situation. These are good honest people, who have in many ways contributed towards helping on the war and bringing it to a successful issue, but now that their hoys are in this plight: the mother cannot sleep at night, the father cannot do his work by reason of the shadow of the trial that is hanging over his son, the boy is perhaps keeping out of the way, and yet no doubt the offence that was committed was really of a very slight character. Now if there is to be a trial I would certainly suggest that this threat should be removed as quickly as possible, and that whatever trials are to be held should take place as soon as possible. I do not want to be regarded as having sympathy with any one who did not do his full duty in connection with this war; but I want hon. gentlemen, particularly the Government, to bear in mind that this country was not educated to the war idea. Canada in my opinion did remarkably well when for the first time in its history she had to face such a serious condition of affairs.
Even if we find after two- hundred years of peace that men without any war blood in their veins were timid in answering the call of their country, it is wise for us to consider carefully what scars we are going to leave because of the war. There are many wounds that can never be healed, and it is for the Government to be very careful that they do not create any more heart burnings in connection with these prosecutions unless it is found to be absolutely necessary for the laying broad and deep the foundations of our national life. After the

Americal civil war nobody was punished as a military defaulter. Surely the poor boy who may have been frightened away from this war is not a worse citizen than the man who shouldered his musket in the Southern States and shot perhaps hundreds of his neighbours. President Lincoln said to him:-"Go home to your wife and children and be a good man after this, and you will have no more trouble." I submit that that is the spirit which should prevail in this country, and that we should get back to peace, harmony and order as quickly as possible. We are glad that the war is over, and if there are sore spots here and there it should be the policy of this Government to prevent further irritation and get back to pre-war conditions. In this morning's papers we have an example of clemency in matters of this kind which I think it well to bring to the notice of this House. I find that although the criminal who shot at the Premier of France was sentenced to death, the Premier intervened and the sentence has been commuted to ten years' imprisonment, and probably that term will be reduced eventually. Here is something for us to think about. The Premier of France, who did so much for his country and for the world, says that the man who attempted to assassinate him shall not suffer the extreme penalty, but shall be dealt with leniently because of the prevailing conditions in his country, because in his opinion under circumstances of this kind we should thank God for the great victory and show that we have no vindictiveness. These are matters, Mr. Speaker, which I wish to submit for the careful consideration of the Government.

I regret, Mr. Speaker, that I have
not had the advantage of hearing the discussion which has taken place this afternoon. I was under the impression that the House to-day met at three o'clock instead of two o'clock; consequently I have not been present during the past hour. The question as to what punishment should be meted out to military defaulters is one which has occupied a good deal of my attention, particularly since the armistice was signed. Shortly after that event the Government, realizing the position in which many men, ordinarilly good citizens, were placed, decided that some effort should be made to produce uniformity in regard to the various sentences which were being imposed upon military defaulters throughout Canada, and early in February a committee was appointed to consider the subject -not only of
ordinary military defaulters, but also of conscientious objectors. That committee made a report to the Government, which report was adopted early in the month of February, and since that time I have been endeavouring, -so far as in my power was possible, to carry out its terms.

speechtext: Colonel McFarland. There is a great variety not only in' the cases themselves, but also in the penalties imposed. There is to some extent a similarity in the excuses which are offered. I am satisfied that a great many men who became deserters became so by reason of the fact that their parents or other members of their families deliberately withheld from them the official military notices which were sent ordering them to report There have been a great number of cases of that kind, where the default has been more or less technical, and, in accordance with the recommendation made in the report of the circumstances, such defaulters have been allowed their liberty after serving from one to two months, or even shorter periods. We have endeavoured to obtain as far as possible in each case a satisfactory report of the circumstances from the trial magistrate or from the records of the military tribunal which dealt with the case. In many cases where these records were not definite, we have relied on the reports of the member of the constituency in which the defaulter happened to reside. speechtext:
The debate appears to me to have gone slightly away in recent minutes from the subject matter of the resolution of my hon. friend (Sir Sam Hughes). There seems to be a degree of horror struck in certain quarters in this House at the idea of a man being shot for desertion when in the presence_ of the German army-which was really trying to kill all of us. I agree with General Sherman that war is hell, but when I am at war and in hell I want to give the other fellow the most of it, and it would be a fatal method of looking at national duty if we got a false sense of proportion on even that subject. A man, after all, up against the foe in France who, when his call comes to go over the top, is late by being absent through getting drunk, or by deserting, when the other men are-going straight into action with their lives in their hands, is guilty of an offence which is not a light offence, because he is endangering the lives of all the men who are associated with him in the war, at the hands of the enemy. I think we should look at this other side of the case before we give expression to horror at the very idea which has been suggested that possibly a deserter from Canada was shot. I do not want to pursue that question any further than just to say that much.
My object in this war, and I think the object of every sane man connected with the Allies, was to get hold of the chief murderer in Europe, and if any man has any doubt about the ability of the Allies to conduct the war, bitter and black and bad as it was for many of us, to a successful conclusion, I would recommend him to apply to the Kaiser if they can find him. He will tell him whether England and the Allies know how to conduct war or not.



With regard to the resolution of my hon. friend (Sir Sam Hughes) it appears to call for what would be a very desirable thing in the opinion of the great majority of the people in this country, as far as I know the majority of the people of this country. I did not hear the whole speech of my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen), and I do not know very much about the legal aspects of this question, but I think there will he a broad sentiment in the country in favour of getting as far as possible equality of sentence. One does not need much law, one only needs to be a level-minded citizen, to see the desirability of such a result being brought about, and to that extent I think the resolution has not been altogether inadvisedly brought before the House. If we could give these defaulters something like equality of treatment I think it would bring general satisfaction in Canada, and would be in accordance with the rough common sense of Canadian citizenship.
I listened with interest to the speech of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie). I do not always agree with my hon. friend in toto. Very frequently, I do not agree with what he says at all, but to-day I had a very large sympathy with his conclusions, and with his evident object in rising, without being carried by the arguments by which he supported his contention. I have not gone as deeply as he seems to have done into the psychology of those who have defaulted;
I do not know whether they and theii friends would thank him for having concluded that the principal cause of theii defaulting was lack of fibre. I think that was his word, or lack of nerve. However, that explanation of the psychology of these particular citizens I leave to my hon. friend and to those particular citizens. Neither did I think that his analogy taken from the United States and President Lincoln was a good one. In that case there was a civil war in which one-half of the country had been doing its best against the other half, and in which the supreme power in the state had been disputed by blood, and I cannot conceive of a statesman with even an average degree of wisdom-and Lincoln had far more than the average-taking any different course from that taken by him. However, I do agree in the main with the advice that my hon. friend gave the Government. We have had too many sorrows and heart-burnings and acute disputes over this war-and I distinguish sharply between the cases to which I referred "when I first arose, which happened during the 
war when everything had to be in to win the war-to keep up animosities after the war is over. Mr. Speaker, I may be misunderstood and disagreed with by many who surround me, for whom I have the highest regard from the fact, at any rate, that we were together in the stress and storm of the war, but I must say now that the war is over, British tradition, I think, would lead us to weigh very carefully the advice which has been given to the House and to the Government by the leader of the Opposition. I do not suggest that criminals should be let off without punishment. That would never do in a civilized country. There is no liberty anywhere except the liberty which is protected by law, and I am sure my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition will agree with that sentiment. Our very liberties depend upon respect for law, and it is the outstanding characteristic of the British Empire that within its bounds more than anywhere else in the world you have the almost perfect combination of respect for law and order, on the one hand, and the greatest possible freedom on the other. Now that the war is won, and well won, .1 think that we might very well go as far as we can in the direction of casting a large measure of blessed oblivion over the small differences that divided us while the war was on. I hold that view very strongly. I think the progress of the months will lead the Government to see the force of that course, and indeed, from what has fallen from my hon. friend the 'Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie)
I think that these instincts are guiding the Government at the present moment. There is really no essential difference between the two sides of this House, il should hope, in regard to the fundamental characteristics of the British Empire and of British justice and of British government in this respect. Why, Sir, what do we see at the present moment? We have seen the British Government recently let the Sinn Feiners out of prison in Ireland. What did we see in South Africa? We saw a course of leniency taken to the point of giving self-government to the Boers in South Africa within a very brief time after the termination of the war, and with the best possible results. I am often struck with this fact, and am rather charmed by it too, that sometimes the sentiments of loyalty in this country, and especially amongst my friends around me, go much farther than they do in Hyde Park, London. I am perfectly sure that every Sunday afternoon in Hyde Park, London, you hear sentiments uttered at public meetings there about monarchy and all conceiv-

able subjects which would speedily get a man a ducking in many parts of the good old province of Ontario, so Ontario is even more loyal than they are in the city of London in this particular.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friends opposite applaud that sentiment. They evidently recognize, as I do, that it is well to err in a good cause. Well, the result of that clemency and that application of British principles in South Africa was very admirable, and just in a general way I wanted to endorse, as I am always anxious to endorse when I can, any sentiments that fall from the lips of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie). He does his best to utter sentiments from time to time which, unfortunately, I cannot agree with, but I am not like him, a Highland Scotchman; my memory is shorter than his, and I am always looking out for good things even in the most unexpected places. I do think we have our hands pretty full in Canada at the present time in reconstructing the country.
I know something about the sentiments of the returned men, and I want to say this for a large number of them with whom I have talked, that they are not at all revengefully inclined. The majority of them know what they were up against, and the returned soldiers, I believe, would in public meeting assembled endorse by a majority the sentiments which I have just been uttering. I may be wrong in that respect, but I have endeavoured to get their sentiments and to learn what they think upon these things, and I feel very strongly that that is their attitude. Let me repeat that I should be very much misunderstood if any one thought I looked lightly upon the crime of desertion or upon any breach of law. But war is an abnormal condition, fortunately, in the affairs of this world, and certainly very abnormal in the affairs of 'Canada, and on the broad principles of British precedent and justice and the kind of sentiment that has animated that old country, with which we are all proud to be connected, in .dealing with those who have been at variance with 'her in times of stress and struggle, I think the Government would do well, in a large number of these questions upon which I do not want to dwell to-day, to think twice, aye, to think three times before they keep heart burnings of irritations and harassments alive amongst our people.

Major-General MEWBTJRN (Minister of Militia): I shall say only a few words on this question, Mr. Speaker. The remarks of onfe of the hon. gentlemen opposite, in reference to a statement made by the Solici-ton General (Mr. Guthrie), might create the impression that a large number of our Canadian soldiers have been shot. As far as I am aware, there were very few such cases. These cases were very few, however, and certainly there have been no reports of any during my term of office. Therefore, I would not like to have it go abroad that there were many such cases. In regard to the question of uniform penalties,-as I stated in the House the other day,-immediately after the armistice, on November 11th, it was quite apparent that we did not require any more of these defaulters as soldiers, and the question was, what was to be done with them? Under the statute they were liable as deserters and defaulters, and personally I never considered that they should be allowed to go scot-free. I do not believe that it is possible in this country,-unless we are going to engage in that work for the rest of our natural lives,-to attempt to arrest all the men of these various classes; but I would like to see some machinery quickly put into operation whereby all the classes mentioned by the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) should be disfranchised and deprived of cer-tain*civil rights for a period of years. This, I think would be approved of by all good people in this country. Those who were defaulters would be thereby penalized.
In view of a question which has been asked in the House in regard to prisoners generally, I cabled some weeks ago to ascertain what policy was in force overseas regarding Canadian prisoners undergoing punishment for military offences in England and France, and what was to be done with them. In connection with the subject 1 may read this statement:
Policy Regarding the Disposal on Demobilization of Canadian Soldiers Undergoing Penal Servitude, Imprisonment or Detention.
1.	Those undergoing sentence for purely military offences will he returned to Canada under arrangements to be completed later, some time prior to the final completion of demobilization. Their sentences will be remitted with effect from the date of sailing. Each soldier will he

left, as far as possible, to complete his sentence before embarkation, but existing powers of remission, etc., will, in the meantime continue to be exercised in special cases.
Each case falling within this class will at the time of final disposal be made the subject of special consideration, and where it appears that existing military conditions due to demobilization render it desirable to make an exception such soldier will be held to complete his sentence.
It is thought that cases of serious insubordination during demobilization might be dealt with in this manner.
2.	Those undergoing sentence imposed by the civil power in England will be left in this country to complete their sentences should they not expire before demobilization has been concluded, but such cases will be reviewed individually prior to the final completion of demobilization with a view to determining whether any of them present such extenuating circumstances as would justify an application to the Home Secretary for a special release. It is not anticipated that many cases of this nature will be encountered.
3.	Soldiers undergoing sentence of imprisonment or penal servitude imposed by military courts, either in this country or in France, for offences of a criminal, as distinguished from a military nature, will be committed to (or left in) civil prisons in England to serve out their sentences. Such cases also will, however, be reviewed prior to the completion of demobilization with a view to determining whether any of them present such extenuating circumstances as would justify remission.
The following additional provisions are applicable to soldiers undergoing sentence in France:-
1.	The general policy outlined above will be followed, but soldiers who are undergoing sen-iencQ for offences not of a serious nature will rbe released from prison on the recommendation of the corps commander and returned with their units to England for demobilization in the usual way. Others, whose offences were of a more serious nature but who are considered to be eligible for release prior to the final completion of demobilization, will be retained in prison to Serve as much of their sentence as possible before the conclusion of demobilization.
2.	Those falling under Class (3) above, will be returned to England and committed to prison here to complete their sentences.
It is proposed, upon the final completion of demobilization to carry out the discharge of all Canadian soldiers left in prison in this country, who have not already been discharged or sentenced to be discharged with ignominy. Nominal rolls will then be prepared and left with the War Office and the High Commissioner for Canada, copies also being forwarded to Militia Headquarters, Ottawa. Upon completion of their sentences the men will be dealt with and, if eligible, repatriated on instructions from the High Commissioner.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
subsubtopic: UNIFORMITY OF ADMINISTRATION AND OF PENALTIES.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while not wishing to prolong this debate, there are one or two points in connection with the discussion that I would like to touch upon, more especially as I was brought into immediate contact with some of the problems during last summer when I had the responsibility of taking the place of my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence (Major General Mewburn) at a very trying time during June, July and August. I do not wish to refer particularly to the resolution except to agree with what my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) has said in pointing out the extraordinary difficulty of equalizing penalties in connection with the administration of justice for infractions of the Criminal Code or for any crimes whatever. I quite agree with my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) that in so far as it is humanly possible with crimes of this kind, it is weil to have equality of punishment. But I think it is quite obvious to anybody who has studied this question at all that the variations and degrees of guilt are, and must be, extraordinarily wide and that there must be a corresponding variation in the penalties imposed.
I wish more particularly to speak of another phase of this matter before the resolution is put through the House, or is dealt with, because I do not think that this House, or the country, should overlook the gravity of the offence that we have been dealing with, from a natioual point of view. My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) pleaded, and I am not complaining in any way about his plea for clemency, for a generous way of looking at this whole matter and, practically, for the abolition of punishment, or at all events,

an early cessation of any rigorous or harsh measures. In the main we would all agree to that. My hon. friend stated that many parents were kept awake at night sorrowing for their boys who had been punished or who had been defaulters. May I point out to him that I took charge of the Militia Department last summer at a most critical phase of the war, when nobody in this country, or amongst the Allies, could face with anything but the deepest anxiety the progress of the various battles going on in Europe and certainly when no man could predict with anything like assurance what the issue might be. Canada was straining every nerve to get every man possible to do his duty to the state whose very existence was in danger, and to send reinforcements to those men who were literally fighting and dying in defence of our own liberty.
When I took charge of the department I found the condition of things practically this. There was scarcely a household in Canada, and in that part of it that I know more especially well, the far West, that had not provided one or more of its members to go and fight in the war and provided them early and voluntarily at a great sacrifice. I found that a great many thousands of men-I would not like to give the exact figures-subject to the call of the state in the very same way as all those other men who had gone had failed to respond ancKwere allowing those others to fight the battle at the risk of their lives while they stayed in safety at home. It seemed to me that at that critical time in our history when everything was in hazard, it was an absolutely impossible thing for us to make a call for more sacrifices from the homes in Canada -which had already provided these people to go to the war and allow to go scot-free thousands of those who were making no effort to do their duty to the state. It became necessary to do one of two things; either to insist that the most severe and harsh punishment should be meted out to those who were deliberately ignoring the call, and violating their first duty to the state, or to make a strong appeal to them in order that they might, before it was too late, recognize their duty, and, in the event of that recognition, to treat them with a generosity which I am sure my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition would have been in entire sympathy with.
Having discussed the matter very thoroughly from every angle, I recommended to my colleagues that we proclaim a general amnesty. While this matter is under discussion I would like to direct the attention of members of the House to the terms of that amnesty, and I would like to put those terms on Hansard for the very reason I have indicated. The amnesty was issued on August 2, 1918, and it was inspired by the belief that nothing short of a measure of this sort would drive home to the thousands of people who were neglecting their duty a realization of what they owed to the state. We put it in such broad and generous terms because we believed that there were thousands of defaulters at that time who had defaulted simply through sheer ignorance or because they had been misled by people in the country who knew a great deal better than they did. Without quoting the whole of the proclamation, I would like to read just two or three paragraphs:
Whereas considerable numbers of men belonging to Class I. under our Military Service Act, 1917, called out on active service in our Canadian Expeditionary Force for the defence of Canada under Our Proclamation of 13th October, 1917, although they have thus become by law soldiers enlisted in the military service of Canada,
Have failed to report for duty as lawfully required of them under the said Military Service Act and the regulations thereunder, including the Order in Council duly passed on April.20 last,
Or have deserted.
Or absented themselves without leave from our Canadian Expeditionary Force,
And it is represented that the very serious and unfortunate situation in which these men find themselves is due in many cases to the fact that, notwithstanding the information and warning contained in Our Proclamation aforesaid, they have misunderstood their duty or obligation, or have been misled by the advice of ill-disposed, disloyal or seditious persons.
And whereas we desire, if possible, to avoid the infliction of the heavy penalties which the law imposes for the offences of which these soldiers have thus been guilty, and to afford them an opportunity within a limited time to report and make their services available in our Canadian Expeditionary Force as is by law their bounden duty, and as is necessary for the defence of Our Dominion of Canada,
Now know ye that we in the exercise of our powers, and of our good will and pleasure in that behalf, do hereby proclaim and declare and cause to be published and made known that the penalties of the law will not be imposed or exacted as against the men who belong to Class I. under our Military Service Act, 1917, and who have disobeyed our Proclamation aforesaid ; or who have received notice from any of our registrars or deputy registrars to report for duty on a day now past and have failed so to report; or who, having reported and obtained leave of absence, have failed to report at the expiry of their leave, or have become deserters from our Expeditionary Force, provided they report for duty on or before the twenty-fourth day of August, 1918.
And we do hereby strictly warn and solemnly impress upon all such men, and as well those

who employ, harbour, conceal or assist them in their disobedience, that, if they persist in their failure to report, absence or desertion until the expiry of the last mentioned day, they will be pursued and punished with all the rigour and severity of the law, subject to the judgment of our courts martial which will be convened to try such cases or other competent tribunals; and also that those who employ, harbour, conceal or assist such men will be held strictly accountable as offenders and subject to the pains, penalties and forfeitures in that behalf by law provided for their said offence.
I desire to point out to the House in discussing the resolution now before it, that the very fact that amnesty was granted in the broadest and most generous terms made it incumbent on all those men who, by ignorance or by deliberate intention, had evaded their duty to the state, to avail themselves of its terms and restore themselves to the position which those citizens occupied who were prepared to do their full duty. When, therefore, it is argued -and I am not pleading for anything but the most reasonable and generous treatment now that the war is over-that we should forget entirely all these things, I will ask the House to 'Consider the position of those thousands of men (for I am glad to say that thousands of men did subse-qwsntly report) who presented themselves in time to avail themselves of the amnesty. In what position does the House think all those men are in, as compared with the thousands of men who deliberately, after the publication of that warning, refused to do their duty to the state, and thereby became doubly defaulters and traitors to their country? The House must not, and cannot, forget that aspect of the question.
My hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) came to see me about that time and we discussed this question. I pointed out to him in the very strongest way that it was up to him, and to every man in this country of influence and power, to use all his influence to convince the men who, through ignorance or deliberation, were not rising to a full sense of their duty in the most terrible period we ever faced, to induce them to come in even at the last hour and discharge their obligation. And if, as I say, in the face of that warning, published broadcast throughout the length and breadth of the land, there were thousands of men who still placed upon themselves the stigma of having failed in that duty, it is not for us to lightly regard this whole question of punishment in some form or another, or to view with complacence the position of those men who took, in the face of such a perilous situation, an atti-

tude which simply meant: I will not move hand or foot for the very existence of the state whose privileges I have been enjoying for years.
Now, Sir, the leader of the Opposition remarked that even the author of the attempted assassination of Premier Clemen-ceau was let off. That may be true, but my recollection of the ultimate result oi the trial in that case is that the would-be assassin was adjudged to be insane, and that was largely the reason for the commutation of the death sentence to ten years imprisonment. Certainly there is considerable doubt as to the sanity of the criminal in that case, and I do not think, taking that fact into account, that it is at all a case parallel with those we are dealing with now. I would admit, and would be the first to do so, that now the war is over harshness should be tempered with mercy, and that there should not be any unnecessary continuation of the methods hitherto pursued or of any desire to unduly punish those persons, however guilty they may have been, who failed the country in the face of the highest call that the State ever issued to them. My hon. friend said we had scars enough already. God knows there have been scars enough in this war. But my hon. friend must not forget also that the men who have had the greatest scars are those who have done their highest duty, and their sorrowing friends and relatives, some of whom now live to mourn their loss, can never entirely view the matter in the same way as those men who are trying to obtain absolute immunity from punishment, who, in the face of the sacrifices that others undertook, made absolutely no sacrifice in any shape or form. I do not think that this country, or any citizen living in it, can afford to minimize the grave dereliction of the highest duty they owed to the State which these defaulters were guilty of. I do not look upon this as an ordinary crime. It seems to me, viewed in the light of oui troubles in the past and our situation at present, that the full obligations 4 p.m. and full privileges of citizenship in this country are not sufficiently realized by those who enjoy them. But this war has driven the lesson home, that if a man becomes domiciled in this country and enjoys privileges-and they are great- of citizenship, whenever the existence oi the State is threatened it is absolutely necessary for him to rise to a full sense of those obligations devolving upon him and to carry them out in their entirety. None of us, therefore, can afford to look lightly at that crime, which is the greatest

crime of all, viz.: That of failing to move hand or foot in the service of the State when the State's life is threatened. That is why I say this: That even in spite oi any desire to mitigate severity and to drop some of the methods that we adopted to bring men to punishment, or in dealing with this subject in any shape or form, we should not forget that this cannot be regarded in any way as a light matter. Personally, I would be strongly in favour of applying some form of disfranchisement against a defaulter. It would mean the sentence to that man: You have failed in your duty as a citizen, and therefore your privileges as a citizen are taken from you, at all events for a time. I believe that such would be a wise course to pursue. Whether that punishment should be applied to the man who has already undergone some form of punishment I need not discuss now. I am only arguing that, for the sake of those who have gone overseas and undergone untold sacrifices in our behalf, or in behalf of the state, in dealing with this matter we should, at all events, render justice, even if that justice is tempered with mercy.

speechtext:
I concur altogether in the last remark made by the Secretary of iState (Mr. Burrell) that the subject brought before the House by the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) is not a matter to be considered or weighed lightly. It is a matter of great moment and great importance, and the House has to consider it as such.
The mover of this resolution has brought before you, Sir, the question which has been discussed in all the papers and by most of the citizens of this country, and which is awaiting a solution. Are we going to solve this question as it ought to be solved, in a broad spirit of justice, or are we going to solve it in the narrow spirit of people who cannot look far enough ahead in the interests of their country? The Acting Minister of Justice has referred to Mr. Justice Langelier. I do not wish to discuss this afternoon the controversy between Mr. Justice Langelier and the Deputy Minister of Justice, Mr. Newcombe, which is a local affair and of not sufficient importance to divert our minds from the broader and more general problem suggested by the motion before the House. But, as a citizen of Quebec and as a member of the Quebec Bar, I wish to tell the Acting Minister of Justice that Mr. Justice Langelier is one of the most respected, most honoured and eminent members of our judiciary, he belongs to a family that has supplied to our Bar and to our judiciary very eminent men -suffice it to mention that his brother was Lieut.-Governor of the province of Quebec after having been Chief Justice of its Superior Court. Mr. Justice Langelier is not a man who would use his position as judge to be a partisan or to defeat the ends of justice, as was insinuated in this House -not by the Acting Minister of Justice, but by some other member on another occasion.
The Government, as regards the city of Quebec, are always in a most unfortunate position. Last year we had riots in our city. The matter was brought before the House, and the explanation given by the Government for the conduct of their representative was the same as that offered by the acting Minister of Justice this afternoon, to wit, that that representative did not belong to any Department of the Government. Colonel Machin was thrown overboard by the Minister of Justice and by the Minister of Militia, and he was cast away by every other member of the Cabinet. He occupied an official position, but it was convenient for the Government that he should disappear, and he did disappear, for a week or so, to reappear a little later. But, Mr. Speaker, the members of this House will not be satisfied with an explanation of that kind. What was Mr. Whitehead doing in the city of Quebec? Was he an official connected with the Government? Did he belong to the Ministry of Justice or to the Ministry of Militia? Mr. Whitehead handed to Judge Langelier instructions; those instructions were official; the judge acted according to those instructions. Were those instructions prepared by the Acting Minister of Justice or by one of his officials? Were those instructions prepared by the Minister of Militia or by one of his officials? That is the question, Mr. Speaker, and the people of this country in general and of the city

of Quebec in particular, as well as Judge Langelier himself, have a right to receive a direct answer for once from the Acting Minister of Justice.

speechtext:
The incident to which the hon. member refers was opened by a communication to the Department of Justice in regard to certain fines imposed on military defaulters in the city of Quebec by the magistrate in question, which fines ranged from $5-which was the usual amount-to $25. The Deputy Minister of Justice thereupon communicated with the Attorney General of the province of Quebec, drawing his attention to the. report and asking that an explanation of it be given; and requesting if the report were true, that representations be made to the magistrate in question that such fines were not incompliance with the law, the Deputy Minister of Justice recognizing that the magistrate was no official of the Department oi Justice or of this Government but was appointed by, and was within the purview of, the Government of the province of Quebec. Then a communication reached the department from the magistrate in question, to the effect that he had been instructed to impose light fines on defaulters. That was the first intimation the Department of Justice ever received that any instructions had gone from the department either to Magistrate Langelier or to any other magistrate or judge in Canada; indeed, we knew that no instructions of any kind whatsoever had gone out. On further inquiry into the matter, a report came to me-I am speaking now from memory; had I known that this matter -was coming up I would have had the whole of the correspondence here -direct from Judge Langelier, |I believe; it was not asked for by us, as our communications up to this time were only with the Attorney General of Quebec. Judge Langelier reported that he had been instructed to follow the course he had taken, and he referred, either in his first or in his second letter, to Colonel Whitehead as the official from whom the instructions came. Colonel Whitehead was an officer of the Dominion Police, which force is under the Department of Justice; it was only in that sense that he was an official of the depart-

ment. Upon hearing that, Colonel Whitehead was immediately suspended. He reported that he had given nothing whatever in the way of instructions, but that he had himself prepared for the guidance of his own officials-he has inspectors, I think, or some other officials under him-a memorandum, which was as partially quoted by Judge Langelier, but it followed with a sentence to this effect: That his officials were to understand that they should in all cases ask for substantial punishment for the offence) but were not to be animated by feelings of severity. This was not in the form of instructions to the magistrate, as I have stated over and over again, and as any hon. member of this House must know, and none better than the hon. member who has just spoken, because to intimate that either we or Colonel Whitehead had any jurisdiction over the magistrate is to intimate an absurdity that could not enter the mind of a reasonable citizen. This memorandum appears to have come to the attention of Judge Langelier. He had been going over with Colonel Whitehead a certain book which police inspectors always carry, but which is not referred to in this case. In reviewing that book, which dealt with the duties of police inspectors, this memorandum came to Judge Langelier's attention. He asked for a copy of it, and a copy was given to him. It contained the portion he quotes, which I repeat again was for Colonel Whitehead's officials, and it contained next the qualifying portion which the judge always refrained from quoting. He then commenced immediately to proclaim that this was received by him from the Department of Justice as his instructions. Well, it would baffle my command of the English language to describe an absurdity more gross or a claim more palpably untrue. No instructions of any kind, let me repeat, ever issued to him or to any magistrate or judge, directly or indirectly,. through an official or through any one else. No instructions were ever intended to issue and none ever did. He got a memorandum which was for the use only of the inspector and for the benefit of the inspector's officials, and chose tj proclaim that as his instructions from us- who, he knew, had no power and no right to instruct him. Hon. members persist in repeating that the Department of Justice so far misunderstood its duties as to attempt to give instructions or advice to magistrates. This gentleman persisted in carrying on a correspondence which the Deputy Minister of Justice very properly refused to continue. That correspondence

I shall he only too glad to have read tc the House; I would have read it myseli had I had any intimation that the subject *was coming up. But it will fail to disclose anything that even savours of an apology. The only time apology comes in is when Judge Langelier, misunderstanding and misrepresenting the facts again, as he did in the first place, replied to some letter and said that he had received an apology. The wit of man would search the correspondence in vain for anything in the nature of an apology. From memory, that is an account of what occurred; it is in essence, a complete account; it is in letter and in spirit an accurate account of what occurred, and nothing else.

We now have the information that Mr. Whitehead is an official of the Justice Department acting as Inspector of Dominion Police in the city of Quebec. Mr. Whitehead hands ovei to the judge written instructions. Well, any man who has had legal experience knows that those written instructions could riot have been prepared or drafted by the inspector himself; they must have been prepared by his superior officer. That superior officer could not give instructions on a matter of that importance without consulting the head of the department; therefore the moment an officer of the Justice Department, the Inspector of Dominion Police, hands printed instructions to a judge in the city of Quebec, we connect the head of the Justice Department, the acting minister (Mr. Meighen), or the minister (Mr. Doherty), who is now away,
with those written instructions. There is no use in running away with the idea thal these instructions were prepared by a mar who is in no way responsible. The explanation of my hon. friend tending to show that these instructions were prepared by an irresponsible official will be accepted by very few in this House. What happened? After Judge Langelier had given a few judgments in accordance with the instructions he had received, some opposition was made and some protest offered from certain parts of the country. As usual, the Government gave way, turned right about face, and tried to deny what had actually been done by its own officers. That was the whole situation.
Let us leave aside the incident of Judge Langelier; in coming to a conclusion in regard to this matter we have to go a little further back. The Secretary of State says that the people of this country had been straining every nerve to win the war. But we all remember something else, Mr. Speaker. If some people were straining their nerves to win the war, others not very far from the Acting Prime Minister and the Secretary of State were straining every nerve not to win the war, but to win the elections. Many gentlemen on your right, Mr. Speaker, when the question oi conscription was being fought out before the people, were thinking not of the Canadians who were over in France facing death, but of the means by which they could defraud the electorate; of the means by which they could deceive their

I bow to your decision, Mr. Speaker. I say that lots of gentlemen sitting to your right were thinking at that time of the means they might adopt to bring about a decision in their constituencies favourable to them, notwithstanding the existence of a feeling adverse to them in those constituencies. Other people were thinking of something else, Mr. Speaker. Other people were trying to secure the farmers' vote in their counties. Farmers are not, like the member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) all well versed in literature. They do not spend their leisure moments reading Shakespeare and the best English authors. What did some of the hon.

gentlemen sitting to your right, Mr. Speaker, say? They went to these farmers and they told them: " Conscription will not apply to you." They were believed. What happened? The Government came back to power. The farmers had voted for a Government that had promised solemnly that the farmers would not be conscripted. In the month of March the new constitutional method invented by the present Government was adopted and an Order in Council wiped out the solemn promise of the members of the Government concerning conscription and the farmers-and the farmers were conscripted. Any hon. gentleman who has a good memory will remember what happened subsequently. The farmers came to this city, and they were curious enough to insist on seeing you, Sir. The Government told them to go home, that the farmers and their sons had to go to war. The agitation continued; discontent was rampant. The Government was frightened once more and instructions were secretly sent to officials throughout the country to this effect: " Bring the farmers to the city, but give them additional furlough, send them back home." They were sent home; in Ontario they were sent home because the Government was afraid of them.
What about the emergency? What about the German peril of March of last year? The farmers were sent home, Mr. Speaker, because the gentlemen sitting on your right were afraid that their promises might bring them to grief in the near future. What were the farmers to understand from all this? Exempted one day, conscripted the next; brought to Quebec one day, sent home on the following. Unsophisticated men could only conclude that what was going to happen was very uncertain and indefinite; so they remained at home. To-day the Secretary of State says that we must not forget to be just. I am of that opinion too, but I think the greatest culprits who should be brought before the tribunal for their action on conscription and the operation of the Military Service Act are some of the gentlemen on your right, Mr. Speaker, occupying Cabinet positions.

This young man Collins had read that statement. He was a farmer and remained at home, because General Mewburn had promised that if he was taken from home he would send him back again. He appealed to our distinguished, candid, frank and sincere friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Crerar): "Why don't you add something to what the Minister of Militia has said? I wish sincerely that that had been the case; I can say that from the bottom of my heart. But it was not the case, and the reason it was not the case was that in certain sections of our country the citizens did not rise to the realization of the full meaning of their citizenship in Canada. My hon. friend from Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) can tell you that when the call for the first contingent was made, it was over-subscribed within forty-eight hours; the second contingent was the same and, so on. If it had been an ordinary war the ordinary voluntary system, which was based upon British law and justice and the desire that small nations might live, would
