speechtext: I do not wish to dispute your ruling, in any way, Mr. Speaker, but the hon. member for Dorchester discussed it for pretty nearly half an hour and I thought that I would have the right to reply. If not, I certainly bow to your ruling.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: UNIFORMITY OF ADMINISTRATION AND OF PENALTIES.
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Dorchester was not discussing conscription except as showing that certain results flowed from the application of the law. The hon. member (Mr. Cockshutt) is attempting to justify conscription itself which is quite a different matter.

subsubtopic: UNIFORMITY OF ADMINISTRATION AND OF PENALTIES.
speechtext:
It is a very fine distinction but, however, I will try to observe it. The hon. member at any rate based his argument on the exemptions that prevailed under the law of conscription. Perhaps I would be in order if I did it in that way. Infractions, it is true, in some eases were not equally punished-in fact, in many cases, were not punished at all. The hon. member for Dorchester calls for justice. If justice were done there would not be sufficient prison room in the county of Dorchester to contain all those who would be serving sentences for not coming forward as required by the Military Service Act. That condition would prevail, not only in Dorchester but in many other counties. As far as I remember the figures, there

were nearly 40,000 defaulters under the law. We know where the bulk of them live. If it is justice that is wanted, justice should be had, and we are ready for it. What the resolution calls for is equal justice to all. We feel that has not been given. Some have been severely punished. We know that in those parts of the country where the voluntary system was the strongest, and where the defaulters were the fewest, the most severe punishments were inflicted not only by fine but by imprisonment. We have sentences ranging from thirty days to a lifetime of imprisonment for not obeying the Military Service law. Is that what justice requires in a country such as Canada? I think not. The resolution calls for justice and for a uniform administration of the law. We should have that and we cannot afford having punished, as we have, so severely a very great number of defaulters in those parts of the country that were ready to round them up, to listen to the cool proposition to come down now and say that where there are so many thousands the law is unequal to deal with them and that therefore we will let them all off entirely. That cannot be contemplated for a moment.
We must have the same uniformity of punishment for those who have not heard the call of their country. If their training in loyalty was not sufficient to bring them to the rescue of Canada and of the British Empire, to the defence of their freedom, and their rights within the law, but necessitated the state stepping in and saying: If you do not go voluntarily you must go under compulsion, then every man who avoided that call should certainly be punished. We set out under the voluntary system. The voluntary system imposes a very heavy responsibility upon the citizen. It says that when your country is in danger you as an individual unit in the country are called upon to do your duty, to go if necessary, and to risk your life in fighting for the defence of your country. What would be said of a case like this? A father has five boys in his house, all good strapping, sound lads; he is attacked by a bunch of bandits over night and, when the old gentleman calls for help, four out of the. five sons only need (to know that the father is in difficulty and needs help to get them to the spot. But the fifth lies in his bed upstairs and says: Let the old man and the other boys fight it out. What would you think of a son like that? Would compulsion be good enough for him? No, he should be disinherited-cut off-branded as
a slacker, a man who, when his parent was in danger, when the family interests were at stake and when all that was dear to that household was calling for his help, played the defaulter.
Is that the kind of man this country would applaud, or would excuse? I think not. Therefore I say that for the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) to argue that these men should be let off, that their offence should be condoned in any way, and that those who were responsible for the issuance cf the Military Service call, and the declaration as to who were exempt under it, should be allowed to go free, is something I cannot comprehend at all. I therefore say that in my judgment the resolution is one that is very well timed and requires the most careful and serious consideration on the part of those who administer justice. Because there could be nothing more lamentable than to have it go out to the country that the administration of justice in Canada is entirely in vain, and that the administrators know it and will not try to change that condition or put the law into operation.
We know that all human laws have inequalities, more or less. We know that sometimes a hungry man who steals a loaf of bread pays as heavy a penalty as the man who defaults with five or ten thousand dollars. We know that such things occur, and we know they are not right. In this case we had the moral law, calling for voluntary service, and I consider that is just as strong on the true citizen as is the law of the land. In addition to the moral law, which called upon every citizen to do his part, we had to enact the conscription law, which said: If the moral law is not strong enough in its claims on you, we must put something back of it that is. Therefore the law of force was enacted in Canada, and the men whose cases we are considering to-day are the defaulters and the slackers under it. They did not come to' the assistance of the country when it needed their help. They did not respond when the call went forth that the British Empire and civilization were in imminent danger. Therefore I say that these men, having failed to answer that call, we cannot afford to disregard the punishment that should be meted out in every province alike, from coast to coast-an absolute evenhanded sentence-to every one that failed to obey the law. That I think is evident, and in my judgment, Mr. Speaker, there can be no two opinions about the matter. I hope the resolution of the hon. member

for Victoria will have the unanimous support of the House, and that some uniform sentence will be imposed on every slacker in the country.
Mr. J. E. S, D'ANJOU (Rimouski) (translation) : Mr. (Speaker, I have listened with very great attention to the remarks fallen from the lips of my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt). I wish he could catch my meaning as well as I understood his own remarks. I understood my hon. friend to say that, the guilty party, the chief culprit responsible for the establishing of conscription in Canada was the province of Quebec. Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the province of Quebec opposed conscription, because she had a right to do so. Our province, in doing so, followed in the footsteps of Australia, one of the great Dominions in the British Empire which twice opposed the passing of a conscription law by two referendums and during an appeal to the electorate, Ireland also objected to the enactment of such a legislation, not on account of the Irish being cowards, seeing that the Irish, whenever their rights were in jeopardy, have shown themselves able to take care of themselves, but because they looked upon such legislation as inimical to their interests, the more so as Ireland, just as the other parts of the Empire, had furnished its full quota during the late war.
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, our friends from the province of Ontario improve every opportunity of throwing discredit on the province of Quebec, by slandering and reviling her. I have the honour of representing here a constituency which did supply a full quota during this war. I do not think there are many representatives from Ontario who could boast of counting amongst their boys men who marched so fearlessly to the front and fought so well in the great cause of civilization and human liberty as lieutenant Briand and lieutenant Eeable, who both were awarded the Victoria Cross and who are electors in the county which I have the honour of representing here.
The province of Quebec was willing to do her duty and she did it. But it must not be lost sight of, Mr. Speaker, that voluntary enlistment was going very well and that, if it fell off, it was because of the orders given by the Prime Minister, in a letter sent to the former Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes), telling him that things were going too fast and that it was necessary to check voluntary enlistment which was going on too rapidly. And why were those orders given? Because,

even in those days, our hon. friends opposite were already planning the enactment of conscription, not in order to win the war, as stated by all the hon. gentlemen who have spoken before, but to win the elections and to remain in power.
Mr. Speaker, I take it that the motion which is now before us is an insult to the people of this country. Canada has played an effective and glorious part in the great struggle which is now over and it seems to me that, on the eve of the final peace treaty being signed, the Government should look at the whole matter with more generosity, and instead of enacting legislation providing for uniformity in the punishments inflicted on defaulters, they should bring down a general amnesty Act and grant to those young men a lasting and enduring peace. As I said in my remarks on the Address in answer to the Speech from the Throne those young .men for the most part acted in good faith, and more particularly the farmers and the sons of farmers who belived that it was in the interest of the country that they should remain steadily at work on their farms, striving patriotically to increase food production for our soldiers overseas. Besides, the Government realized it perfectly well,-even though they were actuated in so doing from political motives-when they passed an order in council, a short time before the elections, in order to exempt from military service the farmers and the sons of farmers. Therefore, those young men who did not comply with the law, who believed that they should rather remain on the farm in order to increase the production of foodstuffs are not altogether guilty, because they heeded the advice given them by the Government, and because the farmers of Ontario were told that they would not be called to the colours, owing to the desirability of increasing food production for helping our Allies. The hon. Minister of Public Works, in his remarks on the Address, stated that a year ago there was nothing which the civilized world needed so much as shipping; that shipping was more vital to winning the war than were men or shells, and the greatest cry of the allied armies was for ships, ships to carry American soldiers across the ocean and ships to carry food to the allied armies.
Therefore, Mir. Speaker, in my opinion, such a motion as the one presented this afternoon by the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Sir Sam Hughes) should be thrown out and all the members ought to protest against and vote down such a resolution. I take it, Sir, all the hon. members

who are actuated by patriotic feelings and desire to promote harmony and peace in the country, should clasp hands and ask the Government to pass forthwith an amnesty Act and put a stop to all vexatious proceedings against the young conscripts who, as I said, have acted in good faith. They have heeded the advice given them in high quarters. They gave heed to the advice and followed in the footsteps of the Unionist candidates who, during the last electoral campaign, throughout the length and breadth of the country, had told them that if they voted for the Union Government, the farmers would not be disturbed and would be free to remain on their farms to increase production, and so work for the triumph of the Allies.
A few days ago, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member from Beauce (Mr. Belaud) asked the Acting Prime Minister, the hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) whether it was the intention of the Government to provide during this session for the repeal or abrogation of the Military Service Act, as soon as demobilization is completed. All we could get from the hon. Prime Minister was a non-committal answer. I hope that this Act, upon the conclusion of peace, will be repealed. For my own part, when demobilization is completed, and after peace has been signed, should the Government deem it proper to repeal that Act, I shall ask-and I hope I shall find a seconder in this House-that that law be erased from our statute-books. The representatives of all the nations who are now sitting at the peace conference want conscription to be done away with in every country of the world, as the last was fought with a view to destroying militarism. We entered the war and fought against the Germans in order to uproot that pest of militarism which has been inflicted on Canada by the Conscription Act. It is of the utmost moment that conscription be done away with for ever, the more so as after the gigantic war which has just come to an end, we may have other wars, but in a distant future, and there is no reason why such a legislation should remain on our statute-books.
Before closing my remarks, Sir, I may add that I am strongly opposed to this resolution and that, were I called upon to vote, I should most heartily register my vote against it, the more so as it is not in the interest of the country that it is presented. Nowadays, in the press, in Parliament, all are bending their efforts towards promoting harmony, peace and concord among the various racial groups of Canada,
in the interest of the country, as our common aim. Why then should questions be submitted to the House which are not making for union and harmony, but rather for disunion. It is time we called a halt and put a stop to such a state of things. It is high time we realized that we are all Canadians, not citizens of the province of Quebec or Ontario, but first and last Canadians striving for the development of the country, so that peace and harmony may revive and be reborn in Canada, in the best interests of the country.
Mr. GEORGE B. NICHOLSON (Algoma East): The resolution submitted by the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) should appeal to the hon. members of this House and to our fellow-countrymen who feel that justice should be done. A more equitable means should be devised to punish defaulters under the Military Service Act and deserters from the Canadian army. But, having said that, it does not follow that because we want to see justice done and a uniform method of punishment devised, these defaulters are going to be given a clean bill of health and permitted to go about as citizens of Canada, which they are not and never were. I would follow the course outlined by the hon. Minister of Militia; I would take these men at their own valuation of themselves: they have by their acts said to their fellow-citizens that they do not want to take the responsibilities of citizenship in this country; therefore I would deprive them of the privileges of citizenship. That is the logical way in which to deal with them. After having listened to the hon. Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen), the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie), and the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie)-men who have had a wide and varied experience in the courts of this country-as a layman I can do nothing else but come to the conclusion that simply by bringing these defaulters and deserters before our magistrates we cannot get uniformity of justice-to say nothing of the experiences we have had in the past twelve or fifteen months in connection with the operation of the Military Service Act. The defaulter under the Military Service Act is in reality in identically the same position as the man who deserted at the front. He was in the class of men who were called upon to come forward and stand valiantly behind our soldiers, who were giving their very lives in defence of their country, and he refused or failed to do so. I have very little sympathy with the argument put forward that a large number of these men were misled, that their parents

or friends got them into a false position. I have had something to do with a very considerable number of these men. I have followed the course they have pursued up through the section of the country in which I live, and it required very little leading to get them to hi'de in the bush or. anywhere else that would save them from doing their duty as citizens of Canada. The way to deal with them-let me repeat it-is to take them at their own estimate of themselves and disfranchise them of the civil rights which they have failed to appreciate.
I would ask your permission, Sir, to refer very briefly to one or two things said by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon). First, with regard to the attitude of the Government towards the farmers. It is true that Government candidates in the election of 1917 said that in so far as it was possible exemption should be granted to men who were producing foodstuffs. It is also true that the Government, so far as I have been able to learn, consistently followed that policy. Exemptions were allowed to farmers in the class of men from 20 to 34 years of age called up under the Military Service Act. But when it was found that in various parts of this country there was an organized effort to defeat the Military Service Act, that tribunals and judges had determined that they were not going to permit it to be effective if they could help it, some other means had to be found to support our troops in France-who were at that time standing, figuratively speaking, with their very back to the wall -and one-fourth of the total number of men had the exemptions withdrawn from them, men from 20 to 22 years of age, but the exemptions to the farming community in this country from 22 to 34 years of age were continued as before. I make that statement, and it cannot be gainsaid.
There is one other matter referred to by the member for Dorehester, and it touched me to the very quick as a member of this House. He stated, Sir, that members on your right who had supported the Military Service Act, who had gone out and done their very best to secure reinforcements for our troops at the front, were actuated not by motives of loyalty to our men, but by a determination to win the election.

Hear, hear.
Mr. GEORGE B. NICHOLSON: Hon. members say, "Hear, hear."

Hear, hear.
Mr. GEORGE B. NICHOLSON: Not one
of those who sit there and say, "Hear, 
hear," Sir, has the record for service and sacrifice-

He was right.
Mr. GEORGE B. NICHOLSON: It does not lie in the mouth of the hon. member for Dorchester to make any such accusation. I hand back to him the miserable, cowardly slander that that is the motive which actuated hon. members on this side of the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The remark of the hon. gentleman is not parliamentary.
Mr. GEORGE B. NICHOLSON:	Mr. Speaker, I bow to your ruling. If my command of the English language is not sufficient to properly characterize my opinion of the hon. member for Dorchester in the House of 'Commons, I will tell it to his face outside, if he will let me.
When any member stands up in this House and says that men who have given the very last they have in the world to-win the war are actuated by any other motive than that of a desire to support the men at the front, he is making a statement that he cannot support and that he dare not make to the faces of those hon. gentlemen outside the House.

I had no intention of speaking on the subject of the resolution of the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes), but as I listened to the remarks of speakers on the other side I felt that in justice to myself I should say a word or two. I heartily approve of the resolution. Indeed, I would approve of a much stronger one,-one that would go further than any one has detailed here to-day. I was struck with the remark of the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) as to what Judge Langelier had done for the Bench. I should have been much more interested to learn what Judge Langelier had done in the way of soliciting the good offices of the people of his district to join the colours and go to the front. With the hon. member for Dorchester it was a case of drawing a red herring across the trail all throughout. The hon. gentleman spoke of the Quebec riots, which culminated in the burning of the military service records. These riots were witnessed by at least one member of Parliament who stood on the scene of action and did not offer a hand to stop it, to intervene, to interfere. The justification for my saying that he stood there is his own word in this House. It looked to me as if men in high positions in the province of Quebec, members of this House, were glad to see the

military service records burned. It was concomitant with the feeling that prevailed in the province against military service.
The proposal has been put forward here that slackers, as they are termed, should be disfranchised. What punishment is disfranchisement? A man who in the time of stress and trouble seeks the bush oi leaves the country should not be dealt with in any such way by the Parliament oi Canada. A man who would not fight for his country has no right to live in it; he should be deported, not disfranchised. He should be sent out of the country; he is a disgrace to himself and to the country in which he lives. The member for Victoria should make his resolution stronger; should make it provide that these men be sent out of the country. They are not fit to live in it, they know it themselves and the country knows it.

He has too good a
heart for that.

I fear so. The member for Temiscouata (Mr. Gauvreau) sometimes agrees with me and I with him. When the question was put about penalties in this House, there was too good a heart in the Minister of Justice (Hon. C. J. Doherty). I asked the minister when the military service penalties were being imposed not to put such a power in the hands of the magistrates; I asked him to make the minimum fine $200. But the heart of the Minister oi Justice was soft; he misjudged the people with whom he had to deal. He turned to me and said : "We do not wish t* fill the jails or to collect fines; we wish to fill the ranks of the army." Well, these men went to the bush and the army ranks were not. filled. The tender heart was there-I leave that with the hon. member to think about.
The member for Dorchester said that the people of this country were straining every nerve to win the war. What right has he to speak for the people of this country and the nerve they strained? What right have most members from the province of Quebec on the opposite side to stand on the floor of this House and boast of nerve being strained to win the war? Presumption unqualified ! Why, if you look at the campaign that was propagated you will find that it was not conscription against which Quebec fought; it was not conscription that caused evasion of the Military Service Act; it was a propaganda engendered and put up for an excuse -language; language was the reason; this argument of the member for Dorchester is
an afterthought. I remember seeing in the Ottawa papers an appeal by the Patriotic Fund Association of Ottawa asking certain churches in the city to urge their congregations to spend money for patriotic purposes, to contribute to patriotic funds. And I saw an article by five French clerics in this city which, in substance, said, no, we will do nothing of the sort; we will ask our people to raise money to be spent not to fight the battles of the country and of the Empire, but to fight the battle of language. The argument has been made that the people were easily misled. I do not know that they were so easily misled, but they were misled by appeals of that kind made by people who should have known better, by people who should have much better respected the liberty they enjoy than to issue such an appeal to their co-religionists.
The member for Dorchester speaks about straining nerve to fight the battles of the Empire. I just looked at the votes of the soldiers in a few of the counties in the province of Quebec in the last election. In Kamouraska it is officially reported that only fifteen votes of soldiers were reported out of a total vote of three thousand six hundred.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not wish unduly
to interrupt the hon. member. He has a right to reply to any argument made by the member for Dorchester, but I hope that he will bring his remarks more closely to bear upon the resolution before the House than he is doing at present.

I do not apprehend that Your Honour wishes to make a ruling until you have heard me a little further. I intend to apply these remarks directly to the resolution under discussion. I submit that I am entitled, in view of the rules of the House and of the course which the debate has taken, to show where the large body of slackers are likely to be found, and to show it by an argument based upon the fact that they did not go to the front. That deals with the question of uniformity and punishment. I wish, therefore, to proceed with the argument; but if Your Honour feels that I may not do so, I shall submit to your ruling. In the county of Joliette, 3 soldiers' votes were polled out of a total vote of 4,500.
Will the hon. member permit me to make an explanation?	*

No, thank you, not at
this stage. There will be lots of time for explanations; I do not wish to be interrupted in the midst of a very interesting table

of figures. In Dorchester 15 soldiers' votes were polled out of a total vote of 4,700; in Bagot 19 soldiers' votes out of a total of 3,400; in Berthier, 8 out of a total of 3,800. In the German county of North Waterloo, Ontario, 659 soldiers' votes were polled out of a total of 9,000. If in North Waterloo the soldiers' votes had been cast in the same proportion as they were in Dorchester, there would have been only 30 out of the 9,000. But in this riding, which is eighty-five or ninety per cent German, the soldiers polled 659 votes in favour of fighting against the old German Fatherland. I put that against all these ridings in the province of Quebec. I will leave it to the country to say whether there is anything fair in a man getting up on tjhe other side of the House and saying that the people of the province of Quebec have strained every nerve to win the war.
How many French-Canadians were sent to be slaughtered?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
My hon. friend i3 insulting our whole race.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The rule is very distinct and clear that an hon. member having the floor may not be interrupted except on a point of order or to ask a question with his consent. The hon. member who has the floor has declined to answer questions, and except a point of order be raised I must ask that he be not interrupted.
He should not be allowed to proceed as he is doing.
Take your medicine.
You mix it yourself.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I asked the hon. member who has the floor to bring his remarks more closely to the subject under discussion, and he assured me that he purposed making an application of his remarks. I must therefore give him an opportunity to make good his endeavours.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

Shame!
Mr. MORPHY I do not wonder at hon. gentlemen opposite getting excited and crying "Shame." I turn and say to them: Clean your own doorstep, and take your own shame, because it is there the shame lies, and you deserve it. I regret that this debate has been precipitated, but in common with many members on your right, Mr. Speaker, I deeply resent and always will resent such taunts as were thrown across the floor of this House this afternoon by the hon. member for Dorchester, whose county has the magnificent record, apparently, of having sent fifteen soldiers to the front, in spite of his " straining every nerve to win the war." Why, county after county in rural Ontario has sent 600, 700, 900 and 1,000 men. The mark stands out strong upon Quebec, and it will stand there until Quebec redeems herself and becomes regenerated, and takes a humble position in the councils of this country.

Will my hon.
friend tell me the number of soldiers who voted in Chambly and Vercheres?

The hon. member has
that information at his own hand. He has the right to get up on the floor of the House and say what he thinks, and I do not think it is necessary for me to do any menial work for him.

When I came to this House this afternoon my intention was not to take part in this debate, but to discuss the simple and gentle subject of titles in Canada, but as I am not going to have an opportunity of discussing that subject I propose to add a few words to the discussion that has taken place. Coming from the city of Kingston I cannot sit in my seat and allow such statements 4s were made here this afternoon by the hon. member for Dorchester to go unchallenged. I might say that I sent a message across the floor of this House by one of the pages to a Whip on the other side asking him to advise the hon. member for Dorchester that I proposed to say a few things about him, and that I would prefer he should be in his seat rather than absent when my remarks were being made. But no doubt the hon. member proceeds on the assumption

that " He who fights and runs away will live to fight another day," and has decided not to come back to this Chamber.
The hon. member for Dorchester says he is against conscription. I quite agree that he is against conscription; against not only military conscription but industrial conscription as well. He not only is against conscription, but he is and has been against the war since its very inception.
I will not ask you, Sir, to take my words for this, but I propose to read to the House a few extracts from the speeches made by the hon. member for Dorchester when he ran in a by-election in his county in the year 1917.

I rise to a point of order. I understood your Honour to rule, when the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) was speaking, that he was not to discuss this question of service or no service as it was not to the point.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: My ruling was with respect to a discussion of the question of conscription. I take it that the hon. member for Kingston desires to reply to the hon. member for Dorchester, who quoted certain statements made during the election in the county of Victoria. I think it would not be competent for me at this stage to pronounce the hon. member out of order, but if at a later stage the point of order is again raised I shall then be in a better position to judge.

I would not think of discussing conscription in the abstract. What I am endeavouring to prove is that the hon. member for Dorchester is just exactly what he said he was-against conscription *-and the way to prove the consistency of a man's action is certainly to compare his conduct of to-day with his conduct and speeches of some time ago. What better standard is there by which to judge a man?

I rise to a point of order. My point is that the hon. member for Dorchester had no business to go beyond this resolution, and simply because he was permitted to go beyond the terms of the resolution, it is not permissible for some other hon. member to go beyond the resolution to reply to him. I know of no rule by which that can be done.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member has raised a point of order. I was not in the chamber during the greater portion of the speech of the hon. member for Dorchester, but while in the Chair I allowed him to read an extract from the election address of the
hon. member for Victoria. The hon. member for Kingston has a right to reply to the speech of the hon. member for Dorchester, and I shall be in the judgment of the House in ruling when he has gone beyond the proper bounds in making reply.
May I rise to a question of privilege or a point of order? I was not charged with writing the telegrams of ministers.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is not a point of order.
It is a correction.

At the time the leader of the Opposition rose to his feet I was about to draw the attention of the House to certain remarks made in the election of 1917 by the hon. member for Dorchester, but if the House will pardon me for a moment I will step aside from the original argument as intended and draw the attention of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) to the fact that while I understood he was only a temporary leader of the Liberal party, I had no idea that his leadership was of such a temporary character that he could not keep his followers in the House in order for one afternoon. If the hon. the leader of the Opposition is correct in his contention that the hon. member for Dorchester was out of order in what he said, then, Sir, I would suggest with all deference that the leader of the Opposition should have risen in his place and called your attention to the fact that one of his followers-one of his new followers-was out of order in making the attack he made a few moments ago. Consistency is a virtue even in politics. I shall quote only a few extracts from the speeches made by the hon. member for Dorchester in 1917. One of his statements, as quoted in the Montreal Gazette, was:-
Are we to ruin our country from the point of view of men of wealth and everything else for England? I say, no, without hesitation.
He was more than a anti-conscriptionist there. He was against the war because he failed to realize that it was Canada's war just as much as it was England's. Again, in another address he delivered in his riding, he said:
I signed my card,-
This was in reference to registration.
-hut I say that I am opposed to conscription, whether industrial or military. If this national service means what it did in England I am ready to fight with all possible means against it.
13.38

He therefore established by these two speeches his opposition to the organization of this country for the prosecution of the war to a satisfactory and victorious conclusion. I only quote these remarks to show that the hon. member for Dorchester was consistent this afternoon, at least in this respect, that he was and always h^s been against conscription. But I want to go further than that and to direct the attention of of the House and of yourself, Sir, to the fact that in a letter that the hon. member for Beauce i(Mr. Beland) wrote, or was alleged to have written, to his sister when he was a prisoner in Germany, he stated that the speeches of the hon. member for Dorchester were reported at great length in the German papers and were there used to demonstrate the supposed fact that Canada was growing weary of the war- weary at a time when it was essential that the strength of the Allies should be kept at'its highest point. If what I say is not correct, I would ask the hon. member for Beauce to rise in his place and say so, and I will willingly retract. But if the statements I have made are correct, I think it is beneath the dignity of the hon. members who are taunted for their support of conscription to sit silent in this House and allow vociferous utterances and honeyed phrases to lead us aside from a discussion so momentous as that which has taken place this afternoon. The member for Dorchester says he wants justice. I say, let him thank God that he has not got justice; because if he received justice for those men that failed to do their duty and failed to realize what the responsibilities of citizenship meant, men in his county and throughout this country who failed to realize the wonderful opportunity that they had, would be punished, not with a fine or trifling imprisonment, nor by the deprivation of citizenship, but punished on the principle that there should be " an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth," and 4hat they should give their lives but not as those heroes did who went to the front to take the place of the men who defaulted in the time of their country's need. The hon. member for Dorchester held this Government up to contempt because he says in 1917 one promise was made to the country whereas a different policy was pursued in 1918. Suppose one policy was followed in 1917 and another in 1918. Are we blind to conditions and to facts? Have we no remembrance of the awful days we went through between the autumn of 1917

and the early spring of 1918? Do hon. members forget that in the autumn oi 1917 we hoped that the war would soon be over, but in the spring of 1918-I think on the 21st of March-there was foreboding in the House when we realized that the line of the Allies was as thin as a thread and that all that stood between the enemy-and civilization was that thin, khaki-coloured line that stretched from the sea to the bounds of Switzerland? Do hon. members forget these things? The hon. member attempts to hold this Government responsible, because, stirred by a stern sense of duty, they may have changed their policy. He says the Minister of Militia should be pilloried and held up to public contempt, and the Minister of Agriculture treated similarly. Why? Simply because, imbued with a true sense of national necessity, they may have abandoned positions they originally held to be tenable, and, in the face of a great danger, realized that everything should be subordinated to the great necessity that existed, and that the national effort should be centred on securing reinforcements to hold a line that was fast growing thin through the wastage of casualties. Are we on this side of the House-perhaps affected by a call that other men did not hear-to sit silent and not reply to taunts and criticisms such as have been levelled against us? Am I, coming from a riding that has giv n approximately 2,000 men to the service of the state in this great war, to stand by and be taunted with charges of inconsistency and an insinuation that my conduct was actuated by a desire to win an election?

taunted by a man who received only some 15 soldier votes in the last election? It is the height of inconsistency to ask those who have sacrificed much to stand by and listen without complaint to insults such as this. We used conscription to win elections? I remember in the late summer of 1917 when I left the House of Commons after the vote on the Military Service Act had been taken, an hon. member said to me: "Niekle, you and I have put a knife to our throats to-day because we will never be able to carry conscription in our ridings;" and I said to him, as I say to-day, that if we had put a knife to our throats and had gone down to defeat and eternal political oblivion, a thousand times would that have been better than that we should have been traitors to the men who cheerfully went, to save our	cause, if	need be,	to death.
We endeavoured to use conscription to win elections? Sir, nothing was further

from our thoughts. We used it not to win elections, but to endeavour to win the liberties of the world. Democracy? Democracy is all right in its way, and there is no more thorough-going democrat in this House than the member for Kingston; but the member for Kingston realizes that there are two aspects of democracy-that of privilege and that of duty; and if this country was good enough as a place to live in it was good enough to fight for and to die for, if necessary. I do not wonder that the member for Algoma East (Mr. Nicholson) was apparently in some heat this afternoon, for I can understand the frame of mind of a man who gave his only son for the great cause, when language such as was used by the member for Dorchester is hurled across the floor of the House. Used conscription as a means to win elections? The life blood of his son in one scale and the election in the other. Which should win? The member for Algoma East paid the supreme sacrifice; he gave to the country his only son in whom his ambitions were centred in the conviction that he was making some contribution to the great cause. Yet the leader of the Opposition says that now it is all over we should forget. Forget what? The sacrifices that were made? The member for Dorchester says he was always against conscription. I was against conscription in the early days of the war, and I never faltered in my faith that this country would respond, until I used every effort that the mind of man could devise to bring to our colours those who were defaulting, but when I realized that national necessity demanded that extreme measures should be taken I was just as enthusiastic for conscription as I was at first against it. The leader of the Opposition says we should forget. Am I to forget the homes from which were taken sons that never will come back? Am I to forget the homes in which weeping women to-day are mourning the loss of loved ones? Am I to forget that while I advocated conscription I also advocated a fair and just determination on the part of the Government to see that all those should go who ought to go and that some of those who went from my riding went to take the place of others that should have gone but did not? Am I to forget that the people of my riding made sacrifices that were necessary because of men who failed to do their duty?
The hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) says Clemenceau, the Tiger oi France, was generous in his forgiveness. True, he was generous in his forgiveness; but the argument is not on all-fours, because between Clemenceau and the assassin it was in part an individual relationship. If Clemenceau is prepared to forgive a crazed assassin, that is for Clemenceau and France to decide. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) says that free speech exists in England, that England is tolerant of those who care to speak and that therefore we should be tolerant of those who did not obey the law. That is not on all-fours with the principle that has been enunciated this afternoon. We pass a substantive law declaring that each man who is of age and has the physical capacity should go to the front and do his duty. I cannot imagine anything more unfortunate in this country than that we should have the principle of substantive law ignored. I cannot think oi anything more unfortunate than that the view should prevail among the young men of this country that in a time of national peril, when Parliament asembled determines that men must go, that we must have conscription, and when the nation, in an election, ratifies that principle, this law should be disobeyed and that these young men should be permitted to say:	Forget out
ignoring of the law and allow us to go free, because we found that compliance with it was not at all palatable to us.
There is not one bit of revenge in my nature. No one would be more willing to drop the whole thing if it were merely a question of the breaking of an obligation betwen one individual and another. But that is not the question to-day. It is a question of justice to the men who went; it is a question of justice to the homes that are sad to-day because men went and others did not go.
Democracy demands that privileges and duties are to be recognized together, and as a true democrat I say that those who are not prepared to fight for their country should certainly not have an opportunity of participating in the national life through the franchise, which really is the exercise oi kingship.

I am sure that my hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Nickle) would not desire to misrepresent me in a matter of fact. He said that I pleaded that we should be tolerant with those who disobeyed the law. I twice said something the very opposite of that. I am sorry, even at this stage, to disagree with my hon. friend in any point; that was the only flaw in a very able speech, but it is a flaw to put into one's mouth what one did not say.

subtopic: THE LATE DR. THOMAS BARNARD FLINT.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: THE LATE DR. THOMAS BARNARD FLINT.
speechtext:
Before the Orders of the Day are called, I feel it my duty to make appreciative reference to a former and much respected official of the House of Commons of whose death we learned yesterday. I refer to the late Dr. Thomas Barnard Flint, who for a period of nearly sixteen years occupied the important position of Clerk of the House.
The late Dr. Flint was a man of wide culture and scholarly attainment. In his youth he won high academic distinction in the educational institutions of his native province and at Harvard University, from which he graduated. Becoming afterwards a barrister, he occupied a number of important public positions in Nova Scotia.
Subsequently, in 1891, he was elected to the House of Commons, of which he remained a member until 1902. During that period he was chief whip of the Liberal party for the Maritime Provinces and occupied also the position of Chairman of the Committee on Standing Orders. He became Clerk of this (House in 1902, retiring owing to ill-health early in 1918. He was a man profoundly versed in constitutional law and in the rules and practice of parliamentary procedure. A notable contribution to the latter branch of knowledge was his third edition of Bourinot's Practice and Procedure, which has been of great value to the members of the House.
We of the present House who were members during the time that he occupied the position of Clerk will always remember him as a most courteous, obliging and affable official, always ready to assist in any way within his power, and an official of high efficiency and capability in the important position which he occupied.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: THE LATE DR. THOMAS BARNARD FLINT.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I join with the leader of the Government in what he has said about our departed friend, Dr. Flint. There is in the House to-day hardly any person who was here when Dr. Flint first became a member of Parliament. So rapid are the changes in the public life of this country and in the personnel of the House of Commons that it is surprising how quickly the Parliament of twenty years ago disappears and new men fill the seats in this House. Ever since I came here until a short time ago, when Dr. Flint left the chair, that distinguished official was the Clerk of the House of Commons. This is an office of great responsibility, requiring many excellencies of head and heart, and I think all of us who came into contact with Dr. Flint while he occupied' that high office, must concur in what has been said by the leader of the Government, namely, that he was a splendid official, a man who brought education, patience, and' affability to the discharge of the various duties devolving upon him as Clerk of this House. We regret his demise, and he will be missed by his wide circle of friends, and although he had left the position of Clerk of the IHouse, we had all hopes, as he himself had, that we would have an opportunity of coming in touch with him and that for many years he would be in companionship with his old friends. His departure was more sudden than we looked for, but after all it is perhaps the best way to get out of this world and to avoid lingering illness. On behalf of the Opposition, I join in what has been said so well by the leader of the Government,

For instance, question No. 2 on the Order Paper is a simple matter, but it seems to have been standing for nearly a month. The other matter which is more serious and concerning which I should perhaps have given notice to the Acting Prime Minister, but I did not have the opportunity to do so, is that measures which have been forecasted in the speech from the Throne, should, as soon as is convenient to the Government, be brought down so that all members may know what the programme is going to be. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Government will be glad to take into consideration the representations of the leader of the Opposition with reference to legislation to be introduced into the House.
The Order Paper contains a very substantial body of legislation. I do not recall any session of Parliament at which so much legislation has been ready for the attention of the House as at the present one, which in that respect is an exception. We have a considerable amount of additional legislation prepared which is not yet on the Order Paper for the reason that it is desirable that the Order Paper should be further cleared up before this legislation is brought down. At all events the House is certainly not awaiting any action on the part of the Government so far as legislation is concerned.
With regard to questions, I sympathize with my hon. friend's point of view. I observed that many questions which had been standing for some time had not been answered, and I have taken some pains to ascertain from the various departments why answers have not been submitted at an earlier date, it may be owing to the war or to the greater range of government activity.

But I find that many questions that are asked should really stand as orders for returns for the reason that it is quite impossible to answer them within a reasonable time. In connection with many of these questions the Secretary of State (Mr. Burrell) is obliged to communicate with all the departments, and it takes considerable time to get those returns in order that he may make answer to the House. My hon. friend has called attention to question No. 2 -" What was the total expenditure of every kind, made by or on behalf of the Fuel Control Board of Canada, from its inception to the end of 1918?" That seems a very simple question, but nevertheless, when it is taken into account that there may be many expenditures which have not yet gone through the books of the Department of Finance, it is difficult to answer such a question without delay. I repeat that there are many questions on the Order Paper which really should be made orders for returns. We have hesitated to ask that they stand as orders for return because our desire has been, if possible, to bring down information to the House in answer to the questions. I assure my hon. friend that I have given the matter personal attention and it is the desire of the Government to have the answers submitted to the House just as promptly as possible, consistent, of course, with our giving accurate answers. In addition to what I have stated, I may say that we shall endeavour to give answers to questions just as quickly as we possibly can, and of that I can assure my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This resolution precedes a Bill which will appropriate the sum of $350,000,000 to meet expenditures connected with the war and the demobilization of our forces, and outlays for other purposes arising out of the war. The Bill will also provide for the necessary borrowing powers to raise the sum in question, or such part of it as may be necessary. It has occurred to me, and I put it forward as a suggestion to the Committee, that as I -shall lay before the Committee to-day certain summaries dealing with all our expen-

ditures for war purposes since the beginning of the war, and an estimate, somewhat in detail, of our expenditures during the coming fiscal year so far as we can forecast them, it might better serve the purposes of intelligent discussion of the subject if I placed the figures upon Hansard so that the Committee may be able more fully to discuss them when in Committee stage on the second reading of the Bill. I put that forward as a suggestion now for the Committee to concur in or not as it may deem advisable. My reason for doing so is that the figures which I shall give are necessarily complicated and will be difficult for hon. members to follow. Having them on Hansard, where they may be studied for .a few days, it would seem to me that the Committee would be in a better position when in the Committee stage on the Bill to discuss them. I do not desire to be understood as in any way wishing to limit such discussion as the members of the Committee may desire to-day upon the subject.
I believe that last year the debate took place in the Committee stage of the Bill. That was done by consent between the 'Government and the Opposition through their respective leaders and I believe it was concurred in as the most convenient method of dealing with the subject. Needless to say, in the Committee stage upon the Bill, if the course I suggest is concurred in, the fullest freedom will be given for discussion; in fact, such freedom, I think is amply provided for by the Rules of the House when in Committee.

What is proposed by the minister is perfectly satisfactory to us and I think it will assist the minister in
getting the figures on Hansard consecutively so that they will be more useful to us than if they were broken in upon by any remarks from this side of the House.

speechtext: The six shillings per day per man was to cover all the services that I have mentioned in respect to the Canadian forces at the front. That arrangement held good up to September 1, 1917, when it became apparent that this war was* different from all previous wars in respect of the immense amount of heavy gun ammunition required. The House, of course, will recall the battles of the Somme, and the scale of artillery fire in all engagements during the latter years of the war. After the agreement had been acted on foi some time, it was found that the expenditure of ammunition for small arms and other guns and for air service was so greatly in excess of the figures upon which the charge was based, that it was suggested by the Imperial Government that the six shillings should be increased to nine shillings and four pence. It has been found since that even the nine shillings and four pence may not be adequate to take care of the heavy charges for ammunition, and the present position is this: That there is something in the nature of an arbitration proceeding between the Imperial Government and the Canadian Government, and, I understand, the other Overseas Dominions as to what that per capita charge per day should be. In this connection the Auditor General, Major Sutherland, has left for London, and together with a firm of chartered accountants will represent this Government in the inquiry which is being had as to the proper charges for expenditure for ammunition.

The ordinary commercial and financial methods, by reason of the machinery of international credits and exchange having been thrown out of gear by the war, are no longer effectual for the purpose of enabling us to carry on our international trade.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: How does this system operate in practice?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
It operates in this way in practice. In the period before the war Canadian wheat, flour and other foodstuffs, and manufactured products that were sold abroad were sold in the ordinary way. That is to say, a bill of exchange would be drawn upon the consignee abroad to which would be attached the bill of lading and other securities, and the seller in Canada would hand the bill of exchange witn the other documents to his bank. The bank might either send those forward to London and sell them there or sell them in New York, which is the exchange centre for this continent. No question of governmental assistance arose at all, because the bills were taken in hand by financial institutions and were ordinarily sold in New York, and by draft on New York, money was brought to Canada.
Owing to the breakdown in international exchange between Europe and America there has for the last two years not been a free exchange market in New York, although there has appeared to be one. The fact is that for the last two years or more and until very recently the Imperial Government has been obliged to provide for the maintenance of sterling exchange on an artificial basis. It was " pegged," to use an expressive financial term, at $4.76, but it was not generally realized in Canada, and I do not think it is to-day, that bills oi exchange drawn by Canadians in respect of goods sent abroad and sold in New York were not really sold upon a free market in the old sense. Very large sums of money, as large as $1,000,000,000 in 1916, had to be provided, in dollar credits in New York by the Imperial Government for the purpose ' of holding up sterling exchange to $4.76. That was one of the reasons why restrictions upon imports were imposed by Great Britain and by continental Europe, because not only was there scarcity of shipping, but it was an object to them to diminish to as great a degree as possible the amount of money which they had to provide on this side for the purpose of holding up sterling exchange. Consequently, during the last two years of the war, practically all buying on'behalf of Great Britain and her European Allies was done through an International Commission. For instance, the Wheat Export Company, which is the buying agency of the Imperial Government in Canada, was the sole purchaser of wheat and flour. I use that just as an example. It was not open to firms dealing in grain
to sell their grain as in the period before the war, draw bills of exchange in respect of it and negotiate them with their banks. In other words, the exchange situation, although on account of its being a complicated matter, this is not generally realized by the public, had much to do with the restrictions placed upon imports by Great Britain and other European countries. The idea was to limit imports to Europe to necessaries, because money had to be provided in New York to keep sterling exchange up to $4.76. Many of those restrictions still remain. What I have said remains good with regard to wheat and flour to-day. Until recently it was true with regard to bacon which now has a free market. It is true to-day with regard to beef. Great Britain, although in command of almost unlimited resources in sterling in Great Britain, cannot pay in sterling for her purchases on this side of the water; she must pay in dollars either in the United States or in Canada. On account of the exchange situation being as it has been for the past two years, Great Britain has not been able to furnish dollar credits on this side of the water as she was in normal times. As a result Great Britain would not have been able to make purchases in America unless she could obtain dollar credits either by borrowing in the money market in the United States or from the American Government or from the Dominion Government here. As far as our producers, both farmers and manufacturers, are concerned, they do not know and I suppose they do not particularly care where the money comes from as long as they receive it in the usual way.
But it can only be provided for purchases of our foodstuffs and our manufactured goods and other exports-I will not say all, but a great volume of them -by provision of credits in Canada for Great Britain and the other governments. It is of the greatest importance to Canada to participate to the utmost in export trade. We have incurred a very heavy indebtedness during the war and that indebtedness can only be met as to interest and sinking fund, with a view to gradual liquidation, by Canada playing an increasingly important part in exports of agricultural and manufactured goods.
A nation is very much like an individual. An individual can pay off his indebtedness only if he produces more than he consumes, and the same. holds true with regard to a nation. The nation can only reduce its national indebtedness and meet the interest obligation upon its debt re-

maining from time to time by producing more than it consumes, and its excess production must be sold abroad. I hope I am not wearying the committee, but the question has been asked me.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: I understand from the minister that we are providing credits for Great Britain, and therefore we have a contra-account to file when the final settlement is made. Has my hon. friend any idea of that account?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
According to our books to date, and not taking into account that extra charge which we shall have to pay for ammunition, the indebtedness of Great Britain to Canada is about $200,000,000. Let me explain to the committee how this has worked out in practice. We had our Canadian Expeditionary Force overseas in Great Britain and the Continent and borrowed from Great Britain, in monthly amounts, such sums as we required to pay our expenditures in Great Britain and to pay Great Britain the maintenance charges of our troops in France. On the other hand, Great Britain was expending in Canada for herself and her Allies immense sums for the purchase of wheat, flour, and other foodstuffs, airplanes and munitions, and almost since the first year of the war Canada has been advancing to her the money which she required here for those purposes. Those advances are consequently a set-off to the advances which were made by Great Britain to us in London; but in addition, as I said a moment ago, there is a balance of $200,000,000 in favour of Canada. To what extent that $200,000,000 will be reduced by the added charge which will have to be paid in respect of the expenditure of unexpectedly large amounts of ammunitior in France and Belgium since Septembei 1, 1917, I cannot say, and until we know that we are not in a position to state wit! any degree of accuracy what the amount is that is owed to Canada by Great Britain. Now I have been speaking of what is owed to the Canadian Government by Great Britain, but in addition, the Committee may know that the banks of Canada have also substantially helped the Imperial Government by making advances for the purpose of purchasing grain and other Canadian products during the past three years. That money was borrowed by the Imperial Government from the banks, maturing in a year from the date of the advances, and it has been renewed from time to time during the war. In that con-

nection I would point out an important feature, namely, that it will be a very great advantage to Canada after the war to have an indebtedness from Europe to the Government and to our banks. It will be an important factor in our exchange situation, because when sterling exchange becomes normal again we shall be able to collect that money by drawing on London, and that will tend to strengthen and stabilize our own exchange.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Have we any account with France or Italy?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friend has raised that question because it is evident I am not wearying the Committee. When the war came to an end we realized that the world was going to be confronted with a very serious industrial and commercial situation. On account of the restrictions upon imports to the European countries and the gen'eral demoralization in Europe caused by the war, we thought it highly desirable to offer credits not only to Great Britain but to other European countries as well, to finance purchases which they might make in the Dominion. As soon as the armistice occurred we at once brought the matter to the attention of the French Government. Negotiations have been had because we should have been very glad indeed to make very substantial advances by way of credits in Canada to our great Ally, France. So far the French Government 'has not felt that it required Canadian credits, but the offer remains open and the matter is still under negotiation in Paris. I cabled Mr. Lloyd Harris and the Prime Minister weeks, in fact, months ago, that we should be very pleased to create a substantial credit for France amounting to $25,000,000 or $50,000,000 or whatever sum she required. Then we felt that Belgium would need to make substantial purchases on this continent, and we entered into negotiations with that country with the result that a credit of $25,000,000 has been arranged for under agreement for the purpose of enabling the Belgian Government to purchase goods and products in Canada. An agreement was also entered into with the Rumanian Government for a credit of $25,000,000.
\Mr. CAHILL: Order in Council?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
It is under the authority of an Order in Council. There is also a $25,000,000 credit to Greece. I may say that we considered very carefully with the British Government and the Imperial

Treasury the question of security and the desirability of making the advances in question, and we are satisfied that we will be justified in making them.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Are these credits earmarked for certain classes of goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
They are not
marked for specific goods, but the position is this: Wheat and flour are being bought by Britain and we are furnishing credits for them. We also provide credits to Great Britain for the purchase of beef, and with regard to the European countries-I am speaking only from memory-one-fifth will be for agricultural products, one-fifth for raw material, and three-fifths for manufactured products. That is, what they require to purchase in Canada they will purchase that through the Canadian Trade Mission, or through missions of their own, or through firms or companies they may employ for that purpose.
