subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: If the purchasing is done through the Canadian Trade Commission here, they are in close touch with all the manufacturers of the goods in question. They have connected with them representatives of the various sections of Canadian manufacturers and agricultural producers and the object is to give every one an opportunity to tender. I can show that to my hon. friend very clearly from the correspondence.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: I understand that our representative, Mr. Lloyd Harris and his associates in Europe at the present time, have been commissioned by the Government to look after business for the Canadian manufacturers. I understand, also there is an independent agent looking after these orders in Europe and distributing them in Canada at the present time. I think the name of the gentleman is Mr. Yapp.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Whom does he represent?

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
I fancy he is representing the woollen industry and he is obtaining orders in Europe at the present time. He is negotiating with the woollen manufacturers regarding the distribution of these orders. I understand too that the woollen manufacturers were called together in Toronto not long ago and, together with one of the managers or leading men of the Trade Commission, they distributed these orders.
These orders were distributed with the understanding that they would be confirmed subsequently by the Government. The question I wish to ask is: Have these orders been confirmed by the Government and, if so, how? Have they been confirmed by Order in Council?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: I am sure they have not been confirmed by Order in Council. The Canadian Trade Mission in England have been promoting and obtaining on the continent, trade for Canada, and we have strongly urged upon the manufacturers and agricultural producers of Canada to send representatives over there and not leave the matter entirely to the Government, but to make use of the facilities we have afforded through the Mission in England, and push their business. The Dominion Government are in privity with governments only, the Governments of Great Britain, Belgium, Rumania and Greece, and, if we extend credit to France, the Government of France. The Belgian Government will, let us say, send a commission out here or act through some established company or firm for the purchase of goods in Canada. That is for them to determine. They say to the Dominion Government. If wa purchase $25,000,000 in Canada, will you lend us the money? We say: Yes, we will lend you the money. On account of the conditions existing in Europe, it is not possible for the transaction to be carried out in the usual way as it would be before the war. In other words, Canada cannot get the business unless we furnish the credit. I am not familiar with the transaction to which my hon. friend (Mr. Pedlow) refers, but if a representative of the woollen manufacturers of Canada obtained an order from a foreign Government, let us say the Rumanian Government, they would come quite within what we have in view. It would be proper for the Rumanian Government to place that order as they might think best either through a commission of their own or ask the Canadian Trade Commission in Ottawa to place the order for them. In placing orders our commission have to consider the .several manufacturers. They have their specifications and they have to purchase to the best advantage and up to the standard required by the Rumanian Government. The price must be fair and reasonable and the purchase would be financed by an advance made to the Rumanian Government through our banks here and through which payment would be made for the goods supplied.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: What function does Mr. Lloyd Harris perform in regard1 to contracts .of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: It would be Mr. Lloyd 'Harris' duty to assist the representatives of the Canadian producers in obtaining business in Great Britain or on the continent. Some of the business might be obtained without any Government credit at all. It might be Mr. Lloyd Harris' duty to enter into negotiations with foreign governments and I have no doubt that in that he would be assisted by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) for the purpose of offering them credit for the purchase of goods in Canada. While this business is of unusual character-

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Very much so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: -that is in peace times-'it is precisely what has been carried on during the war. In order to obtain a market for the goods and commodities which we have to sell we had to furnish credit to Ithe Imperial Government here. In order that the House may realize the extent to which we have made advances during the war, and which advances, as I explained, are much more than a set off to the advances made by Great Britain to us for the maintenance and upkeep of our troops in Great Britain and on the continent, I should like to place upon Hansard some figures showing how these credits we have furnished to Great Britain have been expended in Canada.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Do I understand that the Government is pledging the credit of Canada in order that specific and particular manufacturers should do business outside of this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
I would not put it in that way. The Dominion Government is extending credit to foreign governments in order that the export trade of this country may be promoted and increased. I would be very apprehensive of what would happen in Canada in the period succeeding the war unless the Government had the courage and resource to furnish credit for the purchase of our agricultural and manufactured products. I believe-and I am prepared to argue this at any time-that we occupy the best position with the sole exception of the United States, and I do not know that I should even make that exception, of any of the belligerents vdio have been in this war. I believe this is due not only to the great natural resources and productiveness of Canada but to the fact that

the Government has taken the necessary measures to provide for the continuance and expansion of our export trade.
Mr. JACOB'S:	In other words, we can
compete against the world?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
We can compete against the world provided our people have the financial facilities. Supposing the Dominion Government had said:	No money
for credit in Canada. What would have happened? Our wheat, flour, beef, manufactured goods, cheese, and salmon could not be sold abroad, and the export business of this country would practically come to a standstill.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Would you restrict the exportation of butter just now5

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend
knows that raises a very important question. If the Dominion Government at the close of the war deliberatly took the position, "No more credits for export trade," I would not want to be Minister of Finance in this country.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: I would ask the minister, do we not, in the event of .Rumania not paying, have to assume the obligation: It certainly would not be the manufacturer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: I do not contemplate the possibility of Rumania not paying

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: When you give credit you must do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: If I contemplated that possibility I would not give the credit. We have made inquiry into this matter, and we are satisfied that if we advance the money for the purpose of purchasing here that Rumania will observe her international obligations.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Is it within the knowledge of. the minister that a large number oi trading companies have been formed in the United States to do this very class of business without any assistance from the United States Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
Yes, we advanced that amount for Great Britain for cheese. Then, as I have shown, we made advances for the purchase of all the salmon pack of British Columbia, We also made enormous advances to the Munitions Board, not only for munitions, but for the carrying out of their large shipbuilding and airplane programme throughout Canada. Then we made advances for the purchase of other foodstuffs, and coming down to the present time, I am now arranging an advance for the purchase of the exportable surplus of our wheat and flour. Now my hon. friend saya those advances were made to Great Britain, and so they were, but if Canada is going to engage in international trade, it will have to do what they -are doing in the United States, although, of course, on a smaller scale, which will be to grant credits to other countries for the purchase of goods in Canada.
My hon. friend has asked whether the credit is especially for the manufacturers. It is not only for farmers for their wheat and foodstuffs, but for the manufacturers of food products and of all kinds of goods. If we had all these factories standing idle in Canada to-day by reason of the lack of provision for the credits, what about the question of providing work for dependent people? It is not only a question of manufacturers getting orders, but of their being able to keep their staffs employed and preventing unemployment in this country.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
Might I point out to the
minister that the agricultural commodities

are going to Great Britain, whereas we can only hope to sell the manufactured goods to Rumania, Serbia, iCzecho-Slovakia, and the other new countries that are now being created at the Paris Conference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
Let us assume
that is so. Heie Canada confronts one of the most critical periods in the history of the world, and in her history also. The Government had two courses open to it. One is to say: "Now the war is at an end and we will furnish credits only for the financing of our foodstuffs; we will not furnish any credits for manufacturers at all". The one thing that a country should' guard against, especially at the close of a war and a long war such as this, is unemployment. We do not want unemployment iii this country. We want the factories to be engaged, and the workpeople to be at work; and there would have been a very different story told in Canada to-day if the Government had not taken the measures which it. has taken to maintain the factories in operation and obtain business. I have already said that I believe we are in one of the best positions in the world by reason of the course which the Government has adopted. I think it is perfectly clear that Canada, like the United States, must provide credits to foreign governments for the purchase of commodities in this country, if we are to s-ell to them, for a more or less indefinite period until exchange between Europe and the United States becomes far more normal than it is to-day.	.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Irrespective of guarantees? The point I make is that we are pledging the credit of this country to countries which, to say the least, are not in a very good financial position at the present moment. If Canada is to cast about looking for trade, is it advisable that she should deal with those countries that have been overrun for the last four or five years which are practically on the brink of bankruptcy and threatened on all sides by Bolshevism and everything that implies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: I do not expect that this world is going to continue practically in a state of war. It is my hope and belief that an enduring peace is going to be brought about during the next few weeks. If it is not I should almost despair of the future. The five great Powers that won this war, will, one of these days, sign a treaty of peace., and when that treaty of peace is signed I do not think that the conditions which prevail in Europe to-day will continue.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Will those conditions continue here? Will unemployment continue here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: I desire to say to my hon. friend what I said before. If he will look up the records of all the countries in the world that have been in this war, he will find that Canada is to-day in the best position with regard to labour, employment and prosperity.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: That being so, why should we want to look' for trade to insolvent countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: The retort is very obvious indeed; if the Dominion Government had not taken the course which I mention, had not had the courage and the resource to announce that it would push for overseas business, and establish the credits to enable that business to be carried on, there would to-day be much more unemployment in Canada than.there is.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: As a matter of fact, has one dollar's worth of goods gone forward from Canada to those countries since those negotiations were entered into?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Goods are in process of manufacture. I would remind my hon. friend that there is one very important thing no country can afford to lose, and that is confidence. We maintained it during the war and we have maintained-,it since. The policies which this Government adopted of establishing an Overseas Trade Commission and of financing purchases by Great Britain in this country represent the difference between our position to-day and rwhat it might have been-a prospect I would not like to contemplate. Courage and resource are required by the Government during this period succeeding the war, and if they lack those qualities, the people are going to suffer.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Every one admits that courage is necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Yes; but it is rare.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: What was the purpose oi the Government a few days ago in asking for a vote to make good a deficit of $100,000,000, if they are in a position to loan money to every more or less insolvent country in the wrorld?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
We have a deficit because last year was a war year, and we will have a deficit this year because this year in a sense is also a war year. But if my hon. friend desires to ensure recurring

deficits for many years to come, he would
take measures

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Of precaution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
which would
prevent the expansion of our international trade. On the other hand, if he desires this country to meet its interest obligations and to reduce its national debt, the best course that he could pursue, I submit, would he to adopt a policy of meeting financial conditions and providing credits which will enable it to sell its goods abroad at a profit. Our future depends upon our increased production and our ability to find markets for it; and these markets cannot be found under present conditions unless credits are extended by us. I agree with the hon. member that there may be a difference of opinion whether particular credits should be extended or not; that is a question upon which the Government must make up its mind after inquiry from those whose opinions it deems valuable; but as to the principle of continuing to establish credits this year for the purchase of our agricultural and manufactured products, I do not think it is open to question, because I do not see how our trade could go on unless we pursue that course.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: What about next year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: We will see. Last year there was no free market for bacon; there is a free market now. The manufacturers of bacon can send their goods forward and sell their bills of exchange as they could before the war. But that cannot be done with regard to wheat, and flour, and many other commodities, and with regard to those commodities purchasing can only be done by governments and upon credits furnished to them. If the Dominion Government today said: No more credits for the purchase of our wheat, flour, and cheese and the products of our manufactories, you would have a panic in this country.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
Our business with Great Britain during the war was transacted very much the same as my hon. friend did in his boyhood days: he took a basket of eggs to the market and got tea for them. We had to exchange; we furnished Great Britain certain things and she furnished certain things to us. But the idea of hoping that this country is going to be in a position to finance its manufacturers in foreign markets by creating a false market for our manufactured goods, I cannot conceive of any man of reason entertaining. No. nation ever got into the business of
exporting manufactured goods until it was an importer of foodstuffs. Great Britain is the greatest exporter in the world and she is a great importer of foodstuffs; the same with Germany-	.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the House would like to hear the hon. minister complete his statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
I did not want to interrupt my hon. friend because I have taken nearly all the time of the Committee this afternoon. I do not understand my hon. friend when he says we must lbe importers of foodstuffs if we are to be exporters of manufactured articles. If he will look at the trade returns for the few years before the war he will find that we were exporters of both agricultural and manufactured products, agricultural products being largely predominant, but if he will follow down through the war years he will find a colossal increase in the export of our manufactured goods,
5 p.m. largely consisting of munitions.
This country developed an extraordinary ability for manufacturing munitions and other war commodities. When the war came to an end, if all the munition plants had ceased operating what would have happened to the 200,000 workers in munitions and allied industries? The problem was to substitute other business for the munition business. We must endeavour to find markets abroad for our agricultural and our manufactured products, or not only will our farmers and manufacturers suffer, but our work people will suffer, and our merchants who depend on our work people will also suffer; in fact, the whole country will suffer. I believe that the sooner 'Canada and all other countries can get back to normal trade conditions, so that all this business may be conducted through the regular commercial and financial channels, the better. I do not want to have to find one dollar to finance the purchase of foodstuffs and manufactured products from this country. " Well, then, why do you do it?" you may ask. Because we are in this period succeeding the war, the most critical in the history of the world, and we have to do it in connection with our manufactures and our commerce, which have become badly dislocated by reason of the sudden termination of the war. The Government must endeavour to meet that situation. I hope that we are meeting it wisely, but I have to tell the House that courage and resource are required if we are not to have very serious conditions. We must find a market

abroad for our agricultural and our manufactured products, and we must keep our work people engaged so far as in our power lies. If my hon. friend puts forward the proposition that apart from a condition of war, or the period succeeding the war, the Government should not interfere in financing the purchase of the products which we have for sale abroad, but leave that financing to the institutions established for the purpose, I agree with him.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Right from now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
Not from now. I wish I could say from now. It would be a great relief to the Government at this time if we could say: Old conditions are restored; there is nothing abnormal. Let trade take its course, and let finance take its course and play its part. We would be very glad to do that. But look at the conditions prevailing to-day. You have international exchange demoralized, as I mentioned a little while ago; you have highly artificial restrictions on trade by reason of the prohibition of imports and licensing systems.
We have an entirely artificial condition in the world of international trade. My own view is that we will probably come out'of that more quickly than even experts think.
I am hopeful enough to believe that this period will not last as long as men whose opinion is probably entitled to more weight than mine think it will; that when trade comes back to its usual channels exchange may rectify itself more quickly than some financiers imagine. But until it does, we must conform to the conditions that we find in the world; otherwise our people will suffer and our trade and industry will suffer. I am sure no one in the House desires that to happen.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
Where does the minister propose to get the money that he will require this year, including the $350,000,000?
I understood him to say that he had some $54,000,000 on hand and would require only $296,000,000 of the $350,000,000. Does he propose to float a loan abroad, or will he get the required amount by increased taxation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
The Dominion
Government is in funds to a very large amount at the present time-speaking from memory, to the extent, I think, of a couple of hundred million dollars. That is one reason why $50,000,000 only in excess of the actual expenditure is asked for. I have not had it in mind that we shall need the full $250,000,000 for the credits, but we have 
la-rge expenditures for other things and it will be necessary, I think, later in the year to make a loan in Canada. We have certain maturing obligations in Great Britain and United (States and it may be necessary to . borrow there later, but for the present we have not in contemplation any 'loan. With the armistice coming so suddenly and unexpectedly, it is rather fortunate that we were in funds. The Dominion has some temporary obligations of which I will inform the House in the Budget Speech; but on the whole our debt is pretty well funded, and there is nothing within the next five years, so far as I can see, that need cause any serious apprehension; that is to say, as to our being able to borrow to meet any deficits we may have. But I am the first to say that just as soon as we get through this very trying period, retrenchment must be the order of the day. What we are doing to-day we shall not be able to continue to do. The Dominion Government will not continue in the years that are to come to extend credits to finance our exports; just as soon as free markets are obtained, that will not be necessary. Trade and finance will be as before the war and the Dominion will have its Budget as it had before the war, only, of course, on a very much more extensive scale.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Does the minister expect that out of the $350,000,000 he will have enough for the increased pensions to soldiers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: The item for pensions is in the Main Estimates.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: There has been some discussion in the past as to whether we provided funds in New York to take care of interest obligations in connection with Great Britain's borrowings. Exchange, of course, would be against us at the time we provided that money. Did we, as a matter of fact, provide money to take care of Great Britain's interest charges falling due in New York, and to what extent, if we did, was the exchange chargeable to ourselves or to Great Britain?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
We have not provided any money to Great Britain except for purchases in Canada. On the contrary, we have received from Great Britain a great deal of money in New York funds; in other words, what we have received from Great Britain there ha3 helped our exchange. Of course, that had to be so. Canada has large interest and other obligations in London; she has also interest obligations in New York and during the war many short

date maturities of our Governments, provincial and municipal, and of corporations, fell due there. That meant that Canada had to provide the necessary money there to take care of these obligations. That, with the fact that we had an adverse balance of trade with the United States, accentuated our exchange situation. That was relieved from time to time by money provided by Great Britain in New York and drawn upon by the Dominion Government. I should not like to be misunderstood with regard to Great Britain. Great Britain and Canada have worked together in this war; nothing has so compelled my admiration as the courage and resourcefulness of Great Britain with regard to the tremendous financial tasks which have confronted her.
I am speaking particularly of those on this side of the water. We have been in continuous communication with Great Britain in respect of her finances in Canada and in the United States, and certainly we have nothing to complain of. On the contrary, we have much to be grateful for in what Great Britain has done in a financial way in order to enable her to purchase to the utmoslt of her power in Canada. Great Britain desired to buy all our agricultural produce and all our manufactured goods that she could buy during the war. She appreciated the war effort we were making and she supplemented to the utmost of her financial power the credits which were made available for the purpose of those purchases in Canada. I desire to pay as strong a tribute as I can to the action of the Mother Country with regard to those matters.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
I was very glad that the
minister was allowed to make his statement consecutively so that when the Bill which is founded on this resolution is brought before the House we shall have an opportunity of discussing it freely, and of making use of the figures which have been given.
I profess to have the ordinary man's intellect, but this system of trade is new to me, and, I think, deserves serious consideration. Hon. gentlemen behind the Prime Minister whom I regard as not having any greater intelligence than myself seem to treat this thing as if it were an every day occurrence, a very small matter, a subject for hilarity and laughter. But I fancy they do not really understand the situation very much better than I do. It is a very serious matter when we have to create trade by the use of our own money foT the purchase of our own goods. If a manufacturer goes to the Bank of Montreal for an advance of money on goods which he has in his store,
he must warehouse those goods and give the key of the warehouse to the bank. The banker advances the money on a certain percentage of the goods that are warehoused. The manufacturer gets the money, the goods are warehoused and the bank has security for them. In this case the Government of this country becomes the banker and lends the money. The manufacturer sells his goods, the goods go out of this country, and so the Government has no security at all. That is the inviting proposition which is put before this House by the Government, and upon which we are entering, and which hon. gentlemen supporting the Government cheer and laud and think it is absurd for any person on this side to ask anything about.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that Canada has no security and that we are giving the goods away? I do not think that is the case.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman enlighten me by explaining what security the Dominion Government has for the money it is advancing?

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: If the goods are shipped to Belgium, it has the security of the Belgian Government.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: Rumania?

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: The same thing applies to Rumania.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
If the Belgian Government is reliable, why does it not advance money in Europe to its own people for the purchase of these goods? Some hon. members shake their heads, but if the Belgian Government is able to furnish money to its own people to buy goods in Europe, why cannot it advance money to its own people here and let them purchase our goods? That is the way the matter strikes the ordinary man, and we would not have this backing of the Belgian people by the Belgian Government in order to get this money which the Belgian Government does not possess and cannot get unless the Canadian Government accepts a long term promissory note which some day may be good. The long term note of the Belgian Government which the Minister of Finance purposes taking, is not negotiable to-day; it will not be negotiable to-morrow; it will not be negotiable next year. The minister does not know when it will be negotiable, but he hopes it will some day. He puts that note in his pocket or in his vault and keeps it there, or he leaves it with his banker with instructions to cash it when it de-

serves to be cashed. That is all the security we are getting for this money, and the situation is a very grave one, although it may turn out all right. As far as the manufacturer is concerned, what is the difference between sending those goods out of the country without getting any security for them and the manufacturer warehousing them if they do not take up too much space? If a manufacturer of boots and shoes in Montreal says to the Government: I cannot go on with manufacturing boots unless you give me credit, the minister could very well say to him: If you are going to continue manufacturing those goods and if you warehouse them and give us a lien on them, we shall give you money to the extent of $500,000, or $1,000,000, as the case may be, and the manufacturer promises to put the goods in the warehouse. The people who are working in the factories are kept going just the same and are getting their wages. The boots are being stored away and, if the manufacturer cannot repay the money, the Government has this security that the goods are on hand. The Government's object is to give our people work, and I am in favour of that being done, but at the same time I want to make sure that the money of our country is secure, but it is not a system of trade to be encouraged and lauded and be proud of that we are furnishing money to foreign Governments to come here and buy our goods and take them away without giving us any security at all. If it is absolutely necessary to do this, it is a new and grave situation, and before the Government launches upon it to any great extent, the Canadian people should thoroughly understand the matter.
There is also a vicious element about this business. As has been pointed out to-day, credit has been given to certain persons in Kumania, and through certain channels, over which the ordinary business man in this country has no control, they get the right to come into this country to buy goods. Through some influence in this country they are steered into certain factories and to certain manufacturers here and there from whom they buy. those goods. The money of Canada is drawn into those channels and directed to friends of the Government or friends of those people on the other side who have goods to sell, while the ordinary everyday man, who has no friends at court and no connection with those influences on the other side, is not in a position to get this trade. I am sure every person who desires the general prosperity of Canada wants a free opportunity 
given to everyboy who is in any trade to do his best in the open market with his goods, but here we have everybody in Canada furnishing the money, through the taxes we pay, but the trade that is produced by the use of that money is directed into certain specified channels through certain specified agencies created either directly or indirectly by this Government. That is not fair. If we are using the money of the people to create trade, that trade should be as general as possible and not directed into certain places where it will find its way to favour either friends of the Government or anybody else. Those are things that should be avoided. It was pointed out today that a certain convention of agents from foreign countries and agents of manufacturers had a meeting in Toronto the other day for the purpose of allocating this business. That is the first we heard of it here, and if that is being done, it is evidently being done to the advantage of people who have inside information. If this must be done, it must be because it is highly necessary and there is no other way out of it, and in that case we have no right to be priding ourselves on our great ingenuity and forethought in securing trade for this country. Almost any man, no matter how blunt he is, when he has the power, can take money from the people of this country, hand to a man and say: Here, as long as this money which I have furnished for you lasts, come and buy our goods'with our money; when it is gone, I do not know what will happen, but here is the money, start plying trade with our people while this money lasts. This is a grave problem which should receive the serious consideration of every hon. member.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext:
I understand, my hon. friend to ask why the Belgian Government does not supply the money to make these purchases without asking the Dominion Government's assistance. The Belgian Government would have no difficulty whatever in supplying money in Belgium, but on account of the breakdown in exchange between Europe and Canada, the Belgian Government can purchase in Canada only if she gets dollar credits here. Belgian exchange has broken down as English exchange has. The result is that Belgium, like Great Britain, is unable to get credits in either the United States or Canada unless the money is loaned on this side of the Atlantic. Belgium was one of the most prosperous and wealthy countries in the world, and I have a very high opinion of the industry and en-

terprise of the Belgian people and a great hope in their future. I think the future ot Belgium is assured and that her finances will be wholly restored by indemnities from Germany. But apart from indemnities, the enterprise of her people, and their capacity for trade, together with the natural resources of the country and its colonial possessions, give promise of a great future for the nation. I may tell by hon. friend that the Dominion Government is not desirous to raise money by way of loans and advance it to foreign governments unless for the purposes I have mentioned, but I have pointed out that under present conditions our international trade cannot be carried on unless dollar credits are furnished here. Unless such credits were furnished here it could not be carried on with Great Britain, much less with other countries I have mentioned. The alternative is easily seen; our products, agricultural as well as manufactured, would not find a market. I have had a great deal to do with the financing of wheat, flour, and foodstuffs, during the past two years, and can assure the hon. gentleman that if wheat buying in this country stopped you would hear from all the growers of wheat immediately, for they must sell their wheat to pay their accounts, to pay their help, and to carry on their business as growers of grain. It is absolutely necessary that the money should be provided to take care of that wheat crop and the flour produced by our millers, and if we have to lend money to Great Britain or any other country in order to ensure the purchase of the products of our fields, it is clearly the duty of the Government to do so. There is no other course open. If through timidity we said we would not borrow any more money to. make advances to Great Britain, it would mean that the grain raised on Canadian farms would remain there and would never get into the elevators and be sold on the markets of the world, and there would be a panic all through the West and throughout this country. In connection with the financing of last year's wheat crop, we have paid out nearly $70,000,000 and $90,000,000 more must be provided for the financing 'of the purchase of the exportable surplus of last year's wheat crop- I refer to exportable surplus of wheat and the amount that will be exported as flour. These are vast sums, but I affirm that we must provide money if these commodities are to be sold. I have been speaking about agricultural products, and the same thing applies to our manufactured products sold in Europe. On account of the exchange situation that exists, we must provide
dollar credits here. Business cannot be carried on in the old way, and'therefore the Dominion Government must extend credits which will enable purchases to be made. People who manufacture here must have the money because they have to pay for the raw material, pay their work people, and keep their companies going by providing for overhead and fixed charges. We could adopt the course which I 'think my hon. friend has in mind and say, " No credits for overseas business." Well, I venture to say that if my hon. friend were in my position and took that view he would not hold it a week hence.

subtopic: WAR EXPENDITURE BY DEPARTMENTS AND COMMSSIONS.
speechtext: The minister is mistaken if he thinks that I say there should be no encouragement to overseas business. As far as Great Britain or France and other substantial countries are concerned, it is all right; but to go into the highway and byways to deal with people whom we do not know is, I think, objectionable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:

Now, my hon. friend spoke about the desirability of having orders placed fairly in Canada. I concur in every word he said in that respect, and I affirm <to him to-day that although I have had the task of the provision of these credits, I have had no complaints from any one that there has been any partiality in ithe placing of orders, nor have I in the slightest degree interested myself in the disposition of any of the orders. On the contrary, in November last I arranged with the British Government for a credit of $50,000,000 from the Dominion Government for the purchase of timber in Canada, and I may say to my hon. friend that if we had not arranged that credit the

timber industry of British Columbia would to-day have been in a very serious condition. I took the matter up in correspondence and was very careful to emphasize the fact that, as Canada as a whole was providing the money, the orders should, as far as possible, be distributed fairly throughout the country. I made that point, using the very argument my hon. friend has used, and I have heard no complaints whatever. If we provide credits for Great Britain, Great Britain owes to us that money and will pay with interest. The firms that supply that timber must be firms that can supply according to specifications and at proper prices, because you cannot expect a Government to which you loan money for the purposes of doing Canadian trade to give orders unless the prices are right, nor to accept delivery unless the specifications have been conformed to. It is very essential that in purchases made in Canada by the British people or the British Government specifications should be strictly observed and business conducted properly, and consequently the buying agency has an important task. ,So far as timber buying is concerned it is going through the usual channels, and I expect ana have heard no complaints. Consider what the provision of that $50,000,000 credit has done and will do for this country. It will Keep our timber industry flourishing, and as lue timber is bought in Canada it will provide cargo freights for shipping to Great Britain. Therefore, it is in every way a highly desirable transaction. Indeed, if we did not provide that money, Great Britain could not get dollar credits here and would buy in the United States.
Only recently it was brought to my attention from British Columbia-falsely as it. turned out-that instead of buying in British Columbia, Great Britain was buying in the United States. I have no doubt she is buying in the United Slates but she is only able to buy in the United States if given credit there and she can only buy here if we give her credit. The alternative is that either this business is to be done in Canada or not according as we furnish credits or do not. If we want the business Canada must furnish credits to Great Britain. I desire to assure my hon. friend that in so far as I know there is no favouritism in the placing of the orders and, if it comes to his attention that there is,
I would be glad if he would let me know because I would not stand for that kind of business. There is another matter that I desire to mention. When we appointed this

Canadian Trade Commission, which was complementary to the Canadian Mission in London, the chairman of the Reconstruction Committee, my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Maclean) submitted the memorandum to council which was adopted and became an Order in Council. If hon. gentlemen will read it they will see the functions and powers conferred on this commission. They will also see that various Canadian industries may, through their representatives, keep in close touch with the commission. Suppose that an order for furniture is obtained in Europe; those in the furniture business in Canada, or theii representative, will be in touch with the Canadian Commission here. I am sure that I should have heard if there had been any favouritism but I have not heard one word to that effect. If there is any complaint on that score I can assure my hon. friend that I would be one of the first to stop it because if we are financing with the money of The Dominion of Canada our export trade, it should be on terms that are as fair as possible to our Canadian producers, subject to the necessity of the party buying only the goods that he desires and at a fair price.

I think the country at large will breathe easy in view of the statements and assurances given by the Minister of Finance this afternoon. He speaks with absolute confidence of the conditions that obtain in connection with the financial affairs of the country and he should know whereof he speaks. I am very much pleased indeed to have that assurance. But I would like to call the attention of the minister to one feature of the situation that I think will require some consideration on his part. I refer to the matter of Canadian exchange. During the past winter the sterling exchange rate has been maintained at about 4.76. It is well known in commercial circles that exchange on London must be brought in this country through New York. Unfortunately our balance of trade with the United States is not as favourable as it is with London and notwithstanding the fact that the sterling exchange rate stood at 4.76 until' the peg was removed some few weeks ago, it was of very little advantage to the Canadian purchasers of exchange on London. The reason for that is that in order to buy exchange on London the purchaser in Canada must buy it through New York. 1 have always been at a loss to understand why we should not have an exchange rate

direct with London. In view of the fact that we have not at the present time, and never have had that direct exchange, the advantage of a favourable balance of trade with Great Britain, and of our position of financial strength, is of little value to the purchaser in Canada of exchange in London because it is absorbed in the exchange rate in New York. The position of affairs is that the advantage of the exchange rate between Canada, New York and London is absorbed almost .entirely by the rate we must pay in buying our exchange through the New York market. I would like to see the day arrive when Canadians can purchase their exchange direct on the market in London.
I desire to call the attention of the Minister of Finance to a concrete case in connection with the placing of business with the Canadian woollen manufacturers.
I have these facts on authority that is beyond question. The War Trade Board placed orders within the last two weeks amongst -woollen manufacturers in this country. I do not claim that there was favouritism shown in the placing of these orders. That is not my claim, but what I do claim is that if these orders had been placed in the open market the material would have been purchased at a price possibly 20 per cent lower. For instance, the contract called for a material weighing 22 ounces to the yard. The price paid to these woollen manufacturers was 11 cents per ounce, or $2.42 per yard for the material sold to the War Trade Board on account of the Rumanian orders. I know as a matter of fact there are manufacturers in this country who, if this business had been placed on the open market, would have been delighted to have supplied the material at 9 cents per ounce or $1.98 pei yard. The material is made up of one third wool, one third shoddy and one third cotton. I do not know the extent of these orders that have been placed for woollen materials but I do know from information I have received that this special agent who organized the woollen manufacturers association obtained a commission of 2} per cent on the transaction. If these orders amounted to $6,000,000 -I am not saying that these are the actual figures.-this agent has got $150,000 on this transaction.

The House again in Committee on Bill No. 37-Hon. N. W. Rowell-respecting the Department of Health, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 4, subsection (h)-collection, publication and distribution of information to promote good health, and improved sanitation:

speakeroldname: Hon. N. W. ROWELL (President of the Council):
speechtext:
While it is evident from this
subsection that the Department of Public Health does not intend to go into the collection of vital statistics, it has been suggested that the matter should be made perfectly clear by inserting suitable words to indicate that the department will not duplicate the work of the Bureau of Statistics. This may be done by inserting at the beginning of the subsection the words, " Subject to the provisions of the Statistics Act."
I suggested the other evening that another phase of the work which is, perhaps, not fully covered by the subsection as it stands might be covered by the addition of the words " social welfare." but as objection was taken I did not press the point. I now, suggest, however, that the subsection be so amended that it shall read as follows:
Subject to the provisions' of the Statistics Act, the collection, publication and distribution of information relating to the public health, improved sanitation, and social and industrial conditions affecting the health and lives of the people;
We all recognize that in future more attention must be paid to the health and physical well-being of those who are engaged in industry. In the past, emphasis has been placed on property; in future, emphasis must be placed more largely on life. The country is deeply concerned in all matters connected with the carrying on of industry that affect the life and health of the people. Information should be gathered and published touching that aspect of health as well as the more general classes of subjects which we include in the words " public health." The latter words of the amendment have been suggested to me by Mr. Moore, president of the Trades and Labour

Congress of Canada, and I think the suggestion is a good one.

I submit that the words "and social and industrial conditions affecting the health and lives of the people" will empower the new department to legislate upon matters that are subject to the jurisdiction of Provincial Governments. The department may deal with conditions of health as applied to industries and with the conditions prevailing in the buildings wherein these industries are carried on. But when they are empowered to deal with social conditions as well, we have the same objection that we had to the inclusion ol the words "social welfare" in this subsection. In the amendment which the minister proposes the idea of giving the department control over matters affecting social welfare is carried out-under different terms, that is all. For my part, I prefer the subsection as originally drafted, although 1 am disposed to accept the restriction imposed by the words "subject to the provisions of the 'Statistics Act," which, in my judgment, is a good one. I am in favour of the Bill, but I believe thait there should be no encroachment upon provincial rights. In an article published on 19th March last, the Ottawa Journal-Press expressed the opinion that public health was a matter which, under Ithe terms of the British North America Act, had been handed over to the provinces; that health, like education, was a provincial matter. It is desirable, of course, that there should he co-operation among provincial boards of health. But in drafting this Bill this committee should be very careful not to interfere with provincial rights, and I would, therefore, be quite satisfied if the minister who is in charge of the Bill would not insist on the words:
-and social and industrial conditions affecting the health and lives of the people,
I have the greatest possible admiration for trades and labour organizations, and I am a staunch supporter of every legitimate claim which is made by such organizations, but I feel it is my duty to decline to accept in a Bill a clause which in my opinion is an encroachment upon provincial rights.

I commend this clause very highly. I do not think it is possible to compass the objects of this federal Health Bill in any better way. The clause provides practically for a publicity department in connection with this enactment, and that publicity department has the duty of setting forth before the House and the'public the facts relating to public health as they

affect industrial and social conditions in this country. I can see where it will do a great deal of good in indicating the lines of progress along which the federal department of public health will proceed, 'and I really cannot see wherein it could operate so as to encroach upon provincial rights and the autonomy of the provinces in this work in which we are all presumably interested. The clause is, I understand, intended to permit the federal health department to secure reports as to conditions in factories and workshops regarding ventilation, lighting and the evil influence which may result from dust contamination. These are all very important to workers. The department, I assume will also ascertain and make known conditions as to noxious vapours and poisonous fumes which, in certain factories where large quantities of nitric acid and sulphuric acid are used, are very serious menaces to the workers, and also as to aerial infection of illuminating gas vapours and of the carbohydrates, some of which are extremely noxious. These, I take it, are some of the points concerning which it would be the duty of the department of health to investigate the facts. Then again, we have the great and all-important question of the ages at which children are working in factories where the conditions in employing child labour are, from a sanitary standpoint, far from satisfactory. The hours are often such as to retard the right and healthy development of child workers, and in some parts of this Dominion, notwithstanding the present enactment in force in this country, there are many children under age who are working under unsanitary and unsatisfactory conditions, in factories and rooms that are dark and ill-ventilated, and these conditions ought to be known to the Government and to a federal health department. I consider this clause is designed to bring the facts before the public, and by informing the public generally we may hope to remedy conditions which I am sure no member of this committee would willingly have continued. I think the clause will be in its effect a distinct benefit in the working and development of this federal health department.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: I think in the case of a doubt such as exists in regard to this amendment, the Government should put in a proviso that no such regulations will be put into force without having first received the approval of the Board of Health of each province.

I think my hon. friend
(Mr. DuTremblay) misunderstands the clause, and I think the hon. member for Nicolet (Mr. Trahan) also misunderstood it. This deals only with collecting and distributing information in connection with industrial conditions. There is no power to legislate at all, and this does not, therefore, infringe upon provincial rights.

On subsection (i):-such other matters as may be referred to the minister by the Governor in Council.
Will the minister explain the meaning of this clause?

Let us take the illustration I gave my hon. friends the other evening, the question of administration of such a fund as the Government's fund to aid in housing. That has a very close relation to the question of public health, and at present it is being administered by a committee of the Cabinet. I should think it would be a very appropriate thing for the Governor in Council, if thought fit, to entrust the administration of that particular branch of the public service to a department like this, and, therefore, power to do So is given. There are at the present time certain departments dealing with matters that more or less intimately affect the public health in certain aspects of their work. These Acts are not mentioned in the schedule because there may be a difference of opinion as to whether the administration of those Acts which touch a certain aspect of public health should be entrusted to this department or not, or whether the administration should be 'continued under the existing departments. This would simply permit the Governor in Council to transfer to this department the administration of certain branches of work closely connected with public health which are now being administered by other departments of the Government.

Section 4 reads:
The duties and powers of the minister administering the department of health shall extend to and include all matters and questions relating to the promotion or preservation of the health and social welfare of the people of Canada.
All the necessary powers seem to be included in this; and I cannot therefore see the need for Orders in Council. The minister says he may decide this and that, but all powers are stipulated in this clause.
1.368

If we have all the power already in the first part there can be no harm in having it in the second. It simply indicates the method by which the power can be exercised; it must be exercised by Order in Council. To give an illustration: The Department of Indian Affairs has a medical branch having the medical care and supervision of the Indians on our reserves. It is not proposed by this Bill at the present time to transfer the administration of that branch of the service to this department, but it might be considered desirable in the future to do so and provision is made by which it may be done. Clause 4 is quite broad enough to cover all power-this provides machinery by which a certain aspect of work carried on in one department may be transferred to another.
Mr. McKiENZIE:	Subsection (i) gives
the minister authority in " such other matters as may be referred to the minister by the Governor in Council." If that were found in any law referring to the Department of Railways we would know at once that the word " Minister " meant the Minister of Railways, but in this matter there is no minister. The President of the Council told us the other night that this was to be merely a branch of some department, or at least that it would be under some present minister. As there does not seem to be any special minister in connection with this work this clause is not very significant.

The hon. member will
see that section 2 provides that there is to be a Department of Health, " over which a minister of the Crown to be named by the Governor in 'Council shall preside." That is the minister referred to in subsection (i). Ilf my hon. friend would prefer, the word " department " might be substituted for the word " minister."

I understand that this Bill will enact a law that will receive the cooperation of the provinces, and it seems to be understood that there will he no infringement of provincial rights. With regard to section 4, it seems to me that everything is covered and there is no need to enumerate such matters as are there dealt with. There you have covered everything in connection with these subsections, and the specification of all these matters will Tesult in trouble with reference to provincial rights. Amongst other things, you mention child life and child welfare. That is a clause that I shall not discuss just now, but it is a very delicate question, and the power here conferred should be applied with great discretion having regard to provincial rights. In every province there is a great deal of work done in regard to child life and child welfare, and I think that it is within the right of the province to look after such matters as these. This matter in particular has to do with the school system and the habits and customs of the people in the different provinces, which should be entirely within their jurisdiction. As far as the other matters are concerned, it seems to me that they could be safely left to the Dominion Council of Health as it will be constituted. If you leave in this Bill a clause of this kind reserving to the deputy minister the right to modify or change certain conditions of his own accord subject only to Order in Council, I think it will certainly interfere with provincial rights, and instead of being an Act to help the provinces to promote the welfare of the people, it is more likely to bring confusion and prove a detriment rather than an aid to public health. I would therefore suggest that this clause should be amended and made more definite in its meaning.

When we had this Bill last under consideration, we submitted a clause which I understood was to stand for further consideration. I would like to ask the minister if he has that clause in mind and if he proposes to incorporate it in this Bill. The clause that I submitted was this:
Provided' that nothing in this Act shall authorize any officer or authority created, by or appointed under the authority of this Act or under any regulation made hereunder to exercise any jurisdiction or control over any provincial health officer or any provincial or municipal board of health or other authority operating under the laws of any province.

I had intended suggesting that the clause moved by my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Sheard), slightly modified, but not changing its effect,

Before this section is
adopted I would like to point out that there
[Mr. Rowell. 1

I have said before, and I need hardly repeat, that I can imagine no great advancement, nor any great benefit, is being likely to result from the operation of the federal health law, unless-as it is a pivotal point of operation-the work of a scientific hygienic laboratory goes on in connection therewith. It would appear to me that the hon. minister might meet the views of those who support the Bill, because he is in the happy position of promoting a measure which meets with universal approval; we are all trying to get to the same end; some think it might be better gained one way, some another way, but as to the purpose of the Bill there is no difference of opinion. Therefore I would suggest to the hon. minister that he might very properly declare, en toutes letters, as we say in our province, that is in set terms, that we are going to have in Canada such a bureau or laboratory of research as has been most eloquently urged by the hon. member for Muskoka, who, as a member of a very learned profession, medicine, is much better able to talk with authority on these things than a mere lawyer.

Much has been said in
support of a laboratory in connection with the Department of Public Health with which I heartily agree; in fact, I would go so far as to say that a Department of Public Health without the facilities of a laboratory is out of date before it is established. But I do not find myself in hearty agreement with the advocacy of such a laboratory as has been suggested this evening. I believe that what we ought to have in Canada is one great national laboratory, a laboratory which would carry on the work required for industrial and scientific research; a laboratory with which could be associated the laboratory we now have in connection with our Inland Revenue Department, a hygienic laboratory, and a laboratory which would take up every work which will be required in Canada in the future. I believe that to insert this clause in the Bill at the present time would simply have the result of establishing one more branch laboratory in connection with our national work. To my mind what we want is to co-ordinate the laboratories which we now have, and add such a branch as has been suggested to carry on the health work. But

the Government must give a good deal of consideration to it, and I sincerely trust that within the next year a great national laboratory will be established, following the system and plan of the Pasteur Institute of Paris and Ithe great laboratory at Washington. I would therefore advocate that the Government omit this from 
the Bill at Ithe present time and take into consideration the establishment of such a laboratory as I have suggested.

When I first saw this Bill I searched through it for some mention of a laboratory, because I could not imagine that we could have a Health Department established without it. I must confess that at my first reading I was not able to find any provision for it, but on going through the Bill again I came to the same conclusion as the hon. minister, that one of the clauses covered the point. I think, however, that it would be very much better for us to definitely state that such a laboratory is to be established. Because, Sir, I cannot imagine the hon. minister wanting this department to be a failure, and without a laboratory-and a better one than anything we have in the Dominion to-day-it is certainly going to be a failure. If you establish such a laboratory as has been proposed you will immediately rally to the support of this department the entire medical profession of the Dominion, and otherwise I doubt if you will get its support to any great extent.
Although I am not of the medical profession,-I am one of the allied professions,-yet I have had a good deal to do with the medical profession in Canada, and I cannot subscribe to many of the criticisms in the press these days of the medical profession and their relation to this health department. I have always found them a very progressive body, and I think they have made more progress than any other profession-except, of course, the one I belong to and which claims my loyalty-and I am confident that the medical profession of Canada are equal to the medical profession of any other part of the world. Of course, if we expect them to maintain their position we must give them the opportunities to continue their progress. Therefore I say we should make up our minds to establish this laboratory at the earliest possible time. If that is to be done, there is no reason why it should not be so stated in this Bill, for then you will immediately get the sympathy of the medical profession throughout Canada and at once make it a success. I suggest that this be done, and I support as strongly as I can the position taken by the hon. member for South Toronto.

I rise in support of the suggestion, and also to say a word in justice to the provincial Boards of Health-

Some speakers have criticised those boards- ,
No.

I mean they have criticised them unconsciously in saying that public health work cannot be carried on without a laboratory. I agree in the necessity for instituting a research laboratory, but according to my understanding none of the provincial Boards of Health is so equipped.
Mr. 9HEARD: The Ontario board has had one for ten years.

Perhaps the hon. member is right; 'I did not think they had. However, I wish to support the idea. I think we should have a research laboratory. Some mention was made of research laboratories in the United States. 'One of the finest in the world is the Rockefeller Institute which is supported by funds supplied by John D. Rockefeller. Some of the war lords of this country who have made millions out of the war might show a proper sense of proportion by helping to establish in Canada a practical research laboratory along the lines of the Rockefeller Institute in the United States.

So far as the general
view expresses the importance of a research laboratory, I am heartily in accord with it. I have intimated that the power to establish a research laboratory is quite clearly set forth in section 4, but there appears to be a general desire on the part of the members of the House that some words should be included in the Bill to indicate specifically that the establishment of such a laboratory is within the powers of this department. We should not have a series of laboratories established in various departments. It is very important that the work should be done as economically and efficiently as possible. In consenting to such an amendment as I have suggested, I am not committing myself or the Government to the bringing down of an appropriation for the purpose this session; that is a matter that will have to be taken up by the Government when Estimates are under consideration. If I assent to any reference to research laboratories going in, I am assenting to the specific mention of the fact that this department contemplates the esablish-ment and maintenance of a laboratory. The establishment and maintenance of a national laboratory for public health and research work.
I think it would be more suitable to give it that place in the section.
If this provides for an expenditure of money, it would have to be preceded by the consent of the Governor in Council.
It would be simply defining the powers of the department. We are not voting any money, nor is the Government committing itself to any expenditure.

The control of venereal disease by quarantine at the various ports of entry or by such other methods and investigations as shall limit the spread of these diseases throughout the Dominion of Canada.
