speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The amendment mentioned by the member for South Toronto was defeated upon division the other night in committee.
The amendment that was defeated was much more drastic than the one at present proposed.
To what extent will the hospitals come under the observation or control of this departments
The Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment maintains hospitals for soldiers.
These are military hospitals.

Yes, and hospitals wherein men who have been soldiers are cared for. But the ordinary hospitals of the country, with the exception of the marine hospitals, are wholly under the jurisdiction of the provinces.

The object of this
measure must appeal to us all, especially in the light of the statistics the minister gave us the other night as to the alarming loss of child life. What I fear most is that the Act is so general and so vague that we shall have a large and necessarily expensive organization, the object of which is excellent, hut which will have nothing in particular to do. According to the word-

ing of the Bill, we are to have co-operation, co-ordination-a great word in these days- conservation, inspection, and supervision, but there is nothing specific to do. One is almost reminded of the reference frequently seen in the comic papers to the man who is "all dressed up and no place to go." I do not say this in a spirit of objection; but I shall offer a suggestion as to something for this department to do- and it has a bearing on my question with regard to the hospitals. There is in the Mother Country and in some of our neighbour States quite a large body of what I may call social legislation of a progressive character-legislation respecting minimum wages, old age pensions, and a variety of things of that nature. To all of these we must hereafter give more attention than we have in the past, but we cannot deal at once with them all. One class of legislation that, I think, might well engage the particular attention of this department is the encouragement and extension of maternity hospitals. Talking not long ago with the manager of an organization of charities in one of our large cities, I was much interested in the account he gave of the work in which they were engaged. He said-not in a boastful way-" We are looking after our people from the cradle to the grave. We do better than that: we anticipate the cradle, because we are organizing maternity hospitals." There are in some of our communities-including Ottawa, I am glad to say-a number of these institutions. They are necessarily local in their character; they are all more or less expensive, because they have to charge fees. But if there is anything in the way of social legislation which we should deal with seriously, it is the taking of steps to provide that the woman who is approaching the time when her child is to be born shall be surrounded by all the conditions which will give her comfort, which will give her medical attendance, which will give her proper food and rest both before and after the time when the child is bom. That is the best kind of work for the conservation of child life. Where there is a hospital of this character it might well come under the direction of this department, and where there are not such hospitals, they might well be established. I do not mean to say that any uniform plan could be adopted, but wherever there is such a hospital, I should like to see this board get in touch with it and see that it is en-
couraged. This is clearly a case where there could be co-operation between the federal, provincial and local authorities, and it is a most promising field for useful work. Indeed, I know of no branch of social legislation which offers such large opportunities. I do not need to dwell on the subject, because hon. members who are of the medical profession can say all that I can say and say it much better, but if there is in the world anything in the way of social legislation which we need, it is something which at that critical time in the life of the mother and child will ensure that she is provided with medical attendance, comfort, food, and all the conditions which will go to enable her to perform the function of motherhood with safety to herself and benefit to the community at large.

The only aid which the
federal Government could, under the British North America Act, give in the ease referred to by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) would be -a subsidy or a monetary grant to hospitals in the counties. Eleemosynary institutions and all hospitals, specifically mentioned in the British North America Act as being under the control of the legislatures of the various provinces. That is the only reason why, I fancy, this Bill has not undertaken to set out what has been mentioned.

I do not wish to say that the Bill should set this out specifically. I am quite content, if the object is a good one, to leave it in the hands of the minister. I repeat my first statement, that in many things which are distinctly within the control of the provincial legislatures, we are yet dabbling a good deal. The road question is a distinctly provincial one, and yet we are delving into it; and if this matter is taken up, I am sure we shall find a great deal of co-operation on the part of the loqal and provincial authorities who will permit my hon. friend to do something. I find that, while we are all sensitive in this matter of provincial rights, when any proposal made to encroach upon provincial rights is accompanied with a generous grant, there is not generally very much objection

With all that the hon member for Shelburne and Queens has said as to the importance and urgency of the question he has raised, I am in most hearty accord. I think, however, it is a matter coming within the jurisdiction of the provinces. So far as the Federal Government may act, I think, that power is to-day conferred by subsection (a). Subsection (b)

was added to (a), and (a) now provides for co-operation with the provincial, territorial, and other health authorities in the conservation of child life and the promotion of child welfare. Those words are, I think, broad enough to cover what my hon. friend has in mind, and if Parliament should see fit to make a grant for such purposes, it would be quite competent for Parliament to do so.

I
should, just like to .support the expression, of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens. I recognize the constitutional objection, but I also recognize that in the interest of this country many so-called constitutional objections will have to disappear in the future. In my judgment there is nothing that would do more good to help a lot of needy people than the suggestion the hon. member has thrown out, and I am in favour of going even further and giving every poor man, woman and child in this country free medical service from the cradle to the grave. I believe the time is coming when we shall have to do this in the national interest.
Mr. STEELE.: I should like to add a few words to express the pleasure I have felt in seeing the unanimity that has existed throughout the whole discussion in committee on the question of the establishment of a department of health. If there is one matter that has been proposed to be put under that department that has met with more perfect unanimity than any other it is child welfare. From the Atlantic to the Pacific prominent people who are deeply interested in this subject have expressed their hearty approval of the'establishment of a federal department of health, if for no other reason than that the subject of child welfare might receive greater attention and consideration. I want especially to express my pleasure that, on this occasion at least, Quebec and Ontario can stand hand in hand in support of that which is going to be a great blessing to both provinces. This is a question on which Ontario and Quebec are not disunited. We have evidence of that in the expressions of hon. members from Quebec to-night and on previous occasions. I want to quote an extract from an article published in La Presse a few weeks ago. That paper, which I understand has, perhaps, the largest circulation of any French paper published in the country-
Of any paper in Canada.

The largest circulation of any paper in Canada. That magnifies the
value of expressions of opinion by La Presse. It says, relating to child welfare:-
At a time when war and another evil not less cruel than war has thinned our ranks, who will refuse to admit the necessity of making an urgent effort to fill the void? The time has come w'hen more attention than ever should be paid to guarding the cradle.
That brief extract expresses in a few words the sentiment of the great majority of the people of this country. La Presse,
I have no doubt, had in view conditions which unfortunately prevail in Quebec, and which, perhaps, place that province- and I am saying this in no disrespectful spirit-in a place by itself in this country as regards infant mortality. I should like to quote the figures just to illustrate that. If I compare Quebec with Ontario, hon. members will understand that I am not doing it for the sake of disparaging Quebec, but simply to show how the infant mortality rate in Quebec can be improved in the future. In 1915, there were in Quebec 33,274 births, with 12,775 deaths under one year of age. That is a terrible percentage In Ontario-and Ontario is not by any means in the first class in this respect, because some of the other provinces stand higher than Ontario, but I use the Ontario figures because they are the only ones I have-there were 67,032 births in 1915, with 6,838 deaths under one year of age. With about 20 per cent more births in Quebec in that year, there were very nearly 100 per cent more deaths under one year of age, and if we carry that to deaths under four years of age, we find the discrepancy still greater. To illustrate the matter still further, let me quote the figures for Montreal and Toronto.
In 1916, in Montreal there were 186 deaths of children under one year of age for every 1,000 births. In Toronto in the same year, the number of deaths was only 93 per 1,000 births, or exactly one-half. There are many cities in which the mortality is less than that, but throughout the whole province of Quebec and the city of Montreal there is great room for improvement, and I would urge on the people of Canada a careful consideration of the views expressed by La Presse.

I do not rise to contradict any of the statements made by my colleague and friend, the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele), but rather to corroborate to a certain extent what he has said, especially as regards the cooperation that should exist between Ontario and Quebec. I am sure that not

only in the matter of public health but on many important public questions both provinces can by mutual good will accomplish an enormous good for the country. There is no doubt that the introduction of this Bill has engendered some anxiety on the part of those who are sensitive on the subject of local autonomy, but after a careful study of it, and in view of the amendments which have been introduced and accepted by the Government, I think that sufficient guarantee is afforded for the strict preservation of provincial rights. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queens referred with a touch of ridicule to the word "co-ordination," but it seems to me that the bringing under one control of the different activities of the Federal Government in its relation to public health, is rather advisable. The Department of the Interior, the Department of Agriculture and the Inland Kevenue Department, have all something to do with the .general subject of public health, and who will deny that the co-ordination of these branches under one head would make for effective and efficient service? The British North America Act does not assign the matter of public health to either federal or provincial jurisdiction; but it is evident that in certain cases, for instance, the inspection of schools, the jurisdiction would be in the provinces. In some of the larger fields, such as preventing the propagation and dissemination of contagious diseases, the question of jurisdiction may not be so clear, but up to the present time the most important matters connected with public health have been under	the jurisdiction of	the provinces, and in accordance	with this
interpretation of the British North America Act, provincial board's of health have been established all over Canada. My hon. friend from South Perth, doubtless without any ill design on his part, made particular reference to the situation in Quebec regarding the high infantile death rate. I may say that the Provincial Board of Health of Quebec is one of the best-organized in Canada, and Quebec was .the first province to be divided into sanitary districts. It has ten such districts, and at the head of the organization is a sanitary inspector who holds a diploma of public health issued by a university. There are in Quebec, and probably there may be in Ontario and the other provinces, elaborate laboratories of chemistry and bacteriology to which physicians have access in the diagnosing of diseases, and to which samples of milk and drinking 
water can be Drought for analysis from any part of the province. There is also a very efficient department of statistics.
Have you a research department?
We have not, except for the purpose of ascertaining whether water that is meant for public use is potable.
That is not research.

No. As far as school hygiene is concerned, there is an effective system, but I confess that the rate of infantile mortality is higher in Quebec than in some other provinces. One must not overlook the fact, however, that the population in Quebec is very thinly spread over quite a large territory and also that the birth-rate is much higher. It will be obvious, therefore, that families experience a greater degree of difficulty in caring for their children. In this respect a considerable improvement has taken place in the last ten years, especially in the city of Montreal. Regarding nuisances, dwelling and industrial establishments, we have laws in the province of Quebec that call for the highest praise and admiration. During the last session of the provincial Legislature measures were adopted which I think deserve the commendation of all who have at heart the advancement of public health Coming to the more delicate subject which has been touched upon by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens, venereal diseases, on the recommendation of the Superior Board of Health legislation was adopted during the last session of the Legislature. I will not delay the work of the Committee by reading that law, but it contains three very important clauses which were inserted in the Public Health Act of Quebec. I have no objection at all to inserting in this Bill a clause' referring to the establishment of a bureau or laboratory for scientific research. Provided we are assured there is no intention of infringing or encroaching upon the rights of the provinces, we on this side of the House as well as hon. gentlemen on the other side, are willing to co-operate with the Government.

I desire again to refer
to section 5 which reads as follows:
The Governor in Council shall have power to make such regulations as may be necessary to give effect to and carry out the objects of this Act, and to impose penalties for any violation of such regulations.
I am not inclined to give many powers to the Governor in Council. With regard

to this question of inflicting penalties, we have had during recent times examples which are not very reassuring to us. If the Government use this power in the same manner as they have used similar powers in the past, the burden will be a very heavy one. I would be very glad if the minister would drop the words "to impose penalties for any-violation of such regulations." If he is not willing to do so I am of the opinion the amount of the penalties should be limited in the Act. It will not be very satisfactory if-the Government, by Order in Council, inflict a penalty of $5,000 for a violation of the regulations. As an alternative I would suggest that the words "not exceeding $25," or "$50," be added after the word "penalties".

In order that the
operation of this law, may be successful, it must proceed along lines of co-operation, co-ordination, harmony and peace. Why have penalties at all? If it is found in the operation of the Act that co-operation, co-ordination and other considerations oi that kind are not sufficient, then the minister may come back at a future day and ask us to "make the punishment fit the crime." Let us adopt the principle of trusting the people, of trusting the provinces. Let us strike out those words giving power to impose penalties and appeal to the good sense and reasonableness of the people as a whole. I imagine that the operation of this Act would have to do largely with provinces and municipalities. Let the Big Stick not be in evidence at the beginning of this matter.
The clause is simply the usual one in Bills of this kind.

But this is a very unusual Bill.
, Mr. ROWELL:	Where you have the
power to make regulations, if those regulations are to have any effect, there must be the usual provision for a penalty. There is no danger Of harshness under this Bill. My hon. friend is quite right in saying that the whole framework of the measure contemplates co-operation. That is evident from the very next clause providing for a federal council of health bringing in all the chiefs of the provincial departments. My hon. friend surely does not seriously think there is anything wrong with the clause.

I would dislike the committee to think that I would take up the valuable time of this House in presenting a proposition that was not serious. If
you have to deal with a man or woman along the lines of co-operation and coordination I would advise the minister that it would be well to keep penalties in the background. I understand that in a new department of this sort some latitude may be given to the Government to make regulations by Order in Council-much as we dislike that method-but you will not be able to get people to co-operate with you if you hold heavy penalties over their heads. I think it is well not to have these words in the Bill.
Where you are administering the Quarantine Act, the Adulteration Act and such Acts as that, you must have penalties in order to give the Government power to carry out the provisions of these Acts.

I agree with what hon.
members on this side of the House have said. I think this Committee should have some idea at least of the penalties that are going to be imposed before Parliament is asked to sanction penalties.

The penalties would absolutely depend upon the character of the regulations. You will see that there is power here to deal with the inspection and medical care of immigrants and seamen, the administration of marine hospitals, and the supervision of railways, boats, ships, and all methods of transporation. If you were dealing with transportation companies you would have to have an absolutely different penalty from that for some offence of a private individual of a different character. That is the reason why it is difficult to specify it. It depends entirely on the character of the offence and of the party with whom you are dealing.

I just imagine that would be the case, and therefore I think there is a great deal to be said for what my hon. friend from Nicolet (Mr. Trahan) advances, that you should have a maximum and a minimum penalty so that you can work in ' between the two.

I have no objection to
making the maximum $200. The penalty is very moderate, particularly if you are dealing with corporations.

If I understand the
object of this Bill it is to protect a certain class of people to a certain extent against another section of the community. Those against whom the penalty is aimed can well afford to pay it. Anybody who does not observe the regulations should be fined, and heavily fined, because sometimes it

happens in the case of a large corporation that it will pay a very large fine and not observe the law at all. I have seen that occur in the past.
On section 6-Dominion Council of Health.
^Mr. ROWELL:	I would suggest that
" three " be changed to " five " in the fifth line of this section, relating to the number of members to be appointed.
Is there any special reason why the number should be increased?

It has been represented to me, since the Bill was drafted, that on such a council it may be very desirable to have, say, the President or Chairman of the Canadian National Society of Social Hygiene, or a man of that type. Then it is contemplated, I understand, to form a national organization for the purpose of combatting venereal disease. If such an organization were formed it would be a very proper thing to have the chairman of it on this board. Furthermore, having regard to the very deep interest which organized labour is taking in this Bill and in its promotion; I think it would be desirable to have a representative of labour on the board. And there certainly should be a woman representative, for very good reasons. I have, therefore, thought it wise to increase the number of representatives from three to five, so as to make it possible to include representatives of those interests that are so directly concerned with matters of public health.
Is it contemplated to give any remuneration, beyond expenses, to these five members of the proposed council?
No, it is not contemplated to give them any remuneration.

I suggest a verbal alteration which may not be necessary, 'but will perhaps tend to indicate more clearly what is contemplated. I propose to insert in the second line from the bottom the words in respect of this Act." The section will then read that the Council "shall be charged with such duties and powers in respect of this Act as the Governor in Council may prescribe."
I have no objection to the amendment, although that is what the section means in its present form.

speechtext: The press men, when they get sick, call in a doctor just the same as we do.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not know that was the situation.
Or call in the undertaker.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Before leaving the subject I would like to congratulate the House

upon the passage of legislation which in my judgment will confer more benefit upon the workers of this country than any other piece of legislation this House has enacted. Health can be bought by the rich, but it is those without large incomes who are the sufferers from the contagious diseases against which this Bill is directed. Therefore, I 'think this Bill, when it goes into effect, will do more in the long run for the welfare of the workers of this country than any other piece of legislation that has been passd by this Parliament.

I must take exception to the statement of the hon, gentleman (Mr. Keefer) that I tried to take away from the medical profession any credit for this Bill.
I remember my words very distinctly, and if the hon. gentleman will take the trouble to look them up in Hansard he will find that what I said was that the labour organizations were among the first to advocate the creation of a department of public health. Those were my words and I adhere to them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The medical profession wore the first to advocate it, in 1866 in Canada.

I do not dispute that, and I presume that if the hon. gentleman went back a couple of thousand years he would find an even earlier advocate in the person of Aesculapius. The hon. gentleman would have acted with more fairness if he had quoted me as pointing out that the medical profession were supporting the establishment of this department whole-heartedly and very high-mindedly, because that was the statement I made.

Before the section passes, I would ask the President of the Privy Council whether, in view of the uncertainty that exists throughout the country, he can state who will be the minister at the head of this department, whether it will be a medical practitioner or a layman?
The Western papers contain statements to the effect that the hon. Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) is to be appointed. Would it be a breach of confidence on the part of the hon. minister to enlighten the House?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

On the schedule:

I called the attention of the House the other day to the fund administered by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and I presume that the schedule would be the proper place to add "Chapter 113 of the Revised Statutes?"

The Canada Shipping
Act, Chapter 113, Sections 406 to 408 inclusive, I think should be added to the schedule.

What becomes of the fund to the credit of the Health Branch of the Department of Marine and Fisheries?
I understand that a considerable amount of money has been collected from ships at the various ports, and that the fund so formed is for the purpose of caring for sick seamen. I would like to know if the hon. minister has considered the destination of that fund, or whether the Minister of Health to be appointed will have charge of it.

As the fund is collected for administration under the general provisions of the Act, I did not think it was desirable to take its collection out of the hands of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries who now administers it under the Act, but I think there is no doubt the fund must be applied to the purposes specified in the Act and would be avail-10 p.m. able for paying the expenses oi these hospitals just as it is today. The effect of the change, that is, the placing of sections 406 to 408 of the Canada Shipping Act in this schedule, would be to place the actual administration of the hospitals under the Department of Health, as those are the sections which specify the particular minister who shall administer the hospitals. I think the money would still go in exactly the way it goes to-day, and as it should go.

It has been impressed on the attention of the Marine Department for years that something should

be done for sick seamen owing to the fact that this money had been collected from ships at our ports and had accumulated to a large amount, and that in many places hospitals had not been provided. My object ^ in putting my question to the hon. minister is to find out if the new department will look after sick seamen in a better way than that work has been done in the past.

I would move that the Animals Contagious Diseases Act, the Inspection of Canned Foods Act, and the Penitentiaries Act be included in this schedule. I do not think any argument is needed for including the Animals Contagious Diseases Act, because this is the only natural place for it. Many diseases, such as tuberculosis and anthrax, affect both animals and men. I might point out that diseases are intensified apparently by going through the animal kingdom, and the human being contracts them in an aggravated form. The Inspection of Canned Foods would naturally fall under the work of this department, also the penitentiaries. Very often we have the feeble minded and the partially demented in our penitentiaries, and they require medical supervision.

I do not care whether you include the inspection of penitentiaries and of canned foods, but I do object to animal diseases being put under this organization, because I think the work is remarkably well handled as it is, and it belongs properly to the Agricultural Department.

I might point out to the hon. member the fact that tuberculosis in the animal kingdom is increasing rapidly. I am speaking from memory and subject to correction, but I think the percentage last year increased from 2.9 to about 3.6. That does not look as if that particular branch was being very well handled.
The hon. member need not point that out to me; I know as much about it as he does.
Then I am surprised at the hon. member making that argument.

The Acts to which my hon. friend (Mr. Peter McGibbon) refers are now being administered by three separate departments of the Government: the Animals Contagious Diseases Act by the Department of Agriculture, the Penitentiaries Act by the Department of Justice; and 
the Food Act by the Department of Trade and Commerce. The transfer of these services to this department involves an important question not only of policy but of administration. There is power under the clause we have already passed for the Governor in Council to transfer the medical administration under any one of these Acts to this department, should it appear expedient to do so. In view of that fact I would suggest that the hon. member should not press the amendment at the present time. The matter will be considered by the Government in due course.

In view of the minister's remarks, I withdraw the amendment.
Amendment withdrawn, and schedule agreed to.

Mr. HOWARD PRIMOSE WH'IDDEN (Brandon): Has the Government any information concerning the probable date when the Peace Treaty will be ready for ratification and is there a possibility of the Government setting aside a time for consideration by the House of the League of Nations Covenant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have no official information as to the date upon which the Treaty of Peace will be signed. I am not aware that the date has been fixed. Yesterday an order was made for the printing of the Covenant, and at a later date it will be open to the House to discuss the matter, if it so desires.

Will members
of the House have an opportunity of seeing the Peace Treaty before it is signed on behalf of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think not.
When the Treaty is ready for signature I should think it would not be possible to have it discussed by the several legislatures of the countries concerned. It is very desirable that the Peace Treaty should be signed as soon as possible after it has been agreed upon by the five great powers, in order that peace may be restored to the world. I apprehend what my hon. friend has in mind: that the various countries are to be bound by the decisions of the Peace Conference, and that it would be advisable, if practicable, to have the Treaty discussed by the several legislatures concerned. >But I do not believe that such a course is practicable, nor am L aware that it has been adopted in connection with former peace treaties. Under the constitution of the United States, treaties have to be approved by the Senate, but as regards the present treaty H. think-I am simply giving my own opinion-it will be signed by the plenipotentiaries appointed for the purpose. Whatever subsequent ratification may be necessary by the different legislatures will be given effect to.

Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Acting Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 40, to amend the Juvenile Delinquents Act, 1908.
88J
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This Bill does nothing
more than define the term "Roman Catholic" as used in 'the present Act. There is no definition in the Act as it now stands, and there is a certain class of Catholics who decline to be known as Roman Catholics. Consequently, a definition is necessary. I have an amendment to propose when we are in Committee.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-"Roman Catholic" defined:

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I beg to move:
That section 1 be amended by striking out the words ' head of the Roman Catholic Church ' in lines 9 and 10, and substituting therefor the words ' Holy Roman See.'
'Sir SAM HUGHES:	I cannot hear a
word.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This may not be very
easily understood by my hon. friend.

There are Roman Catholics who belong to the Eastern Church and Roman Catholics who belong to the Western Church, and I am informed that in order to unite them they want to have placed in the Act the official title of the head of the Roman Catholic Church, and that official title, recognized by both branches, is " Holy Roman See."

Would my hon. friend kindly tell me that again? Seeing that the Minister of the Interior could not tell me what the Holy Roman See was, I shall appeal to the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) to enlighten me on that point.
There are two branches of the Catholic Church-
Of the Roman Catholic Church.
-of the Roman Catholic Church: the Western branch and the Eastern branch, and in respect to these young delinquents the members of the church asked-
With the assistance of the Parliament of Canada.
Yes-the members of the church have asked to be allowed to give the official name to the head of the Roman Catholic Church. The official name is the " Holy Roman See."
I would be very glad if the Minister of the Interior would explain to me what is meant by the " spiritual jurisdiction of the head of the Roman Catholic Church."

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps I had better explain the Bill and then the bon. gentleman (Sir Sam Hughes) will understand it. The Juvenile Delinquents Act now provides for taking care of juvenile delinquents in homes.
What homes?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are dhurch homes. If a juvenile delinquent is a Protestant the A at provides that he shall go to a Protestant home. If he is a Roman Catholic he is taken care of in a Catholic home. A difficulty arose in connection with the working of the Act in consequence of the fact that there was no definition of ithe Roman Catholic sect, or branch, as the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) says, known ordinarily as Greek Catholics. They refused to be described as (Roman Catholics and consequently they were being discriminated against under the Act, as they were described as belonging to a class to which they did not belong, and, not belonging to that class, there was no supervision over the children. The Act is now being amended so as to define " Roman Catholic " in such a way as to include them. They are anxious to have 'this amendment.
Who are " they?"

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That branch of the Greek Catholic church. They have secured incorporation from this Parliament under the title of the Ruthenian Greek Catholic Episcopal Corporation of Canada. This amendment will have the effect of placing their children in the same position as Roman Catholic children because it defines "Roman Catholic** in terms wide enough to include them.
Why not define Methodist wide enough to include them also?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These people desire that their children be placed in Catholic institutions.
Have you any evidence of that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, they have asked for the Bill. They are Catholics; they recognize the authority of the Pope, or rather of the Holy Roman Catholic See.
No, they do not.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They inform me that they do and that they desire to be included so as to secure the privileges of that communion. It is they who are asking for the Bill and for this amendment because they recognize the head of the Roman Catholic Church as head of the Holy Roman See. They are not of the Roman Catholic Church but they recognize the Holy Roman See as the head of their church the same as he is the head of the Roman Catholic Church.
H-o-l-y!

'I think that if the situation were understood it might clear the way for the consideration of this Bill. There is a Greek Catholic Church as well as a Roman Catholic Church. Some 250 years ago there was an effort made in Poland to get a union of the two rites. There are people who are known among Greek Catholics as Uniats and who are willing to accept the jurisdiction of the Roman Catholic Church. These people are known in the western provinces to-day as Greek Catholics in communion with the Church of Rome, and, in so far as they are concerned, I see no objection to the Bill going through. But, as far as the Greek Catholics are concerned, I think the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) i? right; they do not recognize the authority of the head of the Church of Rome.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Then, they do not come under the Bill; they are not affected.

I did not know that this Bill was going to be taken up to-day; otherwise I would have looked into it with more interest and paid more attention to it than I have. But it might as well be understood here that there is an attempt being made through Parliament by an organization of the Roman Catholic Church to get control of a number of people who are not Roman Catholics, or to control their children. This is the old story; worldwide; nothing new about it whatever.
They are trying to save the children.

We will not enter into that aspect of the case now. Whether a man calls himself a Roman Catholic oi not, Parliament is going to legislate by this Bill to take away his children and send them to a Roman Catholic institution in case they should come before the court, and in doing so Parliament is interfering with the absolute free will of the subject by forcing him to have his children placed in a

Roman Catholic institution whether he is a Roman Catholic or not. There has been an attempt made on the part of the Roman Catholic Church for centuries, ever since the thing was formed in the fifth century-after Christ-because it was not until the fifth century after Christ that it was ever heard of-an attempt which has been going on for generations, to get control of the Greek Catholics, of the people of Greece, Turkey, Macedonia and the States of the Balkan peninsula. The attempt is being made to secure control over the people of those Balkan States and to bring them in under ithe auspices of the Roman Catholic Church, as Greek Catholics owing allegiance to the See of Rome. The game is well understood by those who have studied it up. I am not finding fault with the Roman Catholic Church for pushing their propaganda, but I .am finding fault with the Parliament of Canada in yielding to that propaganda by legislation of this 'kind. We might as well talk frankly about these things. I cannot agree with ithe opinion that I see in the press of the country that matters of this kind should not be discussed in Parliament at all. Nor do I agree with the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) in the view that questions concerning religion should not be brought up in Parliament at all. Are we to stay quiet and let these corporations come in and get control all over the country? Not at .all. This is the place to fight it out, to call a spade a spade, to talk in plain Anglo-Saxon, and that is what I propose to do. It is generally understood-there is no secret about it-that-the assassination of the heir apparent to the Austrian throne was brought about because he was persona non grata to the Church of Rome, because he was a liberal in religion and not an ultramontane. It is generally understood that the policy of Germany, had she been triumphant in this war, was to make herself mistress of Belgium, Poland, and Lithuania, and the large additions of Roman Catholics to the German Empire by the carrying out of that policy would result in the Roman Catholic population of that empire becoming vastly greater than the Protestant population, with this addition also: that in the states now controlled by the Bolsheviki the Greek Church would be weakened and Russia would be brought under Rome's influence, Italy would be restored to the church, France would be restored to the church, leaving outside its control only the two great powers of Great Britain and the United States, but resulting in the re-establishment of the temporal power of the Pope of Rome over Christendom to the extent which I have mentioned. The aims of the Roman Catholic Church are well known; there is no secret about it at the present time. It is practically well known, and generally understood that the "hidden hand '' interfered with the enlistment of splendid boys who were anxious to fight for their country in the late war-interfered with the enlistment of those boys all over the country.
I certainly object to the spirit of this measure which states that whether any such person as is referred to in this Bill calls himself a Roman Catholic or not he is to acknowledge and be subject to the spiritual jurisdiction of the head of the Roman Catholic Church. Why should we legislate for the jurisdiction and control by the Church of Rome over the future of such people as these who do not belong to that church? I am by no means satisfied that the operation of these homes is as beneficial as it should be in the public interest. It seems to me that these organizations are getting their hands in everywhere and trying to establish themselves wherever they can get a foothold and that in this Bill they are trying to get a recognition that does not belong to them. I certainly object to the passage of this Bill, at all events until such time as the whole matter has been looked into and the House has been placed in possession of full information on the subject.

I would ask the Acting Minister of Justice if he is aware that by a recent decree the word " Roman " has been stricken out of the title of the Catholic Church. So that now instead of being " the Holy Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church " it is " the Holy Catholic and Apostolic Church?" This change may make a very serious difference with respect to the Bill before the Committee. '

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Let me deal with the
matter in this way for the benefit of the hon. member for Victoria and of the Committee: The Juvenile Delinquents' Act does not make anybody a Protestant or a Catholic. It provides two classes of homes to which children may go-one class for Protestant children, and one class for Catholic children.
Might I nob-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Just let me finish-

But I would like to



'The CHAIRMAN: Order. The hon. member can only interrupt an hon. member who is speaking if he gets permission.
I am well aware oi that, but I want to ask him a question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

He did not object.

speechtext: I understood him to object.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would have preferred not to be interrupted at the moment, but now that I have been I will await the question of the hon. member for Victoria.

Never mind, you can [DOT]go on now.
Mr. MEI'GHEN: I was saying, when interrupted, that the Act provides two classes of homes to which children who are delinquents may be sent, its intention, being that Protestants be sent to Protestant homes and Catholics to Catholic homes. As long as that is the case, as long as it does not attempt to admit any child who could possibly be a Protestant to a Catholic home objection could not be made by the hon. member from Victoria. In the same way if the Act does not attempt to send any child who is a Catholic to a Protestant home, it could not be objected to. By what stretch of the imagination could any person come to the conclusion that under this Act a Protestant could be sent to a Catholic home? The Bill defines a Roman Catholic as meaning and including any person who acknowledges and is subject to the spiritual jurisdiction of the Holy Roman See. That is all. If such a person makes that acknowledgment he is not a Protestant. I really do not pretend to be an authority on such matters, but the alphabet would teach me that. It may be he is not a Roman Catholic. If so we do not make him such, and do not attempt to; it is pure nonsense to suggest that we do. But he is a Catholic, and as between the two classes, the Protestant and Catholic it is undoubtedly the Catholic institution to which he should go, if that child is of a parentage that recognizes the authority of the Holy Roman See. It may

be he is a Greek Catholic. It may be he is in the class defined by our Act of 1913 incorporating the Ruthenian Greek Catholic Episcopal Corporation of Canada; but if he is a Protestant, belonging either to the Protestant Greek church or any such ecclesiastical body, he does not recognize the authority of the Holy Roman See and cannot be affected by the Bill.
How are the Jewish children provided for?
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have the Act here and can look up its provisions. They are not affected by this Bill, but I think there are other provisions in the Act which have reference to them.
I do not think there are.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Possibly not.

Now that the point has been raised I think it would be well when we are making amendments to the law to see to it that some provision is made for the care of Jewish children in Jewish homes. It would appear from the discussion as though there were no Jewish juvenile delinquents, but I wish to say, as a matter of fact, that there are. We look after such delinquents, and customarily they are placed with Jewish families. .
Oh, no. My hon. friend is wrong. Jewish delinquents are placed in the Boys' Farm and Training School at Shawbridge.

I am referring to private and not public homes. They are put in private homes and looked after. I think it might be well when we are making these changes in the law that there should be some recognition in this House that we have Jewish juvenile delinquents.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The point does not concern the Bill, but I promise to take the matter which the hon. gentleman has brought to my attention into my consideration. I will have it reviewed in the department and speak to him again about it.

In the first place I wish to resent the use of the word " Catholic " as it is being universally applied in this House. There are a great many people in connection with the English Church who resent the use of the word as applying only to the Roman Church. A great many of the so-called English Catholics regard themselves as just as important a body as the Roman Catholic Church. When you have

reference to those people they consider themselves just as much Catholics as do those persons who belong to the Roman Church. Therefore if the Acting Minister of Justice wishes to adhere to constitutional usage he will take cognizance of that fact. There are not only Protestant Catholics but there are millions of other Catholics who do not belong to either organization, and I fail to see why the child of any man who is not a recognized Roman Catholic should be sent to a Roman Catholic institution. There are public institutions in the country, supported by the municipalities, that are undenominational. That is where such children will go, and this game of grabbing children and bringing them up in this or that faith should be stopped. This kind of business has done more harm than good. The Government ought not to recognize any such ecclesiastical jurisdiction as is proposed here; the people concerned should be free to select their own religious faith.
Do not let any church have an opportunity of grabbing this or that child owing to the fact that the father does not know what church he belongs to. If the Roman Catholic Church gets a child under this hybrid organization of the Greek Catholic Church, that child goes to Rome just the same and Rome gets an additional voter. There is no use trying to get around the fact that this measure is not for the good of the child. I would suggest that the Bill be held over for further consideration to give us an opportunity to get behind the scenes and secure the real facts of the case. This Bill has been smuggled in from the Senate; I never heard of it until a moment ago. It is being rushed through the same as that clause was rushed through a year or two ago in the Military Service Act in connection with divinity students.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not want the Committee to think that any attempt is being made to rush this Bill through. It has already been through one House of Parliament.
They are asleep in the Senate the same as we are.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The reason "Roman

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

Who are they,
some heelers?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
