Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Minister oi the Interior) moved the second reading of Bill No. 38, to amend the Canada Evidence Act.
He said: I will explain the purpose of this Bill. The present Canada Evidence Act provides that any entry in a book kept in any department of the Government is receivable in evidence if proved by the oath or affidavit of any officer of the department. But it has been held that that provision does not apply to books kept, for example, in the Auditor General's branch, which is not a " Department " within the meaning of that term, nor the books kept by a Commission of the Government, for example, the Railway Commission, the Canada Trade Commission, or the War Purchasing Commission. Very great incon-
Cllr. Meighen.f
venience and expense is necessitated as a result, because the proof must be made then by the production of the book itself, and usually by the production of the officer of the department. This is to make the present law applicable not only to departments but also to all branches of the Government service.

Mr. Speaker, some years ago I remember we had an investigation before a Committee of some land speculation in connection with the Department of the Interior, and the question of filing departmental documents came up before the Committee. If I an? not mistaken, the then member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury), who was interested in the matter, insisted that the Committee was entitled to see the original. It seems to me that the same rule should apply to a case before a court of the land.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is competent to discuss only the principle of the Bill on the second reading. The hon. gentleman will serve his purpose better and cause the proceeding to be regular if he waits until the House goes into committee on the Bill.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and the House went into committee on ithe Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On Section I-to make section 26 apply to all offices under Dominion Government.

Generally, it is not necessary to file the original entries, and possibly inconvenience would result if they were required to be filed in every case. But in both criminal and civil cases it may become of the utmost importance that the originals be filed. In that case, what would happen under this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I shall give my view of the law, but I do not wish to give it as final. The present Act provides that the production of a sworn copy of an entry in a book of a department shall be evidence of the entry and of the facts stated in it. The amendment says that that provision shall apply to all branches of the Government service. The effect of the present legislation is to enable a litigant to submit certain evidence, namely, the copy
4	p.m. of an entry instead of the entry itself, and to be in a position then to say that he has produced evidence of the entry and of the facts noted in it. But the litigant is not now prevented by the present legislation, nor will he be prevented by the new legislation, from demanding the orig-

inal as well. If he wants to go to the expense of bringing the proper officer from Ottawa, or wherever he may be, and have the book produced, he may do so, but this gives him a cheaper alternative.
This legislation does not change the old law; it merely exitends it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Extends it; that is all.

A man who is putting in a copy of an entry may contend that that is evidence, and the other side may demand the original. In general iaws of this kind, discretion is sometimes given to the judge to decide whether he shall accept the copy or grant the request of the other side for the production of the original. Possibly it would do no harm to add to this section the words " unless the court or judge otherwise orders." It would then be open to the judge to say 'that either party could have further or better evidence if necessary. I do not think any discretion is left to the judge here to order anything more than the certified copy.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The difficulty with the hon. member's suggestion is this: -a litigant who himself was satisfied with a copy of the entry would not know whether or not he was preparing his case properly by relying on a copy. He might come to court with his copy and then have the judge rule that he must produce the original. That might mean an adjournment of the trial, particularly if the trial was taking place, say, in Victoria and the papers were in Ottawa. But as the law will stand when this Bill is passed, if a litigant is satisfied with the copy he goes ahead and gets it, and he knows that that is proof. If, on the contrary, his opponent is not satisfied with the copy, all he has to do is to go to the' expense of getting the original.

If one is going to rely on a copy of a deed instead of an original, he must give ten or eleven days' notice that he is going to use a copy. It is then open to the other side to refuse to accept the copy and to ask for the original. If the same general law applies to the copy in this case as applies to the copy of a deed, surprise could not happen.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If we were to adopt that in the Canada Evidence Act as extendable to books of account in the Government service, we would have to consider very carefully an amendment to that effect, because provision would have to be made for notice. I suggest that this point raised by
the hon. member stand for consideration in connection with another Bill. He might then, if he thought fit, himself introduce the suggestion.

Would it not be well to specify that the officer of the department who is to certify to these copies shall be the officer who has been particularly in charge of the books? He might be required to state in the affidavit that the books have been under his charge or 'that he knows of them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: lit is provided here that the officer must be an officer of the department, commission or board. I-do not think you can go further than that, because in some cases the books may not be under the special supervision of any particular officer; they may be open to entry on the part of several officers. It would seem to be sufficient that the entry be sworn to by an officer of the department in question. Then it must also be proved that the entry is made in the usual course of business in that office, and that oath must be taken by the officer who takes the affidavit. Consequently, it is necessary in every case that an officer who is familiar with the use of that book take the affidavit.
My hon. friend says there are books that are not under the charge of any special officer. That would be a very rare exception?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps so.

There are various
branches in each department. I should not like to take from the Superintendent of Dredging a certificate as to something that was done in the office of the architect of the Department of Public Works or vice versa, and yet under this Bill that could be done.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The present law is not changed in that respect.
No, but if we are going to amend it, we should improve it, and if we are going to improve it, we should go the whole way.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is no complaint
that it is not perfect as it is.
Then why amend it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Because it does not go far enough.

Has the scope of the section not been enlarged by the insertion of these words:
or in any commission, ]jon ru or oilier ttrancli.

I would have no objection to the section reading:
A copy ot any entry in any book kept in any office or department of the Government of Canada,
But the words:-
or In any commission, board or other branch.
are extremely wide and vague. They include practically everything that pertains to the Government of Canada and to every department. I object to such a vague term unless I am told that the same disposition existed in the old law. In that case I would not ask that the law be changed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The words are wide
but they are by no means vague. Previously this right extended as to any department; it could be applicable say to a Dominion land office or a timber office in New Westminster, if there was one there. It would be applicable anywhere. That being the case, why should it not be applicable say to the War Purchasing Commission? Every portion of the public service of Canada is a clearly defined area of service, and there can be no doubt or vagueness about it. Why then should one portion of the service of Canada be different from another? This simply gives the right to use a sworn copy of a book of entry if such book is used in the public service of Canada.
Will the minister kindly read the-original section?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The original section is this:
(2i6). A copy of any entry in any book kept in any department of the Government of Canada, shall .be received as evidence of such entry, and of the matters, transactions and 'accounts therein recorded, if it is proved by the oath or affidavit of an officer of such department that such book was, at the time of the making of the entry, one of the ordinary books kept in such department, that the entry was made in the usual course of business in such department, and that such copy is a true oo.py thereof.
That is the same, with the exception of the word "commission.''
A wide change is made in the drafting of the new section, because the words "in any office" are new and the words "or in any commission, board or other branch" are equally new.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, intentionally so.
If they were not new, there would be no amendment.

I object to enlarging to such an extent the scope of this section, because this amendment makes it cover practically

all the books kept in the use of the Dominion Government. We do not know where that is going to stop. 'For example, the entry book of a man who is keeping wages accounts on a dredge would fall under this section.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the law now, because he is in the Public Works Department.

If that is the law, it is wide enough now, and we are going to make it even wider. I cannot appreciate the length or the scope of this section drafted as it is. It seems we shall always be at a loss to know what falls under the section and what does not.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Could the hon. gentleman suggest any institution that would be in doubt? What is the difficulty of telling whether any service or institution is or is not part of the public service of the Dominion of Canada.? That is all a question of who issues the cheques.

The difficulty here is
that the certificate of any department of Government should not he taken as evidence unless it is a permanent, fixed' department of Government. These boards are in existence to-day, but twenty years, or ten years, or perhaps three years hence many of these boards or commissions shall have wound up their business and gone oul of existence. They will be no longer a branch of the Government, and the difficulty would arise that, although they were a branch of the Government when this Bill was passed to-day, to-morrow or a year or more afterwards they will not be a branch of the Government and would their certificate then be admissible as evidence? The minister should take care not to recognize in connection with this draft any branch of the service that is not permanent. If it he found that the Auditor General's Department is not within the old section, I can readily understand the necessity of bringing it in, because so far as we all know it is an absolutely fixed department of Government. But the Food Board, the Fuel Board, the War Purchasing Commission, are all for war purposes and will disappear with the war. I do not think the minister would care to say that the certificate of an officer of any of those boards, after they had wound up their business and dissolved, should be recognized as evidence in the courts of the land.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's
remarks might have point if we were pre-

venting any litigant from getting the original, but we are not; we are merely giving him an amendment which he can use. We do not provide for certificates; we provide for a sworn copy of a book of entry. Why would not a sworn copy of a book of entry of the Food Board be just as fair evidence in a court as a sworn copy of a book of entry of a Dominion land office out in Grand Prairie? There is no difference in the world. The temporary character, if it is temporary, of a commission, does not in any way affect the strength or sufficiency of the evidence.
If a man is an officer of a Food Board, that is a public service board, not an institution for private profit, so as to give an incentive perhaps to manipulating entries'. All we say is that, as that is a public service board, the sworn copy of an entry shall be evidence. That is, I presume, based upon the assumption that the public service is honestly carried on, and that the incentive to wrong-doing does not exist with the man carrying it on as it does in a private concern. It is just as applicable in every respect to any part of the public service as it is to the Department of the Interior or the Department of Public Works. Another principle is this: WTe do not want the books of the public service out of use by being used as evidence in courts all over the country.
The Food Board or any other board or commission that has finished its work returns its commission and is dissolved. It goes out of business as a branch of the public service.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But we need the records here.
Are you going to hunt for a man who was an officer of that board or commission to get a certificate from him? If so, where are you going to find him?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We say, if there is an officer who can make that affidavit, all right. We do not say that he must make an affidavit whether he is in a position to or not.
(Suppose that the books of the Food Board, when the board is dissolved, pass into the hands of some department of the Government. To what officer should I go for a certificate?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If there is nobody to give it, you cannot get it; so the amendment would not apply.

It might be absolutely necessary to have a certificate, and I would
be willing to take the certificate of an officer of the department in whose custody the books were. I do not think it is necessary to mention these commissions at all, because their books will be turned over to some department of the Government from which department a certificate could be got. Suppose the books of the Food Board are turned over to the Labour Department, and the certificate of the Deputy Minister of Labour is produced in court, the judge might say: "I cannot see any connection between the Department of Labour and the Food Board, and it is necessary for you to produce a certificate from an official of the Food Board." I would be perfectly satisfied if the Act were so constructed that a certificate could be got from an officer of the department which took over the books.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I apprehend that is the effect of it. For example, there are some commissions that are portions of a department. Consequently any officer of that department can take an affidavit, provided he knows that the entry was made in the usual and ordinary course of business, and that a true copy has been made of it. There are other commissions, the more permanent ones as a rule, that are not under any department. The War Purchasing Commission for instance has not been under any department, and I do not think the railway commission, strictly speaking, is under any department. Consequently, it would be necessary to apply to an official of one of those commissions, and consequently, this Act must be applied to them.
The Railway Commission is a permanent one.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is true, but if the others are of a temporary character the hon. gentleman's objection cannot be taken, because the officer of the department himself can make the affidavit.
Why name these commissions at all? I see no necessity for it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is just to save expense.

The only necessity foi the amendment, if I understood the minister correctly, was to include the Auditor General's branch. Now this Parliament will be sitting from year to year, and if there is any need for widening the scope of the Act the need can be met as it arises. The only difficulty the minister has now is that the Auditor General's branch is not covered by

the present Act. Why not amend the Act to- include that branch, and deal with further difficulties as they arise? The Canada Evidence Act is a pretty old one and I have never heard any complaint against it. I have always thought it was doing very well, but if it is found defective, we can amend it as the need arises. But do not say good-day to the devil before you meet him. I think that would be a much safer method, particularly when you are dealing with practice, for this has to do, not only with evidence, but with practice and procedure.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It seems to me this is the simpler way. There is the same reason for this enactment in one branch of the service as in another. It will mean greater convenience and a saving of expense. The originals are open to be produced, and there is no obligation to make the affidavit.

The objection taken by
my leader gives greater force to what I have suggested. We all know that there are commissions which are only of a temporary character. When those commissions have finished their work, their books will be turned over to some department of the Government, and will be in the care of an officer of that department who keeps books of a similar nature. This section provides for a certificate that the entry was made in the usual and ordinary course of business of such office. Now the man to whom these books are turned over cannot very well take this affidavit. I think it would cover the case if we said that the officer in charge of the books can give a certificate that a correct copy of the entry has been made. When a commission has ceased to exist, it is not possible for the officer of the department to which the books are turned over to certify that the entry has been made in the usual and ordinary course of business of such commission, but he can certify that a true copy of the entry has been made.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the officer in whose charge the books come later cannot take an affidavit that the entry is made in the usual and ordinary course of business, the section would not apply to him. It would have to be done by the officer who could take the affidavit, and that is just what my hon. friend wants.

In that case the office*! of the department would have to appear before the court, and the litigant would be put to considerable expense, which is what we want to avoid. If we saw that a certificate shall be given by the officer in [ Mr. McKenzie. ]
charge of the books it would not be necessary to summon him before the court with a lot of books.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That would be making the Act far wider than we intended, and the leader of the Opposition himself is moving to make it narrower. I do not think we should make the Act so wide as that. I do not think a man who merely has the custody of the books and knows nothing about the entries should be allowed to make that affidavit. He could give a certificate, but he could not make an affidavit. Suppose the Food Board is closed, and its books are in the custody of the Department of Trade and Commerce. It will not be suggested that the Deputy Minister of Trade and (Commerce should be allowed to certify or give evidence that an entry made in the books of the Food Board by somebody else two years before when they were not in his charge at all was made in the usual and ordinary course of business, and was consequently a correct entry, and that his- certificate should be an effective evidence of that entry. That would be going too far to meet my commendation.
I am not asking that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If not, something pretty close to it.

What we want is the contents of the books as evidence. Why should not the Deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce, for example, certify that the copy produced is an exact copy of what the book contains, and if necessary, supplement that certificate with an affidavit? That would give you as much information as the books themselves, the only difference being that one would be a copy, and the other the original. This certificate ought not to contain these words because he cannot say that the certificate, supplemented by an affidavit, would be sufficient evidence for the court.
'Mr. MEIGHEN: That is going a lot farther than I suggested we ought to go.
If a man makes an affidavit and swears that the entry was made in the ordinary course of business, that is the extent to which we are asking the committee to go. The leader of the Opposition says that is too far. My hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) says it is not far enough. I am in the happy position of being in between the two.
This section would only apply to living commissions. If a commission had gone the law would not apply?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This section will apply to both. It deals with the books of the public service and the entries contained therein.

Of a commission actually in existence, hut if the records of the food board are transferred to the Department of Trade and Commerce, this would not apply to any extract you might make from the books of the food board?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not unless there was somebody who could take that strict affidavit.

I think this drafting is very poor English. The words " in any office " must give the judicial interpretation to the clause. It says:-
A copy of any entry in any book kept in any office or department of the Government of Canada, or in any commission, board or other branch of the public service.
The words " in any office " must be understood in all those different places. If these commissions and boards are absorbed by departments they certainly have no offices and there is nothing kept in any office belonging to them; consequently there is no application oi the principle of the amendment at all. I think the minister would be well advised if he would take that into consideration and see if he could not do without the use of the words " commission and boards."

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would rob the Act of a very useful portion if I did so. I do not see any bad English in it, or ithat it could be improved, nor do I feel like recommending to the committee to strike out the words " or in any commission, board, or other branch of the public service." I think the strictest affidavit should be demanded, but the use of an affidavit as ito every portion of the public service is based on the same principle as its use as to a part of the public service.
Do I not understand the minister to strike out the words "commission" or "board"?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

If we are not to understand that a copy can be made better than the original, I think the clause should he amended by adding to it the following words:
Provided in any case the original book containing such entry is still in existence and can be produced in support of the copy.
Supposing the original book has been destroyed, there would be no proof possible
without a provision of this kind. If the original book has been destroyed, and by that fact proof of the contents of the original book has become impossible, are we going to make a copy of the book better than the original, or are we going to allow the original to live again or to be revived in the copy? This might lead to great injustice and fraud. Supposing copies are taken to-day from books which actually belong to a commission or board, now in existence, or out of existence but whose books are still available. Supposing different copies are taken from those books either with or without any special intention. It may afterwards happen that these books are destroyed by fire or otherwise. With this Bill as it is drafted, in a month, or a year, or in ten years from now, any witness could come along and say: Here is a copy taken from such and such a book which was then in existence but which does not exist any more. Then we would have to take it for granted that this copy was, as it purported to be, a true copy and was the actual representative of the entry that was made in the original book. We would have no possible means of ascertaining whether it was true or not. If the party who was using this copy wanted to commit a fraud of some kind, it could easily be done. I am presenting this argument on the principle of the statute of fraud which exists under the old French law and which was made to cover instances of this kind. The minister pointed out that there was no objection to using a copy with the object of giving it the same meaning and the same weight as might be attached to the original because the original could always be produced by a person who would think of denying the authenticity of the copy. The argument was well in point and it convinced me, but it does not bring me to the same conclusion when the original is destroyed and we have to take it for granted that it will be sufficient for any witness to come along and declare that this is a true copy. Such copy will then remain in the record as proof of an original book which does not exist and the asserted authenticity of which cannot be contradicted. I am not saying this with a view to criticising the minister but I would ask him as an eminent lawyer to give consideration to this point.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am afraid the acceptance of the point would do violence to -the first principle of evidence. The hon. gentleman says that you should not be allowed to use a copy unless the original is

in existence at the time of use. Very clearly, the original must have been in existence at the time of use. Very clearly, the original must have been in existence at the time the copy was made or the affidavit could not have been taken. Now suppose the original has been destroyed or lost since. Upon what principle should we say that the sworn copy could not possibly be used as evidence in court? Why it is the best evidence that exists, and it is the best evidence that always must be used. It would be far better, of course, if the original were available and could be summoned in the event of a dispute as to the entry, but if it cannot be made available and if we have got the best evidence that there is, why rule out that evidence? What would be the result? You rule out the sworn copy and what have you left but the memory of some man who was in office and whose testimony could be produced in court. The hon. gentleman could go further and rule that out. If his amendment is right you might just as well relegate one class of evidence into oblivion with the other. However the rule in court is to take the best evidence that is available. Because the best is not quite good enough, do not destroy it. Yet that is the purpose of the hon. gentleman's amendment.
Section agreed to, and Bill reported.

On the motion of the Hon. J. D. Reid (Minister of Railways) the House went into Committee-Mr. Boivin in the Chair-on the following resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the incorporation of Canadian National Railway Company, under which the railways, works and undertaking of the companies comprised in the Canadian Northern System may be consolidated, and together with the Canadian Government railways, may be operated as a national railway system; and to provide that the Governor in Council may nominate such persons as may be deemed expedient, not "less than five nor more than fifteen, to be directors of the said company, and upon such nomination being made the persons so nominated, and their successors, and such other persons as may from time to time be nominated by the Governor in Council as -directors, shall be incorporated as a company; that provision be made for the tenure of office, removal and vacancies of directors; for annual meetings, for capital stock, with or without shares, vested in the Minister of Finance on behalf of His Majesty; for the location of the head office; for payment of directors by the company in such sums as the Governor in Council may approve ; for limited responsibilities of the directors ; for the making of by-laws and organizing the company; for an executive committee of the

Board of Directors; and to provide that whenever under the provisions of the Railway Act, or any other statute or law, the approval, sanction or confirmation by shareholders is required, such approval, sanction or confirmation may be given by the Governor in Council; and further to provide that the Governor in Council may from time to time by Order in Council entrust to the company the management and operation of any lines of railway or parts thereof, and any property or work® of whatsoever description, or interests therein, and any powers, rights or .privileges over or with respect to any railways, properties or works, or interests therein, which may be from time to time vested in or owned, controlled or occupied by His Majesty, or such part or part® thereof, or rights or interests therein, as may be designated in any Order in Council, upon such terms and subject to such regulations and conditions as the Governor in Council may from time to time decide; such management and operation to continue during the pleasure of the Governor in Council, and to be suject to termination or variation from time to time, in whole or in part, by the Governor in Council; that should His Majesty at any time heretofore have acquired or hereafter acquire the stock or the controlling interest in the stock of any railway company, or of any other company having corporate powers or properties which may be conveniently exercised or operated by the Company, the Governor in Council may transfer, or cause to be transferred, such capital stock or- any part thereof to the Company, or may iby proxies or otherwise enable the Company or any nominee of the Governor in Council to exercise the voting power thereof at any meeting of shareholders, upon such terms and conditions as the Governor in Council may from time to time determine; and further to provide that the provisions of the Railway Act and of the Expropriation Act, with certain exceptions, and where not inconsistent with the proposed legislation, shall' apply to the Company; that provision be made as to the signatures to and deposit of plans for lands taken under the Expropriation Act, and the compensation payable therefor; that notwithstanding anything in the Government Railways Act or any other Act, the provisions of the Railway Act respecting the operation of a railway (as distinguished from the provisions of such Act respecting the construction or maintenance of a railway) shall apply to such of the Canadian Government Railways as would 'but for the passing of thiis proposed legislation ibe subject to the Government Railways Act, during such time as the operation and management thereof is entrusted to the Company under these enactments; that provision be made for actions, suits or other proceedings by or against the Company, and foi appeals, and defences available to the respective corporations, includiing Hi® Majesty; and also that notwithstanding anyth itig in the Government Railways Act or the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, all expenses incurred in connection with the operation or management of the Canadian Government Railways under these provisions shall be paid out of the receipts and revenue of the Canadian Government Railways, and in the event of a deficit occurring at any time during any fiscal year the amount of such deficit shall from time to time be payable by the Minister of Finance out of any unappropriated moneys in the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada, the amounts paid by the sodd Minister to be included in the estimates submitted to

Parliament at its first session fallowing the close at s'ueh fiscal year; and in the event of a surplus existing at the close of any fiscal year such surplus shall be paid into the said Fund ; that provision be made for the fiscal year of the Canadian Government Railways; for declaring any of the Companies comprised in the Canadian Northern System to be works for the general advantage of Canada; for the abandonment of any line with the approval of the Governor in Council, and upon the recommendation of the Board of Railway Commissioners; and, with the consent of a majority of the registered security holders affected, dismantling or disposing of the same; for the extension of the time of commencement and completion of any line of railway of any Company comprised in the Canadian Northern System ; for agreements with other Companies; for acquiring any securities issued hy, or make advances to, or receive advances from, the Canadian Northern or any other Company in the Canadian Northern System, with other provisions relating to such advances and loans; for constructing and operating railway lines, branches and extensions with the approval of the Governor in Council and upon any ioca tion sanctioned by the Minister of Railways and Canals; for the use of the name " Canadian National Railways " as collective or descriptive designation of all lines of railway or railway works* under its control; and1 for the change of name of any Company comprised in the Canadian Northern System or of any other Company of which the properties or the controlling interest in the stock is vested in or held by His Majesty; for the issue of bonds, debentures, debenture stock, perpetual or terminable, or other securities; for the deposit and registration of mortgages, and instruments in any way affecting mortgages under section 140 of the Railway Act; for the 'Company, with the approval of the Governor in Council; to acquire, hold and dispose of shares in the capital stock, bonds and securities of any railway company or other specified company; and for the construction or operation of the railway along highways, streets or other public places with the consent of the municipality.

This resolution occupies nearly two pages of print and it is so constructed as to form really only one sentence. If the Chairman is required to read it all in one breath, can he stand it? I do not think he can.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope the Committee will dispense with the reading of it.

The resolution deals with a variety of subjects, and should be divided into paragraphs. As it stands it is very difficult for any one to comprehend without considerable study, especially one whose mother tongue is not English.

It is proposed to incorporate a company to be called the Canadian National Railway Company, which will operate the existing Government railways, the Canadian Northern system, and any railway which may hereafter be .acquired by the Government. The Bill to be introduced after the passage of this resolution will contain thirty clauses.
And this resolution consists of but one phrase.
The Bill provides for the appointment of a number of directors, and deals with capital stock, head office of the company, and various other matters.
If the members of the Committee were in possession of copies of the Bill it would be a good help. I suppose the Bill is based on this resolution.
Yes. I would like to have the resolution adopted so that the Bill might be printed and distributed among the members, thus enabling them to study the details of what is proposed.

But if we adopt the resolution we commit ourselves to all that it contains. There are certain features of it which are not in the public interest, to which I am absolutely opposed, and against which I desire to enter a protest.

By adopting the resolution, hon. gentleman commit themselves to the principle of incorporating a company or organization to operate all the Government railways, but not to the details of the proposed legislation. There will be sections bringing the Government lines under control of the Railway Commissioners, and making the position of the Government lines correspond to, say, that of the Canadian Pacific, in so far as control by the Railway 'Commissioners is concerned.

If there is nothing proposed here that differs from the organization of an ordinary railway company I have no objection, to offer. But I would remind the hon. gentleman that the general Railway Act gives ample power with respect to every imaginable position in which a railway company may find itself. I do not object to the incorporation of a special company to take over the management of a national system of railways, but surely if the existing legislation is ample for, the regulation of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and all other railway lines which have come into existence since it was incorporated, it ought to be sufficient with respect to the Government railways or any new lines which "may hereafter be brought under Government control. Outside the ordinary procedure which is followed by any private company when it wants the authority to operate a railway, I do not see that any special legislation is needed here.

I had the solicitors of the department prepare this Bill on the lines suggested by the hon. member; that is, taking as a model the charter of a privately owned company like the Canadian Pacifiic railway, and altering it as necessary to make it applicable to a Government owned railway. Possibly when the Bill comes before the House we may have to change its form, but the whole object of this measure is to organize a company to operate all our Government railway systems, and to take in other railways tha* we may purchase or lease in the future. Of course, it would be much better for the members to have the Bill in its printed form as I have submitted it. I do not think this resolution commits hon. members to the details of the Bill that I have in mind, but I suppose the hon. membei for Three Bivers (Mr. Bureau) is right in stating that it may possibly commit them to the policy of a different organization for carrying on the administration of oui railways. It is necessary to have some changes; for instance, one of the clauses oi the Bill which will come up for discussion deals with the operation of the Intercolonial railway. In the past the revenues o' that railway have been deposited to the credit of the Hon. Receiver General, ther a certain amount each month has been sent to Moncton, .to be .paid out by the officials there. Now, the revenues of the Intercolonial and the Transcontinental and our other railways will, according to this Bill, go into one fund, and the operating expenses will be paid out of that fund. I do not see how we can possibly operate our railways as a uniform system unless we adopt some such plan. Then the Intercolonial railway will have to be put under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners; and there are many other matters in connection with our Government railways. All I ask is to have the resolution passed so that the Bill may be printed and gone into thoroughly, and if it needs amendment I will be very glad to consider any suggestion from hon. members.
We will see how we gei along.

It does seem to me that before we take up this resolution we should have some clear cut pronouncefnent from the Government as to what the future railway policy of this country is to be. Are we to have a policy of public ownership; or are we going, as far as we can, to have a policy of private ownership? I quite

understand that at the present time the Government have been forced to take over certain railways, and they may be forced to take over others. But this is a matter of extreme difficulty and one which demands the greatest care, attention and study, and we will be able to understand it a great deal better if we can have a clear cut pronouncement.

Whether we want to or not we have got public ownership to the extent of thirteen or fourteen thousand miles of railway, and the object of this Bill is to provide a means of operating as one uniform system the various railways composing that mileage. Therefore the introduction of this proposed Bill would not affect our present position so far as public ownership is concerned in relation to our present Government railways. The passing of this resolution does not really pass the Bill; the latter is there for the Committee to consider. There will be plenty of opportunities to discuss the question of policy mentioned by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) when the Railway Estimates are before the House. I have Estimates to the amount of about $80,000,000 to be passed in connection with our Government railways, and then will be the proper time to bring up the question of policy. This Bill is only to provide for the operation of the railways already under our control, and whether we want public ownership or not we have got it in relation to those lines. I do not think that there is the least chance of transferring our present Government Railway system back to private ownership, and consequently we have to provide some means of operating that system.

Last year the hon.
Minister of Railways put a resolution on the Order Paper asking the House to vote some millions of dollars to be expended by his officers out of the revenues of the Government railways without the expenditure being passed upon by Parliament. That resolution raised such a storm of protest from both sides of this House that the hon. minister withdrew it. Now we have the same thing this year in the form of a Bill. A Bill is to be introduced to form a company, and that company is to take charge of all the revenues of our Government owned railways and spend those moneys according to its best judgment, without having regard to the will of this House at all. II am absolutely oppo'sed to any proceeding of that kind It may be inconvenient and may involve

a lot of work to have this House deal with details of that kind, but II submit, Sir, that we as representatives of the people cannot pass over our responsibilities to any irresponsible body. I was never very much in favour of public ownership, but it does not matter whether I am in favour of it oi not, I fully agree with the hon. minister that we have this state of affairs on our hands now and we have to make the best of it. But I feel that I am responsible to my constituents to see that the expenditure of public moneys is such as to give the country the best possible value, and whether the expenditure be on wharves or harbours or railways, I submit that we, as representing the people of Canada, should have our hands on the purse strings and that not a dollar of public money should be expended except as authorized by this House. That is my view, and I think it is only proper to state it to the hon. minister; and I am not talking here for anybody but myself at the present moment. I cannot agree to the principle that public moneys are to be passed over to an irresponsible body in the shape of a corporation, which after it is incorporated will have full discretion, and we will not have the slightest control over it at all. That is not my idea of public ownership. Public ownership means that the people, represented by the members of this House, shall have control over those expenditures, except as they may delegate their powers to some board or commission of management. Politics is the science of government. When people say: "We must take this matter out of politics," they mean that it shall be taken away from patronage, graft, or mismanagement. I am willing that works of this kind shall be taken out of politics in that sense, but I do not agree that the people who own and operate enterprises shall have nothing to say about their management. Politics must exist in public ownership in so far as that involves the fullest possible control by the people. If this proposed organization is put in charge of the railroads owned by Canada, that is the end of our control over them. I am bound to tell the minister that I cannot commit myself to this proposal.

The Canadian Northern Railway Company, owned by the people, are collecting their revenues and making expenditures without any orders from and without any Act of Parliament. The different railways owned by the Government have different ways of collecting revenue and making expenditures, and it is necesm
sary to get one uniform system. Let us, therefore, get the Bill before the House in order that we may have a discussion on each, clause. The proposals embodied in the Bill may not meet with the wishes of the House or of the Committee. In my judgment, it is the best way of handling the situation, but the House may think differently, and I am willing to amend the Bill in any way that the House may think appropriate.
What is the object oi the resolution, then?
Under Rule 77, any Bill involving an expenditure of public moneys must be preceded by a resolution. That is the only reason why the resolution is on the Order Paper.

I hope the minister will not think me unduly insistent when I ask for a declaration of the policy of the Government. Public ownership, whether we wish it or not, has been imposed upon the people. If we were holding the railways only with the idea of disposing of them to private companies in, perhaps, as short a time as possible, one particular kind of organization might be better than another; but if we made up our minds to adopt the permanent policy of the public ownership of railways, some different system of organization would be necessary. The Government therefore, should state clearly whether they are for the principle of Government ownership as a definite policy for Canada. I know that that involves a heavy responsibility. There is a tremendous amount to be said on both sides of the question; if it were important that my views should be known, I should be sorry to have to declare myself at the present moment either for or against the principle. But after all, that is the responsibility of the Government; the port that they are steering for should be made known to the people before we are asked to vote for a resolution of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know just how many years ahead the hon. member thinks we should place ourselves in order to determine the port. I think the Government is well advised to take its bearings by ports that are in sight, not to fix a policy with reference to yet unborn decades. So far as there is any necessity of stating policy, the Government's policy as to railways has been stated and repeated over and over again. As to the roads that we now own, our policy is to continue to own them and 'to operate



them; we have no intention of selling them to any private corporation. Cer-5 p.m. tain roads we do not own. The Grand Trunk Pacific is one; our policy as to that has been brought down to the House, and we are engaged in the carrying out of that policy. The Grand Trunk is another; we have stated repeatedly our policy as to the Grand Trunk; we have stated what we are doing. The Canadian Pacific is another; the Government has not intimated to Parliament any intention of acquiring the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I do not know what more the hon. gentleman desires; I certainly do not know what more is necessary to the consideration of this resolution. Every time the subject of railways is mentioned in Parliament, is the Government, as to its policy, to see years or centuries ahead? All the Government has to do is to adjust its course with reference to circumstances now known; we have stated our course with reference to all railway circumstances now known. All that is necessary to a consideration of this Bill is a determination of the question whether it is the part of wisdom to operate such roads as we now and may in the future own under the system set out and by the principle clearly defined in this Bill, namely, by the establishment of a holding and operating company, the Canadian National Railways.

We own railways; we are meeting, so to speak, as shareholders. When we are considering anything bearing on the management of the roads which we own, we have a right to know where we stand as a body of people owning a certain property. We have taken over the Canadian Northern, with its various branches and ramifications.
Would the minister be able to tell us just what responsibility the Canadian people have assumed financially in taking over that road? The minister would, of course, have no difficulty in giving us the mileage of the road, and he might tell us if we are operating the full mileage that we took over. What does he think the rolling stock of the road is now worth, and does he say that the road is fairly well equipped as regards rolling stock? How much money have we expended on equipment since we took over the road, and how much money does he think necessary for operation and equipment during the current financial year? How do receipts and expenditures balance as regards the operations of the Canadian Northern as apart
TMr. Meighen.]
from the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental? What is the whole indebtedness that is now upon the Canadian Northern, and what is the present indebtedness per mile, without taking into account any assets, because whether there are assets at all or not, is another matter?
Without repeating what I have said about the Canadian Northern, I should like to have the same information as regards the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental. The people of Canada, and in particular hon. members here, when we are dealing with this very important subject and entering upon further management of the railway and thinking about a change in the management, should be furnished with full and complete information. Laying information of that character on the table of the House is a very poor way of giving it to hon. members, because they really do not get it at all, as it is not easy to get copies made of documents that are laid on the Table and filed in one of the offices of the House. Such information should be brought down, read in the House and put upon Hansard. In that way every hon. member and also the newspapers would have an opportunity of seeing it. This information should be put at our disposal before we commence to discuss seriously the future policy of Canada as regard public ownership and operation of railways. I do not profess to be a railway operator, but we have for a long time been accustomed to the machinery that we had in managing the finances of the Intercolonial railway. Many people may smile at the Intercolonial railway and say that it was not a success, but it has been doing a great deal of good and has been a splendid institution for the whole of Canada, particularly older Canada. That, however, has nothing to do *with the matter of getting in the revenue and paying out the money necessary for operating the road and for its extensions and rolling stock. We in the House are used to that system; we understand it; we know how it is operated. For myself, I cannot understand why the rest of the railway should not be operated, so far as finances are concerned, under the same method. There may be a better policy and a better way of making money; but as regards the incoming of revenue and the outgoing of expenditure, I do not see the necessity of amending the machinery and making thinsrs more difficult. I am in favour of a simpje, straightforward, clean-cut way of dealing with public matters, so that he who runs may read, and I am op-

posed to complications. I understand that I can be answered as regards this, that there are securities, such as bonds and other floating liabilities, that are now outstanding in connection with the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific and that are now being carried along by the machinery	of those	companies, and
that it is necessary to keep that machinery	going in order to keep
afloat those securities. Any person who holds those securities as against any of those companies would be only too glad to accept the undertaking of the Government, wherever we have to meet in full those responsibilities. Wherever we are not responsible at all, we should wipe those things out of existence and not bother further with them, if that is all that is standing in the way. This method of carrying along and seeing to the operation of twenty or thirty companies in connection with property owned by one body, namely the Government of this country as representing the Canadian people, is extremely clumsy. They should all be put under one management, so that we would all know" what we are doing and how the matter stands. That is why I am in favour of a simple and comprehensive method of operating the road, with only one ownership and one paymaster.

The hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) asked what responsibility we took in connection with the purchase of the Canadian Northern railway. As a lawyer he knows that we simply purchased the stock, and there is no obligation other than to continue to operate the road. He is entitled to and must have the information he requested in connection with the whole railway system, comprising the Canadian Northern, the Intercolonial and the Transcontinental. But I do not see how that affects this resolution, as we can furnish that information when we take up the Estimates or when we are in committee on the Bill to be founded on this resolution. The way he suggests of operating all the railway systems that we now have or may have hereafter is the way in which we have been operating the Intercolonial railway in the past, that is, by the Department of Railways. The hon. member knows that there has been a great deal of criticism on the part of the people on account of the Intercolonial railway being operated by that department. No matter what minister was in charge, there were always insinuations that there was patronage and favouritism. How could
the hon member expect a department of railways to operate 15,000 or 20,000 miles of railway? I should not like to have the job. The Intercolonial railway was enough for any one man, and I do not know what will happen if the Department of Railways has to operate this whole mileage. It would not be in the interest of the railways or of the public. These railways should be operated by a board of the very best men in the Dominion of Canada.
Under the department.

Certainly, they are
practically officials of the department.

The directors of this
company will not be.

They will be appointed by the Government, and we should have men in whom the people would have the utmost confidence. They must make their reports to Parliament, and when this Bill is before the House, ff it is necessary to insert in the Bill other clauses than those I have provided regarding the furnishing of reports, we can amend the Bill accordingly. I submit, however, that it is hardly fair to ask that this resolution stand. Before the Bill founded on this resolution is taken up again I can give all the information that has been asked for.

I hope that when the
Bill is brought down my hon. friend will restore to Parliament some of its rights. I have observed the phraseology of the resolution and notice that in almost every three lines the Governor in Council is practically given authority to run the whole national system of railways. We are at the beginning of a new era in railway operation in Canada. I understand that the great railway systems in this country are to be nationalized, and I appeal to my hon. friend to respect the rights of Parliament more than has been done in the past. If the people of Canada are to control the large railway systems, it seems to me Parliament should have a say in the mattery it should not 'be left entirely to the Governor in Council. The resolution provides, for instance, that "the Governor in Council may from time to time by Order in 'Council entrust to the company the management and operation of any lines of railway or parts thereof, and any property or works of whatsoever description, or interests therein." Surely Parliament should be consulted when new systems of railways are to be acquired. It is the people who are paying for the acquisition of these railway systems, and

the Governor in Council should not have exclusive authority in these large matters.

The Bill will not give the Governor in Council power to acquire railways without Parliament Being consulted. We could not take over the Grand Trunk Pacific, for instance, without first getting the approval of Parliament. Our object is this: After having acquired a railway system, the stock will be transferred to this company, our own company, which will operate the road.
Why should not Parliament, instead of the Governor in Council, determine ithe way it shall be operated?
That is a question for the House to decide.
It is a question that we want explained on the resolution.

If lve acquired the
Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk Pacific we should have to introduce legislation for the approval of Parliament, and Parliament would have the power to say whether the road should be operated separately or not. >If, however, we acquired the Grand Trunk Pacific in the same way that we acquired the Canadian Northern, this present legislation would give the Governor in Council power to declare the road a part of the national system. If we did not have that power, the road would have to be operated separately from the national system.

I have studied the
phraseology of the resolution, which I find very obscure. Although I hope my hon. friend is right, it seems to me that I am right. Off we are to have a new system of state-owned railways, the 'Government should come to Parliament with a clear-cut measure-with a new charter for the taxpayers of Canada-and the right should be reserved to Parliament, who are the elect of the people, to pass upon such important legislation. It is legislation not only for a few years, but for all time to come. I am really alarmed at the powers which the resolution seeks to give to the Governor in Council, and the way it ignores the representatives of the people.
There is another point. The resolution provides:
-and also, that notwithstanding anything in the Government Railways Act or the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, all expenses incurred in connection with the operation or management of the Canadian Government railways under these provisions shall be paid out of the receipts and revenue of the Canadian Govern-

ment railway^, and in the event of a deficit occurring at any time during any fiscal year the amount of such deficit shall from time to time be payable by the Minister of Finance out of any unappropriated moneys in the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada, the amounts paid by the said minister to be included in the estimates submitted to Parliament at its first session following the close of such fiscal year.
I am afraid this is not in accordance with business principles. In an important matter of this kind, involving thousands and thousands of miles of railway, we should have a clear-cut system; we should know what our requirements and our estimated expenditure will be. The directors should not be empowered to spend any moneys that have -not been provided for by this Parliament. I stand for the rights of Parliament and, I repeat, I am positively alarmed at the liberties taken by the Government at the expense of the Parliament of Canada.
Another feature of this resolution which I hope my hon. friend will explain is this: Are we or are we not going to acquire a certain number of railways? We are acquiring two transcontinentals, practically, and their branch lines. I see that the resolution provides for the abandonment of any line with the approval of the Governor in Council. My hon. friend must explain what is the meaning of that feature of the resolution. You cannot expect, if you acquire a transcontinental, that you will run only the paying sections; you must run trains not only on the main line but on the branch lines as well. Would it be fair to the people if, after you have acquired the transcontinentals or the main lines, you should then, by a stroke of the pen, without consulting the representatives of the people in these special districts, abandon some of the branch lines? You provide for this in the resolution. Here is the phraseology:
That provision be made for the fiscal year of the Canadian Government railways; for declaring any of the companies comprised in the Canadian Northern System to be works for the general advantage of Canada; for the abandonment of any line with the approval of the Governor in Council, and upon the recommendation of the Board of Railway Commissioners; and. with the consent of a majority of the registered security holders affected, dismantling or disposing of the same.
This strikes me as being a very dangerous power, and I hope that when my hon. friend comes before the House with his Bill he will make it clearer than it appears by the resolution. By all means let my hon. friend restore to the Parliament of Canada the rights which are being invaded by this resolution. I know that you cannot run the Government without Orders in Council and

without the Governor in Council, hut when you are framing a new policy of a most important nature, namely, the nationalization of the railway system of Canada, with the exception of the Canadian Pacific railway, you should come, so to speak, with a new charter and not take unto yourselves the whole wisdom of the people. We have not yet surrendered our rights. We speak for the people of Canada. The question of transportation is one of the utmost importance, and the people should have their say. I know that wide powers should he given the Board of Directors, hut that hoard should he amenable to the representatives of the people. Otherwise it could not be the people's railway; it would be the railway of the hoard of directors governing and directing entirely the administration through Orders in Council. If the people are willing at present-and I think they are in that mood; it may only be a passing mood-to gite their consent to the principle of nationalization, they are not going to surrender their right to have a say in the matter of administration. When the Bill is introduced, respect for the rights of the people should be more pronounced than is apparent from this resolution.

I think my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) is unnecessarily alarmed. When he reads ithe Bill he will find that it does not proceed along the line suggested by him. He objects to the money for operating purposes being paid to the company and not to consolidated fund account as in the past. Of course, there are only the two ways of doing it-either pay the money into consolidated fund or to the railway company. If you'pay into the consolidated fund, as has been done in the pasit with the Intercolonial and Transcontinental, you must come to the House with an estimate of expenditures and the money will be paid out from time to time.
Why not?

If we do that with the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific, and, if we take it over, the Grand Trunk Railway, instead of the money being paid into the corporations as has been done in the past, or into one corporation, it will have to be paid into the consolidated fund and then we will have to pay that money out from time to time according to the calls made. It would hardly be workable, in the interest of the railway or the country, to pay such a large amount into the consolidated fund and then pay it out
again, as we did with the Intercolonial railway. But this is a matter for the consideration of the Committee, and if there is any objection to the plan proposed, or if the Committee think 'that the other way is better, we can change it.
The difficulty is that the minister has no check on the expenditure. How is he going 'to control the payments if the matter is left altogether in the hands of the railway company?

The expenditures were made in that way on the Intercolonial railway. What difference will it make whether the money for operation is paid into the consolidated fund or to the credit of the company? If paid into the consolidated fund we would simply have to pay out each month so many millions of dollars to their credit and let them spend it in operation.
The Intercolonial is not in the same position as the Canadian Northern; it is directly undeT Government management.
I know. We could check the expenditure when the accounts were laid on the table of the House at the end of the year. If necessary we could have that in the Bill.
In the meantime the money is paid out.

It was on the Intercolonial, too. The revenue was collected and we did not know anything about the expenditure until a year afterwards. However, both ways of doing it can be considered when the Bill is before the House.

There is this difference, that on the Intercolonial system we discuss what is to become of the money before it is paid out. Under ithe system now proposed we would be discussing the matter after the money is paid-a very striking difference.

Of course there will be an item in the Estimates for expenditure upon our railways, and the railway situation could be discussed each session. lit is a big question, and I want the assistance of every member of the House to determine whether there could be any improvement in the proposed method of dealing with it. But before that is done I must introduce the Bill in what I consider to be the best way.
The hon. member has raised a question

in regard to the possible abandonment oi railway lines. That question is very important, because if we take over the .Grand Trunk railway it may not be in the interest of the country that we should operate parallel lines. I have in mind the stretch oi line between Kingston or Napanee and Toronto, where three railways are operated. The Grand Trunk has a double track system through this territory, also the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian Northern, and all the lines run side by side and in close proximity. It may be in the interest of the country to take up one of those lines.
I suppose that is to enable them to get in and out of cities.
No, the line is two hundred miles long.
And do the lines run side by side?

Yes, within five hundred feet of each other. Now, as a protection or safeguard, the Bill will contain provisions that in the event of the abandonment of a line of railway the consent of a majority of the security holders and of the Railway Commission must be obtained.
Hon. gentlemen will see that a railway cannot be abandoned simply on the authority of an Order in Council; the Board of Railway Commissioners must say whether that railway is necessary or not in the interests of the country, and whether or not its operation should be discontinued. I have spoken of the railways operating between Toronto and Napanee, but there may be other places in Canada where it is not in the public interest that the operation of two or three parallel railway systems should be continued.
The provision that the consent of a majority of the owners of the railway securities must be obtained simply means the Minister of Finance. That is no protection at all.
It is a legal question, and as to that I would not pit my opinion against the hon. gentleman's. If there is anything in his contention the defect can be remedied in the Bill itself.

I would like to say a word or two with respect to the question of financing the Canadian National railways when they become organized, as we hope they will be. If hon. members will separate in their minds the question of operating costs from the question of capital expenditure they will be able to arrive at a conclusion as to the only means 
by which a railway can be financed in its operation. I am not familiar personally with the methods which have been followed in the past in regard to the Intercolonial, but from a perusal of its records I do not think the system that has been followed on that railway has been of such an ideal character that it should	be
taken as a pattern for the future. If we are going to acquire and operate twenty thousand miles of transcontinental railway lines, for the Parliament of Canada to undertake to vote in its estimates each year the funds sufficient to carry on the operation of those railways satisfactorily will be utterly impossible. The operating costs oi a railway bear an exadt relation to the amount of traffic that is moved. It runs, as a rule to from sixty-eight to seventy-eight per cent of the gross income, and the gross income of Canadian railways, indeed of railways all over the world, varies from year to year to the extent of millions of dollars, nay, tens of millions of dollars. The income and operating expenses of the Canadian railways in 1919 may not be any greater than seventy-five per cent of whal they were in 1918, being entirely dependent on the commercial prosperity of the country. How then are you going to determine, twelve months ahead, what it would cost to operate the system of Canadian National Railways? What should be done is for the operating officers to pay the operating costs out of the revenue as it is received. That is the method which is followed by every railway company in Canada or in any other part of the world. Take the annual report of any one of our great railway companies and you will not find either the stockholders at the annual meeting, or the directors at the monthly meeting, undertaking to determine what funds are to be paid out for the ensuing period for operation. The stockholders at their annual meeting confirm the recommendations of the directors as to the capital expenditure; and it seems to me, when we are proposing legislation, that before anything definite is done in connection with incorporating a company or a board of trustees to manage and operate the Canadian National Railway System, we should provide that the fixing of the amount of capital stock, the projection of new lines, the acquisition of new railway stock, and all these things should be passed upon by Parliament as representatives of the people, and at the same time should make a com-

plete review of the operation of the road for the preceding year to see what our employees-because they will be our employees-have been doing with the money they have secured from operation, giving us a complete statement of the operating expenditures and revenue returns. If hon. gentlemen will examine the question I believe they will find that that is the only method by which they can successfully transmit to any independent or semi-independent body the operation of our Canadian National Railways.
Now, a point in connection with the authority which is vested in the Governor in Council, and the elimination of politics. We may become as idealistic as we like, but in the final analysis the Governor in Council, as the executive of Parliament, will have to be responsible, and it is through them that authority will have to be transmitted to the board of management of the operating company. You can designate it in any terms you like, but in the last analysis the Government must be responsible, and if the management of the railways is not efficient, it is not the management that the Canadian people are going to criticise, the Government and Parliament will be held responsible by the people. We cannot delegate that responsibility to anybody else. As a layman with a limited knowledge of railway matters, I cannot see that Parliament is delegating any of its authority, because the Government is responsible to Parliament for its every act, and if Parliament is not satisfied it has the means to chastise the Government.

Assuming that the Government and Parliament do appoint such a commission, and that the Government and Parliament find, as many railway companies have heretofore found, that they have been mistaken in their selections and have apponited such a class of men, for instance, as the owners of the Grand Trunk selected to construct the Grand Trunk Pacific, then what?
At the next session of Parliament put them out for cause. Just like the Railway Board is now constituted; its members are not subject to dismissal, except for cause, during their ten year term.

That is just exactly the point. Parliament might appoint these men and keep them there so long as they are efficient; but Parliament can never delegate its authority to those men absolutely; Parliament through the Government, must retain authority to dismiss these men if they are not doing their duty.
I did not think for a moment that Parliament would not have that power.

Before bringing in this resolution I think the Minister of Railways would have done well to follow the advice of the present Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) and also, of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) when this subject was under debate in 1917. That this company when formed should be removed as far as possible from political control, they both went so far as to say that Parliament should have the sole control. But here -we are undertaking to manage thirteen or fourteen thousand miles of railway, and thousands of employees, as a purely political machine. This legislation would give the Minister of Railways the right to appoint and dismiss directors as he desired. I agree with the hon. member who spoke before recess that this problem should be carefully
worked out so that we can get the best possible results from this railway system. It is a huge undertaking. It is the first time in the history of the world that such a large railway system has been put in the hands of a government as a government-owned proposition. The history of public ownership in Australia has been that the roads w;ere managed in the first place by a department of the government, and failed. Then they were turned over to a commission, and succeeded fairly well. Later the roads were taken out of the hands of the commission and put back in the hands of the government, and made another failure, and they are now back in the hands of a commission. The same is true of Italy. All the private-owned roads were taken over by the state, but were afterwards turned over to private ownership after public ownership had failed. The roads were again taken over by the state and managed by a commission; again handed back to private ownership, and again taken over by a commission. The same is true of Belgium. In fact, the only country where public ownership of railways has been a success, so far as I can learn from the books in the library of Parliament and the Ottawa library, is Prussia, where the roads were managed purely as a military machine. It was a success there because every employee of the road was under military rule while in railway employ. They charged exorbitant rates and were able in that way to make a profit for the government.
I do not believe it is the intention that we should go into public ownership of railways in this country as a profit-making business-that we should charge exorbitant rates to make a profit. I rather think that the intention of the Government, if they have a defined policy in the matter, would be to give the lowest possible rates consistent with making the road pay. Regardless of what the management may be, I think it would be the intention to increase the rates until the system paid. Unless they intend to do that they must ask the taxpayers of Canada to make good the deficits, and that brings up the question: Is it right that the taxpayers should make up for inefficiency in management, or because freight and passenger rates were not sufficient to make the roads pay? Personally, I think the people who use the railroads should pay rates sufficient to meet the carrying charges of the roads. If the system is to be handled purely as a political machine, as it is now, it is foredoomed to failure, there is no question about that.

That has been the experience of every nation in the world that has attempted to operate a railway system on that b_sis. When the minister says it is impossible to take the system out of the hands of the Government, that is true to some extent, but it is possible .to leave the system under the control of Parliament and not directly under the control of the minister. Por instance, a committee might 'be set up of ten from the Government and five from the Opposition side, five from the railway employees, and five from the 'Bailway Commission, which would name the directors; the directors in turn would be responsible .to Parliament. If you select five men, and they in their discretion decide to select two more, let them have power to do so. Surely out of five or seven men there would not be more than one or two who should be dismissed between the prorogation and the reassembling of Parliament. We ought to get five or six of the best railway men to be had in Canada. I would not advocate going outside of Canada, because I think our railway problems are peculiar to this country. I would pay these men good salaries, as much as, or perhaps a little more than, private roads would pay them, and the roads should be managed at a profit.
