After the system had been put in the hands of a commission, some conclusion should be reached as to the .capitalization! of the roads. In arriving at the proper capitalization, a fair basis would be to take the present value. For instance, if the Toads have cost the country $8,000,000, but are found by a competent commission to be worth only $5,000,000, adopt that as the basis on which you expect money to be earned.
Then I would suggest that the employees be given the opportunity of participating in the profits. After putting aside sufficient for ordinary maintenance and upkeep of the railways, the employees should receive ten per cent of the first one per cent net earned; on the second one per cent, twelve per cent; on the third one per cent, fifteen per cent; on the fourth one per cent, eighteen per cent; on the fifth one per cent, twenty-one per cent, and on the six one per cent, twenty-four per cent. That would give the employees one per cent of the net profits after the road had earned six per cent clear of running expenses and upkeep. Some hon. gentlemen may say there would be no profits. I am afraid that under the proposed plan there would be no profits. The system should be put in the hands of an independent commission, and should be put on a basis on which it could hope to earn

money, because, after all, we must expect to catch up with this thing some time. Then make a division of the profits with the employees, including every man from the directors down, who would be permanent so far as possible and devote their whole time to the road. Divide up one per cent among all the directors, officers and employees of the road, after six per cent had been earned clear of operating expenses and upkeep, and I would say that after six per cent the employees should receive twenty-five per cent of each one per cent net earnings, until the commission decided that the earnings were sufficient to justify a lowering of the rates. In that way the system would be taken out of politics as far as possible, and yet would be subject to parliamentary control. Parliament, after all, is the supreme body in this country, and if we found that the arrangement did not work satisfactorily, something else might be tried. I repeat that the plan proposed in this resolution has been tried in every country that has undertaken public ownership of railways, and has made a failure in every country except Germany.
It is a foregone conclusion that it will be a failure here. I remember that a few days ago the minister was asked in the House what quantity of ties was being obtained from the Northern Construction Company. Hon. members from Western Canada will know who the Northern Construction Company are. They are Mackenzie & Mann, the people who are at the present moment the controllers of the Canadian Northern railway. They have their employees, who have been with them for years, working as contractors and managing the contracts of the Canadian Northern Railway system.

I would like to correct the hon. gentleman there. Mackenzie & Mann, the two men from whom the stock was purchased, are not in any way connected with the Northern Construction Company, and, as far as I understand, never were.

The Northern Construction Company is well known to be the Mackenzie & Mann people who built practically the whole Canadian Northern railway through Western Canada. Any man from Western Canada knows that. When the question was asked here by my hon. friend from Prescott (Mr. Proulx), the minister said:
It is not in the public interest to give this information.
We are going to spend tens of millions of dollars on these railway projects, and the

minister is going to ask for $75,000,000 or $80,000,000 this year. Under these circumstances, Mr. Chairman, you can readily understand what the position will be ii when we ask him about these expenditures he will reply to us that it is not in the public interest that we should know from whom the company buy their ties, whal company is acting as contractors for the construction of the new roads that they propose building, or from whom they are buying their rolling stock or the hundred and one things which railway companies must buy. In the present instance the company bought from some person whose identity the minister does not want to disclose; otherwise he would be willing to answer that question. That is where this railway proposition is going to land us,-it is going to develop into a political machine operated by political parties, and the same people who have been robbing this country foi the last quarter of a century are going tc continue to get graft out of the Canadian Northern and the Government railways through purchases. If we are going to be in the position that millions will be spenl with no way of finding out what the money has been spent for, or who is getting the benefit of that expenditure, you will understand where this railway muddle is going to land us. The hon. Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White), in 1917, made a statement which I think is worth referring to because it shows what was in his mind at that time:
Thie Dominion Railway Company Board could hardly be self -cons t i t u t e d because it would have to be constituted in the first place by some authority, but after it was constituted the vacancies arising would .be filled by the remaining members; dn other words, It would be a complete sovereignty in itself

self-perpetuating. It would .be outside the control of the Government and outside the control of Parliament-although I am not quite sure as to the latter statement because Parliament, I suppose, has power over anything under its jurisdiction. No it would not be free of Parliament.
I think that is just where it should be. That is practically the same statement as was made by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) last year. He said:
I think hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House, and I know we all have a common purpose in this, will agree that a great railway system such as that which is now being acquired ought not to be administered directly by any department of the Government. I think we may start with that.
Apparently it was in the minds of both these hon. gentlemen that they should not make this a department of the Government,
or that they should not have it directly under the control of the ministers. But we know that they have it in their power by Order in Council to name the directors and to cancel their appointments at will. There should be some safeguard by which these directors will know that if they give good sendee and value for the money they receive they will be continued in office. You cannot expect to get railway men, even il you pay them $50,000 a year, to accept these positions unless they see some future before them. Every man of the Canadian Pacific Railway system has an opportunity of getting to the top, but there would be no such opportunity under this plan because their names could be withdrawn by the minister at will.
This resolution, if I understand it correctly, which I very much doubt, because there is nobody, even the minister himself, who does understand it, apparently gives power to the Governor in Council to purchase, operate and construct railways and branches of railways. He has power to acquire any railway in Canada without coming to Parliament and he has power to construct branch lines, build betterments, establish divisional points, and make extensions and improvements at the expense of the tax payers. The minister will probably say that he has not as much power as that, but that appears here in black and white, if the resolution means anything- although he is not unlikely to get up and say it does not. It is almost impossible to get anything out of the resolution: in fact, it was suggested here this afternoon that it should have been cut up into paragraphs so that it might be understandable. If it does not mean that he can build and acquire railways, it says so; if it does not mean that he can spend all the unappropriated funds of the Dominion of Canada, it says so. I do not know whether it means that, or whether it means what the minister says it means, which is something entirely different from the way the resolution reads.
I pointed out a few days ago an instance in which, apparently, for the benefit of some private interest, there were some twenty-three engines and engine crews moved from Calgary to a town named Hanna, in Alberta. Calgary is well situated and has ample water, housing accommodation and every convenience for the trainmen. These men were moved to Hanna where they had no water for themselves and they had to keep two trains hauling water fifty miles to furnish the engines out

of the town of Hanna. I talked to a number of railway men in that district, and not one of them could tell me why those engines should be moved. There was a question on the Order Paper asking the minister why the change was made, but apparently it was not in the public interest to answer the question.
Did the hon. gentleman ask the acting superintendent, Mr. O'Donnell, why these engines and crews were moved to Hanna?

I was afraid he might tell me that it was because Mr. Hanna and some of his friends owned real estate in iHanna, and I did not like to embarrass him. I would like the minister to explain why that was permitted and whether it was permitted by the Government,

I can hardly think that is a fair statement to make about Mr. D. B. Hanna. He does not own any real estate, and I must resent any reflection on D. B. Hanna, president of the Canadian Northern Railway system. I say that D. B. Hanna is an honest man, one of the straightest men in Canada, and if the hon. member will repeat over his own signature in the newspapers to-morrow morning what he has said here to-night about graft going on in connection with the Canadian Northern Railway Company, I am more than satisfied he will get all the information he wants, and will have no more trouble in so far as making statements of this kind is concerned.
I feel-and I think I should make the statement here now-that the men whom we have appointed to manage the Canadian National railways are honest, straightforward men; and I hardly think it is fair for any member of this House to accuse them of graft, and of being dishonest and dishonourable men, unless he will assume responsibility for his statements either in this Chamber or outside of it. If any one can tell us anything that would tend to show that these men are not carrying out their duties properly I, for one, will do everything I can to ferret the matter out, and, if the accusations are established, have the guilty parties removed. But what will kill public ownership in the future, no matter whether it is Mr. Hanna or any other man whom we appoint, is the action of members of Parliament in reflecting on their honesty and character as the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) has done. I say that it is not fair for these men whom we place in these responsible positions. I say this al-
though I have no brief for D. B. Hanna or any other member of the board. The hon. member has insinuated that the members of this board were appointed for political reasons. Two members of that board were employees of the Canadian Northern, and I would like to see any man in this House, or out of it, make any statement against the character or reputation of those two officials. Reflections have been indulged in concerning the members of the Railway Board consisting of Messrs. D. B. Hanna, A. J. Mitchell, Robert Hobson of Hamilton, Jones of Montreal, Barnhill of St. John, and Cant-lie of Nova Scotia. I only wish these statements were made outside of the House where the men accused could take action to defend themselves. It is, unfortunately, a privilege of Parliament that a member can reflect in this House upon the honour and reputation of an outside citizen, and he cannot be brought to book for his accusations. I repeat that these men against whom imputations have been made are honest and upright men.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Cahill) insinuates that we propose to manage these railways under the Department of Railways and Canals. We are not doing that at the present time, far from' it. The Railway Board is operating the Government railways entirely irrespective of the department, and there is no interference with them in any way, shape or form.
Before the hon. gentleman concludes his speech I would ask him who appointed these directors?

Of course they were
appointed by the Governor in Council. The hon. gentleman says that this board should be run in the same way as the Railway Commission, entirely outside of politics. Very well, who appointed the Railway Commission? They are appointed 'by the Government. Originally all the members of the commission were Liberal appointees. I regarded them as honest men, and believe they carried on the affairs of the commission regardless altogether of politics. We had confidence in those men because they were men of honour and reputation. We have appointed the directors of this Railway Board, they are men in whom the people of this country have confidence. Yet the hon. gentleman raises an issue about the appointment of that board, whereas the leader of the Opposition wants the Department of Railways and! Canals to operate the railways the same as was done in the case of the Intercolonial railway. I think these

two honourable gentlemen should get together and agree on some policy, because at present their views are very divergent.
So do the members of tire Government disagree.

The point I wish tc make is that the hon. gentleman has reflected on the character and reputation of the Board of Directors that we have appointed. All I ask him to do as a man of honour, which I believe he is, is to state in the public press to-morrow what he has said here to-night, and I will take a chance as to what will happen.

I would like the minister to answer the questions put to him before he starts to talk about his appointees. And when he asks me to reconcile my views to those of other hon. gentlemen on this side, I would ask him and his colleagues in the Government to reconcile their differences. Why, the leader of the Government is on record as opposed to the very principle that the hon. gentleman is advocating to-night. Yet the hon. gentleman gets up and flails the wind with his arms about somebody making false statements. The Railway Commission were appointed in the very way that I want these, men to be appointed.
The Board of Directors of the National Railways were appointed in the same way as the Railway Commission.

The members of the Railway Commission are not at the beck and call of the Governor in Council, the Minister of Railways, or anybody else. They are appointed for ten years, and I want these Directors who are managing the Government railways to be appointed in the very same way. I am not making any reflection upon Mr. Hanna. I am sure it would be resented in the country were I to suggest that Mackenzie & Mann, oi Hanna, ever did anything in Canada that was not above reproach. It would be regarded as an awful calamity and bring a storm of criticism about any man's ears who even suggested that Mackenzie & Mann ever did anything out of place in this country. And when my hon. friend gets so heated it is evidence to me that he intends to continue just as he has been doing in the past. When he talks about Mr. Cantlie in Nova Scotia, somebody else in Hamilton, and somebody else on the Western Prairies, as being directors, I tell him that they are directors when they are called together. I do not believe any one
of them would pretend to know more about railway business or railway management than any other ordinary citizen. They are not railway men, and they will only take their advice from Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann's appointee, through the Minister oi Railways-D. B. Hanna. Why does not the the minister tell us what he proposes to do with these branch lines? Why does he not tell us that he wants them taken out of politics instead of getting up and indulging in a harangue and defending Mackenzie & Mann, D. B. Hanna, or somebody else? The people of Canada do not care a hoot whom you have so long as you appoint efficient railway men to manage these railroads and make them pay. If you put these roads in the hands of efficient railway men, then you may expect at some time get good service, and you may expect to get the railroads out of the mire that they are in at present. Instead of doing that, however, the minister will blandly get up here from year to year, as long as he is privileged to sit on the Treasury Benches, and ask from thirty to eighty million dollars to pay deficits in the operation of these railroads. What interest has Hanna, or anybody else, in the efficient management of these railroads so long as he is at the beck and call of the Minister of Railways. His position is only good while he lives up to the instructions received from the minister, not a moment afterwards. IT say that these men! should be absolutely free from political control, and should be placed under the control of Parliament, so that if they do not serve the country properly, Parliament's attention may be directed to it and a change effected. The system which the minister has adopted is simply repeating the same mistakes that have been made in every country that has adopted the public ownership of railways. Every one of them has handed the management of the railways over to the political machine. Even in France, as late as 1908, when the authorities took over the North Western Railroad, they increased the employees twenty per cent on that road in the first two years of Government operation, until it was taken out of the hands of a member of the Government and placed under the control of a commission. This is a fair subject of debate, Mr. Chairman, and we should give the best possible attention to the question of how our national railroads are to be managed, because I can assure my public ownership friends that if our national railway system is used as a political machine to furnish political jobs, we are going to have a huge

deficit every year, and our people will become disgusted and say: Let us get rid of this thing and hand it over to somebody else. I think we have a fair chance to make this railway system a success. It may be true that we are a little over-built, but our lines run through a good productive country, and if we have a sane policy we will soon catch up to our railroad development and have sufficient traffic to make the system a success, unless we install the wrong kind of management and, as the hon. minister has pointed out, appoint a grocer of Montreal, an iron manufacturer of Toronto and another one of Nova Scotia. These gentlemen, I understand, are getting $2,000 a year each for the time and attention they devote to looking after this $900,000,000 investment. It is not reasonable to expect any man to devote sufficient time to an undertaking of such magnitude for that remuneration. You must get the besl railroad men obtainable and put them ir charge with -as little .political interference as possible. If you do not do that, if you adopt the hon. minister's plan to spend all the unappropriated funds of the Dominion, and allow him to bluster this thing through with the support of his friends at the back of him, you will end in a worse position than we were when we took over these roads. It has cost us more during the past year than in any previous year, and at the rate we are going on our deficit in a period of ten years will far exceed the amount we paid Mackenzie and Mann. 'I am not advocating the continuance of that plan. We have the opportunity in our own hands. Let us put our national railway system on a sane business basis and -try to get the best we can out of it. If the rest of the ministers would show as much gall in attempting to put anything through as the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals does-
He cannot beat you for it. We would like some of your own nerve.

As I understand it, the resolution has not yet been read and is not before the House. I think before it comes up for discussion the hon. minister would be well advised to take this long-winded resolution, capture the draftsman who is responsible for it, and then- take it to some person else and see if he cannot put it in such shape that the hon. minister can at least attempt to explain what it means.
The resolution is before the Committee.
It has not been read, I understand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It has been read as far as it will be.

Either the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) has been ill-advised, or he is trying to put something over on .the House to-night that he does not think will be contradicted by some one who knows. I happen to live in the little town of Hanna, and I can tell the hon. gentleman why the trains have been pulled out of Calgary and put into Hanna. It is because that is the point from which the railway can be operated the cheapest. As far as water goes, the railroad company happen to have a dam at Hanna now which stores enough water to supply the railway for two years. The water backs up for about a mile, it is about two hundred yards across and in the neighbourhood of about thirty feet deep in the centre. I am very pleased that the -hon. gentleman has given me a chance of advertising my own business to-night. I happen to be the official townsite agent for the town of Hanna. I have sold practically every lot, and I am here to tell the House that the Canadian Northern Railway did own that townsite, but I know every lot owner there and I can state that iMr. D. B. Hanna does not now and never did own one lot in that townsite. If the balance of the hon. member's arguments are as strong as on these two points I would advise the House not to take too much stock in -them.

I have listened very
earnestly and intently to the discussion on this resolution. I was very much surprised, indeed, at the case as presented by the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux). He pointed out that this resolution, extensive though it is and contained all in one sentence, has in almost every second line a reference to the Governor in Council or to Orders in -Council. As the representative of the constituency of -South Renfrew I came here .with the feeling that I would be consulted occasionally on matters of importance to the country and to my constituency, but to my surprise day after day we are .treated to a dose of Orders in Council and proposals for Orders in Council. We were assured that once the emergency conditions incident tc the war were over legislation of this kind would cease and this House would return to normal conditions. We are to-night engaged in discussing a resolution to make provision for the years after the war, and I see that the same spirit prevails in it. There seems to be no provision whatever

from start to finish, save one exception, whereby the people's representatives will be consulted in regard to the management of our national railways. The only exception, Sir, is when there has been discovered, as we are assured there will be, a deficit in the operating expenses. I have gone over this resolution and have extracted the following matters that will be attended to by Order in Council.
The Governor in Council will have power by Order in Council to nominate the directorate. The Governor in Council will also have powrer to incorporate the company. The Governor in Council will also have power to arrange the tenure of office of the directorate. The Governor in Council wall also have power to remove the directorate. The Governor in Council will also have power to annul meetings and to arrange annual meetings. The Governor in Council -if the Bill that the hon. Minister of Railways proposes bringing down is based on this resolution-will also have power to arrange the capital stock of the company. The location of the head office is also left to the Governor in Council. If members to your right, Mr. Chairman, do not object now to this matter being left in the hands of the Governor in Council, they will when they find that the matter has been arranged over their heads-and there will be some trouble in store for the Minister ol Railways. The people's representatives should have at least some say in the matter of the location of the head office; it should not be left entirely in the hands of the Governor in Council. The payment of the directors is left to the Governor in Council; the people's representatives are not to be consulted with regard to that matter. The Governor in Council will be charged with the appointment of the executive. The Governor in Council may transfer property or do what he pleases with if [DOT]-I would almost like to use an adjective in this connection, but perhaps it would not be parliamentary. The Governor in Council may acquire new property withoui saying why, wherefore, or by your leave. Funds belonging to the Government railways may be expropriated by Order ii Council. The abandonment of property may be accomplished by Order in Council without any consultation of the people's representatives. The minister referred to the possibility of this being done. I assure him that he would be wise in his day and generation to consult Parliament in that matter, because vested rights will be affected. Towns and villages have sprung up
along the railway lines, and if railway accommodation is taken away from these places the value of property will be depreciated and the rights of the people seriously affected. The Government cannot play ducks and drakes with the railroads without consulting Parliament.
The Governor in Council may construct new lines without consulting the representatives of the people in Parliament assembled; may issue bonds and debentures, arrange mortgages, dismantle or dispose of roads-all by Order in Council. The Governor in Council has almost the power of omnipotence in his hands; he is a law unto himself; his powers are almost beyond the limit. The Minister of Railways and Canals is vested almost with the power oi a god. I do not want to impute improper motives to him, but this resolution is a pretty extensive order, and I for one do not intend to endorse the proposal. I have often taken home and slept over a letter written in a hasty. moment, and invariably that letter has never been mailed. I suggest that the Minister of Railways take this resolution home with him to-night anc sleep on it. If he does, I am sure that he will bring down a more sane and sensible proposal than the one he has put before the House.
I notice also that the Minister of Railways proposes to arrange capital with or without shares by Order in Council; t( make by-laws by Order in Council; to arrange proxies at the annual meeting bj Order in Council-I do not know that he has omitted anything which it would be possible for him to do by Order in Council. That is not to be wondered at, as this resolution is made up of the longest sentence 1 ever read; in a page and a half, semicolons are the only marks of punctuation. The minister also intends by Order in Council to make agreements with other companies and to make money advances to the Canadian Northern railway. This disposition of affairs is, in my judgment, the nearest possible approach to omnipotence on this side of the grave. The only matter reserved to the elected representatives of the people is that of paying deficits-there is cold comfort in that. This matter affects the future welfare of our country. 'Hon. gentlemen who vote for this resolution or for any Bill which may be based upon it are simply voting away the rights that our forefathers fought for and handing them over to the Governor in Council.
I almost feel like moving an amendment to the resolution, which would have the

effect of striking out all of the words of the resolution after the word " resolved." On second thought, however, I shall merely make a suggestion by way of some-
9 p.m. thing else for the Minister of Railways to sleep over. I would suggest that all the words after the word " resolved " be struck out and that the following be substituted therefor:
That this House do now prorogue and that the business of the country be carried on, according to the Union Government practice, by Order in Council.
Does the hon member suggest that each of these powers asked for under the resolution should be submitted to Parliament?

Certainly not, but the
more important ones-I referred to them during the course of my remarks-should be submitted to Parliament.

If not through the Governor in Council, what means does the hon. member suggest by which the Parliament of Canada may express to the board of management or the board of directors of the operating company of the Canadian National railways the determination of Parliament to carry on along any particular line, with regard either to the construction of new lines or to methods of operation?

I suggest that the Government submit to Parliament from time to time such matters as the location of the head office. I am sure the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) would be one of the first men to object if the head office were located at the city of Quebec. I would also suggest that the Governor in Council refer to the Parliament of this country any proposed acquisition of new properties before they confirm the proposition. I would also suggest that they refer to this Parliament any proposition for the abandonment of any railway property, before abandoning it. I suggest also that the Minister of Railways submit to this House any proposition he has for the construction of new railways, before going ahead with the woitk. I would suggest also-and I might say this is in reply to the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson)-that before the minister disposes of any railroads in this country, he refer the matter to this Parliament for its consideration and determination. I would also refer several other matters that I perhaps have not at my finger ends at the moment, but they are, I am sure, such matters as would suggest themselves to
| Mr. Pedlow.]
such an experienced railroader as the hon. member for East Algoma.

I would like to make one or two observations with regard to this matter, just for the purpose of endeavouring to get some of my hon. friends down out of the air as regards the management of the Canadian National railways. The Governor in Council, in relation to the management of the Canadian National railways, are in exactly ithe isame position as the directors of a railway company, and if the shareholders of the privately-owned railway desire to have their wishes carried out, they are going to do that through their board of directors and their executive officers. If my hon. friend will look into this matter carefully, he will find that the Governor in Council are simply taking to themselves the authority to carry out the expressed will of Parliament, whatever that will may be. I particularly wish to refer to what the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) said as to the moving of train crews from Calgary to Hanna. He made a direct and specific charge against the management of the Canadian National railways. Personally, I cannot recall ever having had the pleasure of meeting any of those men; I do not know anything about them. But I do know the man who was responsible for moving the train crews from Calgary to Hanna, namely Acting General Superintendent O'Donnell, who is superintendent of the Canadian National railways at Winnipeg. If the hon. member for Pontiac has any criticisms to offer as to Superintendent O'Donnell as a railroad official, I should like him to make them in this House or out of it. I have known Mr. O'Donnell from the time he began his railway career. The hon. member stated that water had to be hauled fifty miles into Hanna. The heavy traffic is in and out of Hanna. How far will the hon. member suggest that one of those 180 per cent locomotives would run with one supply of water? If the work is going to be done out of Hanna, the water must be brought in, it does not matter what system is used to get it in, nor does it matter whether train crews are located in Hanna or not.
The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) said that he knew the hon. member for East Algoma would object to the head office going to Quebec. The head office of the greatest railway system in the world and the one I admire the most is in the province of Quebec, and I do not care whether the head office goes to Timbuctoo,

because that does not make a particle of difference.	.
Mr, BUREAU: It might be too far out.

The whole
question in connection with this is-how are we going to control the men whom we put into positions of responsibility as regards the management of our railways. The hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) says: Appoint them for ten years and remove the management from politics. Supposing we put in for ten years a board of management, and the first year we find they are inefficient, that they are the type of men who have been exploiting this country in the management and operation of railways- what are we going to do with them?
I -think the hon. member misunderstands me if he says that I said ten years. I did not mention any such period. I said that the railway commissioners were appointed for ten years.

I understood
the hon. member said he wanted them appointed on the same basis as -the railway commissioners who are appointed for ten years. If we are going to appoint them, we must not pledge ourselves to appoint them for ten days, unless they are going to do the work properly. All this Utopian talk of removing the management of the Canadian National Railways from politics might just as well be forgotten. We must put in control men whom we think to be efficient. If they do the job, let us -support them; if they do not do the job, let us find somebody who will. And, if the people of Canada are going to have the railways operated right, they will send to the House of Commons men who will see that these men do their work properly. That is -the only way by which it can be done.
One word with regard to the present Board of Directors. I do not believe I would know one of them if I were to meet him on the street. How many men on the Board of Directors of the Canadian Pacific railway are practical railway men in the sense that they eould take hold of the railway and operate and manage it? The president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is a lawyer who was taken into the office of the ex-president, Sir Thomas Shaugh-nessy, and trained as an executive officer pure and simple. What are all the others? They are not practical railway men in the 6ense I have mentioned, but men of sufficient capacity to find men who can operate the road. And in the final analysis, if the
Canadian National railways are to be operated successfully, we must have at the top one man who is a practical railroad man, who has the final say, and we must surround him with a group of intelligent, earnest men, willing to place their services at the disposal of their country, and to apply themselves to whatever projects they have in mind, who will find specialists in railway operation. Let me again ask the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill), in all his declarations with regard to inefficiency and incompetency on the part of the men who are operating the Canadian National railways what about -Mr. Hunger-ford, Mr. Warren, Mr. Brady, Mr. Hayes? Will he say these men are inefficient, incapable? I happen to know some of the men who are engaged in the operation of the road. They may not have the Canadian National railways into the complete system in which we would like to see it; they may not be the right men, but they should be given an opportunity of showing whether they are or not.
Without political interference.

Let us get right down to bed rock on this matter. Let the hon. member mention one case in which there has been political interference in the operation of the Canadian National railways since this Board of Management was selected. Let him mention one case in which they have been interfered with in the selection of an officer under them, or in what they are doing in their efforts to co-ordinate and put into a successful position so far as operating is concerned the Canadian National railways, and then we shall know where to start from. Will the hon. member do that?
I might refer the hon. member to about 1916 or 1917 when the-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is before the Board was appointed.
But as long as the Intercolonial was controlled from Ottawa, there was political management-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Better answer the question.
-and while there was this political management, there was the Minister of Railways sitting in the House of Commons-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Sit down.

-opposing members on the floor of the House, and the Minister of



Railways, still a member of this House, apparently lost his position as Minister of Railways,

I asked the bon. member a specific question. He has charged the president of the board of management of the Canadian National Railways with incompetence and grafting, and has charged the Government with political interference with the present board in the management of the railways. Now it is fair to ask the hon. member to state one instance in support of his charge. I do not know whether these charges are true or not. The hon. member may be in a position to floor me in a minute, and if he is I will join hands with him in an effort to clean the thing up. But I ask for one specific case.
What particular thing are you referring to?
It is for the hon. member-
Order. It is absolutely impossible for two hon. members to speak at once.

The hon. member will
have to sit down for me to answer.

I submit that until the hon. member can point to one instance where the present management of the Canadian National Railways has been actuated by anything but a desire to serve the public, it is absolutely unfair for him to make the charges he has made here tonight. Let me emphasize what the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) has said. If we are ever going to get men of the capacity we require to manage these railways-men of the type managing the Canadian Pacific, for instance-we must make up our minds to stand behind them honestly if they serve us faithfully, and not make charges against their honesty or capacity unless we are in a position to back those charges up. The biggest proposition that the people of Canada ever grappled with is the management of these railways, and we have to get men of the right sort to manage them. But do you think we will get men of the right sort if they are going to be hounded from one end of this country to the other as political heelers and grafters? Would you get a man of the type of Lord Shaughnessy, the late David Mc-Nicol, MacTier, Murphy, Scully or Coleman to enter the public service of this country so long as men will stand up here 
and traduce their character without offering one scintilla of evidence in support of the charges they make? I do not think you would, and I repeat, until these men have shown their incapacity-I do not know whether they are the right men or not to manage the road-it is our business to support them in their work.

When the Committee rose at six o'clock I put two questions to the minister. I suppose he will claim he has answered one. I desire now to know why he has left the fixing of the salaries of the directors to the Governor in Council? We fix the salaries, of the judges, the railway commissioners, and the civil service commissioners in this House, and I should like to know-I am asking merely for information-why we should not fix the salaries of these directors.

The Bill provides that the Governor in Council shall fix the salaries. Of course, the Government will be responsible to the House. It is a debatable question, I admit, whether they should be fixed by Parliament or by the Governor in Council, but we can discuss that matter in committee on the Bill, and if it is the general desire of the committee . the Bill can be amended.

I am not criticising at
all. The Bill will no doubt come up for a second reading to-morrow, which will not give us time to study the matter. I .say that we are departing from the practice that has been followed by Parliament heretofore in connection with the railway commissioners, the civil service commissioners and the judges, the members of the highest tribunal in the land; and I should like a reason why Parliament should not fix the salaries of these directors.
The reason why it is left to the Governor in Council is because the people are the shareholders, and the shareholders axe the ones who elect the directors and fix their salaries.
The shareholders elect the directors.
We are the shareholders, in this Parliament. We hold proxies from the people.

I quite understand the difficulties of my hon. friend. This legislation is very complex, and it is just as well that from the beginning we should stand fast by the principles of parliament-

ary government. In my humble judgment, there are many objections to the details of this legislation, some of which I pointed out this afternoon, but my main objection is against the use by the directors of the new company of moneys from the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada without any parliamentary vote.
It must be voted afterwards.

Yes, locking the stable after the horse is gone-and I say that with all due respect. I think the minister appreciates my argument. He will realize that the amendnrent I am going to move will not prevent him from putting this new organization into shape. I understand that at this session he will ask Parliament for a large amount of money, running into the millions of dollars, for the administration and operation of the railway system.
I am quite sure he has received from Mr. Hanna and the other directors an estimate of the cost of administrating and operating the system during the next fiscal year. Parliament will provide a fund to administer and operate the whole system, and I think it is enough for us to create this new power, with all the privileges we are conferring on it, without surrendering all our rights to that directorate.
As regards the financial end of this administration, we should stand fast by the principle that no money is going to be spent without first having been voted by Parliament. That is an elementary principle that should appeal to both sides of the House.
I would therefore move, Mr. Chairman, an amendment to this resolution. I regret the resolution is not paragraphed and numbered as Bills usually are, because I cannot see at what line this amendment comes, as the resolution is too long and too compact in its arrangement. But I would move to amend the resolution about two thirds down the page reading:
And in the event of a deficit occurring ait any time during any fiscal year the amount of such deficit shall from time to time he payable by the Minister of Finance out of any unappropriated moneys in the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada, the amounts paid by the said5 Minister to he included in the estimates submitted to Parliament at its first session following the close of such fiscal year.
As I propose to amend it, the clause would read as follows:
And in the event of a deficit occurring at any time during the fiscal year the amount of such deficit shall from time to time be payable by the Minister of Finance provided that said amount is paid out of moneys voted hy Parliament
Striking out the words:
Out of any unappropriated moneys in the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada, the amounts paid by the said minister to be included in the estimates submitted to Parliament ait its first session following the close of such fiscal year.
This is a question of principle with me.
I cannot surrender my rights in that way.
Let me explain to the hon. member the position we would be in if that amendment carried.
You are going to create a fund for next year.
No.

You are going to ask
Parliament for a huge appropriation for the running of the railway. You are able to get an estimate from Mr. Hanna and the directors.	1

We do not 'propose doing that at all. There are two ways of operating this system. One is, as suggested by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie), the way we have been operating the Intercolonial railway. That would mean placing in the Estimates the amount that it would take to operate the Canadian Northern and the Intercolonial. The other is to follow the method by which the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific are operated now. The receipts would all be collected by the railway and the cost of operation only would be expended from that fund. For the building of new lines we would have to get a vote of Parliament. We started out on the first of April this year with the Canadian National Railway system. Suppose that during this present fiscal year we should have a deficit of 84,000,000 or $5,000,000 on what we called the Government railway system prior to taking in the Canadian National railways, and another $10,000,000 of a deficit on the Canadian Northern, a. total deficit of $15,000,000. As all the money that we have for operating the railway is collected hy the railway, we could not meet these deficits until the next session, and we would not have money to operate the railway or to meet the deficits that would arise from month to month. A deficit does not come at the end of the year. In the month of April you will probably have a deficit, and so on during the twelve months. That clause is put there in order that we may keep the railway in operation, and, at the next session of Parliament we will come down for a vote. If this amendment should carry it would mean that the rail-

way would have to be closed down because we could not get any money to operate it. The directors have no power to borrow any [DOT]money as they go along. Let us take this *question up clause by clause and discuss ;it. I do not want to hurry or rush the Bill through. I court discussion of every clause of it in order that we may see whether we can put it in better shape than I have it. My whole desire is to get the very best Bill possible in order to ensure the successful operation of this railway system. If we get all the railways together, and it looks as if we will, we will probably have a billion dollars invested in them. I appeal to the members of this House to go into the Bill clause by clause and see if there is any way we can improve it, I appeal again 'to the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) not to press his amendment because its adoption would make it impossible to operate the railway inoperative. We could not carry it through to the next fiscal year.

I grant that my hon.
friend is in earnest in this legislation. The country is in a mood to stand by a system of railway nationalization. While it may be a passing mood, and while the country may not be disposed later on to maintain the system, it seems to be in favour of it at the present time. My hon. friend knows that there are men in the Grand Trunk system who know almost exactly, twelve months in advance, what the earnings, the surplus or the deficit will be. Does my hon. friend believe that the board of directors or the managers of the Canadian Pacific do not know what the traffic will yield during the next year? My hon. friend may think it is a matter of guessing but it is not. The president of the Canadian Pacific last year, in his report, based on the information that was conveyed to him by his officers all along the line, pretty well estimated the business during the current year. So it has been in former years. The officers of the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Canadian Northern could tell my hon. friend what the approximate earnings of the road for the next twelve months will be. We are going into this nationalization business; why not start right? Why not tell the people at once what the approximate deficit will be for the next fiscal year? It is easy. My hon. friend will have access to the books of the Grand Trunk Pacific? It is almost certain that the officers of the Grand Trunk system will be the officers of the Government.
The minister has retained almost every official of the old Canadian Northern Rail-IMr. J. D. Reid.]
way System. I share the confidence that my hon. friend has in Mr. Hanna. I have known Mr. Hanna for several years, and I think he is one of the ablest railway men in Canada, possibly in America. Mr. Hanna knows the Canadian Northern Railway System from A to Z, and I can assure my hon. friend that if he were to ask that gentleman to-morrow to give him his views as to the probable earnings of the system for the next fiscaL year, Mr. Hanna would be in a position to give him that information pretty accurately. So that it is relatively easy for the hon. gentleman, as the head of the Railway Department, to ascertain what it will cost to administer and to run the railway system during the next fiscal year. After all, the people are entitled to that information, and though the truth may not be palatable to them, it is just as well that they should get this estimate, and not give a board of directors the wide powers which he is conferring by this resolution. The principle involved is for me an elementary principle, and one which, if defeated by such legislation, would mean practically the annihilation of parliamentary control. I stand fast by my rights as a member of the House. I represent the people, and as such I wish, and claim, to have the control of all the moneys to be spent by the Government, whether it is for a small breakwater on the coast of Gaspe or for a big transcontinental railway system. I do not care what the amount is, what must be considered is the principle involved. Why, should my hon. friend be afraid to ask for such powers to be conferred on a board of directors, which after all must come under parliamentary control, because we ourselves have created the organization.

Can the hon. gentleman name any railroad company in Canada, or elsewhere, that observes the condition laid down in this amendment in regard to making an estimate of the amount of money required to carry on the undertaking for the year?

I have not the last annual report of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company under my hand, but if my hon. friend will refer to it he will see what are the prognostications, if I may use the expression, of Mr. Beatty. In any railway of that magnitude, the president, after having consulted the chief officers of all sections of the road, would be able to say approximately what the expenditure would be for the ensuing twelve months.

If the hon.
gentleman will refer to the report again he will find that that expenditure is the expenditure on capital account, and it is the only subject in regard to which Mr. Beatty wili venture to lay an estimate before the Board.

I believe the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Le-mieux) is perfectly sincere, and I think the House is anxious that the whole situation should he clearly understood. Therefore, let me submit a question like this: Assuming there is a difference of one hundred million bushels of the grain crop that has to be moved out of the Northwest this coming season from what is anticipated. Assuming that the Canadian National Railways are confronted with the proposition oi handling a crop similar to the of 1915. What would happen to any estimate the directors might make as to the costs of operation? Every dollar that is spent on the operation of the railway-and I am repeating what I said this afternoon, and which is perfectly obvious-has a direct relation to the amount of traffic to be moved. Now the amount of traffic that is moved from year to year varies, according to the industrial condition of the country, the crops to be handled, and everything that goes to make up the traffic. If one looks back over the reports of the Canadian Pacific and Grand Trunk railways, he will find that the operating costs varied, sometimes to the extent of ten or fifteen million dollars, one year from the other. The operating cost of every railway in Canada was increased by millions, due to the award of the Board of Adjustment which sat in connection with those railroads. That is liable to happen in the middle of any year. What would be the result if a twenty-five per cent increase in the rate of wages paid to the employees was forced upon the management of the Canadian National railway, in the middle of a season Parliament not being in session, and they being tied down to a certain estimate, which they must not exceed, as to what they should expend from month to month? Every practical man will tell you that such a thing is utterly impossible for them to carry out: the railway management simply go on spending the revenue as they get it. Should there be an operating deficit it will be found that the Canadian Pacific, the Grand Trunk, and all other lines, have a fund somewhere from which they can draw in the event of one month not being as good as another. But to require the management
of the Canadian National Railways to make an estimate of operating expenses a year ahead is practically impossible.

I remember distinctly that during the last session of Parliament a resolution involving the same principle which is under discussion here was placed upon the Order Paper by the Minister of Railways. I also remember distinctly that the resolution in question was finally withdrawn, which means that operations were continued during the year on the old basis.
I would like to know from the minister what the experience has been of the past year's operations on that basis?

The Intercolonial was not handed over to the new management until about the latter part of the year or the first of January, and the cost of operating for that period was taken out of the funds voted by Parliament. What is really meant by the amendment before the committee, if I understand it aright-and if not I am open to correction-is that the revenue for the fiscal year of the Canadian National Railways and of any other railway which may be taken over is to be deposited to the credit of the Receiver General, and whatever the costs of operation may be (whether it be two, three, or four hundred million dollars) should be voted in an estimate submitted to the House. I do not see how that can be worked.
How did it work out last year?
The Canadian Northern System worked in the way it always has done.

The minister has not explained why it is not possible to apply the same system to the other Government railways that he is applying to the Intercolonial Railway. As I understand that system, the minister makes up his mind before the opening of the fiscal year how much he will need for the operation of the Intercolonial during the ensuing twelve months, and Parliament votes that money. That system has worked out well in Canada for a great many years.
We are now proposing to allow these new railway directors to expend as much money as they please; there is to be no check on them whatever. They may run our national railway system in the most extravagant way, and Parliament pledges itself at the end of the year to pay the bill. Would it not be more business like for these directors to come to Parliament and say: We esti-

mate that our earnings for the coming year will be so many million dollars, but we feel certain that we will not be able to operate the road on those earnings, and we will want so many more million dollars to pay our bills before the end of the year. Then the people would know what they had to pay. By the system proposed we are throwing the whole matter into the hands of the board of directors and are losing control by Parliament altogether. I have always felt that the statement made by the Minister of Railway at the commencement of every fiscal year was very important; he outlined the business of the Intercolonial Railway for the year and told us what he expected to get' in revenue and what he expected to have to spend. By this system we are abandoning that good policy which has been pursued for a long time, and the hon. minister has not given us any good reason for its abandonment. Before he turns down the amendment of my hon. friend-which I am inclined to support- I think the hon. minister should tell the House why he cannot apply to our National railway the system which has been in vogue on the Intercolonial.

While I am to some extent in sympathy with the amendment as proposed by the hon. member for Mai-sonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) and consider it good in theory, it seems to me that the principle it enunciates is impracticable, for this reason:	Unless you were a
weather prophet it would be almost impossible to forecast the earning capacity of a great transportation system such as we are operating. The winter we have just passed through illustrates what I mean. The mild season has been the most effective fuel controller that we have had for years, .and it not only saved coal in our homes, but it saved coal in the operation of the railways; and it also resulted in a gain of millions of dollars in our western country through not having to remove snow. In some winters there has been a great expenditure of money to keep our roads open even in Western Canada, where our snowfall is not usually as heavy as in the East, and that expenditure is something very hard to estimate. We who have lived in the western country a number of years know that it is almost impossible, particularly at this season of the year, to forecast the crop. Growing wheat successfully depends altogether on weather Conditions, and in some years we will have probably 100,000,000 bushels more to move than in other years. So I do not see how 
it is humanly possible to forecast within even a few million dollars the probable earnings and operating expenses of a railway system such as we are handling. It seems to me that if we voted a certain sum of money as forecasted, probably during the course of the year, we would be faced with a deficit of from five to ten million dollars, and if we have no means of making good that deficit how are our operating officials going to pay expenses and keep the system running?
Amendment negatived; nays 36, yeas 16.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

I do not quite see why there was such strong objection to the amendment of the hon. member for Maisonneuve which has just been voted down. There can be no good derived from experience at all if we are to be forever groping in the dark in matters of this kind. Surely, after nearly fifty years experience with over one thousand miles of Government railway managed by successive min-listers, we should by this time havesome fairly reliable data of operating costs per mile per year. There is not a business firm in this country that has been in operation for half that length of time but can tell from year to year within a very small fraction what have been their operating costs and what they are going to be next year. Take a big city like Toronto, the civic authorities are able to estimate the cost of running the city each year. Take the Canadian Pacific Railway, the management can tell more than a year ahead what the system is going to cost. I can very well imagine that if any of us were present at a meeting of the shareholders of that company, and that question were asked, an estimate would be made and submitted to the meeting. There is no disposition on the part of hon. members on this side of the House to closely figure what the hon. minister might require for the running of his road. We are willing to give him a million dollars leeway if he wants it; it does not make very much difference, because if he does not require it it will not be expended. He says he has honest officials; we believe he has, and we believe there will be an honest effort made to run the road economically. But we want to have the right to say how much shall be expended and how much set aside for operating expenses, allowing an ample sum to meet contingencies. That is all; we are not desirous of cutting down the amount and crippling the running of the road; there is no such

suggestion; but we do not want to leave a free hand for the expenditure of public money without any parliamentary check. I would like to tell hon. members, and particularly those who have only been in this House for the last seven or eight years, that when my hon. friend, the Minister of Railways, sat in Opposition when the older Conservative members were sitting in Opposition they made an outcry against spending the money without the vote of Parliament. My good friend the member for East Lambton (Mr. J. E. Armstrong), the railway expert of the Conservative party, was loud' in his objections. But how have the mighty fallen! These gentlemen who had such a great respect for the representatives of the people in those days, and who were pernickety about, the expenditure of even a fifty-cent piece if it was not first voted by Parliament, now want to launch upon the expenditure of millions about which the people of Canada have absolutely nothing to say. It was a good, sound doctrine that they were preaching then, and it is a good, sound doctrine for Liberals to preach to-day.	I stated very clearly and explicitly in the earlier part of this discussion that I had only one opinion on this matter: That no moneys of the people should, in the absence of an emergency, be expended unless the expenditure is first passed upon by Parliament. I asked the minister for certain information about the standing of the Canadian Northern and the other railway systems which we own. I suggested that that information be put on Hansard before the second reading of the Bill is moved, so that members of the House may see what the real situation is. I notice that the member for Beauharnois (Mr. Papineau) put a question to the minister some time ago concerning the indebtedness of these roads, in the following words:
1.	On what date did the Government take possession of the Canadian Northern Railway System?
2.	What is the total amount of the liabilities of said railway system, which the country assumed on taking possession?
To which the following answer was given by the Minister of Railways:
1.	The Government received the controlling interest in the stock of the Canadiafi Northern Railway, on Ootober 1, 1917.
2.	The Dominion of Canada purchased the stock in the Canadian Northern Railway, but did not assume the outstanding liabilities which remained as debts of the company. According to the Government auditors the total outstanding liabilities as of October 1, 1917, including funded debt was $434,312,747.34.
That is not a satisfactory answer, or one that the Canadian people will accept. When a man buys a house with a mortgage on it, he must pay the mortgage off before he owns the house. We paid 10 p.m. a certain amount of money for stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and when we took over that stock we also took over the debt on the road. The people of Canada, therefore, should know what sort of bargain they made when they bought this property and what are its commercial chances for the future. We are paying the running expenses of the road; we are paying for rolling stock and improvements; we own the road just as much as we own the Intercolonial, and we must pay all bills in connection with it. The old Canadian Northern system as a company has no real, live existence except in matter of name; we took everything they had and we have to pay their liabilities. The question is, what did we take over; what value do we get for the responsibilities and liabilities we assumed? These are matters upon which I expect the minister to give us full and complete information before he moves the second reading of the Bill.

I should like to put on Hansard a statement made by Lord Shaughnessv the last time he appeared before the annual meeting of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company as president, with regard to the operating costs and income of that system. He said;
Compared with the returns for the calendar year 1916 the Thirty-seventh Annual Report of the Directors now before you for consideration and approval shows an increase in gross revenue from transportation of $12,660,000, but this amount was more than absorbed by the working expenses, which increased $16,590,000, so that the net income from transportation in 1917 was less by $3,930,000 than it was in the previous calendar year.
Notwithstanding the larger volume of traffic in 1917, it will be gathered from the statistics incorporated in the Report that there was a substantial decrease in traffic train mileage and loaded car mileage, indicating still further improvement in operating efficiency. In normal times this should be reflected in the working expenses, but its effect was minimized by the higher scale of wages and the enchancefl cost of fuel and other materials required for the maintenance and operation of the railway that prevailed during the year and that added $15,250,000 to the operating expenses.
This is a statement put before the stockholders after the event. It could not have been put before them before the event, i am confident that if any hon. member will take pains to inquire carefully into the situation, he will find that the Canar

dian Pacific management never undertake to say within five or ten million dollars what is going to be expended in operating costs. Without any question they do make a complete statement as to capital expenditure, and the House of Commons of Canada should see to it that the directors and management of the Canadian National railways submit for our consideration their programme with regard to such expenditures. But the operation of railways can be carried on only out of earnings, unless we are going to do as the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) suggests, namely at the beginning of the year vote a large block of money that we are sure will cover every contingency, without having any details whatever and without knowing how it is going to be expended, and then say, as we said to the officers of the Intercolonial in the heyday of their existence: Go to it; we will take care of the deficits when they come in at the end of the year.

The resolution reads:
For constructing and operating railway lines, branches and extensions with the approval ot the Governor in Council and upon any location sanctioned by the Minister of Railways and Canals.	.
I do not object as to the branches, because the Railway Act provides as to what length of branches can be constructed under a charter. When a company desires to build a railway, they have to come before Parliament in order to get a charter. I understand that the Governor in Council may have to deal with the branches, but is there any particular reason, if the management desire to build a railway, why they should not ask the permission of Parliament to build it so that the matter would come be-for the Railway Committee and be discussed there, thus giving every member of the House an opportunity of stating whether he approves the location, and of pronouncing upon the advisability and advantages of the construction?

When we have the Bill before us, I will go into the matter more fully. The old Canadian Northern Railway have charters for extensions, which charters have been in existence for some years. Those extensions are now being constructed and a number of them will be completed this year. Plans must be approved in the usual way, just as is the case with the plans of other railways. With regard to the construction of new lines or branches

That is the power that
is given here.

-the Canadian National Railways will have power to extend, but we shall have to come to Parliament for any moneys, with which to build those extensions. Money that is received from operating the railways, we permit them to apply only to operating expenses. If there is construction, they have to come to Parliament for the money. There is a section with regard to bonds, but they have to come to Parliament for this money. This clause does not give power to the management to go ahead and build lines without coming to Parliament. If I cannot show that such a proviso is m the Bill, we can amend the Bill accordingly.
After the Bill is introduced and distributed, how much time shall we have to look over it before it is rushed through?

I do not propose rushing it through. If it is introduced to-day, I do not expect to bring it up again until after the Easter adjournment. Hon. members will therefore have all of next week and part of the week after to consider the Bill.
The minister surely does not expect that we are going to study a railway Bill during the holidays.
I will give the hon. member plenty of time.
Has the Government paid for the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway?
So far as I understood, it was all paid for.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I understand the stock has all been paid for except a block which is pledged with the Government of British Columbia

Oh, yes.
Mr. MEIGHEN-as against the construction of a certain line in that province by the Canadian Northern. That, not being deliverable as yet, has not been paid for.

The clause which the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) was discussing states that the management have power to construct subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. If the minister is satisfied that this is a mistake and if hia intention was that they should come to Parliament, then it would be well to change the wording from " the approval of the Governor in Council " to " the approval of Parliament." Would the minister be willing to adopt that change?
I could not change that now, because I think the hon. member, when he sees the Bill, will see that the point he raises is covered.

This is a very important resolution we are voting on, and we are doing so without very much information.
If the minister is not sure that what is in the resolution is what he is going to have in the Bill-
Mr. J. D. iREID: What this means is just what I stated. In every railway Bill a clause is inserted providing that the plans must be approved by the Minister of Railways and Canals. Notwithstanding the fact that a charter has been granted by this Parliament, the plans must he approved by the minister.

A railway company has its plans deposited with the Minister of Railways and Canals, and approved, after the charter is granted. The minister says this is to allow the company to build railways on charters already granted by this Parliament?
Yes.

Why not change it to read:-
__For constructing railways for which charters
have already heen granted to the Canadian Northern.
If the Government takes over the Grand Trunk Pacific, then another Bill will be necessary.

That could be covered by inserting in the Bill:-
For constructing lines which already have heen approved hy Parliament and for which charters have been granted.
If the minister is not quite clear as to whether he wants that clause left in the resolution in that way or not, I wbuld move an amendment that it be taken out of the resolution.

I would like it left in. I cannot change it in the resolution tonight. I prefer the resolution as it is, because I do not understand the clause as the hon. member suggests it. Of course, if the hon. member wishes to move his amendment he can do so.

Is it the intention of the Government to go on constructing branch or other lines of railways by Order in Council with the approval of the Minister of Railways and without consulting Parliament? They have in this resolution absolute power to do so, and if there is any money in the treasury of Canada to spend one of the things on which they can spend it is the construction of branch lines or other lines of railway. If it is not the intention of the Government to build branch or other lines without first submitting the proposition to Parliament for approval that clause should not be in the resolution.

I mentioned that a short time ago. Of course, we have no intention of building branch lines or constructing railways anywhere without first coming to Parliament for a vote. When a vote is asked for, a full explanation is always given of the Government's proposals.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Algoma (Air. Nicholson) a moment ago read a report from Mr. Beatty relating to the Canadian Pacific. I have here a very short article giving the results arrived at by the United States Government with state ownership of railways. It is as follows:
New York, April 7.-For the month of February it is announced that the railways of the United States under Government operation show a deficit of over thirty-six million dollars, notwithstanding increases in fares and reduction of service by curtailing trains and packing the cars.
This actual loss, added to the hundreds of millions of loss in the previous twelve months, which must be made up by taxation is creating widespread hostility to Government ownership. Writing of the results of Government control of the railways the New York Sun says: " Price fixing and Government ownership have had such exhaustive trials as would have been totally impossible in times of peace. In many cases, as notably the railroads, the experiments were made under the most favourable circumstances and with a degree of public toleration if not approval that normally would have been impossible.
" In every case, without exception, the experiment has been ruinous to the socialistic theory. Service was not improved. It was rendered inefficient and unreliable to an incredible extent. To crown all. in order to maintain this mad carnival of abuse, crushing taxes have been laid upon the people and new burdens of taxation and debt loom up ahead, along with a total disorganization of business. These are the blessings that Government price fixing and Government management of public utilities have brought to the country. There is no single case that can be quoted to the contrary.
"Both political parties admit that the nation would vote overwhelmingly against Government ownership. Even the papers that advocated the policy, and politicians who supported it, now admit it was a terrible error."
In view of the fact that both political parties in the United States are against
Government ownership and that in the

month of February, the shortest month in the year, the railways of the United States under Government ownership showed a deficit of over 836,000,000, I think this resolution should be very carefully reconsidered.
Resolution reported, read and concurred in.
Mr. J. D. REID thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 70, to incorporate the Canadian National Railways Company.

speechtext:
Before moving the adjournment of the House, I wish to refer to the judgment just delivered by the Railway Commission on the question of the order of the Railway War Board as to the change of time on the railways. As hon. members will know from a perusal of the ' judgment, the position taken by the Chief Commissioner, concurred in, I believe, by Mr. Commissioner Nantel, is to the effect that the fixing of standard or local time is, in so far! as the determination of the broad question is concerned, a matter of provincial jurisdiction, and that the only jurisdiction which the Board of Railway Commissioners has is exercisable only when they are convinced that interference on their part is necessitated by the public protection or safety or the public convenience. Founding their opinion upon that basis, the judgment is that they cannot interfere with the time fixed by the Railway War Board. That being the case,
I beg to suggest that the House on adjournment to-night, having regard to the convenience of members of Parliament, and having reference, of course, only to the sittings of this House, do adjourn until Monday at three o'clock, local time,

At all events, the members of the House will appreciate the fact that the Government has come to terms with common sense by adopting the time which is accepted outside of the main entrance of the
